prompts.why: A hardware enclave keeps data encrypted in memory and isolated from the host and hypervisor while it is in use. Encryption at rest and in transit does not cover processing.

prompts.label: Call center agents verify callers with their SSN but should see only the last four digits on screen
prompts.why: Masking hides most of the value on display while the application still works with the real data behind it.

takeaway: At rest: full-disk encryption, tokenization, hashing for passwords. In transit: TLS or SFTP, with DLP to stop leaks. In use: secure enclaves and masking. Tokenization removes the real value; encryption only hides it.

scenario: Risk A: ransomware on the main file server. The server, its data and the cost of downtime are valued at $500,000, and one attack would cost 30% of that. The company expects one such attack every four years. EDR plus immutable backups would cost $12,000 per year and cut the exposure factor to 5%. Risk B: laptop theft. About six laptops are stolen each year and each costs $1,500 to replace; full-disk encryption means no data is exposed. An insurance policy costs $4,000 per year and pays for each stolen laptop minus a $500 deductible.
stem: Calculate each value and choose each risk response.

prompts.label: Risk A: single loss expectancy (SLE)
prompts.why: SLE = asset value x exposure factor = $500,000 x 0.30 = $150,000.

prompts.label: Risk A: annualized loss expectancy (ALE) today
prompts.why: One attack every four years is an ARO of 0.25, so ALE = $150,000 x 0.25 = $37,500. Multiplying by 4 instead would give $600,000.

prompts.label: Risk A: ALE with EDR and immutable backups
prompts.why: The control changes the exposure factor, not the rate: SLE becomes $500,000 x 0.05 = $25,000, and ALE = $25,000 x 0.25 = $6,250.

prompts.label: Risk A: response
prompts.answer: Mitigate: the control is worth $19,250 a year after its cost
prompts.why: It reduces the ALE by $37,500 minus $6,250 = $31,250 and costs $12,000, a net benefit of $19,250 per year. Counting the $31,250 without subtracting the cost overstates the value.
choices: Mitigate: the control is worth $19,250 a year after its cost
Mitigate: the control is worth $31,250 a year
Accept: the control costs more than the loss it prevents

prompts.label: Risk B: ALE today
prompts.why: Each theft costs the full $1,500 (exposure factor 100%), and six a year is an ARO of 6, so ALE = $1,500 x 6 = $9,000. An ARO can be greater than 1.

prompts.label: Risk B: expected yearly cost with the insurance policy
prompts.why: The company still pays the $4,000 premium plus a $500 deductible on each of six claims ($3,000), for a total of $7,000.

prompts.label: Risk B: response
prompts.answer: Transfer: buy the policy, which lowers the expected yearly cost by $2,000
prompts.why: Insurance costs $7,000 a year against $9,000 of expected loss without it, so transferring the risk saves $2,000. The deductibles mean the company still bears part of every loss.
choices: Transfer: buy the policy, which lowers the expected yearly cost by $2,000
Transfer: buy the policy, which removes all cost of theft
Accept: the policy costs more than it saves

takeaway: SLE = AV x EF, ALE = SLE x ARO (the ARO can exceed 1). Compare a control's yearly cost with the ALE reduction it buys, and count deductibles when you price insurance.

scenario: A database server gets a full backup every Sunday at 23:00 and an incremental backup every other night, Monday to Saturday, at 23:00. On Thursday at 15:00 its storage array fails and all data on it is lost. Restoring the full backup takes 3 hours, each incremental takes 30 minutes, and verifying the database afterwards takes 1 hour. Assume the restore starts immediately. The business impact analysis sets an RPO of 4 hours and an RTO of 6 hours.
stem: Answer each item about the restore and the recovery objectives.

prompts.label: Backup sets needed to restore the database
prompts.answer: Sunday full, then the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday incrementals in order
prompts.why: Each incremental holds only the changes since the previous backup of any kind, so every one since the full backup is needed, applied in sequence.
choices: Sunday full and the Wednesday incremental
Sunday full, then the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday incrementals in order
The Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday incrementals only

prompts.label: Backup sets needed if the nightly backups had been differentials instead
prompts.answer: Sunday full and the Wednesday differential
prompts.why: A differential holds every change since the last full backup, so the most recent one plus the full is enough. That is why differentials restore faster but grow larger each night.
choices: Sunday full and the Wednesday differential
Sunday full, then the Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday differentials

prompts.label: Data lost in this failure
prompts.why: The last good backup ran on Wednesday at 23:00 and the failure came on Thursday at 15:00, so 16 hours of changes are gone.

prompts.label: Time to restore and verify using the incremental sets
prompts.why: 3 hours for the full, plus three incrementals at 30 minutes each (1.5 hours), plus 1 hour of verification, is 5.5 hours.

prompts.label: Does the restore meet the 6-hour RTO?
prompts.why: 5.5 hours is inside the 6-hour RTO, though with little margin; a Friday failure would add another incremental and use it all up.

prompts.label: Does the current schedule meet the 4-hour RPO?
prompts.answer: No, because up to 24 hours of changes can be lost
prompts.why: RPO is about how much data can be lost, and with backups once a night the worst case is almost a full day. Meeting the RTO says nothing about the RPO.
choices: Yes, because a backup runs every night
Yes, because the restore finishes within the RTO
No, because up to 24 hours of changes can be lost
No, because the restore takes longer than 4 hours

prompts.label: Change that would meet the RPO
prompts.answer: Add transaction log backups every hour
prompts.why: Hourly log backups cap data loss at about an hour, inside the 4-hour RPO. Switching to differentials or nightly fulls changes restore speed, not how often data is captured, and offsite copies protect against site loss.
choices: Switch the nightly incrementals to differentials
Run a full backup every night instead
Add transaction log backups every hour
Copy each backup to an offsite location

takeaway: Incrementals need the full plus every incremental since; differentials need the full plus the latest one. RPO is set by how often you back up, RTO by how long the restore takes, and meeting one says nothing about the other.

scenario: A small accounting office is adding guest Wi-Fi and moving its printer and door badge controller onto their own VLAN. One stateful firewall routes between the VLANs and the internet and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins. The firewall answers DNS and DHCP itself, so that traffic is outside this rule list.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-OFFICE] ──┬── STAFF    192.168.10.0/24   staff PCs
                           │      MGR01    192.168.10.25   office manager's PC
                           │
                           ├── GUEST    192.168.20.0/24   visitor Wi-Fi
                           │
                           └── DEVICES  192.168.30.0/24
                                  PRN01    192.168.30.20   printer: print jobs on TCP 9100,
                                                           admin web page on HTTPS only
                                  BADGE01  192.168.30.30   door badge controller

All office VLANs together: 192.168.0.0/16
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Guest devices cannot reach anything on the office networks.
Guests can browse the web, but only over encrypted connections.
Staff PCs can send print jobs to PRN01.
Only the office manager's PC can open the printer's admin web page.
No other staff traffic can reach the device VLAN.
Staff can browse websites on the internet over HTTPS.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: Guests must not reach the staff or device VLAN, and 192.168.0.0/16 is the one destination offered that covers both. It has to sit above rule 2, because rule 2's Any destination would otherwise let guests reach internal HTTPS pages such as the printer's.

Guests browse sites anywhere on the internet, so the destination is Any, and only TCP 443 is opened because port 80 would carry unencrypted HTTP. Rule 1 has already removed every internal destination.

Every staff PC prints, so the source is the staff subnet, but the destination is the printer alone on the port the exhibit gives for print jobs (TCP 9100). Ports 515 and 631 are other printing protocols this printer is not using.
Only MGR01 may manage the printer, so the source is its single address and the port is the HTTPS admin page. This exception must sit above rule 5, which would otherwise deny it.

This deny protects the whole device VLAN, including the badge controller, and must sit above rule 6. Without it, the staff HTTPS rule with an Any destination would let every staff PC open the printer's admin page.
Staff browse the internet over HTTPS, so the destination is Any on TCP 443. It is safe only because rules 4 and 5 have already decided all staff traffic to the device VLAN.
The cleanup rule blocks everything not allowed above, such as the printer or badge controller reaching the internet. It must be last, or it would block the allowed traffic below it.

takeaway: Two ordering rules cover most firewall PBQs: a single-host exception goes above the subnet deny it is an exception to, and a deny protecting a segment goes above any broad allow whose Any destination would include that segment.

scenario: Administrators need remote access to servers without exposing RDP to the internet. Remote administrators connect to a Remote Desktop Gateway in the screened subnet, which forwards their sessions to a hardened jump host, while administrators in the office use the jump host directly. FW-CORE routes between every segment and the internet, is stateful, and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-CORE] ──┬── DMZ      172.18.0.0/24
                         │     RDGW01  172.18.0.10   Remote Desktop Gateway: HTTPS transport on
                         │                           TCP 443, UDP transport on UDP 3391
                         ├── MGMT     10.60.5.0/24
                         │     JUMP01  10.60.5.10    jump host, RDP on TCP 3389
                         ├── ADMIN    10.60.9.0/24   administrator workstations
                         └── SERVERS  10.60.20.0/24  Windows servers (RDP, TCP 3389) and
                                                     Linux servers (SSH, TCP 22) share this subnet

RDP's UDP transport is disabled on JUMP01 and the servers.
Directory and DNS traffic are handled by rules outside this task.
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Remote administrators can reach the gateway from anywhere on the internet using its HTTPS transport.
The gateway's UDP transport also works from the internet.
The gateway can forward sessions to the jump host and to nothing else.
Administrators in the office can open RDP sessions to the jump host from their workstations.
Only the jump host can open RDP sessions to the Windows servers.
Only the jump host can open SSH sessions to the Linux servers.
Everything else is blocked, including RDP from the internet.

rows.why: The gateway wraps RDP inside HTTPS, so the internet only ever sees TCP 443 to RDGW01. Opening 3389 to the internet is exactly what the gateway exists to avoid, and remote administrators can connect from any address.
The gateway's optional UDP transport is a separate protocol and port (UDP 3391), so it needs its own rule. A TCP rule cannot carry it, and Any protocol would open more than the requirement asks.
The gateway connects onward to the jump host with ordinary RDP on TCP 3389. The destination is JUMP01 alone, so a compromised gateway cannot reach the servers directly.
Office administrators sit in the admin subnet and RDP to the jump host. Using 10.60.0.0/16 as the source would let any internal device try to log on to it.
The jump host is the single permitted source for server administration. The Windows and Linux servers share one subnet, so 10.60.20.0/24 is the narrowest destination offered.
SSH to the Linux servers is a different port, so it needs a second rule from the same single source. A port of Any would also open WinRM and every other service on the servers.
The cleanup rule blocks everything else, including RDP from the internet, administrator workstations going straight to servers, and the gateway reaching anything but the jump host.

takeaway: Remote access gateways exist so the risky protocol is never exposed: the internet reaches the gateway on TCP 443 (plus UDP 3391 for its UDP transport), and only the gateway and jump host speak RDP or SSH inward.

scenario: All mail for the company passes through a spam filter appliance in the screened subnet. The appliance relays clean inbound mail to the internal mail server and relays that server's outbound mail to the internet. FW-EDGE routes between all four segments, is stateful, and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-EDGE] ──┬── DMZ      172.22.0.0/24
                         │     SPAM01  172.22.0.25   spam filter appliance (SMTP relay)
                         ├── SERVERS  10.5.1.0/24
                         │     MAIL01  10.5.1.20     internal mail server
                         │                           SMTP relay on TCP 25
                         │                           IMAP on TCP 143 and IMAPS on TCP 993
                         │                           client submission on TCP 587, STARTTLS required
                         └── USERS    10.5.10.0/24   staff workstations

All internal networks together: 10.5.0.0/16
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Mail servers on the internet can deliver mail to the spam filter.
The spam filter can pass clean inbound mail to the internal mail server.
If the spam filter is compromised, it must not be able to reach any other internal system.
The internal mail server sends all outbound mail through the spam filter.
The spam filter is the only system that delivers mail to other mail servers on the internet.
Staff mail clients can retrieve mail from MAIL01, but only over an encrypted connection.
Staff mail clients can send mail through MAIL01 using authenticated client submission.
Everything else is blocked.

rows.why: Server-to-server mail delivery is SMTP on TCP 25, and any mail server on the internet may be the sender. The destination is the appliance only, never the internal server.
The appliance relays clean mail to MAIL01 alone on TCP 25. This allow has to come before the deny in rule 3, which blocks every other path from the appliance into the LAN.
This deny contains a compromised appliance. It must sit above rule 5, because that rule's Any destination on TCP 25 would otherwise let the appliance open SMTP connections to any internal host.
Outbound mail goes from MAIL01 to the appliance on SMTP. Rule 3 does not interfere, because it only matches traffic whose source is the appliance.

Only the appliance delivers to the internet, so it is the single source. Other mail servers can be anywhere, so the destination is Any, which is safe because rule 3 already removed internal destinations.
IMAPS on TCP 993 is IMAP inside TLS. Port 143 is plain IMAP, which the requirement rules out, and 995 is POP3S, a different retrieval protocol.

Mail clients submit outgoing mail on TCP 587, which the exhibit says requires STARTTLS. Port 25 is for relaying between servers, and port 465 (submission over implicit TLS) is not offered by this server.
The cleanup rule blocks everything else, including workstations sending mail straight to the internet, which is how spam-sending malware is stopped.

takeaway: Mail flow PBQs separate the hops: TCP 25 for every server-to-server relay, 587 for client submission, 993 for IMAPS. Put the deny that contains a screened subnet host above that host's broad outbound allow.

scenario: A company is redesigning DNS. Its public zone is hosted on an authoritative server in the screened subnet, with a secondary server run by a hosting provider. Staff must use the internal resolvers, which forward every query to a protective DNS service over an encrypted channel. FW-CORE is stateful and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
Internet ── [FW-CORE] ──┬── DMZ      172.16.53.0/24
                         │     NS1     172.16.53.10   authoritative server for example.com
                         ├── SERVERS  10.8.1.0/24
                         │     RES01   10.8.1.53      internal resolver
                         │     RES02   10.8.1.54      internal resolver
                         │     (10.8.1.52 and 10.8.1.55 are unused)
                         └── USERS    10.8.10.0/24   staff workstations

Secondary DNS server (hosting provider): 203.0.113.53, polls NS1 for changes
Protective DNS service:                  198.51.100.100, accepts DNS over TLS only
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Only the hosting provider's secondary server can copy the zone from NS1.
Anyone on the internet can look up names in the public zone on NS1. Its answers are small enough to fit in UDP, and no source other than the secondary may open TCP connections to NS1.
Staff workstations can resolve names only through the internal resolvers, including large answers that fall back to TCP.
The internal resolvers forward queries only to the protective DNS service, using its encrypted transport.
Staff can browse the web over HTTPS.
Everything else is blocked, including staff workstations sending DNS queries straight to the internet.

rows.why: Zone transfers run over TCP 53, so allowing TCP 53 from the secondary's single address is what lets it copy the zone. No other source gets TCP 53 to NS1.

Ordinary lookups use UDP 53, and the requirement says NS1's answers fit in UDP, so UDP alone serves everyone. TCP or Any would let any internet host attempt a zone transfer, which NS1 should also refuse in its own configuration.

Both resolvers sit inside 10.8.1.52/30, the narrowest choice that covers them, while 10.8.1.53 alone would leave RES02 unusable. Protocol Any on port 53 permits UDP queries and the TCP fallback for large answers.
DNS over TLS runs on TCP 853, and the protective service accepts nothing else. Port 53 would send queries in cleartext, and Any destination would let the resolvers bypass the filtering service.
Staff browse the internet on TCP 443. A port rule cannot tell DNS over HTTPS apart from ordinary web traffic, so stopping DoH to public resolvers needs a proxy or next-generation firewall policy.
The cleanup rule blocks direct DNS from workstations to the internet, DNS over TLS to any other service, and every other unlisted flow.

takeaway: In DNS designs, TCP 53 carries zone transfers and large answers: give it to the secondary, and to clients only when large answers must work. Lookups use UDP 53, DNS over TLS uses TCP 853, and DNS over HTTPS hides inside TCP 443.

scenario: A company is deploying IP phones on their own voice VLAN, using SIP over TLS for signaling and SRTP for encrypted audio. The internal firewall routes between the VLANs, is stateful, and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins. Replies pass automatically, and because the media is symmetric RTP, PBX01's half of each audio stream is treated as the reply to the phone's half.
exhibit:
VOICE    10.40.50.0/24    IP phones
DATA     10.40.10.0/24    staff PCs
  VADM01   10.40.10.15    voice administrator's PC
SERVERS  10.40.60.0/24
  PBX01    10.40.60.10    call manager
                          SIP on UDP and TCP 5060, SIP over TLS on TCP 5061
                          media (RTP and SRTP) on UDP 16384-32767
                          admin console on HTTPS
  PROV01   10.40.60.20    phone provisioning server, HTTPS
  NTP01    10.40.60.123   time server
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Phones can register and set up calls with PBX01 using encrypted signaling.
Phones can exchange call audio with PBX01.
Phones can download their configuration from the provisioning server.
Phones can synchronize their clocks with NTP01.
Only the voice administrator's PC can manage PBX01 through its admin console.
Everything else is blocked, including any traffic from staff PCs to the phones.

rows.why: SIP over TLS runs on TCP 5061. Port 5060 is unencrypted SIP, which the requirement rules out. The phones keep this TLS connection open, so PBX01 sends incoming calls down it as return traffic.
Audio travels as RTP or SRTP over UDP, on the range the exhibit gives. Signaling and media are separate flows, so one SIP rule is not enough, and a TCP rule would never match the media.
The provisioning server serves configuration files over HTTPS. Port 69 is TFTP, an unencrypted protocol many phones fall back to, which would expose their configuration.
NTP is UDP 123, and the destination is the time server alone. Accurate clocks matter for phones because TLS certificate checks fail when the time is wrong.
Only VADM01 manages the call manager, so the source is its single address and the port is the HTTPS console. The data subnet as a source would let every staff PC try to log on.
The cleanup rule blocks staff PCs reaching the phones, phones reaching any other server, and unencrypted SIP, none of which any rule above allows.

takeaway: VoIP needs at least two rules per path: signaling (SIP on 5060, or SIP over TLS on TCP 5061) and media (RTP or SRTP on a UDP port range). Choose the secure port whenever the requirement says encrypted.

scenario: Developers work in an isolated VLAN that must never reach the internet directly. They use an internal code repository and an internal package mirror, and the mirror is the only system allowed to fetch from the public registries. The firewall is stateful and processes rules top to bottom, first match wins. Its policy ends with a built-in default deny that is logged, so this table has no cleanup rule.
exhibit:
DEV      10.90.20.0/24   developer workstations
  CI01     10.90.20.50   build server, receives webhooks on TCP 8443
TOOLS    10.90.5.0/24
  GIT01    10.90.5.10    code repository: Git over SSH on TCP 22,
                         web interface on HTTPS
  PKG01    10.90.5.20    package mirror, HTTPS
STAGING  10.90.30.0/24   staging servers, SSH on TCP 22

Public package registries: many changing addresses behind CDNs
DNS is handled by rules outside this task.
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Developers can clone and push code on GIT01 using Git over SSH.
Developers can review code in GIT01's web interface.
Developers can install libraries, but only from PKG01.
GIT01 can notify the build server whenever new code is pushed.
Only the build server can deploy to the staging servers, using SSH.
PKG01 can refresh its copies from the public registries over HTTPS.

rows.why: Git over SSH uses TCP 22 to the repository server. Port 9418 is the native Git protocol, which has no encryption or authentication. CI01 is inside the developer subnet, so it can pull code through this rule too.
The web interface is a second service on the same server, so it needs its own rule on TCP 443. Combining both into one rule with port Any would open every service on GIT01.
Libraries come from the mirror over HTTPS, with PKG01 as the only destination. A destination of Any would let developers download straight from the public registries, which the design forbids.

The webhook is a new connection from the repository to the build server, on the port the exhibit gives. Allowing GIT01 to the whole developer subnet would let a compromised repository reach every workstation.
Only CI01 deploys, so the source is its single address rather than the developer subnet. Developer workstations reaching staging are dropped by the default deny, so no extra rule is needed.

Registries sit behind CDNs with changing addresses, so Any is the only workable destination. The rule stays tight because the source is one server and the port is HTTPS only, and no narrower destination offered covers the registries.

takeaway: When the policy ends in a logged default deny, you do not need a cleanup rule, and you do not need explicit denies for flows nothing allows. Write only the allows, each with the narrowest source, destination and port.

scenario: A hospital is isolating its medical devices, many of which run operating systems the vendor does not allow the hospital to patch. The internal firewall routes between the VLANs, is stateful, and applies one rule list top to bottom, first match wins. Every blocked attempt must appear in the firewall log, and this firewall does not log its built-in default deny.
exhibit:
MEDDEV    10.120.40.0/24   patient monitors and infusion pumps
  CT01      10.120.40.60   CT scanner
CLINICAL  10.120.30.0/24   clinical workstations
  BIO01     10.120.30.15   biomedical engineering workstation
SERVERS   10.120.10.0/24
  HL7-01    10.120.10.20   integration engine, receives HL7 messages on TCP 2575
  PACS01    10.120.10.40   image archive: DICOM on TCP 104,
                           DICOM over TLS on TCP 2762, web image viewer on HTTPS
  NTP01     10.120.10.123  time server

Medical devices are managed through HTTPS pages on each device.
stem: Complete the rule table so that it meets every requirement and follows least privilege.
requirements: Monitors and pumps can send patient data to the integration engine.
The CT scanner, and no other medical device, can send images to PACS01, but only over an encrypted connection.
Medical devices can synchronize their clocks with NTP01.
Only the biomedical engineering workstation can manage the medical devices.
Clinical workstations can view images in the PACS web viewer.
Everything else is blocked and logged, including any attempt by a medical device to reach the internet.

rows.why: The monitors and pumps share the device subnet, so it is the narrowest source offered that covers them (CT01 is included, but no choice excludes it). The destination is the integration engine alone, on the HL7 port given in the exhibit.
Only CT01 sends images, so its single address is the source. TCP 2762 is DICOM over TLS. TCP 104 is the same protocol unencrypted, which the requirement rules out.
NTP uses UDP 123, and every device needs time, so the source is the device subnet and the destination is NTP01 only. Accurate time keeps medical records and logs consistent.

BIO01 is the only permitted manager, so it is a single-host source, and the destination is the device subnet because every device has a management page. The clinical subnet as a source would expose unpatchable devices to every workstation.
Clinicians view images through the PACS web viewer on HTTPS. The destination is PACS01 alone, not the whole server subnet.

An explicit cleanup rule is required here because the built-in default deny is not logged, and the requirement says every blocked attempt must be logged. It also blocks medical devices from reaching the internet.

takeaway: Unpatchable devices are protected by isolation: allow only the exact flows they need, pick the TLS port for the encrypted version of a protocol, and add an explicit logged cleanup rule when the default deny does not log.

scenario: After a change, the lobby kiosks (10.30.66.0/24) can suddenly open remote desktop sessions to servers, and the monitoring subnet (172.16.99.0/24) can no longer reach them. The ACL below is applied outbound on the router interface that leads to the server subnet 172.16.20.0/24 and the lab subnet 172.16.21.0/24. It is processed top to bottom, first match wins.
exhibit:
#  Action  Proto  Source           Destination      Port
 1  permit  tcp    10.30.0.0/16     172.16.20.10     443
 2  permit  tcp    10.30.0.0/16     172.16.20.0/24   any
 3  deny    tcp    10.30.66.0/24    172.16.20.0/24   any
 4  permit  udp    10.30.0.0/16     172.16.20.53     53
 5  deny    ip     any              172.16.20.0/24   any
 6  permit  ip     172.16.99.0/24   172.16.20.0/24   any
    (implicit deny ip any any)
stem: Trace each connection attempt through the ACL and choose the outcome and the rule that decides it.

prompts.label: 10.30.66.12 to 172.16.20.30, TCP 3389 (a kiosk opening RDP)
prompts.why: Rule 1 does not match because the destination is not 172.16.20.10. Rule 2 matches: 10.30.66.12 is inside 10.30.0.0/16 and the destination is in the server subnet on any TCP port. Rule 3, the kiosk deny, is never reached, so it is shadowed.

prompts.label: 10.30.66.12 to 172.16.20.10, TCP 443
prompts.why: Every field of rule 1 matches: the source is in 10.30.0.0/16, the destination is 172.16.20.10, and the port is TCP 443. Evaluation stops at the first match.

prompts.label: 10.30.5.5 to 172.16.20.53, UDP 53
prompts.why: Rules 1, 2 and 3 only match TCP, so this UDP query passes over them. Rule 4 permits UDP 53 from 10.30.0.0/16 to the DNS server.

prompts.label: 10.30.66.12 to 172.16.20.53, ICMP echo request
prompts.why: ICMP is neither TCP nor UDP, so rules 1 to 4 do not match. Rule 5 denies all IP traffic from any source to the server subnet, and ICMP is IP traffic.

prompts.label: 172.16.99.7 to 172.16.20.30, TCP 22 (the monitoring server)
prompts.why: Rules 1 to 4 only match sources in 10.30.0.0/16. Rule 5 matches any source going to the server subnet, so the monitoring traffic is denied before rule 6 is ever evaluated. Rule 6 is shadowed.

prompts.label: 10.30.5.5 to 172.16.21.8, TCP 443 (a lab server)
prompts.why: Every rule names 172.16.20.x as the destination, so nothing matches traffic for the lab subnet 172.16.21.0/24. It falls through to the implicit deny at the end.

takeaway: A broad rule shadows every later rule it fully covers, whether the later rule is a permit or a deny. Fix shadowing by moving the specific rule above the broad one, and check each field (protocol, source, destination, port) before declaring a match.

scenario: A stateful firewall sits between the internal network (10.50.0.0/16), a screened subnet (172.16.30.0/24) and the internet. A packet that belongs to a connection already in the state table is passed before the rule list is checked. New connections are checked against the rules top to bottom, first match wins. Addresses are shown as the rule list evaluates them.
exhibit:
#  Action  Proto  Source           Destination      Port
 1  allow   tcp    10.50.0.0/16     any              443
 2  allow   tcp    any              172.16.30.10     443
 3  allow   tcp    172.16.30.10     10.50.8.20       5432
 4  deny    any    172.16.30.0/24   10.50.0.0/16     any
 5  allow   tcp    10.50.9.0/24     172.16.30.0/24   22
    (implicit deny)
stem: Choose how the firewall handles each packet and what decides it.
choices: Allowed as return traffic for an existing connection

prompts.label: 10.50.3.7:51000 → 203.0.113.80:443  TCP SYN (new connection)
prompts.why: This starts a new session, so the rule list is checked. Rule 1 allows any internal source to reach any destination on TCP 443, and the firewall records the session in its state table.

prompts.label: 198.51.100.4:52200 → 172.16.30.10:443  TCP SYN (a customer opening the website)
prompts.why: Rule 1 does not match because the source is not internal. Rule 2 allows any source to reach the public web server on TCP 443, so the new connection is permitted and recorded.

prompts.label: 203.0.113.80:443 → 10.50.3.7:51000  TCP SYN-ACK (reply to the connection above)
prompts.answer: Allowed as return traffic for an existing connection
prompts.why: The reply matches the session that rule 1 created, so the state table passes it. No rule allows new traffic from the internet to 10.50.3.7, and none is needed.

prompts.label: 203.0.113.80:50500 → 10.50.3.7:3389  TCP SYN (new connection)
prompts.why: This is a new inbound connection, not part of any session. Rule 1's source must be internal, rule 2 only covers 172.16.30.10, and rules 3 to 5 do not match, so the implicit deny drops it.

prompts.label: 10.50.9.4:50600 → 172.16.30.25:22  TCP SYN (administrator opening SSH)
prompts.why: Rule 4 does not match because its source is the screened subnet, not the admin subnet. Rule 5 allows TCP 22 from 10.50.9.0/24 to the screened subnet.

prompts.label: 172.16.30.25:22 → 10.50.9.4:50600  TCP ACK (server's reply in that SSH session)
prompts.answer: Allowed as return traffic for an existing connection
prompts.why: Read against the rules, this packet would hit rule 4, which denies the screened subnet reaching the internal network. It is never compared with the rules because it belongs to the SSH session rule 5 allowed.

prompts.label: 172.16.30.25:41000 → 10.50.9.4:22  TCP SYN (screened subnet server opening SSH inward)
prompts.why: This is a new connection started from the screened subnet, so the state table has nothing for it. Rule 4 denies any traffic from 172.16.30.0/24 to 10.50.0.0/16.

prompts.label: 172.16.30.10:40100 → 10.50.8.20:5432  TCP SYN (web server querying the database)
prompts.why: Rule 3 is a specific exception placed above the broad deny in rule 4, so the web server's database connection is allowed. Had rule 3 been below rule 4, it would be shadowed.

takeaway: A stateful firewall checks the state table first: replies in an allowed session pass even when a deny rule would match them. Only new connections are judged by the rules, so the direction of the first packet decides which rule applies.

scenario: WEB03 (10.0.5.20) is a Linux web server with the host firewall rules below on its INPUT chain. Rules are processed top to bottom and the first match decides. DROP discards a packet silently, REJECT discards it and sends an error back, and the chain's default policy applies when no rule matches.
exhibit:
-P INPUT DROP
 1 -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
 2 -A INPUT -i lo -j ACCEPT
 3 -A INPUT -s 203.0.113.0/24 -j DROP
 4 -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
 5 -A INPUT -s 10.0.9.10 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
 6 -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -j REJECT
 7 -A INPUT -s 10.0.0.0/8 -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT
stem: Choose how WEB03 handles each incoming packet and which rule decides it.

prompts.label: 203.0.113.9:52000 → 10.0.5.20:443  TCP SYN (new connection)
prompts.why: The packet is new, so rule 1 does not match, and it did not arrive on loopback. Rule 3 drops everything from 203.0.113.0/24 before rule 4 can accept HTTPS.

prompts.label: 198.51.100.4:52001 → 10.0.5.20:443  TCP SYN (new connection)
prompts.why: Rules 1 to 3 do not match a new connection from 198.51.100.4, and rule 4 accepts TCP 443 from any source.

prompts.label: 10.0.9.10:50122 → 10.0.5.20:22  TCP SYN (the bastion host)
prompts.why: Rule 5 accepts SSH from the bastion's single address, and it sits above the general SSH reject in rule 6.

prompts.label: 10.0.9.11:50123 → 10.0.5.20:22  TCP SYN (another admin subnet host)
prompts.why: Rule 5 matches only 10.0.9.10, so this packet reaches rule 6, which rejects all other SSH. Rule 7 would have accepted it, but rule 6 shadows it completely.

prompts.label: 203.0.113.50:443 → 10.0.5.20:44010  TCP ACK (reply to WEB03's own download from a mirror)
prompts.why: WEB03 started this connection itself, so the reply is ESTABLISHED and rule 1 accepts it before rule 3 is evaluated. Rule 3 blocks new connections from that range but not replies to WEB03's own sessions.

prompts.label: 127.0.0.1:39000 → 127.0.0.1:5432  TCP SYN (app talking to its local database)
prompts.why: Traffic on the loopback interface is accepted by rule 2. It is a new connection, so rule 1 does not apply, and loopback traffic never leaves the host.

prompts.label: 10.0.4.4:40500 → 10.0.5.20:161  UDP (an SNMP poll)
prompts.why: No rule mentions UDP 161, and the packet is not part of an existing session or from loopback. With no match, the chain's DROP policy discards it silently.

takeaway: On a host firewall, an ESTABLISHED rule at the top lets replies through ahead of any block list, and a broad REJECT shadows any later ACCEPT for the same port. DROP is silent, while REJECT tells the sender the port is closed.

scenario: A data loss review asked the SOC to pull notable entries from the secure web proxy for one week. Each excerpt below comes from a different user or group.
stem: Identify the activity that each proxy excerpt shows.
choices: Data exfiltration to personal cloud storage
Credential harvesting page reached from a phishing email
Malware download disguised with a double extension
Credentials sent over an unencrypted connection

prompts.label:
Sat 02:13  user=dkim  POST https://files.personal-share.example/upload
bytes_out=4,212,880,114  category=Online storage (personal)  action=allowed
(dkim resigned on Thursday; last working day is Friday next week)
prompts.answer: Data exfiltration to personal cloud storage
prompts.why: Gigabytes sent to a personal storage service, at night, by a departing employee is the classic insider exfiltration pattern. DLP and blocking personal storage categories are the usual controls.

prompts.label:
Mon to Fri  31 users in Marketing  → app.quickboard.example
category=Project management (not on the approved list)  2,400 requests
sign-in: corporate email addresses with self-chosen passwords
prompts.why: A whole team adopting a cloud service that IT never approved is shadow IT. The risk is company data in a service with no contract, no security review and no central account control.

prompts.label:
10:42  user=jlopez  GET https://hr-benefits-update.example/start  referer=webmail
10:43  POST https://hr-benefits-update.example/signin  form fields: username, password
category=Newly registered domain (6 days old)  action=allowed
prompts.answer: Credential harvesting page reached from a phishing email
prompts.why: The user arrived from a webmail link, landed on a days-old domain and submitted a username and password form. The account should be reset and the sign-in logs checked for use of those credentials.

prompts.label:
14:05 to 14:09  user=rpatel  CONNECT to 14 different IP addresses on 443
category=Anonymizer / proxy avoidance  action=blocked (all 14)
14:10  user=rpatel  installs a browser extension that offers a free VPN
prompts.why: Repeated connections to anonymizer services, each blocked, followed by a VPN extension, show a user trying to get around the proxy's filtering. Application control should block the extension too.

prompts.label:
16:31  user=amorris  GET https://cdn-share.example/Invoice_4471.pdf.exe
content-type=application/x-msdownload  file signed=no  reputation=unknown
action=allowed
prompts.answer: Malware download disguised with a double extension
prompts.why: The name ends in .exe but is dressed up as a PDF, counting on Windows hiding known extensions. The executable content type and unsigned, unknown reputation confirm it is not a document.

prompts.label:
09:20  user=bnguyen  POST http://legacy-hr.corp.local/login.asp
request body includes the password field in readable text  action=allowed
prompts.answer: Credentials sent over an unencrypted connection
prompts.why: A login form posted over plain HTTP sends the password in cleartext, readable by anyone on the path. The fix is TLS on the application, not user training.

prompts.label:
Staff from six departments visited supplierforum.example, a trusted industry site
each page now loads a hidden frame from 203.0.113.44/landing
that page profiles the browser and serves an exploit for an old plugin flaw
prompts.why: Attackers compromised a legitimate site that their targets already trust and visit, then used it to attack visitors' browsers. Patching browsers and plugins and isolating browsing are the main defenses.

takeaway: Proxy logs show who sent what, where and how much: big uploads to personal storage suggest exfiltration, unapproved SaaS is shadow IT, blocked anonymizers mean filter evasion, and a trusted site serving exploits is a watering hole.

scenario: The firewall team exported summaries of unusual traffic from the edge and internal firewalls over one month. Each excerpt shows a different activity.
stem: Identify the activity that each firewall log excerpt shows.
choices: Port scan of a single host
Sweep of one port across many hosts
Spam-sending malware stopped by egress filtering
Large outbound transfer suggesting data exfiltration

prompts.label:
DENY TCP 203.0.113.15 → 172.16.1.10 ports 1 to 1024 except 443, SYN, 1,023 attempts in 4 s
ALLOW TCP 203.0.113.15 → 172.16.1.10:443, SYN
prompts.answer: Port scan of a single host
prompts.why: One source tries every low port on one target in seconds, which maps the services that host exposes. The single allow simply shows the port the scanner found open.

prompts.label:
TCP 10.6.4.31 → 10.6.0.1 through 10.6.3.254, port 445 only, SYN, 1,022 hosts in 70 s
(10.6.4.31 is a workstation that has never used SMB to reach other workstations)
prompts.answer: Sweep of one port across many hosts
prompts.why: One port across a whole range is a horizontal sweep looking for every host running SMB, typical of worms and lateral movement. A port scan instead tries many ports on one host.

prompts.label:
ALLOW TCP 10.6.2.18 → 198.51.100.77:443 every 300 s (varies by up to 30 s) for 9 days
~1.2 KB out and ~0.8 KB in each time, including weekends and overnight
prompts.why: Small, regular check-ins that continue when no one is working are beaconing. The random variation (jitter) is added by C2 malware to avoid fixed-interval detection, but the pattern still stands out.

prompts.label:
ALLOW TCP from 41,000 source addresses → 172.16.1.10:443, SYN only, 380,000 per second
firewall state table 98% full, almost no handshakes completed
prompts.why: Huge numbers of half-open connections from many sources exhaust the state table and the server's connection queue. SYN cookies and upstream DDoS scrubbing are the usual mitigations.

prompts.label:
DENY TCP 10.6.3.40 → 612 different internet hosts, port 25, in 10 minutes
(10.6.3.40 is a sales workstation; only the mail relay may send on port 25)
prompts.answer: Spam-sending malware stopped by egress filtering
prompts.why: A workstation connecting straight to hundreds of mail servers on TCP 25 is behaving like a spam bot. The egress rule did its job, but the host still needs to be investigated and cleaned.

prompts.label:
ALLOW TCP 10.6.8.5 (file server) → 203.0.113.200:443 from 02:10 to 04:55
38 GB out, 0.2 GB in; the server normally sends under 1 GB a day to the internet
prompts.answer: Large outbound transfer suggesting data exfiltration
prompts.why: Far more data leaving than arriving, at night, from a server that rarely talks to the internet, is the volume anomaly that points to exfiltration. Encryption hides the content but not the size.

takeaway: Read the shape of the traffic: many ports on one host is a scan, one port on many hosts is a sweep, small regular sessions are beaconing, floods of half-open sessions are a SYN flood, and heavy one-way uploads suggest exfiltration.

scenario: During an investigation the SOC pulled the Windows events below from domain controllers and member servers. Each excerpt shows a different activity.
stem: Identify the activity that each set of Windows events shows.
choices: Brute force against a single account
Dormant account re-enabled for unauthorized access
New service installed for remote execution or persistence
Clearing the audit log to cover tracks

prompts.label:
DC01 4625 failed logon x58 for m.chen in 6 minutes, sub status 0xC000006A (wrong password), source WS-221
DC01 4740 user account locked out: m.chen
prompts.answer: Brute force against a single account
prompts.why: Event 4625 is a failed logon, and many of them against one account from one source until 4740 records the lockout is a brute force attempt against that account.

prompts.label:
DC01 4625 failed logon, sub status 0xC000006A, source 10.3.2.77
one attempt each against 640 different accounts in 15 minutes, no lockouts
DC01 4624 successful logon x3 from 10.3.2.77 shortly after
prompts.why: One attempt per account across hundreds of accounts stays under the lockout threshold, the signature of spraying a common password. The 4624 successes mean three accounts used that password and must be reset.

prompts.label:
DC01 4722 user account enabled: t.brooks (left the company five months ago), by helpdesk-07 at 23:48
VPN01 t.brooks connected at 23:55
prompts.answer: Dormant account re-enabled for unauthorized access
prompts.why: Event 4722 records an account being enabled. Reviving a departed employee's account at night, followed minutes later by a remote connection, is unauthorized access using an account nobody watches.

prompts.label:
DC01 4728 member added to security-enabled global group Domain Admins: s.ortiz (Sales), by helpdesk-07, no change ticket
FS01 4672 special privileges assigned to new logon: s.ortiz
prompts.why: Event 4728 shows a sales user being added to Domain Admins, and 4672 at the next logon confirms the account now holds administrator-level privileges. Without an approved change, this is privilege escalation.

prompts.label:
SRV12 7045 a service was installed: name xkqwz, image path C:\Windows\Temp\xkqwz.exe, account LocalSystem
installed over the network from WS-221
prompts.answer: New service installed for remote execution or persistence
prompts.why: Event 7045 in the System log records a new service. A random name, a binary in a temp folder and SYSTEM rights, pushed from another machine, is how remote execution tools and persistence mechanisms run code.

prompts.label: SRV12 1102 the audit log was cleared, by helpdesk-07 at 00:21
prompts.answer: Clearing the audit log to cover tracks
prompts.why: Event 1102 records the Security log being cleared. Right after the activity above, it is an attempt to destroy evidence, which is why logs should be forwarded to a SIEM as they are written.

takeaway: Know the core Windows event IDs: 4624 success, 4625 failure, 4740 lockout, 4672 admin-level logon, 4720 created, 4722 enabled, 4728 added to a global group, 7045 service installed, 1102 Security log cleared.

scenario: A Linux web server was flagged by file integrity monitoring. You are reviewing its auth.log, sudo log and cron log, plus notes from the responder. Not every excerpt is malicious.
stem: Identify the activity that each excerpt shows.
choices: Automated guessing of common usernames and passwords
Unauthorized attempt to gain root with sudo
Unauthorized SSH key planted on a service account
Covering tracks by wiping logs and shell history

prompts.label:
sshd: Failed password for invalid user oracle from 203.0.113.61
sshd: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.61
(2,300 failures for 410 different nonexistent usernames in 40 minutes, about 6 passwords each, none accepted)
prompts.answer: Automated guessing of common usernames and passwords
prompts.why: The usernames do not exist on this server, so this is a bot working through a list of common account names and passwords. Spraying would target real accounts with one password each.

prompts.label:
sudo: kwong : user NOT in sudoers ; TTY=pts/3 ; PWD=/home/kwong ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/bin/bash
(three times in two minutes)
prompts.answer: Unauthorized attempt to gain root with sudo
prompts.why: A user without sudo rights repeatedly trying to start a root shell is a failed privilege escalation attempt. sudo logs and reports these attempts by default, so they are easy to alert on.

prompts.label:
useradd: new user: name=sysupd, UID=0, GID=0, home=/var/tmp/.s, shell=/bin/bash
(run from a root shell started by the web server's process)
prompts.why: UID 0 makes the account equivalent to root whatever its name, and a hidden home directory in a temp folder shows it was created to keep access, not for any real user.

prompts.label:
sshd: Accepted publickey for www-data from 198.51.100.90 port 50122 ssh2
(www-data is the web server's service account; it has never logged on interactively, and its authorized_keys file was created yesterday)
prompts.answer: Unauthorized SSH key planted on a service account
prompts.why: Someone added their public key to a service account that should never log on, giving them password-free SSH access. The key must be removed, and service accounts should have no login shell.

prompts.label:
crontab entry added for root at 03:02: every 5 minutes, download a script from 203.0.113.9 and run it with a shell
CRON: (root) CMD (that entry) logged every 5 minutes since
prompts.why: A scheduled job that keeps fetching and running code from an outside address makes sure the attacker regains control even after a reboot or after one payload is removed.

prompts.label:
auth.log shrank from 4.1 MB to 0 bytes at 03:20
root's .bash_history is now a link to /dev/null
prompts.answer: Covering tracks by wiping logs and shell history
prompts.why: Emptying the authentication log and sending shell history to /dev/null removes the record of what the attacker did. Forwarding logs off the host as they are written defeats this.

prompts.label:
sudo: deploy : TTY=pts/0 ; PWD=/srv/app ; USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/bin/systemctl restart app
(09:15, inside the change window for approved ticket CHG-1182)
prompts.why: The deploy account ran one specific, permitted command during an approved change window. This is the normal, least privilege use of sudo, and it should not be escalated as an incident.

takeaway: On Linux, look for invalid user floods (guessing), NOT in sudoers (failed escalation), UID 0 accounts (backdoor), keys on service accounts, root cron jobs fetching code (persistence) and emptied logs. Check change records before calling sudo use malicious.

scenario: The network intrusion detection system raised the alerts below on the internal network over two days. You are triaging them before deciding which become incidents.
stem: Identify the activity behind each IDS alert.
choices: ARP poisoning for an on-path attack
Worm spreading through an SMB vulnerability
Authorized vulnerability scan that the rule should exclude

prompts.label:
[IDS] TLS client fingerprint matches a known C2 framework | 10.2.3.40 → 198.51.100.61:443
server certificate is self-signed with the framework's default issuer name
prompts.why: The TLS fingerprint and default certificate identify the C2 tool even though the traffic is encrypted. The host should be isolated and the destination blocked.

prompts.label:
[IDS] ARP: 10.2.0.1 (default gateway) changed from 00:1a:2b:00:00:01 to 3c:52:82:4f:11:9a
420 unsolicited ARP replies from 10.2.0.88 in 5 minutes
prompts.answer: ARP poisoning for an on-path attack
prompts.why: A host flooding unsolicited ARP replies to claim the gateway's IP address is redirecting neighbors' traffic through itself. Dynamic ARP inspection on the switch stops it.

prompts.label:
[IDS] Exploit attempt for a known SMBv1 remote code execution flaw
source 10.2.6.14 → 61 internal hosts on TCP 445 within 3 minutes
prompts.answer: Worm spreading through an SMB vulnerability
prompts.why: The same exploit fired from one host at many others in minutes is self-propagating malware. Disabling SMBv1, patching and isolating the source host contain it.

prompts.label:
[IDS] SQL injection pattern in URI parameter | 10.2.9.15 → 10.2.20.30:443 at 01:12
10.2.9.15 is the security team's vulnerability scanner; its scan is scheduled 01:00 to 03:00
prompts.answer: Authorized vulnerability scan that the rule should exclude
prompts.why: The alert is technically accurate but comes from the approved scanner during its window. The right response is tuning, such as suppressing this rule for the scanner's address, not an incident.

prompts.label:
[IDS] ICMP echo requests with 1,400-byte high-entropy payloads | 10.2.4.8 → 203.0.113.12
9,000 packets over 2 hours
prompts.why: Normal pings carry small, predictable payloads. Large, random-looking payloads sent steadily to one outside host mean ICMP is being used as a covert channel to move data.

prompts.label:
[IDS] DHCPOFFER from 10.2.0.77, which is not an authorized DHCP server
offered default gateway and DNS server: 10.2.0.77
prompts.why: An unauthorized DHCP server hands out itself as gateway and DNS, which puts it on the path of every client that accepts the lease. DHCP snooping on the switches blocks it.

prompts.label:
[IDS] Cleartext login on Telnet, TCP 23 | 10.2.1.50 → core switch 10.2.0.2
username and password visible in the session
prompts.why: Telnet sends everything, including the login, unencrypted. The switch should allow only SSH for management, and the exposed password should be changed.

takeaway: Triage IDS alerts by what the evidence proves: tool fingerprints mean C2, gateway MAC changes mean ARP poisoning, one exploit hitting many hosts is a worm, and expected scanner traffic calls for tuning rather than an incident.

scenario: Brightwater Supply (brightwater.com) sends mail only from its own gateway at 203.0.113.25 and through a marketing platform that lists its sending servers at _spf.mailer.example. Every message is DKIM signed with d=brightwater.com. The records below have been live for a month, and the DMARC reports show that only those two sources send mail as brightwater.com.
exhibit:
brightwater.com.                  TXT  "v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.25 include:_spf.mailer.example -all"
sel1._domainkey.brightwater.com.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8A..."
_dmarc.brightwater.com.           TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@brightwater.com; adkim=s; aspf=s"
stem: Choose what each part of the records does, and the change that meets each new requirement.

prompts.label: -all at the end of the SPF record
prompts.answer: Mail from any server not listed fails SPF
prompts.why: -all is a hard fail: a server that matches none of the earlier mechanisms is not authorized. ~all would be a soft fail and ?all neutral, and +all would authorize everyone.
choices: Mail from unlisted servers soft fails and is accepted but marked
SPF makes no claim about servers that are not listed
Every server on the internet is authorized
Mail from any server not listed fails SPF

prompts.label: include:_spf.mailer.example
prompts.answer: Authorizes the servers listed in the marketing platform's own SPF record
prompts.why: An include makes receivers evaluate the other domain's SPF record and pass the message if the sender matches it, so the platform can change its servers without Brightwater editing DNS. It does nothing to DKIM, DMARC or routing.
choices: Sends a copy of every message to the marketing platform
Lets the marketing platform sign outgoing mail with Brightwater's own DKIM private key
Authorizes the servers listed in the marketing platform's own SPF record
Exempts the marketing platform's mail from DMARC checks

prompts.label: A ticketing service will start sending as support@brightwater.com and supplies its own SPF include
prompts.answer: Add its include to the existing SPF record, ahead of -all
prompts.why: A domain may publish only one SPF record, so the new include goes into the existing record before -all. Two SPF records make receivers return a permanent error, and +all would let any server on the internet pass.
choices: Publish a second SPF TXT record at brightwater.com for the service
Add its include to the existing SPF record, ahead of -all
Change -all to +all so the new service is never blocked
Add the service's address to the DMARC rua tag

prompts.label: p= in the DKIM record
prompts.answer: The public key receivers use to verify the signature
prompts.why: DKIM publishes only the public key in DNS, and the private key never leaves the signing server. The body hash travels in the message's DKIM-Signature header, and a failure policy is DMARC's job, not DKIM's.
choices: The private key the gateway signs messages with
The public key receivers use to verify the signature
The policy receivers apply when the signature fails to verify
A hash of the message body

prompts.label: sel1 in the DKIM record's name
prompts.answer: A selector telling receivers which published key to fetch
prompts.why: Each DKIM-Signature header carries s=sel1, and receivers look up sel1._domainkey.brightwater.com to find the key. Selectors let a domain publish several keys at once, for example one per sending service or per rotation.
choices: The name of the mail server that originally sent the message
A selector telling receivers which published key to fetch

prompts.label: adkim=s; aspf=s
prompts.answer: The SPF or DKIM domain must exactly match the From domain (strict alignment)
prompts.why: s means strict, so a DKIM signature from news.brightwater.com would not align with a From address at brightwater.com. Relaxed (r, the default) accepts the same organizational domain. DMARC needs SPF or DKIM to pass and align, not both.
choices: Subdomains of the From domain also count as aligned with it (relaxed alignment)
A message must pass both SPF and DKIM to pass DMARC
The SPF or DKIM domain must exactly match the From domain (strict alignment)
Receivers must reject any message that soft fails SPF

prompts.label: rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@brightwater.com
prompts.why: rua receives aggregate XML reports summarizing which servers sent mail as the domain and whether each passed. Copies of individual failing messages (forensic reports) go to the ruf address instead.
choices: Where receivers send copies of individual failing messages
Where users report phishing that impersonates the company
The contact address for the domain's registrar

prompts.label: Monitoring shows only the two approved sources, and spoofed mail must now be refused outright
prompts.why: p=reject tells receivers to refuse mail that fails DMARC instead of delivering it to spam. p=none would only monitor, ~all weakens SPF, and the reports are still needed to spot new legitimate senders.
choices: Change -all to ~all in the SPF record
Remove the rua tag to stop the reports

takeaway: SPF lists who may send (one record per domain, -all hard fails), DKIM publishes a public key under a selector, and DMARC sets alignment, reporting (rua aggregate, ruf forensic) and the policy, moving from none to quarantine to reject.

scenario: An audit compared the identity provider's current settings (exhibit) with the new standard IAM-07, which follows NIST SP 800-63B. IAM-07 requires: a minimum of 15 characters; no composition rules; no scheduled expiration, but a forced change whenever compromise is suspected; rejection of passwords found in breach lists; no reuse of the last 24 passwords; self-service reset only through a factor the user registered earlier, never knowledge-based questions; and lockout after 10 failures in 15 minutes, unlocking automatically after 30 minutes so an attacker cannot keep accounts locked.
exhibit:
Setting                      Current value
Minimum length               8 characters
Composition                  Upper, lower, digit and symbol required
Expiration                   Every 90 days
Breached password check      Off
Password history             Last 5 passwords
Self-service reset           Two security questions
Lockout threshold            3 failures in 15 minutes
Lockout duration             Until an administrator unlocks the account
stem: Choose the new value for each setting so that it meets IAM-07.

prompts.label: Minimum length
prompts.why: IAM-07 sets the minimum at 15 characters. Sixty-four is the length NIST says a system should be able to accept, not a minimum users could live with.

prompts.label: Composition
prompts.why: IAM-07 drops composition rules, as NIST recommends, because they push users toward predictable patterns such as Summer2026!. Requiring two types, or letters only, is still a composition rule.
choices: Upper, lower, digit and symbol required
At least two character types required

prompts.label: Expiration
prompts.answer: No scheduled expiration; force a change when compromise is suspected
prompts.why: Scheduled changes lead to weak, incremented passwords, so IAM-07 removes them. It still requires a forced change on suspected compromise, which rules out never changing the password at all.
choices: No scheduled expiration; force a change when compromise is suspected
Never expire, and never force a change even after a suspected compromise

prompts.label: Breached password check
prompts.answer: Block passwords found in known breach lists
prompts.why: Screening new passwords against breach corpuses stops the passwords attackers try first in credential stuffing and spraying. A warning the user can ignore does not meet the word reject.
choices: Block passwords found in known breach lists
Warn the user about the breach but still allow the password

prompts.label: Password history
prompts.why: IAM-07 forbids reusing any of the last 24 passwords, so the history must remember 24. Five or ten would let a user cycle back to an old password sooner.

prompts.label: Self-service reset
prompts.answer: A code or push from an authenticator the user registered earlier
prompts.why: A previously registered authenticator proves possession of something the attacker lacks. Security questions and employee IDs are knowledge an attacker can research, and emailing a password to any address hands it to whoever asks.
choices: A code or push from an authenticator the user registered earlier
Email a temporary password to whatever address the user types in
Help desk reset after the caller gives their employee ID

prompts.label: Lockout threshold
prompts.why: IAM-07 specifies 10 failures in a 15-minute window, which throttles online guessing while tolerating typos. Three locks out too many legitimate users, and no lockout allows unlimited guessing.

prompts.label: Lockout duration
prompts.why: An automatic unlock after 30 minutes still slows guessing but stops an attacker from keeping every account locked, which manual unlock allows and which also floods the help desk. One minute barely slows guessing.
choices: Until an administrator unlocks the account
Until the user resets the password

takeaway: NIST-style password policy: long minimums, no composition rules, no scheduled expiry but forced change on compromise, breach list screening, and lockouts that unlock automatically so attackers cannot weaponize them.

scenario: A clinic group is creating a cloud storage bucket for scanned patient records. Requirements: no object may ever be publicly readable, even if someone later writes a bad policy; data must stay in the EU but survive the loss of one region; every request must be encrypted in transit; the clinic, not the provider, must control the encryption key, be able to disable it at once and rotate it yearly without re-encrypting files by hand; people who administer the key must not be able to read records; records must be impossible to delete or overwrite for seven years, even by the cloud account's root user; access logs must be kept where the storage administrators cannot alter them.
stem: Choose the setting for each item.

prompts.label: Public access
prompts.answer: Block public access on, overriding any policy or ACL that grants it
prompts.why: Block public access is a guardrail that wins over any later policy or ACL, which is exactly the requirement about a future bad policy. A deny statement in the bucket policy can be edited away by the next mistake.
choices: Off, relying on a bucket policy statement that denies anonymous reads
Block public access on, overriding any policy or ACL that grants it
Off, sharing files only through pre-signed URLs

prompts.label: Location
prompts.answer: An EU region with replication to a second EU region
prompts.why: Keeping both copies in EU regions meets data sovereignty and survives a regional outage. A single region fails the resilience requirement, and any US region or US-spanning location moves data outside the EU.
choices: A single EU region with no replication
A US region with a replica in the EU
An EU region with replication to a second EU region
A multi-region location that spans both the EU and the US

prompts.label: Encryption in transit
prompts.answer: A bucket policy that denies any request not made over TLS
prompts.why: Denying requests that arrive without TLS enforces encryption for every client and path. Default endpoints may still accept plain HTTP, and the provider's internal network is still a transit path that the requirement covers.
choices: A bucket policy that denies any request not made over TLS
TLS from outside the clinic, plain HTTP inside the provider's network
Plain HTTP, because the files are encrypted at rest

prompts.label: Encryption at rest
prompts.answer: A customer-managed key in the provider's KMS, backed by an HSM
prompts.why: A customer-managed KMS key lets the clinic disable it instantly, making the data unreadable, and logs every use. Provider-managed keys cannot be disabled by the customer, and a key in a config file is exposed to anyone who reads the code.
choices: A customer-managed key in the provider's KMS, backed by an HSM
No server-side encryption, because the provider's disks are encrypted
A customer key stored in the application's config file

prompts.label: Key rotation
prompts.answer: Automatic yearly rotation of the key material
prompts.why: KMS rotation creates new key material and keeps the old versions available to decrypt existing objects, so nothing is re-encrypted by hand. Rotating the application's access keys protects credentials, not the encryption key.
choices: Automatic yearly rotation of the key material
No rotation, so older files stay readable
Download every file and re-upload it under a new key each year
Rotate the application's access keys instead

prompts.label: Key policy
prompts.answer: Security team administers it; only the records app's role can encrypt and decrypt
prompts.why: Splitting key administration from key use is separation of duties: the key administrators can manage and disable the key but cannot read records. Letting storage admins or every principal decrypt defeats that.
choices: The storage administrators both administer the key and use it to decrypt the records
Every principal in the account may use the key
Only the root user may use the key
Security team administers it; only the records app's role can encrypt and decrypt

prompts.label: Retention
prompts.answer: Versioning with object lock in compliance mode for seven years
prompts.why: Compliance mode cannot be shortened or removed by any user, including root, until the period ends. Governance mode lets users with a special permission bypass it, a lifecycle rule only schedules deletion, and versioning alone lets versions be deleted.
choices: Versioning with object lock in governance mode for seven years
A lifecycle rule that deletes objects after seven years
Versioning with object lock in compliance mode for seven years

prompts.label: Access logs
prompts.answer: Sent to a separate security account the storage admins cannot modify
prompts.why: Logs held in another account, outside the storage admins' permissions, cannot be quietly altered by the people they record. Logs in the same bucket inherit the same administrators, and disabling them leaves no audit trail.
choices: Written to the same bucket as the records, under the same administrators
Sent to a separate security account the storage admins cannot modify
Kept on the application server's local disk

takeaway: For sensitive cloud data: block public access as a guardrail, keep copies inside the sovereign region, require TLS, use a customer-managed KMS key with rotation and split admin from use, lock records in compliance mode, and log to a separate account.

scenario: A review sets these requirements for the customer portal at portal.example.com: support TLS 1.2 for older partner clients but nothing older; TLS 1.2 cipher suites must give forward secrecy and authenticated encryption; once a browser has visited, it must refuse plain HTTP for a year on the domain and all subdomains; scripts may load only from the portal's own origin, with no inline scripts; no site, including the portal itself, may show portal pages in a frame; browsers must not guess file types; the session cookie must be unreadable to JavaScript, sent only over HTTPS and never sent with cross-site requests; responses must not reveal the server version.
stem: Choose the value for each server directive or response header.

prompts.label: ssl_protocols
prompts.why: This enables exactly TLS 1.2 and 1.3. TLS 1.3 alone would lock out the older partner clients, and anything listing TLS 1.1, 1.0 or SSLv3 allows deprecated protocols.

prompts.label: ssl_ciphers
prompts.why: ECDHE gives forward secrecy, and GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are authenticated encryption. AES256-GCM-SHA384 uses static RSA key exchange (no forward secrecy), the SHA256 and SHA384 suites keep ECDHE but use CBC, which is not AEAD, and RC4 and 3DES are broken.

prompts.label: Strict-Transport-Security
prompts.why: 31,536,000 seconds is one year (86,400 is only one day), and includeSubDomains extends the HTTPS-only rule to every subdomain. Without it subdomains can still be stripped to HTTP, and max-age=0 tells browsers to forget the policy whatever follows it.

prompts.label: Content-Security-Policy
prompts.why: 'self' allows scripts only from the portal's own origin and, without 'unsafe-inline', blocks inline scripts, which is where most injected XSS lives. A wildcard or https: allows scripts from any site.

prompts.label: X-Frame-Options
prompts.why: DENY stops every site, including the portal itself, from framing its pages, which defeats clickjacking. SAMEORIGIN would still let the portal frame its own pages, which the requirement forbids.

prompts.label: X-Content-Type-Options
prompts.why: nosniff tells the browser to trust the declared Content-Type instead of guessing, so an uploaded file cannot be sniffed and run as script. noopen is an unrelated download option for old Internet Explorer.

prompts.label: Set-Cookie: session
prompts.why: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript, Secure keeps it to HTTPS, and Strict never sends it on cross-site requests. Lax still sends it on top-level cross-site navigation, and SameSite=None sends it cross-site by design.

prompts.label: server_tokens
prompts.why: off removes the version number from the Server header and error pages, so scanners cannot match the exact build to known vulnerabilities. on and build both reveal version details.

takeaway: Web hardening set: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 with ECDHE and AEAD suites, HSTS with includeSubDomains, a CSP without unsafe-inline, X-Frame-Options DENY, nosniff, Secure HttpOnly SameSite cookies, and no version banners.

scenario: You are hardening OpenSSH on a Linux database host with a public interface (203.0.113.40) and a management interface (10.10.0.40). Requirements: SSH listens only on the management interface; administrators sign in with keys, never passwords; root may not sign in directly by any method, so admins use their own accounts and sudo; only members of the sshadmins group may connect; each connection allows three authentication attempts and no more; no graphical forwarding; only authenticated encryption (AEAD) ciphers; a legal warning appears before login. The current file is shown in the exhibit.
exhibit:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config (current)
#ListenAddress 0.0.0.0
PermitRootLogin yes
PasswordAuthentication yes
#AllowGroups
MaxAuthTries 6
X11Forwarding yes
Ciphers aes128-cbc,3des-cbc,aes256-ctr
#Banner none
stem: Choose the value for each sshd_config directive.

prompts.label: ListenAddress
prompts.why: Binding to the management address means the daemon never answers on the public interface. 0.0.0.0 listens everywhere, the public address exposes it to the internet, and 127.0.0.1 would lock out remote admins.

prompts.label: PermitRootLogin
prompts.why: no blocks root by every method. prohibit-password still lets root sign in with a key, and forced-commands-only still allows root key logins for set commands, so both break the any method requirement.

prompts.label: PasswordAuthentication
prompts.why: Turning password authentication off leaves key-based login, which defeats password guessing. Keyboard-interactive authentication should be disabled as well, or it can still prompt for a password.

prompts.label: AllowGroups
prompts.why: AllowGroups sshadmins refuses logins from every account outside that group, even one with a valid key. Listing root contradicts the root requirement, and a wildcard or the sudo group lets in more people than intended.

prompts.label: MaxAuthTries
prompts.why: Three matches the requirement exactly. One would break admins whose agents offer several keys, since each key counts as an attempt, and six or ten give a guesser more tries per connection.

prompts.label: X11Forwarding
prompts.why: Graphical forwarding is not needed on a database host, and disabling it removes a channel an attacker could use to reach an admin's X display.

prompts.label: Ciphers
prompts.why: Both are AEAD ciphers that encrypt and authenticate together. CTR mode is still secure with a separate MAC but is not AEAD, CBC modes and 3DES are weak, and arcfour and blowfish are obsolete.

prompts.label: Banner
prompts.why: Banner shows the file's contents before authentication, which is where a legal warning must appear. The message of the day in /etc/motd only shows after login, and none shows nothing.

takeaway: SSH hardening: listen only on the management interface, keys only, PermitRootLogin no (not prohibit-password), AllowGroups for who may connect, few auth tries, no X11 forwarding, AEAD ciphers and a pre-login Banner.

scenario: A security team is reviewing incidents from the past quarter. For each one, it wants the single control that would BEST have prevented it. Some controls in the list are not needed.
stem: Choose the control that BEST prevents each attack.
choices: Input length limits on form fields
Port security allowing one MAC address per port

prompts.label: Typing ' OR '1'='1 into the login form's username field let a tester sign in without a password
prompts.why: Parameterized queries pass input to the database as data, never as part of the SQL statement, so quote characters cannot change the query. A length limit does not stop a payload this short.

prompts.label: A product review contained a script that ran in every visitor's browser and sent their session cookies to the attacker
prompts.why: Stored XSS is stopped by encoding user content for the place it is displayed, so the browser shows the script as text instead of running it. Parameterized queries protect the database, not the page.

prompts.label: Visiting a forum page made logged-in customers' browsers silently submit a new payee to their online banking
prompts.why: This is cross-site request forgery: the browser attaches the bank's cookie automatically. A secret token in each legitimate form proves the request came from the bank's own page, and the forum cannot know it.

prompts.label: On a cafe hotspot, an attacker served regular users the plain HTTP version of the webmail login page and captured their passwords, although the site supports HTTPS
prompts.why: This is SSL stripping. HSTS makes browsers that have visited before (or that ship the site on a preload list) use HTTPS only and refuse the downgrade, so the attacker never gets a plain HTTP session to read.

prompts.label: Forged responses planted in a branch office's caching resolver sent users to a fake banking site at the wrong IP address
prompts.why: DNS cache poisoning works because plain DNS answers are not authenticated. A validating resolver checks the zone's signatures and discards forged records for signed domains instead of caching them.

prompts.label: A laptop on the user VLAN sent gratuitous ARP replies claiming the default gateway's IP address and intercepted its neighbors' traffic
prompts.why: DAI compares ARP replies with the DHCP snooping bindings and drops ones that claim an address the port does not own. Port security limits MAC addresses per port, but the attacker used only its own MAC.

prompts.label: An attacker tried one common password against each of 4,000 accounts once a day for a week and took over 12 accounts
prompts.why: This is password spraying: one guess per account per day never reaches a lockout threshold, so lockout would not trigger. With MFA, a correctly guessed password alone does not grant access.

takeaway: Match the fix to the mechanism: parameterized queries for SQLi, output encoding for XSS, tokens for CSRF, HSTS for stripping, DNSSEC for cache poisoning, DAI for ARP poisoning, and MFA for spraying that dodges lockout.

scenario: The vendor and partner management office is filing the documents for several relationships and must label each one correctly.
stem: Choose the agreement type that BEST fits each situation.

prompts.label: The hosting provider commits to 99.95% monthly uptime and a one-hour response to critical tickets, with service credits when it misses either
prompts.why: Measurable service targets with penalties or credits for missing them are the definition of an SLA.

prompts.label: Two universities state their intention to share a research lab in future years. The document is not legally binding and sets no detailed duties
prompts.why: An MOU records a shared intent to cooperate without binding terms or specific obligations, which is exactly this statement of intent.

prompts.label: A city and its county, having already agreed to share a dispatch center, sign a document setting out each party's specific responsibilities and cost share
prompts.why: An MOA is more formal than an MOU: it spells out the specific terms and responsibilities each party has accepted, where an MOU only states intent. Two public bodies sharing a service are not forming a for-profit partnership, so a BPA does not fit.

prompts.label: Before any project begins, the company and a consulting firm agree on the general terms (payment, liability and dispute resolution) that will govern every future engagement
prompts.why: An MSA sets the standing legal and commercial terms once, so each later project only needs its own scope document under it.

prompts.label: Under that framework, a document defines the next penetration test: its deliverables, timeline, price and acceptance criteria
prompts.why: A SOW (or work order) describes one specific engagement's work, deliverables and schedule, and relies on the MSA for the general terms.

prompts.label: A candidate vendor will share its internal SOC 2 report only if the company promises in writing not to disclose it
prompts.why: An NDA legally binds the recipient to keep shared information confidential, which is what the vendor requires before releasing the report.

prompts.label: Two companies jointly develop and sell a product, and the document sets each partner's investment, profit share and duty to protect shared customer data
prompts.why: A BPA governs a business partnership: each partner's contributions, profits and responsibilities, including security duties for shared data.

takeaway: SLA is measurable service levels, MOU is nonbinding intent, MOA is agreed specific responsibilities, MSA is standing terms, SOW is one project's scope, NDA is confidentiality, BPA is a partnership's shares and duties.
