scenario: A manufacturer uses the classification scheme in the exhibit. The data owners have asked you to label several data sets and decide how two of them are handled.
exhibit:
Label         Meaning                                         Handling
Public        Approved for public release                     No restrictions
Internal      Routine business data, low harm if disclosed    Company systems and staff only
Confidential  Serious harm if disclosed: contracts,           Encrypt at rest and in transit;
              unreleased financial results, source code       need-to-know access
Restricted    Regulated personal data (PII, PHI, card data)   Confidential rules plus MFA, logged
              and trade secrets: severe harm or penalties     access and DLP; never on removable media
stem: Choose the label or handling for each item.

prompts.label: Product brochures already published on the company website
prompts.why: The brochures have been approved and released, so disclosure causes no harm and they need no restrictions.

prompts.label: The cafeteria menu and the internal holiday calendar
prompts.why: Routine business information meant for staff causes little harm if it leaks, but it has not been approved for public release.

prompts.label: Next quarter's financial results, two weeks before they are announced
prompts.why: The scheme lists unreleased financial results as Confidential: early disclosure could cause serious harm, such as insider trading, but this is not regulated personal data or a trade secret.

prompts.label: The same quarterly results, the day after they appear in the public filing
prompts.why: Classification follows the data's life cycle. Once the results are officially released, the owner downgrades them, because keeping them restricted protects nothing.

prompts.label: The never-patented formula for the company's best-selling adhesive
prompts.why: A secret formula is a trade secret, which the scheme places in Restricted. Its value depends entirely on staying secret, unlike patented inventions, which are published.

prompts.label: A spreadsheet that joins the Internal staff directory with each employee's home address and Social Security number
prompts.why: A data set takes the highest label of anything it contains. Adding Social Security numbers makes this regulated personal data, so the whole file is Restricted.

prompts.label: An external auditor needs a copy of a Restricted payment data extract
prompts.answer: Send it through the approved encrypted file transfer service, with access logged
prompts.why: Encrypted, logged transfer to a named recipient meets the Restricted rules. A USB drive is removable media, which the scheme forbids, a password sent in the same email protects nothing, and an anyone-with-the-link share has no access control.
choices: Copy it to an encrypted USB drive and courier it to the auditor
Send it through the approved encrypted file transfer service, with access logged
Email it as a password-protected ZIP file, with the password in the body of the same message
Share it through a file link that anyone with the URL can open

prompts.label: Laptops whose drives held Restricted data are being retired
prompts.answer: Sanitize or destroy the drives and keep a certificate for each one
prompts.why: Sanitization or destruction makes the data unrecoverable, and the certificate documents it. Deleting files, quick formatting or reinstalling the OS leaves the data recoverable with simple tools.
choices: Sanitize or destroy the drives and keep a certificate for each one
Delete the files and empty the recycle bin
Quick format the drives and donate the laptops
Reinstall the operating system from the gold image and reissue the laptops to new interns

takeaway: Label by the harm of disclosure, take the highest label in an aggregated data set, downgrade data when it is officially released, and apply the handling rules of the label through the whole life cycle, including disposal.

scenario: A company has replaced its remote access VPN with a zero trust architecture. Dana, a finance analyst traveling abroad, opens the payroll application from her company laptop, and her request passes through the steps below.
stem: Choose the zero trust component or concept that each step describes.

prompts.label: Dana's laptop and her user account, which together are requesting access to the payroll application
prompts.why: In the data plane, the subject is the user or service requesting access and the system is the device it uses. Together they are what every policy decision is about.

prompts.label: Because the sign-in comes from a new country at an unusual hour, the identity platform requires a stronger MFA step than it would from the office
prompts.why: Adaptive identity changes the authentication required based on context such as location, time, device and behavior, instead of treating every sign-in the same.

prompts.label: A central service weighs her role, her laptop's patch and EDR status and current threat intelligence against policy, and decides to grant access
prompts.why: The policy engine is the control plane component that makes the allow or deny decision. It decides but does not itself open the connection.

prompts.label: Another service acts on that decision: it tells the gateway to open a session for Dana and issues a session-specific credential
prompts.why: The policy administrator carries out the engine's decision by setting up or tearing down the communication path and generating session credentials for the enforcement point.

prompts.label: The gateway in front of the payroll application lets her session through, monitors it and terminates it when instructed
prompts.why: The PEP sits in the data plane between subject and resource and enables, monitors and terminates connections as the control plane instructs.

prompts.label: Her session can reach only the payroll application, not the subnet it runs on or any other server behind the gateway
prompts.why: Granting access to one resource rather than a network limits what a compromised laptop or account could reach, shrinking the threat scope.

prompts.label: Behind the gateway, the payroll application servers and their database exchange traffic without any further checks
prompts.why: The implicit trust zone is the area behind the PEP where entities are trusted without further checks. Zero trust aims to keep these zones as small as possible.

takeaway: Control plane: adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, the policy engine (decides) and the policy administrator (sets up the session). Data plane: the subject/system, the policy enforcement point and the implicit trust zone behind it.

scenario: A laptop with no IP address connects to the user VLAN, VLAN 20. The DHCP server is on a separate server subnet, so the VLAN 20 router interface is configured as a DHCP relay agent (IP helper). The access switches run DHCP snooping, trusting only their uplinks.
stem: Put the events in the order they happen, from connecting to the first lease renewal.

items.text: The laptop broadcasts a DHCPDISCOVER from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255
items.why: With no address and no idea where a server is, the client can only broadcast, and the broadcast stays on VLAN 20.

items.text: The relay agent forwards the message as a unicast to the DHCP server, adding the VLAN 20 interface address
items.why: Routers do not forward broadcasts, so the relay carries the request across subnets and tells the server which scope to use.

items.text: The server answers with a DHCPOFFER of a proposed address, which the relay passes to the laptop
items.why: The offer comes back through the relay and arrives on the trusted uplink, so DHCP snooping lets it through to the client.

items.text: The laptop broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST naming the server and the address it accepts
items.why: The request is broadcast so that any other server that made an offer learns it was not chosen and can release its proposed address.

items.text: The server confirms with a DHCPACK containing the lease time, mask, default gateway and DNS servers
items.why: The acknowledgment completes DORA, and the snooping switch records the laptop's MAC, IP, port and VLAN in its binding table.

items.text: The laptop checks that no other host is using the address, then starts using it
items.why: The client probes the address with ARP and sends a DHCPDECLINE instead if another host answers, which prevents duplicate addresses.

items.text: Halfway through the lease, the laptop unicasts a DHCPREQUEST to the server to renew
items.why: At T1 (50% of the lease) the client renews directly with its server. Only if that fails does it broadcast to rebind at T2 (87.5%).

takeaway: DORA is Discover (broadcast), Offer, Request (broadcast), Acknowledge. A relay agent carries it across subnets, the client checks for conflicts before use, and renewal at T1 is a unicast request.

scenario: A developer accidentally pushed the private key for the public TLS certificate of www.example.com to a public code repository. The public CA can issue a replacement within minutes, and management has asked that the site never be left without a valid certificate while you respond.
stem: Put the response steps in the correct order.

items.text: Confirm the leaked file is the live key by matching its public key to the certificate the site serves
items.why: Analysis comes first: matching the key to the live certificate proves which certificate is compromised before you change anything.

items.text: Generate a new key pair on the web server
items.why: The replacement must use a fresh key. Reissuing a certificate on the leaked key would leave the site exactly as exposed as before.

items.text: Create a CSR from the new key and obtain the replacement certificate from the CA
items.why: The CSR carries only the new public key, and the CA revalidates the domain before signing the replacement.

items.text: Install the replacement certificate and its chain, and confirm the site now serves it
items.why: Switching to the new certificate before revoking the old one keeps the site valid throughout, as management asked.

items.text: Revoke the old certificate with the reason keyCompromise
items.why: Once nothing depends on it, revocation tells clients to distrust anyone presenting the old certificate with the leaked key.

items.text: Check the CA's OCSP responder or CRL to confirm the old certificate shows as revoked
items.why: Verification proves the revocation has been published, which is what actually protects clients that check status.

items.text: Review how the key reached the repository and add secret scanning to the pipeline
items.why: The lessons-learned step fixes the cause so the next secret is caught before it is pushed. It comes last because the leaked key was already public and only replacement and revocation close that risk.

takeaway: Key compromise: confirm, new key pair (never reuse), new CSR and certificate, install, revoke the old one as keyCompromise, verify the revocation, then fix how the key leaked.

scenario: HR wants a cloud payroll provider that will store every employee's bank details and Social Security number. The leading candidate will share its SOC 2 Type II report only after a non-disclosure agreement is signed.
stem: Put the third-party risk management steps in order, from selection to the end of the relationship.

items.text: Document the business need and the data the vendor will hold, and assign it a risk tier
items.why: The data involved sets the risk tier, which decides how deep the assessment must go. Payroll and SSNs put this vendor in the highest tier.

items.text: Sign an NDA with the candidate vendor
items.why: The vendor will not release its SOC 2 report without one, so the NDA must come before the assessment can start.

items.text: Perform due diligence: review the SOC 2 Type II report, a security questionnaire and the vendor's financial stability
items.why: Due diligence checks whether the vendor's controls actually operated over time and whether the company will survive, before any commitment is made.

items.text: Negotiate the contract, including breach notification, a right-to-audit clause and an SLA
items.why: Findings from due diligence shape the security terms, and these clauses are only enforceable if they are in the signed contract.

items.text: Provision least-privilege integration accounts and the payroll data feed
items.why: Access and data flow begin only after the contract is signed, and only with the permissions the service actually needs.

items.text: Monitor the vendor and reassess it every year using its new SOC 2 reports
items.why: Vendor risk changes over time, so ongoing monitoring and periodic reassessment continue for the whole relationship.

items.text: At contract end, revoke all access and get written confirmation that the data was returned or destroyed
items.why: Offboarding closes the life cycle: the vendor keeps no access and no copies of employee data.

takeaway: Third-party risk life cycle: scope and tier, NDA, due diligence, contract with security clauses, least-privilege onboarding, ongoing monitoring, and offboarding with data return or destruction.

scenario: A flood has knocked out the primary data center, and facilities expect at least five days to restore power. The order system's database replicates asynchronously to a warm site, where the application servers are installed but powered off. The DR plan names a coordinator who must authorize any failover.
stem: Put the failover and failback steps in the correct order.

items.text: The DR coordinator assesses the outage against the plan's criteria and declares a disaster
items.why: Nothing moves until the authorized person declares the disaster, which stops teams from failing over piecemeal or for an outage that will soon end.

items.text: Promote the warm site's database replica to read-write, accepting the changes lost since the last replication
items.why: The database comes first because everything depends on it. Asynchronous replication means some recent changes are lost, which the RPO allows for.

items.text: Start the application servers at the warm site and point them at the promoted database
items.why: A warm site has the servers ready but off, and they need the database online before they can serve orders.

items.text: Place a test order against the warm site to confirm the application works end to end
items.why: Testing before customers arrive catches configuration problems while they can still be fixed quietly.

items.text: Switch DNS to the warm site and tell staff and customers that service is restored
items.why: Traffic is redirected only after the site is proven to work, and the announcement follows the switch.

items.text: When the primary site is repaired, replicate the changes made at the warm site back to the primary database
items.why: Orders taken at the warm site exist only there, so the primary must be brought up to date before it can take over again.

items.text: Fail back in a planned window, then restore replication from the primary to the warm site
items.why: Failback is a planned change, and reestablishing normal replication restores the DR capability for next time.

takeaway: Failover: declare, bring up the data tier, then the apps, test, redirect and announce. Failback: resync the primary from the DR site first, then switch back in a planned window and restore replication.

scenario: An online store's hosting contract promises 99.9% availability in each 30-day month. Last month the store had three outages, lasting 20, 25 and 15 minutes. The store works only when both its web tier (99.9% available) and its single database server are up. The database server has an MTBF of 1,990 hours and an MTTR of 10 hours.
stem: Calculate each value.

prompts.label: Downtime allowed per 30-day month at 99.9%
prompts.why: A 30-day month is 30 x 24 x 60 = 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. 8.76 hours is the yearly allowance at 99.9%, and 7.2 hours is 1% of the month.

prompts.label: Availability achieved last month
prompts.why: Total downtime was 20 + 25 + 15 = 60 minutes, so availability was (43,200 minus 60) / 43,200 = 99.86%.

prompts.label: Was the SLA met?
prompts.why: 60 minutes of downtime exceeds the 43.2-minute allowance by 16.8 minutes. The allowance applies to total downtime in the month, not to each outage separately.
choices: Yes, because no single outage exceeded 43.2 minutes

prompts.label: Mean time to repair (MTTR) last month
prompts.why: MTTR is total repair time divided by the number of failures: 60 minutes / 3 outages = 20 minutes.

prompts.label: Database server availability
prompts.why: Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) = 1,990 / 2,000 = 0.995, or 99.5%. Dividing MTTR by MTBF gives the roughly 0.5% unavailability instead.

prompts.label: Store availability with the web tier and database in series
prompts.why: Components that must all be up multiply: 0.999 x 0.995 = 0.994, or 99.40%. Averaging the two (99.70%) is the common mistake, and a chain is always weaker than its weakest link.

prompts.label: Database tier availability after adding a second identical server with automatic failover (failures independent)
prompts.why: Redundant components fail only together, so multiply the unavailabilities: 0.005 x 0.005 = 0.000025, and 1 minus that is 99.9975%.

prompts.label: Can the whole store reach 99.9% if only the database is made redundant?
prompts.answer: No: 0.999 x 0.999975 is about 99.8975%, just under the target
prompts.why: Anything in series with a 99.9% web tier comes out below 99.9%, so the web tier needs redundancy too. Reporting 99.9975% forgets the web tier entirely.
choices: Yes: with a redundant database the store becomes 99.9975% available
Yes: the store becomes exactly 99.9% available
No: 0.999 x 0.999975 is about 99.8975%, just under the target

takeaway: Allowed downtime = period x (1 minus availability). Availability = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). Multiply availabilities in series; multiply unavailabilities for redundant parts in parallel.

scenario: You must divide 10.20.0.0/24 into the subnets in the exhibit. Allocate them in the order shown, starting at 10.20.0.0, placing each subnet immediately after the previous one and using the smallest subnet that fits each need. Every subnet keeps a network and a broadcast address (the routers do not support /31), and the default gateway always takes the first usable address.
exhibit:
Order  Subnet        Hosts needed
1      Sales         100
2      Engineering   50
3      HR            20
4      Management    10
5      Router link   2 (one address per router)
stem: Choose the correct value for each item.

prompts.label: Prefix length
prompts.why: 100 hosts need 7 host bits: a /25 has 128 addresses and 126 usable. A /26 has only 62 usable, and a /24 would use the whole block.

prompts.label: Broadcast address
prompts.why: Sales is 10.20.0.0/25, covering .0 to .127, and the last address is the broadcast. 10.20.0.126 is the last usable host.

prompts.label: Subnet mask
prompts.why: 50 hosts need a /26 (62 usable), and /26 is 255.255.255.192. A /27 (.224) gives only 30 usable hosts.

prompts.label: Network address
prompts.why: Engineering starts right after Sales ends at .127, so it is 10.20.0.128/26, running to .191. .129 is its first usable host, not the network address.

prompts.label: Usable host range
prompts.why: HR needs a /27 (30 usable) starting at .192, so it spans .192 to .223. Excluding the network (.192) and broadcast (.223) addresses leaves .193 to .222.

prompts.label: Prefix length
prompts.why: 10 hosts need a /28, which has 14 usable addresses. A /29 has only 6 usable, and a /27 would use 32 addresses where 16 are enough.

prompts.label: Default gateway
prompts.why: Management is 10.20.0.224/28, right after HR ends at .223. The gateway takes the first usable address, .225, because .224 is the network address.

prompts.label: Network address and prefix
prompts.why: Management ends at .239, so the link starts at .240. A /30 gives exactly two usable addresses, one per router (a /31 would need router support for RFC 3021 point-to-point links, which these routers lack). 10.20.0.236 lies inside Management, and .248 would leave a gap.

takeaway: Pick the prefix from usable hosts (2 to the host bits, minus 2), allocate the largest subnets first, and each network address is the previous broadcast plus one. The gateway is the network address plus one.

scenario: A manufacturer runs a machine controller on Windows 7 because the vendor's software will not run on anything newer. The security team cannot patch it, so they place it on an isolated VLAN, allow access only through a monitored jump host, and alert on any new outbound connection.
stem: Which control type BEST describes this set of measures?

options.text: Compensating, because they stand in for patching that cannot be done
options.why: The recommended control, patching, is impossible, so isolation, a jump host and monitoring together give comparable protection. That substitution is exactly what a compensating control is.

options.text: Corrective, because they repair the risk left by the unpatched system
options.why: Corrective controls act after an incident to restore or fix, such as restoring a backup. Nothing here is responding to an incident that already happened.

options.text: Preventive, because the isolated VLAN stops attacks from reaching it
options.why: The VLAN does prevent some access, but the question asks about the set of measures and why they exist. They exist to replace a control that cannot be applied, which makes compensating the BEST answer.

options.text: Directive, because they instruct staff how to use the legacy system
options.why: Directive controls are policies and instructions that tell people what to do. These are technical measures, not instructions.

takeaway: When a scenario says the normal fix cannot be applied and lists substitutes, the answer is compensating, even if some pieces also look preventive or detective.

scenario: At 2 a.m. a critical vulnerability in the internet-facing load balancer is being actively exploited. The on-call engineer applies the vendor's hotfix immediately, before the change advisory board can meet.
stem: Which of the following should happen NEXT to keep the change compliant with the change management process?

options.text: Document the change and submit it for retroactive review and approval
options.why: Emergency changes are allowed to skip prior approval, but they must still be documented and reviewed after the fact, usually by an emergency CAB, so the record and the configuration baseline stay accurate.

options.text: Roll the hotfix back until the full change advisory board approves it
options.why: Removing the fix would reopen an actively exploited hole. The process exists to manage risk, not to force a dangerous rollback.

options.text: Update the incident response plan to remove the approval requirement
options.why: The approval requirement is part of change management, not incident response, and one emergency does not justify removing a control for every future change.

options.text: Ask the vendor to confirm in writing that the hotfix contains no defects
options.why: Vendor assurances are nice to have but do not replace the organization's own documentation and review of what changed in production.

takeaway: Emergency changes skip the waiting, not the paperwork: document them and get after-the-fact approval.

scenario: A company using a zero trust architecture decides that access to the payroll application must now also require a compliant device and a phishing-resistant MFA method. Nothing about the network path changes.
stem: Which component is MOST directly updated to implement this new requirement?

options.text: The policy engine, which evaluates requests and decides to grant or deny
options.why: The new rule changes the decision logic, and the policy engine is where requests are evaluated against policy and signals such as device health and authentication strength.

options.text: The policy enforcement point, which opens or closes the session
options.why: The enforcement point only carries out the decisions it is given. It does not need to know why access was granted, so the new rule does not live there.

options.text: The policy administrator, which sends session instructions to the gateway
options.why: The administrator translates the engine's decision into instructions for the enforcement point. It does not decide what conditions access requires.

options.text: The implicit trust zone, which sits between the gateway and the application
options.why: The implicit trust zone is the small area behind the enforcement point. It is something zero trust tries to minimize, not a place where policy is configured.

takeaway: Policy engine decides, policy administrator relays, policy enforcement point enforces. New access conditions are decision logic, so they go in the engine.

scenario: An auditor reviews a web application that stores passwords as SHA-256(password + "Acme2024"). The same appended string is used for every user. Two accounts in the sample have identical stored values.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST recommendation?

options.text: Generate a unique random salt per user and hash with a slow algorithm such as Argon2
options.why: A unique salt per user makes identical passwords produce different hashes and forces attackers to crack each one separately, and a deliberately slow algorithm makes each guess expensive. The current design fails on both counts.

options.text: Replace SHA-256 with SHA-512 and keep the shared salt so existing logins still work
options.why: A longer fast hash does not slow attackers meaningfully, and the shared salt still lets one precomputed table attack every account and reveals users who share a password.

options.text: Encrypt the stored hashes with AES-256 using a key kept on the application server
options.why: If the server is compromised the key is right there, and it still leaves the shared salt and fast hash problems untouched.

options.text: Change the shared salt every quarter and force every user to reset their password now
options.why: Rotating a shared salt keeps all its weaknesses: identical passwords still match each other and one table still covers every user until the next rotation.

takeaway: Salts must be unique per password, and password hashing should be slow (bcrypt, PBKDF2, Argon2). Identical stored hashes for two users is the giveaway of a missing or shared salt.

scenario: A purchasing system and a supplier's system exchange orders. Each order carries an HMAC-SHA256 computed with a secret key both companies share. In a dispute, the supplier claims an order for 5,000 units was never sent by the purchaser.
stem: Why can't the HMAC settle the dispute, and what would?

options.text: Both parties share the key, so either could create it; a digital signature would
options.why: An HMAC proves integrity and that the message came from someone holding the shared key, but both parties hold it. A digital signature uses the sender's private key, which only the sender has, and so provides non-repudiation.

options.text: SHA-256 is too weak for legal evidence; switching to HMAC-SHA512 for every message would
options.why: The problem is not the strength of the hash. A stronger HMAC is still created with a key both sides share, so it still cannot prove which side created it.

options.text: HMACs do not detect tampering; adding encryption with AES would
options.why: HMACs do detect tampering, which is their purpose. Encryption adds confidentiality, not proof of who sent the message.

options.text: The HMAC was not timestamped; adding a timestamp field would
options.why: A timestamp shows when, not who. Either party holding the shared key could still compute a valid HMAC over a timestamped message.

takeaway: HMAC gives integrity and authenticity between parties who share a key, but not non-repudiation. Only a private key held by one party (a digital signature) proves who sent it.

scenario: A hospital's database already uses transparent data encryption (TDE) for its data files and backups. A new rule says database administrators must not be able to read patients' Social Security numbers, although they still need to maintain the database.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the new rule?

options.text: Field-level encryption of the SSN column, keyed outside DBA control
options.why: Encrypting just that column, with keys managed outside the DBA role, means administrators see ciphertext in that field while still running and maintaining the database.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the database server with a key sealed in its TPM chip
options.why: Full-disk encryption protects against stolen drives. Once the server is running, everyone with database access, including DBAs, sees plaintext.

options.text: Rotating the TDE key every 90 days and storing it in an HSM
options.why: TDE decrypts data transparently for anyone who can query the database, so rotating or protecting its key does nothing to stop a DBA reading the column.

options.text: TLS 1.3 between the application servers and the database
options.why: TLS protects the data in transit on the network. It does not change what a DBA can see when querying the table directly.

takeaway: Encryption only protects against the people who cannot reach the key or the decrypted view. TDE and disk encryption stop thieves of files and drives; field-level encryption can stop privileged insiders.

scenario: A bank is building an internal certificate authority that will sign thousands of device certificates per hour. Its regulator requires that the CA's private key be generated inside FIPS 140-3 Level 3 hardware and never exist outside it in plaintext.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: A hardware security module attached to the issuing CA
options.why: An HSM generates and uses keys inside tamper-resistant, certified hardware, performs high-volume signing, and never exports private keys in plaintext. That is the textbook fit for a CA.

options.text: A TPM chip on the motherboard of the issuing CA server
options.why: A TPM protects keys for one machine's boot integrity and disk encryption. It is not built for high-throughput signing and is not the expected answer for a CA key at this assurance level.

options.text: A cloud key management service that stores the key encrypted at rest
options.why: A KMS manages keys, but storing a key encrypted at rest is not the same as generating and using it only inside certified tamper-resistant hardware.

options.text: A secure enclave in the administrator's laptop processor
options.why: A secure enclave protects secrets on one device, such as biometric templates. It is not where a production CA performs high-volume signing.

takeaway: TPM protects a single device, secure enclave protects secrets on a phone or laptop, KMS manages keys as a service, and HSM is dedicated tamper-resistant hardware for high-value keys such as a CA's.

scenario: An analytics team needs to join several datasets on customer card number to study purchase patterns. Analysts must never see real card numbers, and only the payments team may map a value back to the real number. The analytics platform must also stay out of PCI DSS scope.
stem: Which technique BEST meets all of these needs?

options.text: Tokenization with a consistent token per card and the vault held by payments
options.why: Each card number maps to the same token, so joins still work, the token has no mathematical link to the card, and only the payments team can look it up in the vault. Systems that hold only tokens can be removed from PCI scope.

options.text: Masking every card number so that only the last four digits are shown
options.why: Many cards share the same last four digits, so joins would merge different customers, and masking cannot be reversed by the payments team.

options.text: Hashing every card number with SHA-256 before loading the datasets
options.why: Card numbers have so little entropy that unsalted hashes can be brute-forced quickly, and a hash cannot be mapped back by the payments team as required.

options.text: Encrypting card numbers with AES and giving the analysts the shared decryption key
options.why: Giving analysts the key lets them see real card numbers, which the requirement forbids, and encrypted card data generally keeps systems in PCI scope.

takeaway: Tokenization swaps sensitive data for a lookup value with no mathematical relationship to it, keeps the original in a vault, and is the classic answer for shrinking PCI scope.

scenario: After a certificate renewal, desktop browsers load the company's site normally, but many Android phones and an API client written in Python fail with "unable to get local issuer certificate". The new certificate is valid, unexpired and issued by a well-known public CA.
stem: What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The web server is not sending the intermediate CA certificate in the chain
options.why: Desktop browsers often fetch or cache missing intermediates, which hides the problem, while many mobile and programmatic clients only trust what the server sends plus their root store. Installing the full chain on the server fixes all of them.

options.text: The certificate was issued without the server's name in the SAN field
options.why: A name mismatch produces a hostname error in every client, including desktop browsers, and the message would be about the name, not the issuer.

options.text: The public CA's root certificate has been revoked and removed by the browser vendors
options.why: A revoked or distrusted root would break desktop browsers too, and they are working normally.

options.text: The server is stapling an OCSP response that has already expired
options.why: A stale stapled response usually causes a revocation-related warning, not an inability to build the chain to a trusted issuer.

takeaway: "Works in Chrome, fails on mobile or in scripts" after a renewal is almost always a missing intermediate certificate on the server.

scenario: A retailer suspects that its customer database may be stolen in the future and wants to know immediately if a stolen copy is ever used, even if the theft itself goes unnoticed.
stem: Which deception technique BEST meets this goal?

options.text: Insert fake customer accounts whose use anywhere triggers an alert
options.why: Planted fake records are honeytokens. They have no legitimate use, so any login, email or card use tied to them proves the data left the building, even if the theft itself was missed.

options.text: Deploy a honeypot server that imitates the production customer database
options.why: A honeypot detects attackers who interact with the decoy server. It says nothing about whether the real database was copied and later used.

options.text: Place a document called customers_full.xlsx on the file server
options.why: A honeyfile alerts when someone opens or copies that file. It does not help if the attacker copies the real database instead.

options.text: Build a honeynet that mirrors the production network segments
options.why: A honeynet studies attacker behavior on decoy systems. It cannot detect later use of data stolen from real systems.

takeaway: Honeypot and honeynet are decoy systems, a honeyfile is a decoy document, and a honeytoken is a decoy piece of data, ideal for detecting use of stolen data.

scenario: An investigation finds that a firewall rule exposing a database was added using the "netadmin" account. Five engineers know that account's password, and the logs show only the account name and a VPN address shared by all of them.
stem: Which change would BEST ensure this question can be answered next time?

options.text: Give each engineer a named account with MFA and retire the shared login
options.why: Accountability depends on tying actions to one person. Unique, strongly authenticated accounts make every log entry attributable.

options.text: Rotate the shared netadmin password monthly and store it in a password vault
options.why: Rotation and vaulting improve password hygiene, but if the account remains shared the logs still cannot say which engineer acted.

options.text: Forward the firewall logs to the SIEM and keep them for seven years
options.why: Longer retention preserves the same unattributable entries. The missing piece is identity, not log storage.

options.text: Require a second engineer to approve every change before it is saved
options.why: Dual control reduces mistakes and fraud, but with a shared account you still cannot prove which two people were involved.

takeaway: No accountability without unique identities. Shared accounts break attribution no matter how good the logging is.

scenario: A company wants to adopt ISO/IEC 27001. Before budgeting, the CISO wants a list of which required controls already exist, which are partly in place, and which are missing, ranked by how far each is from the requirement.
stem: Which activity provides this?

options.text: A gap analysis against the ISO/IEC 27001 requirements
options.why: A gap analysis compares the current state with a target standard and produces exactly this list of missing and partial controls, which then drives the roadmap and budget.

options.text: A quantitative risk assessment that calculates ALE for each asset
options.why: A risk assessment estimates likelihood and impact of threats. It does not map current controls against a specific standard's requirements.

options.text: An external certification audit by an accredited body
options.why: A certification audit judges whether the company already conforms. Doing it before any preparation would just confirm failure, and auditors do not act as consultants.

options.text: A penetration test of the company's internet-facing systems
options.why: A penetration test finds exploitable weaknesses in specific systems. It says little about policies, processes and most of the controls a standard requires.

takeaway: Current state versus a target framework, with a list of what is missing, is a gap analysis.

stem: A security manager is building a control inventory. Which of the following are BOTH technical AND detective controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A network IDS that alerts on known exploit signatures
options.why: It is implemented in technology and it identifies attacks without blocking them, so it is technical and detective.

options.text: File integrity monitoring on web server configuration files
options.why: FIM is software that detects unauthorized changes after they occur, which makes it technical and detective.

options.text: An inline IPS that drops packets matching known exploits
options.why: An IPS is technical, but because it blocks traffic it is preventive, not merely detective.

options.text: A quarterly review of user access rights by department managers
options.why: Access reviews do detect problems, but they are carried out by people as a process, so they are operational (or managerial), not technical.

options.text: CCTV cameras with motion-triggered recording at the loading dock
options.why: Cameras are detective, but they are a physical control, not a technical one in CompTIA's categories.

takeaway: Score every control twice: category (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and type (preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, compensating, directive).

scenario: Bob receives a contract that Alice digitally signed. His software recomputes the document hash, decrypts the signature with the public key it found in Alice's certificate, and the two values do not match.
stem: Which of the following could explain the failure? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The document was altered after Alice signed it
options.why: Any change to the document changes its hash, so it no longer matches the hash recovered from the signature.

options.text: The signature was made with a private key that does not pair with that certificate
options.why: If the signature was created with some other private key, Alice's public key recovers the wrong value. That happens if someone else signed it or Alice used a different key pair.

options.text: Bob's own private key has expired
options.why: Bob's keys are not involved in verifying Alice's signature at all. Verification uses only Alice's public key.

options.text: The document was encrypted with Bob's public key before sending
options.why: Encrypting for confidentiality is separate from signing. Bob would decrypt with his private key first and then verify the signature normally.

options.text: Alice signed the document with her public key instead of her private key
options.why: Signing software signs with the private key. A 'signature' made with a public key is not something that can be produced or verified in this way.

takeaway: A failed signature check means either the content changed or the signer's key does not match the certificate. The verifier only ever uses the signer's public key.

scenario: An approved change will add a new payments service to the server application allow list on 400 servers. The change ticket lists the business owner, test results and a maintenance window.
stem: Which technical implication is MOST important to add to the ticket before implementation?

options.text: Which other services depend on the change and whether any will need a restart
options.why: Allow list changes often require a service or application restart and can break dependent services. Identifying dependencies and restarts is what keeps the maintenance window from turning into an outage.

options.text: The vendor's list of new features included in the payments service
options.why: Feature lists matter to the business, but they are not a technical implication of changing the allow list on 400 servers.

options.text: A note that the change does not need a backout plan because it only adds software
options.why: Every change needs a backout plan. Adding software to an allow list can still break things and may need to be reversed.

options.text: The names of the help desk staff who will answer user calls during the change
options.why: Staffing is useful operational planning, but it does not address the technical risks of modifying the allow list.

takeaway: Change management technical implications include allow and deny lists, restricted activities, downtime, restarts, legacy applications and dependencies.

scenario: A colocation data center has badge readers on every door and a guard at the front desk. Audits keep finding that employees hold the server hall door open for colleagues carrying equipment, so more people enter than badge in.
stem: Which control would MOST effectively enforce one person per badge at the server hall?

options.text: An access control vestibule that admits one badged person at a time
options.why: A vestibule with interlocking doors physically allows only one authenticated person through per badge, so holding the door for someone becomes impossible rather than just against policy.

options.text: A second guard stationed just inside the server hall entrance at all hours
options.why: Another guard adds observation but relies on people enforcing the rule, which is exactly what is already failing with the front-desk guard.

options.text: Signs at the door warning that tailgating is a fireable offense
options.why: Signs are a deterrent or directive control. They do not physically stop a courteous employee from holding the door.

options.text: CCTV that records everyone who enters the server hall
options.why: Cameras are detective: they would show the tailgating after it happens but would not stop it.

takeaway: When the problem is people holding doors, the fix is a control that removes the choice: an access control vestibule.

scenario: After several contractors browsed systems they had no business reason to use, a company configures every server's SSH and RDP login screens to display: "Authorized use only. All activity is monitored and violations will be referred for prosecution." Anyone who continues past the banner can still log in.
stem: Which control category and type BEST describe this banner?

options.text: Technical deterrent
options.why: The banner is delivered by the systems themselves, which makes it technical, and its purpose is to discourage misuse by warning of consequences rather than to stop it.

options.text: Physical deterrent
options.why: Warning signs on a fence or door are physical deterrents, but this message is displayed by software on a login screen, so the category is technical.

options.text: Technical preventive
options.why: A preventive control actually stops the action, like an ACL or MFA. The scenario says anyone who clicks through can continue, so nothing is prevented.

options.text: Managerial directive
options.why: A written acceptable use policy would be managerial and directive, but this is a warning built into the systems that aims to discourage, not a policy document.

takeaway: Warnings that discourage without stopping are deterrent. Classify the category by how the control is delivered: a software login banner is technical, while a printed sign is physical.

scenario: A company is rolling out data loss prevention for email. For the first 30 days the policy is set to log and alert on messages containing card numbers but still deliver them, so the team can tune false positives before switching to block mode.
stem: During the first 30 days, which control type is the DLP system acting as?

options.text: Detective, because it identifies and reports violations without stopping them
options.why: In log-and-alert mode the messages are still delivered, so the control can only discover and report violations after they occur, which is the definition of detective.

options.text: Preventive, because DLP is designed to stop sensitive data from leaving
options.why: That will be true once block mode is enabled, but during the tuning period nothing is stopped, and the type depends on what the control actually does today.

options.text: Compensating, because it temporarily covers for the block mode that has not been enabled yet
options.why: Compensating controls substitute for a required control that cannot be implemented. Here the same control is simply in a staged rollout, not replaced by an alternative.

options.text: Corrective, because the alerts let the team fix the policy rules
options.why: Corrective controls restore systems or limit damage after an incident. Tuning a rule set is configuration work, and the alerts themselves only detect.

takeaway: Classify a control by what it does in its current configuration: a DLP or IPS in monitor mode is detective, and the same product in block mode is preventive.

scenario: An auditor at a 40-person nonprofit finds that the single bookkeeper both creates vendors and approves payments to them. The organization cannot afford a second bookkeeper, so the executive director now reviews a report of every new vendor and every payment each week and signs off on it.
stem: Which control type BEST describes the weekly review?

options.text: Compensating, because it offsets the separation of duties that cannot be implemented
options.why: The ideal control, splitting the duties between two people, is not possible, so an independent review provides comparable assurance in its place. A substitute for a required control is compensating.

options.text: Detective, because the director finds improper payments after they are made
options.why: The review does detect problems after the fact, which is why it works, but the key fact is that it exists to replace separation of duties, making compensating the BEST description.

options.text: Directive, because the executive director instructs the bookkeeper on approvals
options.why: Directive controls tell people what they must do, such as a policy. The review does not instruct anyone; it checks the bookkeeper's completed work.

options.text: Preventive, because the bookkeeper knows that any fraudulent payment will be noticed by the director
options.why: Knowing you will be caught is a deterrent effect, not prevention, and the review happens after payments are already made, so it cannot stop them.

takeaway: When a scenario says the standard control cannot be put in place and describes a substitute, choose compensating, even if the substitute also detects.

scenario: An audit template requires each control to be tagged as technical, managerial, operational or physical. Reviewers rejected an earlier draft because it tagged procedures carried out by staff as managerial.
stem: Which of the following are managerial controls? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An annual risk assessment that ranks threats to the payment system
options.why: Risk assessments are management activities that guide decisions about which controls to fund, so they are managerial (administrative) controls.

options.text: The information security policy approved by the board of directors
options.why: Policies set direction from management and define what must be done, which places them in the managerial category.

options.text: Security guards who check visitor identification at reception
options.why: Guards are people performing a daily security task, an operational control (some frameworks file them under physical), but it is not a management or policy activity.

options.text: Quarterly phishing awareness training delivered by the security team
options.why: Training is carried out by people as part of normal operations, which CompTIA classifies as operational. The policy that requires the training would be managerial.

options.text: A host-based firewall enabled by group policy on every laptop
options.why: A firewall is enforced by technology, so it is a technical control regardless of the management tool used to deploy it.

takeaway: Managerial controls are the decisions and documents that direct security (policies, risk assessments, governance); the people who carry out procedures are operational controls.

scenario: A data center places a sign beside the server hall door that reads: "All visitors must sign the log and be escorted by an employee at all times." The door already has a badge reader, and a separate sign on the perimeter fence warns that trespassers will be prosecuted.
stem: Which control type BEST describes the sign beside the server hall door?

options.text: Directive
options.why: The sign tells people exactly what they are required to do (sign in and stay with an escort). Instructions that direct behavior are directive controls.

options.text: Deterrent
options.why: The fence sign that threatens prosecution is the deterrent. The server hall sign does not warn of consequences; it states a required procedure.

options.text: Preventive
options.why: The badge reader is the preventive control on that door. A sign cannot physically stop a visitor from walking in unescorted.

options.text: Compensating
options.why: Nothing in the scenario is missing or being substituted for, so there is no reason to call the sign a compensating control.

takeaway: A sign that warns of consequences is deterrent; a sign that tells people what they must do is directive. Read the wording of the sign, not just the fact that it is a sign.

scenario: A configuration management tool checks every web server every 15 minutes. If it finds that the TLS settings or the list of enabled modules differ from the approved baseline, it logs the difference and automatically rewrites the files back to the baseline.
stem: Which control type BEST describes the automatic rewrite?

options.text: Corrective
options.why: Putting a system back into its approved state after an unwanted change has already happened is the job of a corrective control.

options.text: Detective
options.why: The comparison and the log entry are detective, but the question asks about the automatic rewrite, which fixes the problem rather than just reporting it.

options.text: Preventive
options.why: The tool acts after the drift has occurred, so it does not prevent the change. A preventive control would remove the ability to edit the files at all.

options.text: Compensating
options.why: The tool is the intended control for configuration drift, not a substitute for some other control that could not be applied.

takeaway: One product can perform several control types, so split it into functions: spotting drift is detective, and restoring the baseline afterward is corrective.

scenario: After hours, a server room is protected by passive infrared motion sensors wired to the building alarm panel. When a sensor trips, the panel notifies the guard desk, and the guard checks the camera feed before responding.
stem: Which category and type BEST describe the motion sensors?

options.text: Physical detective
options.why: The sensors are part of the facility's physical security and they report an intrusion rather than stopping it, which makes them physical and detective.

options.text: Technical detective
options.why: The sensors are electronic, but CompTIA puts building intrusion sensors in the physical category. Technical detective controls watch systems and data, like an IDS or log monitoring.

options.text: Physical preventive
options.why: A locked door or a bollard is physically preventive. A motion sensor cannot stop anyone; it only reveals that someone is there.

options.text: Operational detective
options.why: The guard's response is an operational activity, but the question is about the sensors themselves, which are equipment, not a procedure carried out by people.

takeaway: Facility sensors, cameras and alarms are physical controls even though they are electronic; an IDS, a SIEM and log review are their technical detective counterparts.

scenario: An audit finds that domain administrators can disable Windows audit logging on servers, and there is no way to tell afterward that it happened. Administrators need full rights to do their jobs, so the auditor recommends making sure any such change is noticed within minutes.
stem: Which control BEST satisfies the auditor's recommendation?

options.text: Forward server logs to the SIEM and alert on audit policy changes or logging gaps
options.why: Logs that leave the server immediately cannot be erased by a local admin, and an alert on policy changes or sudden silence reveals the tampering quickly. That is the detective control the finding asks for.

options.text: Remove the right to change audit policy from the domain administrators group
options.why: This is preventive, but the scenario says administrators need full rights, and the recommendation is specifically to notice the change, not to block it.

options.text: Add a policy statement forbidding administrators from disabling audit logging
options.why: A directive policy states the rule but provides no way to notice when someone breaks it, which is the actual gap in the finding.

options.text: Take nightly backups of every server's event logs and store them on an immutable target
options.why: Backups help recover logs that existed, but they would not show that logging was turned off between backups and would not alert anyone within minutes.

takeaway: Match the control type to the finding: when the requirement is to notice something quickly and blocking is not an option, choose a detective control that sends evidence off the host.

scenario: A workstation was infected by malware that ran for two hours before anyone noticed. The security team is reviewing which of its tools and procedures acted after the infection to limit damage and restore normal operations.
stem: Which of the following acted as corrective controls in this incident? (Select TWO.)

options.text: EDR quarantining the malicious executable and killing its processes
options.why: Once the malware is already running, quarantining it and ending its processes reduces the damage and returns the host toward a clean state, which is corrective.

options.text: Reimaging the workstation and restoring the user's files from backup
options.why: Rebuilding the host and restoring data puts the system back into a known good state after the incident, the classic corrective action.

options.text: The SIEM alert that told the analyst about the suspicious process
options.why: The alert discovered the activity but did nothing to fix it, so it is a detective control.

options.text: The email gateway that blocks attachments with executable content
options.why: The gateway stops threats before they reach users, which is preventive, and in this case it did not stop the sample.

options.text: The acceptable use policy that bans installing unapproved software
options.why: A policy that tells users what they may and may not do is directive, not corrective.

takeaway: Corrective controls act after an incident has started to contain it or restore operations (quarantine, reimage, restore); alerts are detective and gateways are preventive.

scenario: A manufacturer lists its ransomware defenses for the board: email filtering, an inline IPS, EDR in block mode and quarterly awareness training. A tabletop exercise reveals that backups are written to a share the domain admin account can delete, and nobody has ever tested a full restore.
stem: Which addition would MOST improve the company's ransomware resilience?

options.text: Immutable or offline backups with regularly tested restores
options.why: The listed controls all prevent or detect. If ransomware gets past them, the company has no reliable corrective control, and protected, tested backups fill that gap.

options.text: A second EDR product so two engines inspect every file on endpoints
options.why: This adds more of the same preventive coverage. It does nothing for the real weakness, which is the inability to recover after a successful attack.

options.text: Monthly phishing simulations in addition to quarterly training sessions
options.why: More frequent training strengthens a preventive control that already exists, but one click can still lead to encryption with no way to recover.

options.text: A SIEM rule that alerts when many files are renamed on a file server
options.why: Earlier detection is useful, but it still leaves the company unable to restore data, and the tabletop showed that recovery is the missing piece.

takeaway: Check that every control type is covered. A stack of preventive and detective tools without a working corrective control, such as tested backups, leaves one failure unrecoverable.

scenario: A junior analyst prepared the control register below for an upcoming audit. The reviewer says exactly one row has the wrong control type.
exhibit:
ID    Control                                          Category    Type
C-01  NGFW blocks inbound SMB from the internet        Technical   Preventive
C-02  Bollards in front of the lobby glass             Physical    Preventive
C-03  SIEM correlation rule for impossible travel      Technical   Detective
C-04  Restore file server from backup after an attack  Technical   Detective
C-05  Board-approved information security policy       Managerial  Directive
C-06  "Premises under video surveillance" signs        Physical    Deterrent
stem: Which row is misclassified, and what should its type be?

options.text: C-04, which should be corrective
options.why: Restoring a server after an attack returns it to normal operation, which is corrective. It does not discover anything, so detective is wrong.

options.text: C-05, which should be preventive
options.why: A policy states what people must do, which CompTIA classifies as directive. It cannot stop anything on its own, so preventive does not fit.

options.text: C-06, which should be detective
options.why: Signs warning of surveillance discourage intruders, a deterrent effect. The cameras would be detective, but the signs themselves detect nothing.

options.text: C-02, which should be deterrent
options.why: Bollards can look intimidating, but their main function is to physically stop a vehicle, which makes them preventive.

takeaway: Ask what the control does when it acts: stop it (preventive), discourage it (deterrent), find it (detective), fix it afterward (corrective), instruct (directive) or substitute (compensating).

scenario: After a vishing attack, help desk agents must now end any password reset call, look up the employee's phone number in the HR system, and call that number back before resetting anything. The written procedure was approved by the IT director, and agents follow it on every call.
stem: Which category BEST describes the call-back step the agents perform?

options.text: Operational, because people carry out the check as part of daily work
options.why: The step is performed by help desk staff following a procedure, which is what CompTIA means by an operational control.

options.text: Managerial, because the IT director approved the procedure that requires it
options.why: Approving a procedure is a managerial activity, but the question asks about the call-back the agents perform, which is a people-run operational task.

options.text: Technical, because the agents look the phone number up in the HR system
options.why: Using a computer during the step does not make it technical. A technical control is enforced by the system itself, such as MFA or an ACL.

options.text: Physical, because it verifies the identity of a person rather than a device
options.why: Physical controls protect facilities and hardware, such as locks and fences. Verifying a caller has nothing to do with physical access.

takeaway: Who or what enforces the control decides its category: management decisions are managerial, people following procedures are operational, and enforcement by systems is technical.

scenario: A water utility sends tank level readings from field sensors to its control center over a cellular link. The readings are not sensitive, but engineers worry that an attacker could alter values in transit to trigger a false overflow response. The sensors have very limited processing power.
stem: Which control MOST directly addresses this concern?

options.text: Add an HMAC to each reading using a key unique to each sensor
options.why: The concern is integrity: detecting any change to a reading. An HMAC lets the control center verify that the value was not altered and came from a holder of that sensor's key, and it is cheap to compute.

options.text: Encrypt each reading with AES in CBC mode before sending it
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality, which the scenario says is not needed. CBC without a MAC does not reliably reveal tampering, since altered ciphertext still decrypts to some value.

options.text: Add a second cellular carrier so readings always have a path
options.why: Redundancy improves availability, but the threat described is altered values, not lost ones.

options.text: Restrict which control center accounts can view the raw readings
options.why: Limiting who can view readings addresses confidentiality and authorization at the control center. It does nothing to detect values changed on the network.

takeaway: Map the worry to CIA first: altered data is integrity (hash, HMAC, signature), exposed data is confidentiality (encryption), and lost access is availability (redundancy, backups).

scenario: A CFO's email approved a $250,000 wire transfer. Weeks later the CFO says she never sent it. The company's mail servers use TLS between each other, and all outbound mail is signed with DKIM for the company domain.
stem: Which control, had it been in place, would MOST strongly prove that the CFO herself sent the approval?

options.text: S/MIME signing with a private key held on the CFO's smart card
options.why: Only the CFO's private key, protected on her smart card, could produce that signature, so a valid S/MIME signature ties the message to her personally. That is non-repudiation.

options.text: DKIM signing with a separate selector for the finance department
options.why: DKIM proves that a message passed through the domain's mail servers, not which person wrote it. Anyone with a mailbox in that department would produce the same signature.

options.text: Mandatory TLS 1.3 for all connections between the company's mail servers
options.why: TLS protects messages in transit between servers but leaves no lasting proof of authorship once the message is delivered.

options.text: Encrypting the message with the treasury team's public key before sending
options.why: Encrypting with the recipient's public key provides confidentiality. Anyone can do that, so it proves nothing about who the sender was.

takeaway: Non-repudiation requires a signature from a key only one person controls. Domain-level signatures (DKIM), transport encryption and shared secrets cannot prove which individual acted.

scenario: A company is deploying 3,000 smart meters that send readings to a cloud API. Each meter must prove its own identity so a single stolen meter can be blocked without affecting the others, and no person is present to type a password.
stem: Which method BEST authenticates the meters?

options.text: Mutual TLS with a unique certificate issued to each meter
options.why: A per-device certificate authenticates each meter as a system, needs no human, and a single meter can be blocked by revoking its certificate.

options.text: One API key embedded in the firmware image for every meter
options.why: A shared key cannot tell meters apart. Revoking it after one meter is stolen would break all 3,000 devices at once.

options.text: A MAC address allow list maintained at the API gateway
options.why: MAC addresses do not cross routers, so a cloud API never sees them, and they are easily spoofed, so they cannot authenticate a device.

options.text: Time-based one-time passwords sent to the field technician
options.why: TOTP authenticates a person. The meters run unattended, so a human factor cannot be supplied for each connection.

takeaway: Authenticating systems means giving each device its own credential, usually a certificate, so one compromised device can be revoked without disturbing the rest.

scenario: During an investigation, the team asks how long a contractor's VPN session lasted and how much data it transferred. The RADIUS server shows only the entries below for that session.
exhibit:
2026-09-14 22:41:07  Access-Request  user=jlee  NAS=vpn-gw1
2026-09-14 22:41:08  Access-Accept   user=jlee  Class=contractors
(no further entries for this session)
stem: Which AAA function is MISSING from this configuration?

options.text: Accounting
options.why: Accounting records what a user did: session start and stop, duration and bytes transferred. The VPN gateway is not sending RADIUS accounting records, so those questions cannot be answered.

options.text: Authorization
options.why: The Access-Accept with a group attribute shows authorization is working, since the contractor was assigned a role. What is missing is the record of the session itself.

options.text: Authentication
options.why: The request and accept entries show the contractor proved their identity successfully, so authentication is present and working.

options.text: Identification
options.why: The username jlee was supplied and logged, so the user was identified. Identification never records session length or data volume.

takeaway: Authentication proves who you are, authorization decides what you may do, and accounting records what you did; session times and byte counts are accounting data.

scenario: A new CISO at a regional insurer is asked to perform a gap analysis of the security program. The insurer has never adopted a framework, and different managers describe the target as "best practice," "whatever the regulator wants" or "what our competitors do."
stem: What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.text: Define the target state by choosing the framework or requirements to measure against
options.why: A gap analysis measures the distance between the current state and a defined target. Without an agreed framework, such as NIST CSF or ISO/IEC 27001, there is nothing to measure against.

options.text: Run a vulnerability scan of all systems to establish the current state
options.why: A scan shows technical weaknesses, but it is only part of the current state, and without a target it does not reveal any gaps.

options.text: Draft a remediation plan and budget for the most obvious missing controls
options.why: Remediation planning is the output of a gap analysis. Doing it first skips the measurement the CISO was asked to perform.

options.text: Hire an external firm to run a full penetration test against the insurer's entire network
options.why: A penetration test shows how an attacker could break in. It does not compare the program to a set of required controls, which is what a gap analysis does.

takeaway: A gap analysis needs a defined target (a framework or set of requirements) and an honest assessment of the current state; the target comes first.

scenario: A company's zero trust design document describes the flow below for a user reaching an internal HR application.
exhibit:
1. User on a laptop requests https://hr.corp.example
2. Component X intercepts the request and asks for a decision
3. Policy engine evaluates identity, device posture and risk: ALLOW
4. Policy administrator tells Component X to open the session
5. Component X forwards traffic to the HR app and keeps watching it
stem: Which zero trust component is Component X?

options.text: Policy enforcement point
options.why: Component X sits in the data path, intercepts the request and allows or blocks traffic according to the decision it receives. That is the policy enforcement point.

options.text: Policy engine
options.why: The engine makes the allow or deny decision in step 3. Component X does not evaluate policy; it acts on the outcome.

options.text: Policy administrator
options.why: The administrator relays the decision and sets up the session in step 4. It instructs Component X, so it cannot be Component X.

options.text: Implicit trust zone
options.why: The implicit trust zone is the area behind the enforcement point, where the HR app sits. It is not an active component that intercepts requests.

takeaway: In zero trust the policy engine decides, the policy administrator carries out the decision by setting up or tearing down the session, and the policy enforcement point in the data path allows or blocks the traffic.

scenario: Twenty minutes into a user's session with a finance application, the EDR agent reports malware on the user's laptop. The policy engine reevaluates the session and changes its decision from allow to deny.
stem: Which component is responsible for instructing the gateway in front of the application to terminate the existing session?

options.text: Policy administrator
options.why: The policy administrator executes the engine's decisions by establishing or shutting down the communication path, sending the command to the enforcement point.

options.text: Policy engine
options.why: The engine made the new deny decision, but it does not command the enforcement point to close sessions; it hands its verdict to the administrator.

options.text: Policy enforcement point
options.why: The gateway is the enforcement point. It will drop the traffic, but it acts on instructions, and the question asks who issues them.

options.text: Subject
options.why: The subject is the user and device requesting access. It is the one being cut off, not the component that orders the cutoff.

takeaway: The policy engine decides, the policy administrator acts on that decision by creating or terminating sessions, and the policy enforcement point is where traffic is actually allowed or dropped.

scenario: A company's identity provider logged the two sign-ins below for the same user within one week. The user entered the correct password both times and holds the same role in both cases.
exhibit:
Sign-in A  Tue 10:02  Location: Chicago (usual)  Device: managed, compliant
           Result: allowed with password and push MFA, full access
Sign-in B  Sat 23:47  Location: new country      Device: unmanaged browser
           Result: phishing-resistant MFA required, then read-only access
stem: Which zero trust concept do these results BEST demonstrate?

options.text: Adaptive identity
options.why: The checks changed with context such as location, device state and time of day. Adjusting authentication strength and access to the risk of each request is adaptive identity.

options.text: Threat scope reduction
options.why: Threat scope reduction limits how much an attacker can reach, for example with microsegmentation. The scenario is about how authentication changes per request.

options.text: Implicit trust zone
options.why: An implicit trust zone is an area where traffic is trusted once inside. The scenario shows trust being reevaluated on every sign-in, which is the opposite.

options.text: Static role-based access control
options.why: A static role would grant the same access both times. Here the result varied with risk signals even though the user and role were the same.

takeaway: Adaptive identity means authentication and access change with real-time context (location, device health, behavior), so the same user can face different requirements on each request.

scenario: In a company's old design, any user connected to the VPN could reach every server on the internal network. The new design places an enforcement gateway in front of each application, so a connected user can reach only the specific applications their policy allows.
stem: Which zero trust goal does the new design MOST directly achieve?

options.text: Threat scope reduction by shrinking the implicit trust zones
options.why: With enforcement close to each application, a stolen account or infected laptop can reach far less. Limiting that blast radius is threat scope reduction, and each implicit trust zone shrinks to a single app.

options.text: Adaptive identity by adjusting authentication to each user's risk
options.why: Nothing in the design changes how users authenticate. The change is about how far a connected user can reach afterward.

options.text: Non-repudiation by tying every request to an individual identity
options.why: Per-application gateways can improve logging, but proving who performed an action is not the goal the redesign describes.

options.text: Defense in depth by adding a second VPN concentrator at the edge
options.why: A second concentrator adds redundancy at the perimeter and does nothing to stop broad access after a user connects.

takeaway: Large implicit trust zones, such as a flat network behind a VPN, give attackers room to move; moving enforcement points closer to resources is how zero trust reduces threat scope.

scenario: An architect is sorting zero trust components into the two planes CompTIA describes so vendor proposals can be compared. The control plane makes and manages access decisions, while the data plane carries and enforces the traffic.
stem: Which of the following belong to the control plane? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Policy engine
options.why: The policy engine evaluates requests against policy and decides whether to allow them, which is control plane work.

options.text: Policy administrator
options.why: The administrator turns decisions into commands for the enforcement points, so it is part of the control plane.

options.text: Adaptive identity
options.why: Adaptive identity shapes how access decisions are made from context and risk, and CompTIA lists it under the control plane.

options.text: Policy enforcement point
options.why: The enforcement point sits in the traffic path and allows or blocks the actual data, which places it in the data plane.

options.text: Subject/system
options.why: The subject or system is the requester whose traffic flows through the data plane. It does not make access decisions.

options.text: Implicit trust zone
options.why: Implicit trust zones are areas of the data plane behind an enforcement point, not decision-making functions.

takeaway: Control plane: adaptive identity, threat scope reduction, policy-driven access control, policy engine and policy administrator. Data plane: implicit trust zones, subject/system and policy enforcement point.

scenario: A bank branch has a glass lobby facing a busy road. After a car crashed through a similar branch nearby, management wants to protect the lobby from vehicles while keeping it fully open and accessible to customers walking in from the sidewalk.
stem: Which control BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Bollards along the curb in front of the lobby
options.why: Bollards stop vehicles while leaving gaps that pedestrians and wheelchairs can pass through, so the lobby stays open to customers.

options.text: A perimeter fence with a staffed pedestrian gate
options.why: A fence would stop vehicles but also funnel customers through a gate that needs staffing, which conflicts with keeping the lobby fully open.

options.text: An access control vestibule at the lobby entrance
options.why: A vestibule controls people entering one at a time. It does nothing against a vehicle and would slow every customer.

options.text: Security film and brighter lighting on the glass
options.why: Film helps glass hold together and lighting deters, but neither stops a car from driving into the lobby.

takeaway: Bollards are the answer when vehicles must be stopped but people must still pass; fences block both, and vestibules control people, not cars.

scenario: A museum wants an alarm the moment anyone lifts a small sculpture from its pedestal. The gallery is open to the public all day, so visitors walk around the pedestal constantly while the alarm is armed.
stem: Which sensor BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: A pressure sensor under the sculpture's base
options.why: A pressure sensor detects a change in weight, so it alarms when the object is lifted and ignores people walking nearby.

options.text: A passive infrared sensor aimed at the pedestal
options.why: Infrared sensors detect the heat of moving bodies. With visitors constantly nearby during open hours, it would alarm all day.

options.text: A microwave motion sensor covering the gallery
options.why: Microwave sensors detect movement across a wide area, even through some walls, so normal visitor traffic would trigger it constantly.

options.text: An ultrasonic sensor mounted above the display
options.why: Ultrasonic sensors detect motion from reflected sound waves. They would react to visitors moving around the pedestal, not specifically to the object being lifted.

takeaway: Pick sensors by what they sense: pressure senses weight, while infrared, microwave and ultrasonic sense movement, so only pressure works when movement around the object is normal.

scenario: A facilities manager is comparing motion sensors for a warehouse. The vendor explains that some sensors send out energy and measure what bounces back, while others only receive energy given off by an intruder.
stem: Which sensors detect motion by emitting a signal and measuring its reflection? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Microwave
options.why: Microwave sensors transmit radio waves and detect changes in the reflected signal, so they are active sensors.

options.text: Ultrasonic
options.why: Ultrasonic sensors emit high-frequency sound and detect changes in the echoes when something moves.

options.text: Passive infrared
options.why: As the name says, it is passive: it only receives heat radiated by a body and does not emit anything.

options.text: Pressure
