options.why: Pressure sensors respond to weight on a surface and do not emit or measure any reflected signal.

options.text: Magnetic door contact
options.why: A door contact detects when a door opens by breaking a magnetic circuit; it does not sense motion with a reflected signal.

takeaway: Microwave and ultrasonic sensors are active (they emit and measure reflections); passive infrared only receives body heat, and pressure sensors respond to weight.

scenario: A distribution center already records its parking lot with high-resolution cameras. After several overnight car break-ins, the footage was too dark to identify anyone, because the lot lights are switched off after 10 p.m. to save energy.
stem: Which control would MOST improve both deterrence and detection in the lot?

options.text: Motion-activated or continuous lighting across the parking lot
options.why: Lighting discourages thieves who prefer darkness and lets the existing cameras capture usable images, improving deterrence and detection at once.

options.text: Replacing the cameras with models that have a higher resolution
options.why: More pixels do not help when there is no light to capture. The scenario says the footage was too dark, not too blurry.

options.text: Contracting a guard to patrol the lot twice each night
options.why: Patrols help, but two visits a night leave long gaps, and the cameras would still capture nothing usable between them.

options.text: Posting signs warning that the lot is under video surveillance
options.why: Signs add some deterrence, but thieves who see a dark lot will doubt them, and the footage would remain unusable.

takeaway: Lighting is both a deterrent and an enabler of detection: cameras only detect what they can see, so dark areas weaken every other physical control.

scenario: A biotech lab's lobby has badge readers, cameras and an access control vestibule. Several times a week, couriers, job candidates and auditors arrive without badges, and employees let them through because nobody is at the desk to check identity or call their host.
stem: Which control BEST addresses this problem?

options.text: A guard at reception who verifies visitors, issues temporary badges and calls hosts
options.why: Unexpected visitors need someone who can check identification, contact hosts and make judgment calls. A guard provides the human decision that readers and cameras cannot.

options.text: Additional cameras covering the vestibule and lobby from more angles
options.why: Cameras record what happens but cannot verify a courier's identity or decide whether to admit them, so employees would keep letting people through.

options.text: A second badge reader inside the vestibule for two-factor entry
options.why: Visitors have no badges at all, so a stronger reader does nothing for the people causing the problem.

options.text: A written policy reminding employees that they must never admit anyone who lacks a badge
options.why: A directive reminder may help, but it leaves visitors with legitimate business stranded with no one to process them, so employees will keep bending the rule.

takeaway: Guards add human judgment: they handle exceptions such as visitors, deliveries and emergencies that badges, cameras and vestibules are not designed to decide.

scenario: A university security research team wants to study how attackers move laterally after an initial compromise: which credentials they steal, which hosts they pivot to and which tools they bring in. The environment must look like a small corporate network.
stem: Which deception technology BEST supports this research?

options.text: A honeynet of several decoy servers and workstations
options.why: Studying lateral movement requires multiple interconnected decoys an attacker can pivot between. A network of honeypots is a honeynet.

options.text: A single high-interaction honeypot on the internet
options.why: One honeypot shows the initial attack well, but with no other systems to reach, the team cannot observe pivoting between hosts.

options.text: Honeyfiles placed on the university's file shares
options.why: Honeyfiles alert when someone opens a decoy file. They reveal snooping on real systems but do not create an environment to watch movement.

options.text: Honeytokens inserted into the student database
options.why: Honeytokens reveal when stolen data or credentials are used. They do not provide systems for attackers to move through.

takeaway: A honeypot is one decoy system, a honeynet is a network of them, a honeyfile is a decoy file and a honeytoken is decoy data or credentials whose use reveals a breach.

scenario: The security team created the file below on a finance share that every employee can read. No legitimate process uses it, and an alert fires whenever anyone opens it.
exhibit:
File:     FS01  finance$/Admin/Wire_Transfer_Passwords_2026.xlsx
Contents: fake bank portal logins (none valid)
Audit:    alert SOC on any read access

ALERT 2026-10-03 14:22  user=CORP\mtorres  host=WS-0442  action=read
stem: Which deception technique is this, and what does the alert MOST likely indicate?

options.text: A honeyfile; someone using that account was browsing for credentials
options.why: A decoy file with an enticing name that no one needs is a honeyfile. Opening it suggests snooping by the user or by an attacker using that account, which should be investigated.

options.text: A honeytoken; the fake bank logins have been used against the bank portal
options.why: The fake logins inside could act as honeytokens, but this alert is a file read, not a login attempt. There is no evidence yet that the credentials were tried.

options.text: A honeypot; an attacker has taken full control of the file server FS01
options.why: A honeypot is an entire decoy system. FS01 is a real production server, and reading one file does not show that the server was compromised.

options.text: A honeynet; the attacker has moved laterally between decoy systems
options.why: A honeynet is a network of decoy systems. This is one decoy file on a production share, and no movement between hosts is shown.

takeaway: Identify deception technology by its form: a decoy file is a honeyfile and decoy data or credentials are honeytokens. The alert tells you what was touched, nothing more.

scenario: A company is deploying a high-interaction honeypot in its screened subnet to learn which exploits attackers use against its web stack. Legal has approved the project, and the honeypot already sends all activity logs to an external collector.
stem: Which configuration is MOST important before the honeypot goes live?

options.text: Restrict its outbound traffic so it cannot reach production systems or attack others
options.why: A high-interaction honeypot is expected to be fully compromised. Without tight egress rules, attackers could use it to pivot into the network or to attack third parties.

options.text: Give it the same domain-joined image and service accounts that the real web servers use
options.why: Realism is useful, but joining it to the domain with real accounts hands attackers credentials and a path into production.

options.text: Publish its address in DNS under a name similar to the main web portal
options.why: Making it easy to find may attract attackers, but it adds no protection, and leaving the decoy uncontained is the bigger risk.

options.text: Patch it fully so attackers can only use previously unknown exploits
options.why: A fully patched honeypot would see few successful attacks and defeat the goal of learning which exploits are being used.

takeaway: Deception systems are meant to be attacked, so contain them: isolate them from production and restrict outbound traffic so a compromised decoy cannot become a launch point.

scenario: During an approved 1 a.m. to 3 a.m. maintenance window, an engineer upgrades the order database. At 2:15 the post-change tests fail, and the vendor's support engineer thinks a fix might take another hour. The ticket includes a backout plan that restores the pre-change snapshot in 20 minutes.
stem: What should the engineer do NEXT?

options.text: Execute the backout plan and restore the pre-change snapshot
options.why: The change failed its tests, and fixing forward would overrun the approved window. The documented backout plan returns the system to a known good state before business hours.

options.text: Keep working with the vendor and extend the window by one hour
options.why: Extending the window without approval puts an untested fix on production after the time stakeholders agreed to, which is exactly what the backout plan is meant to avoid.

options.text: Leave the database as it is and open an incident ticket for the morning
options.why: Leaving a system that failed its tests in production risks an outage when business starts, and the process already provides a safe way back.

options.text: Ask the change advisory board to approve an emergency change for the fix
options.why: Convening the CAB at 2:15 a.m. for an untested fix is slower and riskier than the documented rollback. The fix can be planned as a new change later.

takeaway: When a change fails its tests and the window is closing, follow the backout plan; fixing forward is a new change that needs its own testing and approval.

scenario: A change to replace the TLS certificate and key on the public API gateway passed internal testing and was approved. After implementation, two large partners' integrations failed because their clients pin the gateway's old public key, a dependency nobody had recorded.
stem: Which part of the change management process was MOST clearly inadequate?

options.text: Impact analysis
options.why: Identifying which systems depend on the gateway's key, and what would happen to them, is the job of impact analysis. The pinned partner clients were never considered before approval.

options.text: Backout plan
options.why: A backout plan would help restore service after the failure, but the root problem is that the dependency was never identified before approval.

options.text: Maintenance window
options.why: Choosing a different time would not have helped. The partner clients would have failed whenever the key changed.

options.text: Test results
options.why: The internal tests passed because they did not include the partners' pinned clients. Testing can only cover dependencies that someone has already identified.

takeaway: Impact analysis asks what else depends on the thing being changed (partners, pinned keys, integrations) before approval; testing only covers dependencies someone has identified.

scenario: The infrastructure team scheduled a Friday 8 p.m. change to upgrade the storage array behind the ERP system. The IT manager who owns the array approved it. At 8:30 p.m. the payroll team, which runs its biweekly payroll batch on Friday nights, called to report the ERP was unavailable.
stem: Which step would MOST likely have prevented this conflict?

options.text: Identifying and consulting the stakeholders who depend on the ERP before scheduling
options.why: Payroll is a stakeholder affected by the change. Involving them during planning would have revealed the Friday batch and led to a different window.

options.text: Requiring the storage vendor to provide written test results for the firmware upgrade
options.why: Vendor test results show the upgrade works, but they would not reveal that payroll needs the ERP on Friday nights.

options.text: Writing a more detailed backout plan for restoring the storage array configuration
options.why: A better backout plan shortens the outage but does not prevent scheduling a change during payroll processing.

options.text: Having the CISO rather than the IT manager approve all storage changes
options.why: A different approver who also does not know about payroll would make the same decision. The missing input was from the affected business users.

takeaway: Change approval is only as good as its inputs. Stakeholders are everyone the change affects, and the people who use a system know its busy periods better than the people who run it.

scenario: A change request will disable TLS 1.0 and 1.1 on all internal web servers next month to meet a new policy. A review of server logs shows that a warehouse scanning application, no longer supported by its vendor, still connects to one of those servers using TLS 1.0.
stem: What is the BEST way to handle this before the change is approved?

options.text: Record the legacy app as an impact and plan an exception or isolation for it
options.why: Legacy applications are a known technical implication of changes. Recording the impact and planning an exception with isolation and other compensating controls keeps the warehouse running.

options.text: Proceed on schedule because the policy requires TLS 1.0 to be disabled everywhere
options.why: Following the policy blindly would break the warehouse scanners. Change management exists to find and plan for this kind of conflict before implementation.

options.text: Postpone the entire change until the vendor releases a TLS 1.2 update
options.why: The vendor no longer supports the application, so an update will likely never arrive, and every other server would stay on weak protocols.

options.text: Disable TLS 1.0 on that server first to see whether the scanners still work
options.why: Testing in production on the one server the legacy app depends on is the riskiest place to find out, and the logs already show it needs TLS 1.0.

takeaway: Legacy applications are a classic change implication: find them before approval, then plan an exception, isolation or replacement instead of discovering them in production.

scenario: A change replaced the expiring certificate on a Linux web server at 9 a.m. The engineer copied the new certificate and key into place and closed the ticket. At noon, monitoring still reports the old certificate, so an analyst runs the commands below.
exhibit:
$ openssl x509 -in /etc/nginx/tls/site.crt -noout -enddate
notAfter=Nov 18 23:59:59 2027 GMT

$ openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -enddate
notAfter=Oct 17 23:59:59 2026 GMT
stem: What is the MOST likely reason the old certificate is still being served?

options.text: The nginx service was not reloaded or restarted after the files were replaced
options.why: The file on disk is the new certificate, but the running process still holds the old one in memory. Many services read certificates only at start or reload, a common technical implication of changes.

options.text: The new certificate was issued with a different subject name than the old one
options.why: A name difference would cause a hostname mismatch, not cause the old certificate to keep being served. The live expiry date shows it is still the old certificate.

options.text: Client browsers are caching the old certificate until the cache expires
options.why: The check used openssl s_client, which makes a fresh connection with no browser cache. The server itself is presenting the old certificate.

options.text: The certificate authority has not yet published the new certificate to OCSP
options.why: OCSP reports revocation status. It has no effect on which certificate file a web server presents during the handshake.

takeaway: Many changes only take effect after a service or application restart or reload; the change plan should include that step, its brief downtime and a check of the live result.

scenario: An engineer was approved to apply a security patch to two core switches during a weekend window. While connected, she noticed a newer firmware release and installed it too, since the window had time left. The new firmware changed a default spanning tree setting and caused a network loop on Monday.
stem: Which change management principle did the engineer MOST directly violate?

options.text: Work in a window is restricted to the activities approved in the change request
options.why: Approval covers a specific, analyzed scope. Unapproved extra work, even if well intentioned, skips impact analysis and testing, which is why restricted activities are part of change control.

options.text: Every change must be scheduled within an approved maintenance window
options.why: The firmware was installed during the approved window, so timing was not the problem. The problem was doing work the window had not been approved for.

options.text: Backout plans must be tested in a lab before the change is implemented
options.why: Testing backout plans is good practice, but the outage came from installing unapproved firmware, not from a failed rollback.

options.text: Standard operating procedures must be followed for all routine switch maintenance work
options.why: A firmware upgrade may well have an SOP, but the core failure was performing a change nobody had analyzed or approved, which is a scope violation.

takeaway: An approved change authorizes only its documented scope; extra work during the window, however tempting, is an unapproved change with no impact analysis or backout plan.

scenario: After an outage, engineers find that the production firewall's running configuration differs from the configuration attached to the last approved change ticket. Several administrators have made small edits over recent months, and no one can say what the previous working configuration was.
stem: Which control would BEST prevent this situation in the future?

options.text: Store device configurations in version control with automatic change tracking
options.why: Version control keeps every configuration revision with who changed it and when, so drift is visible, versions can be compared and a known good version can be restored.

options.text: Require administrators to update the network diagram after each edit
options.why: Diagrams show topology, not the line-by-line rule set, and they would not let engineers restore the previous configuration.

options.text: Write a standard operating procedure describing how to edit firewall rules
options.why: An SOP describes how to make edits correctly but keeps no record of past configurations to compare or roll back to.

options.text: Allow firewall changes only during the monthly maintenance window with no exceptions
options.why: Restricting when changes happen does not record what changed, so the same confusion could follow the next window.

takeaway: Version control gives configurations and code a history: who changed what and when, a diff against the last good version and a reliable rollback point.

scenario: You are reviewing the change request below before it goes to the change advisory board.
exhibit:
CHG-20418  Upgrade customer database cluster, PostgreSQL 14 to 16
Owner:              Database team lead (R. Okafor)
Stakeholders:       Portal, billing and reporting teams (notified)
Impact analysis:    Portal read-only for up to 90 minutes
Test results:       Upgrade and app regression passed in staging
Maintenance window: Sat 01:00 to 04:00
Backout plan:       N/A (major version upgrade cannot be downgraded)
stem: Which change should be made to this request BEFORE approval?

options.text: Add a backout plan, such as restoring a verified pre-upgrade snapshot or backup
options.why: An in-place downgrade may be impossible, but a rollback is still possible by restoring data captured before the upgrade. Approving a change with no way back is the biggest risk in this ticket.

options.text: Move the maintenance window to a weekday evening so fewer staff need overtime pay
options.why: Nothing suggests the Saturday window is a problem, and a weekday evening could affect more customers. The window is already reasonable.

options.text: Repeat the staging tests twice more to confirm the results are consistent
options.why: The tests already passed in staging. Repeating them adds little compared with having no way to recover if production behaves differently.

options.text: Reassign ownership from the database team lead to the CIO
options.why: The team lead who runs the system is an appropriate owner. Moving ownership to an executive does not reduce the risk in this ticket.

takeaway: "N/A" is never an acceptable backout plan; when a change cannot be reversed in place, the plan is to restore from a verified pre-change backup or snapshot.

scenario: Three weeks after a change moved internal DNS to two new servers, a responder handling an outage followed the incident runbook and spent 40 minutes troubleshooting the old, decommissioned DNS servers it still listed. The change itself was tested, approved and implemented without problems.
stem: Which step of the change process was MOST likely missed?

options.text: Updating the documentation, diagrams and procedures affected by the change
options.why: A change is not complete until the documents that describe the environment are updated. The runbook still pointed to the old servers, so responders were misled.

options.text: Performing an impact analysis on applications that rely on DNS
options.why: The change was implemented without problems, so dependent applications were handled. The failure was stale documentation discovered weeks later.

options.text: Notifying every affected stakeholder about the maintenance window well ahead of time
options.why: Stakeholder notification matters on the day of the change. It would not update the runbook that responders used three weeks later.

options.text: Testing the backout plan for restoring the original DNS servers
options.why: A backout plan matters if the change fails, and this change succeeded. The problem is that the runbook was never revised afterward.

takeaway: Documentation updates (diagrams, runbooks, policies and procedures) are part of the change itself; stale documents cause errors long after a successful change.

scenario: A team lead is preparing a change request to replace the VPN concentrator at headquarters. The change advisory board rejects any request that lacks the information it needs to judge risk before granting approval.
stem: Which of the following should be included in the request BEFORE the board reviews it? (Select THREE.)

options.text: An impact analysis of the users and services affected during the cutover
options.why: The board needs to know who and what will be affected, and for how long, to judge whether the risk is acceptable.

options.text: A backout plan for returning to the old concentrator if the cutover fails
options.why: A tested way back is a core approval requirement, since it limits the damage if the change goes wrong.

options.text: Results from testing the new concentrator's configuration in a lab or staging
options.why: Test results show the change has been validated outside production, which reduces the uncertainty the board must accept.

options.text: An updated network diagram showing the new concentrator in production
options.why: The diagram is updated after the change is implemented, once the real configuration is known. It is a post-change step.

options.text: A lessons learned report from the completed cutover
options.why: Lessons learned can only be written after the change happens, so they cannot be part of the approval request.

options.text: Confirmation from users that remote access worked normally after go-live
options.why: User confirmation is post-implementation validation. It cannot exist before the change is approved and performed.

takeaway: Before approval: owner, stakeholders, impact analysis, test results, backout plan and window. After implementation: validation, documentation and diagram updates and lessons learned.

scenario: A consulting firm's laptops are often left in taxis and airports. Consultants save client files in many places, and applications write temporary files, swap and hibernation data containing client content. The firm wants all of it protected if a laptop is lost while powered off.
stem: Which encryption approach BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Full-disk encryption with a TPM and a preboot PIN
options.why: FDE encrypts the entire drive, including temporary, swap and hibernation files, so nothing is readable from a powered-off laptop. The PIN stops the TPM from unlocking the drive for a thief who simply powers it on.

options.text: File-level encryption of the consultants' Documents folders
options.why: Folder or file encryption leaves temp files, swap and hibernation data, and files saved elsewhere unprotected, which the scenario says contain client content.

options.text: Database encryption for the firm's client management system
options.why: This protects data in one server-side database, not the many files stored on consultants' laptops.

options.text: Encrypting client files in transit with TLS when they are synced
options.why: TLS protects data while it moves over the network. Once stored on the laptop, the files are unencrypted at rest.

takeaway: Full-disk encryption protects everything on a lost device, including files the user never thinks about; file-level encryption protects only the files it is applied to.

scenario: A legal department sends contract drafts to outside counsel by email and cloud links. All company laptops already use full-disk encryption. The general counsel wants each draft to stay encrypted wherever it is copied and to be readable only by the named recipients.
stem: Which approach BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: File-level encryption tied to the identities of the named recipients
options.why: File-level encryption travels with the file, so the draft stays protected in email, cloud storage and on recipients' devices, and only holders of the right keys can open it.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on all laptops used by outside counsel
options.why: FDE only protects data at rest on a particular device. The draft is readable the moment it is attached to an email or uploaded from a running laptop.

options.text: Volume encryption for the department's shared document server
options.why: Volume encryption protects data on that server's disks. Copies sent by email or link leave the volume and lose the protection.

options.text: Enforcing TLS for the mail server and the cloud file sharing service
options.why: Transport encryption only protects the file while it moves. Stored copies in mailboxes and downloads folders are unencrypted.

takeaway: Full-disk, partition and volume encryption protect data where it sits; file and record encryption protect the data itself, wherever it goes.

scenario: A SaaS provider stores all customers' records in one shared database table. A large customer requires that its records be encrypted with a key it controls, so that revoking the key makes only its own data unreadable without affecting any other customer.
stem: Which encryption level BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Record-level encryption with a separate key for each customer
options.why: Encrypting each customer's records with its own key lets one customer revoke access to its data alone, which table, database or volume encryption with a single key cannot do.

options.text: Transparent database encryption with one key for the whole database
options.why: TDE uses one key for all data files, so revoking it would make every customer's data unreadable, not just this customer's.

options.text: Volume encryption on the storage that holds the database files
options.why: Volume encryption protects disks against physical theft but uses one key for everything on the volume, so it cannot separate customers.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on every database server in the cluster
options.why: FDE protects data on stolen drives. Once the server is running, all records are readable, and there is no per-customer key.

takeaway: Choose the encryption level by the boundary you need: device (full-disk), partition or volume, database, or individual records; per-customer keys require record-level encryption.

scenario: A developer proposes protecting 50 GB nightly backup files by encrypting them directly with the company's 4096-bit RSA public key, so that only the security team's private key can restore them. A reviewer says the design is slow and impractical.
stem: Which design BEST achieves the same goal?

options.text: Encrypt the backup with a random AES key, then encrypt that key with the RSA public key
options.why: This hybrid approach uses fast symmetric encryption for the bulk data and asymmetric encryption only for the small key, so only the private key holder can restore.

options.text: Encrypt the backup with RSA using a shorter 2048-bit key so the encryption completes faster
options.why: A shorter RSA key is still far too slow for bulk data, RSA can only encrypt small blocks, and the change weakens the key.

options.text: Hash the backup with SHA-256 and store the digest next to the file
options.why: Hashing provides integrity checking but no confidentiality. Anyone with the backup file could still read it.

options.text: Encrypt the backup with an AES key stored in the same folder as the backup
options.why: AES is the right algorithm for bulk data, but keeping the key next to the encrypted file means anyone who steals the backup can decrypt it.

takeaway: Symmetric encryption handles bulk data and asymmetric encryption protects the symmetric key; TLS, S/MIME and PGP all combine them this way.

scenario: A security team learns that an attacker has been recording a company's encrypted VPN and web traffic for months, hoping to steal the servers' long-term private keys later and decrypt everything retroactively.
stem: Which key exchange approach BEST protects the recorded traffic even if a server's private key is stolen later?

options.text: Ephemeral Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman for every session
options.why: ECDHE creates a fresh key pair for each session and then discards it, so stealing the long-term private key later does not reveal past session keys. That property is perfect forward secrecy.

options.text: RSA key transport using a 4096-bit server key pair
options.why: With RSA key transport the session secret is encrypted with the server's public key, so whoever later steals the private key can decrypt every recorded session.

options.text: A long pre-shared key configured on both ends of the tunnel
options.why: If the session keys are derived only from the pre-shared key, anyone who later obtains it can derive them and decrypt the recordings, so a static key offers no forward secrecy.

options.text: AES-256 in GCM mode for the bulk data of each session
options.why: AES-256-GCM is a strong cipher for data, but it does not decide how session keys are agreed, which is what protects against later key theft.

takeaway: Forward secrecy comes from ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE or ECDHE); key transport with a long-term RSA key lets a future key theft decrypt recorded traffic.

scenario: A medical device maker needs firmware on a low-power insulin pump to sign the dosing reports it sends and to verify signatures on updates. The pump has little memory and a slow processor, and company policy requires security at least equivalent to 3072-bit RSA.
stem: Which signature algorithm BEST fits these constraints?

options.text: ECDSA with the P-256 curve
options.why: A 256-bit elliptic curve key gives security comparable to 3072-bit RSA with much smaller keys and signatures and far less processing to sign, which suits a constrained device.

options.text: RSA with a 1024-bit key
options.why: A 1024-bit RSA key is small but far below the policy's strength requirement and is considered too weak by current standards.

options.text: RSA with a 4096-bit key
options.why: 4096-bit RSA exceeds the policy, but its large keys and signatures need much more memory, and signing each report would be very slow on the pump's processor.

options.text: AES-128 with a key shared by all pumps
options.why: AES is symmetric and cannot produce digital signatures, and a key shared by every pump lets anyone who extracts it forge updates.

takeaway: ECC reaches the same strength as RSA with far shorter keys (256-bit ECC is roughly 3072-bit RSA), which is why it is preferred on mobile and embedded devices.

scenario: A company encrypts engineering design files with keys tied to each engineer. When a senior engineer left suddenly, her encrypted files could not be opened. Leadership now requires a way for authorized staff to recover such data under a dual-control process.
stem: Which solution BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Key escrow, with recovery keys held by a trusted party and released under dual control
options.why: Escrow stores copies of keys, or recovery keys, with a trusted party so the organization can recover data when the key holder is unavailable, and dual control prevents misuse.

options.text: Key stretching, so that engineers can always recover their keys from easily remembered passphrases
options.why: Key stretching makes passwords harder to crack. It does not help when the only person who knows the passphrase has left the company.

options.text: A certificate revocation list that is updated as soon as each engineer leaves
options.why: Revoking a departing engineer's certificate stops its future use but does nothing to recover data encrypted with her key.

options.text: A TPM in each workstation that stores the engineer's private key in hardware
options.why: A TPM protects keys on that one machine but provides no organizational recovery copy. If the machine fails or is wiped, the key is gone.

takeaway: Key escrow keeps recovery copies of keys with a trusted party, usually under dual control, so encrypted data survives a lost key or a departed employee.

scenario: A company wants its Windows laptops' drive encryption key released only if the firmware, boot loader and operating system loader have not been altered, and only on that specific laptop. Users cannot be expected to carry any external device.
stem: Which component BEST provides this?

options.text: A Trusted Platform Module that seals the key to measured boot values
options.why: The TPM is a chip on the laptop that records measurements of each boot component and releases the sealed key only if they match, binding the key to that hardware and that boot state.

options.text: A network-attached hardware security module that stores every laptop's key
options.why: HSMs are dedicated appliances for high-volume key operations such as CA signing. They are not built into laptops and cannot measure each laptop's boot chain.

options.text: A cloud key management service that rotates the disk keys daily
options.why: A KMS manages keys for cloud services. It cannot verify that a particular laptop's firmware and boot loader are unmodified before releasing a key.

options.text: A secure enclave that isolates application code in the processor
options.why: A secure enclave protects sensitive code and data while the system runs, but the requirement is to check the boot chain before the OS loads, which is the TPM's role.

takeaway: TPM: a chip on the motherboard that measures the boot process and seals keys to it. HSM: a dedicated appliance for high-volume key operations. KMS: a key service, often in the cloud.

scenario: A company runs storage buckets, managed databases and message queues in one public cloud. It needs a central way to create encryption keys for these services, rotate them yearly, control which roles may use each key and log every use. It does not want to buy or rack hardware.
stem: Which solution BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: The cloud provider's key management service
options.why: A KMS integrates with the provider's services, creates and rotates keys, controls key use with access policies and logs every operation, all without customer hardware.

options.text: An on-premises HSM cluster in the company's data center
options.why: An HSM offers strong key protection, but it means buying hardware and building integration with each cloud service, which the company wants to avoid.

options.text: The TPM chips in the company's administrator laptops
options.why: TPMs protect keys on individual devices. They cannot centrally manage keys for cloud services or log their use.

options.text: A key escrow agreement with a third-party provider
options.why: Escrow keeps recovery copies of keys. It does not create keys, rotate them, enforce usage policies or log use by cloud services.

takeaway: A KMS is the central service for creating, rotating, authorizing and auditing keys across many services; an HSM is the hardened hardware that may sit underneath it.

scenario: A mobile banking app must store the private key it uses to sign payment approvals so that even malware with full control of the phone's operating system cannot export the key. Each signing operation must require the user's fingerprint.
stem: Which approach BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Generate the key inside the phone's secure enclave, gated by biometric approval
options.why: A secure enclave is a hardware-isolated area: the key is generated and used inside it and never exported, so even a compromised OS can only request signatures, and only after the fingerprint check.

options.text: Store the key in the app's private storage, encrypted with a key derived from the user's PIN
options.why: App storage lives under the operating system. Malware with OS control can read the file and capture the PIN when the user enters it.

options.text: Store the key in the bank's cloud KMS and fetch it at each login
options.why: Downloading the key to the phone exposes it to the compromised OS while it is in use, which defeats the goal.

options.text: Obfuscate the key inside the app's code to make it hard to find
options.why: Obfuscation slows down analysis but does not stop a determined attacker with full OS access from extracting the key.

takeaway: A secure enclave keeps keys in hardware isolated from the main OS, so the key can be used but never extracted; it is the phone-side counterpart to a TPM or HSM.

scenario: A DLP review finds that an engineer emailed 40 vacation photos to a personal account over two weeks. The images open normally, but each is about three times larger than other photos from the same phone. DLP scanned the attachments and found no sensitive keywords.
stem: Which technique MOST likely explains these findings?

options.text: Steganography hiding data inside the image files
options.why: Steganography hides data inside ordinary-looking carrier files. The pictures still display normally, the extra size holds the hidden data and keyword scanning sees only image content.

options.text: Tokenization replacing sensitive data with random values
options.why: Tokenization swaps sensitive values for tokens inside data systems. It would not make photos larger or hide data inside them.

options.text: Data masking that obscured the design documents
options.why: Masking hides parts of data from viewers, such as showing only the last four digits. It is a protection technique, not a way to sneak data out in images.

options.text: Encrypted archives renamed with a .jpg extension
options.why: A renamed archive would not open as a normal photo, and DLP tools commonly flag files whose content does not match the extension.

takeaway: Steganography hides data inside innocent carrier files such as images or audio; files that work normally but are oddly large are a classic sign, and content inspection usually misses it.

scenario: A development team needs a copy of the production customer database for performance testing. Testers must never see real names or Social Security numbers, values must keep a realistic format for the application's validation rules, and nobody will ever need the originals back.
stem: Which technique BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Static data masking that replaces the values with realistic fakes
options.why: Masking permanently substitutes real values with fictitious ones in the same format, which gives testers realistic data with nothing sensitive and no way back to the originals.

options.text: Tokenization with a token vault managed by the security team
options.why: Tokenization would work, but it keeps a reversible mapping the scenario says is not needed, adding a sensitive vault to protect and maintain.

options.text: Encrypting the sensitive columns with AES before the copy is made
options.why: Encrypted values do not match the format the application validates, and anyone with the key could recover the originals.

options.text: Hashing each name and SSN with SHA-256 before loading the copy
options.why: Hashes are long hexadecimal strings that fail format checks, and SSNs have so few possible values that the hashes could be reversed by brute force.

takeaway: Use data masking when realistic but fake data is enough and recovery is never needed; use tokenization when an authorized party must map tokens back to real values.

scenario: A vendor announces that attackers modified its download page for three days, replacing both the installer and the SHA-256 value shown on the page. An administrator downloaded the installer during that period and checked it as shown below.
exhibit:
$ sha256sum agent-installer-5.2.1.pkg
9f2c4e07...d3a71b  agent-installer-5.2.1.pkg

Vendor download page (at time of download):
  SHA-256: 9f2c4e07...d3a71b
stem: What is the BEST way for the administrator to confirm whether the installer is genuine?

options.text: Verify the vendor's code signing signature with its trusted public key
options.why: A signature can only be produced with the vendor's private key, which the attackers did not have. A valid signature proves origin and integrity even though the page and hash were replaced.

options.text: Run sha256sum again on another computer to rule out a local error
options.why: The hash already matches. The problem is that the reference value came from the same compromised page, so recomputing it proves nothing.

options.text: Compute an MD5 hash as well and compare it with the published values
options.why: Any extra hash published on the same altered page is also under the attackers' control, and MD5 is weaker than SHA-256 anyway.

options.text: Scan the installer with antivirus software before running it on servers
options.why: A scan may catch known malware, but a targeted, modified installer could easily pass. It does not prove the file came from the vendor.

takeaway: A hash proves integrity only if the reference value comes from a trusted source; a digital signature proves integrity and origin, because only the private key holder can create it.

scenario: After a breach, a company learns that its user table, which stores salted SHA-256 password hashes, was stolen. Attackers with GPUs can test billions of SHA-256 guesses per second. The team is redesigning password storage.
stem: Which changes would MOST slow down offline cracking of the stored passwords? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Switch to Argon2id with memory-hard settings
options.why: Argon2id is a key stretching function designed to need significant memory and time per guess, which erodes the GPU advantage.

options.text: Use PBKDF2 with several hundred thousand iterations
options.why: PBKDF2 repeats the underlying hash many times per password, so each guess costs the attacker as much as hundreds of thousands of ordinary hashes.

options.text: Replace SHA-256 with SHA-512 for every password hash
options.why: SHA-512 is also a fast general-purpose hash. GPUs compute it nearly as quickly, so cracking speed barely changes.

options.text: Increase the salt length from 16 to 64 bytes
options.why: Salts defeat rainbow tables and identical-hash matching, which 16 bytes already does. A longer salt does not make each guess slower.

options.text: Encrypt the hash column with AES using a key stored on the web server
options.why: An attacker who breached the server also has the key, and once the hashes are decrypted, guessing runs at full speed again.

takeaway: Salting defeats precomputed tables; key stretching (bcrypt, PBKDF2, scrypt, Argon2) makes every guess expensive. Fast hashes like SHA-2 are wrong for passwords even with a salt.

scenario: A software company signs each release with its code signing key. A customer's security team asks what a valid signature on a downloaded release actually proves, so it can decide which other controls it still needs.
stem: Which of the following does a valid digital signature provide? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Integrity, because any change to the file breaks the signature
options.why: The signature is computed over the file's hash, so even a one-bit change causes verification to fail.

options.text: Authentication of origin, because only the signer's private key could create it
options.why: Verifying with the publisher's public key shows that the holder of the matching private key produced the signature.

options.text: Non-repudiation, because the signer cannot plausibly deny having signed it
options.why: Since only the signer controls the private key, the signer cannot credibly claim someone else produced the signature.

options.text: Confidentiality, because the file contents are encrypted with the private key
options.why: Signing does not hide the file. Anyone can read a signed release, and verifying the signature requires only the public key.

options.text: Assurance that the software contains no vulnerabilities or malware
options.why: A signature shows who published the file and that it was not changed, not that the code is safe. Signed malware and buggy signed code both exist.

options.text: Availability, because the signed file can be restored if it is corrupted
options.why: A signature can detect corruption but cannot repair it. Availability comes from redundancy and backups.

takeaway: Digital signatures give integrity, authentication and non-repudiation, but not confidentiality; signing is not encryption, and a signature does not prove the code is safe.

scenario: Five shipping companies want a shared record of container handoffs. No company is willing to let another run the system, every member must be able to verify the full history, and any attempt to change a past entry must be evident to all of them.
stem: Which technology BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: A blockchain ledger replicated across all five companies
options.why: A blockchain links each block to the previous one by hash and replicates the ledger to every member, so no single party controls it and altering history is evident to all.

options.text: A central database hosted by the largest member with audit logging
options.why: Audit logs help, but the host controls both the data and the logs, which the other companies refuse to accept.

options.text: Digitally signed PDF reports emailed to every member each night
options.why: Signatures prove who created each report, but there is no shared, linked history, and a member could quietly issue a conflicting report.

options.text: A hardware security module shared by the five companies
options.why: An HSM protects keys. It does not store a shared transaction history or make changes to past entries evident.

takeaway: A blockchain is a distributed ledger whose blocks are chained by hashes; a public one is an open public ledger anyone can verify. It fits when parties need one tamper-evident history without trusting a single operator.

scenario: On October 14, a contractor's client authentication certificate was revoked at 09:00 after his laptop was stolen. At 15:00 the same day, the VPN gateway still accepts the certificate. The gateway checks revocation using the CA's CRL, and its cached copy shows the fields below.
exhibit:
Certificate Revocation List (CRL):
    Issuer:      CN=Corp Issuing CA 2
    This Update: Oct 14 06:00:00 2026 GMT
    Next Update: Oct 15 06:00:00 2026 GMT
    Revoked Certificates: 212 entries
stem: What is the MOST likely reason the revoked certificate is still accepted, and the BEST fix?

options.text: The gateway uses a CRL cached until the next update; enable OCSP checking
options.why: The cached CRL was issued at 06:00 and is valid until tomorrow, so the 09:00 revocation is not in it. OCSP gives near real-time status for each certificate.

options.text: The certificate was never revoked; reissue the revocation from the CA
options.why: Nothing indicates the revocation failed. The cached list predates it, which fully explains why the gateway has not seen it.

options.text: The CRL has too many entries to load; split the CA into two separate issuing CAs
options.why: 212 entries is a small CRL for any gateway to process. Size does not explain why one recent revocation is missing.

options.text: The gateway needs a wildcard certificate to read the CA's revocation data
options.why: Wildcard certificates cover multiple host names. They have nothing to do with how a gateway obtains revocation information.

takeaway: CRLs are published on a schedule and cached until Next Update, so recent revocations can be missed; OCSP, or OCSP stapling, gives current status for one certificate at a time.

scenario: An auditor exports every certificate trusted by the company's laptops and flags all self-signed certificates for review. One of them is the company's own offline root CA certificate, which signs the issuing CAs that issue employee and server certificates.
stem: How should the root CA's self-signed certificate be handled?

options.text: Keep it, since a root CA certificate is self-signed by design and anchors the chain
options.why: A root has nothing above it to sign it, so it signs itself. Distributing it to managed devices makes it the root of trust for the internal PKI, which is the intended design.

options.text: Replace it with a certificate signed by one of the company's issuing CAs
options.why: The issuing CAs are signed by the root. Having a subordinate sign the root would create a circular chain that cannot establish trust.

options.text: Remove it from the trust store, because self-signed certificates should never be trusted
options.why: Self-signed server certificates are risky because nothing vouches for them, but every root CA, public or private, is self-signed. Removing it would break all internal certificates.

options.text: Ask a public CA to cross-sign it so the root becomes third-party trusted
options.why: Cross-signing is costly and unnecessary when only company devices must trust the internal PKI, and the root certificate itself would remain self-signed.

takeaway: Every root CA certificate is self-signed, and trust comes from deliberately placing it in the trust store. Self-signed end-entity certificates are the ones to avoid in production.

scenario: An administrator generated a CSR on a staging server, sent it to the CA and received the signed certificate. She then generated a new private key on the production server and tried to install the certificate there, but the web server refuses to start. She runs the commands below.
exhibit:
$ openssl x509 -noout -modulus -in www_example_com.crt | openssl sha256
SHA2-256(stdin)= 4be1d0...77c09d
$ openssl rsa -noout -modulus -in /etc/ssl/private/www.key | openssl sha256
SHA2-256(stdin)= 7a3391...02e512
stem: What is the BEST way to resolve the problem?

options.text: Reissue the certificate from a new CSR created with the production server's key
options.why: The certificate contains the public key from the staging CSR, which does not match the production key, as the different modulus hashes show. A new CSR from the production key yields a certificate that matches it.

options.text: Convert the certificate from PEM to DER format before installing it
options.why: Format conversion changes the encoding, not the public key inside. The modulus would still not match the private key.

options.text: Install the CA's intermediate certificate in the server's chain file
options.why: A missing intermediate causes client trust errors, not a server that refuses to start because the key and certificate do not match.

options.text: Generate a self-signed certificate on production to use until the CA sends a new one
options.why: This lets the server start but causes trust warnings for every visitor, and it does nothing to fix the mismatch between the issued certificate and the key.

takeaway: A CSR carries the public key of the key pair it was generated from, so the issued certificate works only with that private key; generate the CSR where the key will live.

scenario: A company installs a certificate for *.example.com on its load balancer. Users report that www.example.com and shop.example.com work, but api.eu.example.com and the bare domain example.com both show name mismatch errors.
stem: What is the BEST way to fix the errors?

options.text: Reissue the certificate with example.com and api.eu.example.com added as SANs
options.why: A wildcard covers exactly one label, so it matches neither the bare domain nor the two-level api.eu name. Listing those names in the Subject Alternative Name field covers them.

options.text: Reissue the certificate as *.*.example.com so it matches every subdomain level
options.why: Public CAs do not issue multi-level wildcards and browsers do not honor them; a wildcard may replace only the single leftmost label.

options.text: Install the root CA certificate on the load balancer so clients trust the chain
options.why: These are name mismatch errors, not trust errors. The chain is fine for www and shop, which use the same certificate.

options.text: Enable OCSP stapling so clients can confirm the certificate is still valid
options.why: Stapling speeds up revocation checks and has no effect on which host names the certificate matches.

takeaway: A wildcard such as *.example.com matches one label only, not the bare domain and not deeper names like a.b.example.com; add those as SAN entries.

scenario: A new certificate was installed on an internal web server, but browsers reject the connection with an error saying the certificate is not valid for this purpose. The server name, validity dates and chain all check out.
exhibit:
Subject: CN=intranet.corp.example.com
Issuer:  CN=Corp Issuing CA 2
Validity: Oct 01 2026 to Oct 01 2027
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name: DNS:intranet.corp.example.com
X509v3 Key Usage: Digital Signature, Key Encipherment
X509v3 Extended Key Usage: TLS Web Client Authentication
stem: What is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The certificate's EKU allows client authentication but not server authentication
options.why: The Extended Key Usage lists only client authentication. A TLS server certificate needs Server Authentication, so browsers refuse it for this purpose.

options.text: The Key Usage field is missing Certificate Sign, which web server certificates require
options.why: Certificate Sign is only for CA certificates that sign other certificates. A web server certificate should not have it.

options.text: The subject alternative name must use a wildcard for internal sites
options.why: The SAN already matches the exact host name, which is valid. Wildcards are optional, never required.

options.text: The issuing CA must be a third-party public CA for browsers to accept it
options.why: Internal CAs are fine when their root is in the managed devices' trust store, and the scenario says the chain checks out.

takeaway: Check the purpose fields: Extended Key Usage must include Server Authentication for a TLS server, Client Authentication for a client and Code Signing for software.

scenario: A developer accidentally pushed the production web server's private key to a public GitHub repository. The key was public for six hours before the commit was removed. The certificate it belongs to is valid for another ten months.
stem: What should the security team do FIRST?

options.text: Revoke the certificate and replace it with one issued for a newly generated key pair
options.why: Anyone who copied the key can impersonate the site until the certificate is revoked, and a new key pair is needed because the old private key must be treated as compromised for good.

options.text: Rewrite the repository's history so that the key no longer appears in any earlier commit
options.why: Cleaning the history is worth doing, but the key may already be copied, and removing it does not stop an attacker from using it.

options.text: Renew the certificate early using a CSR from the same private key
options.why: Renewing with the same key keeps the compromised key in use, so the new certificate would be just as easy to impersonate.

options.text: Enable OCSP stapling on the web server so clients get fresh status
options.why: Stapling delivers revocation status efficiently, but the certificate has not been revoked, so the stapled status would still say good.

takeaway: A leaked private key means revoke the certificate and issue a new one for a new key pair; reusing the key or just deleting the leak leaves impersonation possible.

scenario: Maria needs to email a merger term sheet to Dev. Only Dev may be able to read it, and Dev must be able to prove that it came from Maria and was not altered. Both have S/MIME certificates issued by the corporate CA.
stem: Which combination of keys BEST meets both requirements?

options.text: Maria signs with her private key and encrypts with Dev's public key
options.why: Signing with Maria's private key proves origin and integrity, and encrypting with Dev's public key means only Dev's private key can decrypt the message.

options.text: Maria signs with Dev's public key and encrypts with her private key
options.why: This reverses both roles. A signature needs the signer's private key, and anything encrypted with Maria's private key can be read by anyone with her public key.

options.text: Maria signs with her public key and encrypts with Dev's private key
options.why: Maria never has Dev's private key, and a signature must be made with the signer's private key, not the public one.

options.text: Maria signs with her private key and encrypts with her own public key
options.why: The signature part is right, but only Maria could decrypt a message encrypted with her own public key, so Dev could not read it.

takeaway: Sign with your own private key and encrypt with the recipient's public key; the recipient decrypts with their private key and verifies with your public key.

scenario: A payments company protects card numbers in several systems. The fraud team sometimes needs the original card number back, so the architect is listing which protection methods let an authorized party recover the original value.
stem: Which of the following allow an authorized party to recover the original card number? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Tokenization with a secured token vault
options.why: The vault maps each token back to the real card number, so authorized systems can detokenize when needed.

options.text: Symmetric encryption with a managed key
options.why: Anyone authorized to use the key can decrypt the ciphertext and obtain the original card number.

options.text: Static data masking with random digits
options.why: Masking permanently replaces the value with fake data, and no mapping is kept to recover the original.

options.text: Salted hashing with SHA-256
options.why: Hashing is one-way. Authorized parties can compare values, but they cannot recover the original number from the hash.

options.text: Truncation to the last four digits
options.why: Truncation discards most of the number, so the full value cannot be reconstructed from what is kept.

takeaway: Tokenization and encryption are reversible for authorized parties; masking, truncation and hashing are one-way, which is safer when recovery is never needed.

scenario: Three weeks after a round of layoffs, every server in the finance cluster wipes its data at 00:00 on the first of the month. Forensics finds a scheduled script, created eight months earlier under a database administrator's account, that checks whether that administrator's own account still exists before running the wipe. The administrator was laid off.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes the threat actor and the malware?

options.text: A malicious insider who planted a logic bomb
options.why: The code was planted from inside by someone with legitimate access, and it waited for a condition (the author's account disappearing) before firing. That combination is a malicious insider with a logic bomb.

options.text: A nation-state actor who deployed a wiper worm
options.why: Nothing here spreads on its own, and the trigger tied to one employee's account points to that employee, not to a well-resourced outside group.

options.text: A hacktivist who installed a remote access Trojan
options.why: A RAT gives interactive remote control. This was a dormant script with a trigger condition, and there is no political message or cause.

options.text: An organized crime group running ransomware
options.why: Ransomware encrypts for payment and leaves a ransom note. This simply destroyed data, with no demand and no profit motive.

takeaway: Dormant code waiting for a date or event is a logic bomb, and a trigger tied to a specific employee leaving is the classic insider signature.

scenario: Accounts payable receives an email from a long-standing supplier's real address asking that future payments go to a new bank account. The message continues an existing invoice thread, and it passed SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Two weeks later the supplier says it never sent it.
stem: Which control would MOST likely have prevented the loss?

options.text: Verify bank detail changes by calling the supplier's known number
options.why: The supplier's own mailbox was compromised, so every email check passes. Only verification through a separate, pre-established channel catches a change request that comes from a genuine but hijacked account.

options.text: Set the company's own DMARC policy to reject instead of quarantine for all mail
options.why: DMARC protects against spoofing of the company's own domain. This message came from the supplier's real domain and already passed DMARC.

options.text: Block inbound email that contains links or attachments
options.why: The message needed neither. Business email compromise relies on a convincing request, not on malicious content.

options.text: Require TLS between the company's and the supplier's mail servers
options.why: TLS protects the message in transit. It does nothing about a legitimate mailbox being used by an attacker.

takeaway: When the email is genuinely from the partner's real account (vendor email compromise), technical email authentication passes. Process controls such as out-of-band callback verification are the defense.

scenario: A tester finds that visiting https://app.example/#name= runs script in the browser. The WAF and the server access logs show no sign of the payload, because browsers never send the part after # to the server. The page's JavaScript reads location.hash and writes it into the page with innerHTML.
stem: Which vulnerability is this, and where must it be fixed?

options.text: DOM-based XSS, fixed in the client-side script by using safe text APIs
options.why: The payload never reaches the server; the page's own JavaScript moves untrusted data from the URL fragment into the DOM. The fix is in that script, for example using textContent instead of innerHTML.

options.text: Stored XSS, fixed by sanitizing values before saving them to the database
options.why: Nothing is stored. The payload lives only in the link, and it never reaches the server or the database.

options.text: Reflected XSS, fixed by adding a WAF rule that blocks script tags
options.why: Reflected XSS bounces the payload off the server. Here the server never sees the fragment, which is why the WAF logged nothing and a WAF rule cannot help.

options.text: CSRF, fixed by adding anti-forgery tokens to every form on the page
options.why: CSRF forges a request on the user's behalf. This is script execution in the page, which tokens do not prevent.

takeaway: Reflected: off the server in the response. Stored: saved and served to everyone. DOM-based: entirely in the browser, often from the URL fragment, invisible to the server and WAF.

scenario: A gift card API checks the card balance, then in a separate database call deducts the purchase. A tester sends 40 identical $50 purchases in parallel against a $50 card, and 23 of them succeed.
stem: Which vulnerability did the tester exploit?

options.text: A race condition between the balance check and the deduction
options.why: Parallel requests all pass the check before any deduction lands. This time-of-check to time-of-use gap is fixed by making check and deduct one atomic operation, such as a single conditional update.

options.text: An integer overflow that wraps the balance to a large positive number
options.why: An overflow would need an arithmetic wrap, and repeating the same small request would not trigger one. The issue only appears with concurrency.

options.text: Insecure direct object reference that lets one user spend another's card
options.why: The tester used their own card. The problem is timing, not access to someone else's object.

options.text: A replay attack that resubmits one captured purchase request
options.why: Replaying a request in sequence would fail once the balance hit zero. Success depends on the requests arriving at the same moment.

takeaway: Many simultaneous identical requests that all succeed is the signature of a race condition (TOCTOU). The fix is atomicity, not input validation.

scenario: An employee whose password was leaked receives 30 push notifications from the MFA app at 1 a.m., followed by a text from someone claiming to be IT saying the prompts will stop once one is approved. The employee approves one.
stem: Which change would BEST prevent this attack from succeeding again?

options.text: Require number matching or FIDO2 keys instead of simple push approval
options.why: Number matching makes the user type a code shown on the sign-in screen, which the victim does not have, and FIDO2 cannot be approved remotely at all. Either defeats MFA fatigue.

options.text: Lock the account after five failed password attempts within any ten-minute window
options.why: The attacker already has the correct password, so there are no failed password attempts to count.

options.text: Replace push notifications with one-time codes sent by SMS
options.why: SMS codes can be phished by the same social engineering, or intercepted through SIM swapping, so this weakens rather than fixes MFA.

options.text: Shorten the session lifetime after a successful MFA approval
options.why: A shorter session limits how long the attacker stays in, but they still get in once the push is approved.

takeaway: Push bombing (MFA fatigue) beats simple approve or deny prompts. Number matching or phishing-resistant FIDO2 MFA stops it.

scenario: An attacker steals a forum's user table. Within minutes, most passwords are recovered without any further connection to the forum, because every hash was produced by a single unsalted MD5 pass. Days later, the same email and password pairs are used successfully against a bank's login page.
stem: Which two attacks are described, in order?

options.text: A rainbow table attack, followed by credential stuffing
options.why: Cracking unsalted hashes offline in minutes points to precomputed rainbow tables. Reusing the recovered pairs on another site is credential stuffing.

options.text: Password spraying, followed by a brute force attack
options.why: Spraying is an online attack that tries a few passwords against many accounts. The first attack happened offline against stolen hashes.

options.text: A birthday attack, followed by pass-the-hash
options.why: A birthday attack finds hash collisions, not passwords, and pass-the-hash reuses a hash on the network rather than a password on a website.

options.text: A dictionary attack, followed by password spraying
options.why: Using known pairs on another site is stuffing, not spraying. Spraying does not start from known username and password pairs.

takeaway: Offline plus unsalted plus minutes suggests rainbow tables (beaten by salting). Known pairs replayed on a different service is credential stuffing (beaten by unique passwords and MFA).

scenario: An incident report shows an attacker dumped NTLM hashes from the memory of a help desk workstation where a domain administrator had signed in, then used those hashes to authenticate to servers without cracking them.
stem: Which of the following would MOST directly reduce the chance of this happening again? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Only let domain administrators sign in from dedicated privileged access workstations
options.why: If admin credentials are never entered on ordinary workstations, there is no admin hash in their memory to steal.

options.text: Enable credential protection such as Credential Guard and restrict NTLM use
options.why: Protecting LSASS memory makes hashes much harder to dump, and limiting NTLM removes the protocol that accepts a raw hash as proof of identity.

options.text: Require domain administrator passwords of at least 20 characters
options.why: Pass-the-hash never cracks the password, so its length does not matter once the hash is stolen.

options.text: Add a unique salt to the password hashes stored on the domain controller
options.why: The attacker reused the hash directly, which salting at rest does not prevent, and NTLM authentication does not use salted hashes in that way.

options.text: Force domain administrators to change their password every 30 days
options.why: Rotation shortens how long a stolen hash works, but the attacker used it immediately. It does not stop the theft or reuse.

takeaway: Pass-the-hash is about where privileged credentials are exposed and which protocols accept hashes. Password length, salting and rotation do not stop it.

scenario: EDR shows WINWORD.EXE launching powershell.exe with a long Base64-encoded command, which then loads code into memory. A WMI event subscription relaunches the same command at every logon. Antivirus scans of the disk find nothing malicious.
stem: Which type of malware is this MOST likely to be?

options.text: Fileless malware that lives off the land with PowerShell and WMI
options.why: Encoded PowerShell, code loaded straight into memory and WMI-based persistence, with nothing malicious on disk, are the hallmarks of fileless malware using built-in tools.

options.text: A boot sector virus that loads before the operating system starts
options.why: A boot sector virus modifies the boot record and loads before Windows. Here everything starts from Word after logon.

options.text: A macro virus that copies itself into every Word document on the host
options.why: A macro virus spreads by infecting documents, which a disk scan would find. This activity loads code into memory instead.

options.text: A rootkit that replaces system drivers to hide its own files
options.why: There are no hidden files or replaced drivers to hide. The scan found nothing because nothing was written to disk.

takeaway: Office spawning encoded PowerShell, memory-only payloads and WMI persistence point to fileless malware. Behavior-based EDR and script logging catch it; file scans do not.

scenario: Several Linux web servers show CPU at 98% around the clock, the fans are loud, and response times have tripled. No files have been encrypted or deleted. Each server has a process named kworkerds that makes outbound connections to port 3333.
stem: Which of the following is MOST likely occurring?

options.text: Cryptojacking malware mining cryptocurrency for the attacker
options.why: Constant maximum CPU, a process disguised with a kernel-thread-like name and connections to a mining pool port such as 3333, with no data damage, all point to cryptojacking.

options.text: A distributed denial of service attack against the web application
options.why: A DDoS would show heavy inbound request traffic. Here the load comes from a local process making outbound connections.

options.text: Ransomware that is still encrypting files in the background
options.why: Ransomware generates heavy disk activity and renames or encrypts files. No files have changed.

options.text: A logic bomb waiting for a date before deleting data
options.why: A dormant logic bomb uses almost no resources until it fires. This process is busy all the time.

takeaway: Resource consumption with no damage and outbound connections to a mining pool is cryptojacking; the indicator to remember is unexplained, sustained CPU use.

scenario: A traveler types bank.example into a browser on hotel Wi-Fi. The browser shows http://bank.example with no padlock, although the bank only serves HTTPS. The attacker's machine on the same network had been sending forged ARP replies for the gateway's address.
stem: Which attack is the user experiencing, and what server-side control would BEST have prevented it?

options.text: SSL stripping by an on-path attacker, prevented by HSTS with preloading
options.why: After ARP poisoning put the attacker in the path, they kept the victim on HTTP while talking HTTPS to the bank. HSTS, especially preloaded, makes the browser refuse plain HTTP for that site.

options.text: DNS poisoning of the resolver, prevented by DNSSEC on the bank's zone
options.why: The attacker positioned themselves with ARP, not DNS, and the name still pointed to the real bank. DNSSEC would not stop the downgrade.

options.text: A replay attack against the session, prevented by shorter session lifetimes
options.why: Nothing captured is being resent. The issue is that the connection was never encrypted from the user's side.

options.text: A rogue access point, prevented by WPA3 encryption on the hotel network
options.why: The user was on the real hotel network. WPA3 encrypts over the air but does not stop another client on the same network from poisoning ARP.

takeaway: An HTTP address for a site that only serves HTTPS, plus an on-path position, means SSL stripping. HSTS is the server-side fix.

scenario: A customer viewing invoice 10452 changes the URL to /invoices/10453 and sees another customer's invoice. The application checks that the user is logged in but never checks who owns the invoice.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this flaw?

options.text: Horizontal privilege escalation through an insecure direct object reference
options.why: The user gains access to another user's data at the same privilege level by changing an object identifier the server does not authorize. That is horizontal escalation via IDOR.

options.text: Vertical privilege escalation through a flaw in the site's broken authentication flow
options.why: Vertical escalation gains a higher role, such as admin. Authentication worked fine; authorization of the specific object did not.

options.text: Directory traversal through manipulation of the requested path
options.why: Traversal uses ../ to reach files outside a folder. Here the user simply requested another valid record ID.

options.text: Session hijacking by reusing another customer's session token
options.why: The attacker used their own session. They never touched another user's token.

takeaway: Same role, someone else's data is horizontal escalation; higher role is vertical. Predictable IDs without ownership checks (IDOR) are the usual cause.

scenario: An agency learns that network cards bought through a gray-market reseller contain modified firmware that beacons out when traffic is quiet. The cards passed the agency's acceptance tests and run the expected firmware version string.
stem: Which control would BEST reduce this specific risk on future purchases?

options.text: Buy through authorized channels and verify the firmware signatures
options.why: Hardware supply chain attacks are reduced by buying from vetted sources and verifying firmware integrity cryptographically, because version strings can be faked.

options.text: Run a credentialed vulnerability scan against each card once it is installed
options.why: A scanner looks for known weaknesses in exposed services. It will not reveal a deliberately implanted, quiet firmware backdoor.

options.text: Place the servers that use the cards in a separate VLAN
options.why: Segmentation limits damage after compromise but does nothing to keep tampered hardware out of the environment.

options.text: Require a longer burn-in test before accepting new hardware
options.why: The implant was designed to pass functional testing and wait for quiet periods, so longer testing is unlikely to catch it.

takeaway: Supply chain risk is managed at the source: vetted suppliers, authorized channels and cryptographic verification of firmware, not just functional testing.

scenario: A WIPS reports two problems. In a conference room, an access point plugged into a wall jack is broadcasting "Guest-Fast" with no encryption; facilities says an employee installed it. In the parking lot, a device is broadcasting the corporate SSID "CorpNet" with a stronger signal than the real access points and is not connected to the wired network.
stem: Which of the following correctly labels the two devices?

options.text: The conference room device is a rogue AP; the parking lot device is an evil twin
options.why: Any unauthorized AP attached to the network is a rogue AP. One that imitates the legitimate SSID to lure clients, usually not connected to the real network, is an evil twin.

options.text: The conference room device is an evil twin; the parking lot device is a rogue AP
options.why: This swaps them. The conference room device uses its own name and is wired into the network, while the parking lot device copies the corporate SSID.

options.text: Both devices are evil twins because both are unauthorized
options.why: Being unauthorized makes a device rogue. Only the one copying the legitimate SSID is an evil twin.

options.text: Both devices are rogue APs, and evil twins only exist on Bluetooth
options.why: Evil twins are a Wi-Fi attack. The parking lot device is a textbook evil twin.

takeaway: Rogue AP: any unauthorized access point (often an inside back door). Evil twin: impersonates a legitimate SSID to capture clients.

scenario: A lab instrument runs an operating system that reached end of support three years ago. The vendor will not certify the instrument on a newer OS, and replacing it costs $2 million. The instrument must send results to a server on the lab network.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST way to reduce the risk?

options.text: Isolate it on its own segment that can reach only the results server
options.why: Unsupported systems cannot be patched, so the best risk reduction is isolation with a tightly scoped rule, which shrinks the attack surface to the one flow the business needs.

options.text: Install the latest antivirus product and schedule daily full scans
options.why: Antivirus may not even support the old OS, and it does nothing about the unpatched operating system vulnerabilities.

options.text: Disable automatic updates so that a broken patch cannot ever affect the instrument
options.why: There are no more patches for an unsupported OS, so this changes nothing about the real risk.

options.text: Accept the risk because the instrument is too expensive to replace
options.why: Acceptance without any controls ignores cheap, effective mitigations such as segmentation that are clearly available.

takeaway: End-of-life systems that cannot be replaced get compensating controls: isolation, strict allow rules and monitoring.
