scenario: Users across the company who type the correct address of a payroll site land on a look-alike page. The company's internal recursive resolver returns 203.0.113.50 for the payroll domain, while public resolvers return the real address. Endpoints' hosts files are clean.
stem: Which attack has MOST likely occurred, and what would BEST prevent it?

options.text: DNS cache poisoning of the internal resolver, prevented by DNSSEC validation
options.why: Only the company's resolver hands out the wrong address, so its cache was poisoned. A validating resolver rejects forged answers that lack valid DNSSEC signatures.

options.text: Typosquatting of the payroll domain, prevented by registering similar names
options.why: Users typed the correct name. Typosquatting relies on mistakes in the name.

options.text: ARP poisoning on each user's subnet, prevented by enabling Dynamic ARP Inspection
options.why: ARP poisoning is local to one subnet and would not make the resolver return a different IP address for every user company-wide.

options.text: Domain hijacking at the registrar, prevented by registry lock
options.why: If the domain itself were hijacked, public resolvers would also return the attacker's address. They do not.

takeaway: Wrong answers from one resolver only (public resolvers fine, hosts files clean) point to cache poisoning of that resolver. DNSSEC validation is the fix.

scenario: A building's new smart thermostats arrive with Telnet enabled, a universal default admin password, UPnP turned on and a cloud management portal. They need only to reach the vendor's cloud over HTTPS.
stem: Which of the following hardening steps are MOST important before deployment? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Change the default admin password to a unique strong value per device
options.why: Universal default credentials are exactly what botnets like Mirai log in with. Unique passwords remove that easy entry.

options.text: Disable Telnet and UPnP
options.why: Telnet sends credentials in clear text and UPnP lets devices open firewall ports on their own. Neither is needed for HTTPS to the cloud.

options.text: Place the thermostats on an isolated VLAN allowed only HTTPS to the vendor
options.why: Segmentation with one tight outbound rule limits what a compromised thermostat can reach and matches the only business need.

options.text: Install an endpoint antivirus agent on each thermostat
options.why: Embedded devices rarely support agents, and antivirus does not address the open services and default passwords.

options.text: Rename the thermostats so their model is not obvious on the network
options.why: Renaming is security through obscurity. Scanners fingerprint devices regardless of their names.

options.text: Enable SNMPv1 so the facilities team can monitor them
options.why: SNMPv1 uses clear-text community strings and adds attack surface. It is a hardening step backward.

takeaway: IoT hardening: change defaults, turn off unneeded services, isolate on a segment with least-privilege rules, and keep firmware updated.

scenario: At a trade show, several executives later find that their phones' contact lists and calendar entries appear on a competitor's blog. The phones were left in discoverable Bluetooth mode, and no one clicked a link or installed anything.
stem: Which attack MOST likely occurred?

options.text: Bluesnarfing, which pulls data from a vulnerable Bluetooth device
options.why: Stealing data such as contacts and calendars over Bluetooth, without user interaction, is bluesnarfing.

options.text: Bluejacking, which sends unsolicited messages to nearby devices
options.why: Bluejacking only pushes messages to a device. It does not take data off it.

options.text: An evil twin that captured traffic from the trade show Wi-Fi
options.why: The theft happened over Bluetooth with discoverable phones, not through a Wi-Fi network.

options.text: A watering hole attack on the trade show's mobile app
options.why: No one installed or used an app here, and a watering hole compromises a website the victims visit.

takeaway: Bluejacking sends (annoying), bluesnarfing steals (dangerous). Keep Bluetooth off or non-discoverable in public.

scenario: Engineers at several wind turbine manufacturers are infected after visiting an industry association's website. The site itself is legitimate and correctly spelled, but an attacker added a script that only targets visitors from the manufacturers' IP ranges.
stem: Which attack does this describe?

options.text: A watering hole attack on a site the target group trusts
options.why: Compromising a legitimate site that a specific community visits, and filtering for the intended victims, is a watering hole attack.

options.text: A typosquatting attack using a misspelled association domain
options.why: The domain was the real, correctly spelled one. Typosquatting relies on look-alike names.

options.text: A spear phishing campaign sent to the engineers' inboxes
options.why: Nobody received a message. The victims went to the site on their own.

options.text: A supply chain attack on the turbine manufacturers' vendors
options.why: The association website is not a vendor in the manufacturers' supply chain, and nothing they bought was altered.

takeaway: Watering hole: poison a site the targets already trust and visit, often filtering by visitor IP so only the intended victims are hit.

scenario: Data loss alerts show sales staff uploading customer contracts to a free file-sharing service. The sales director set up the account so the team could share files with clients more easily, and IT was never told. Nobody intended to harm the company.
stem: Which threat actor category BEST fits this situation?

options.text: Shadow IT
options.why: Employees adopting unapproved services to get work done, without IT's knowledge and without malicious intent, is shadow IT.

options.text: Malicious insider
options.why: An insider threat requires intent to harm or steal. These employees were trying to do their jobs.

options.text: Unskilled attacker
options.why: An unskilled attacker is an outsider using borrowed tools to attack. No attacker is involved here.

options.text: Organized crime
options.why: There is no criminal group or profit motive, just an unsanctioned service.

takeaway: Shadow IT is well-meaning use of unapproved technology. The fix is governance and approved alternatives, not treating staff as attackers.

scenario: A packet capture shows a client offering TLS 1.3 and modern cipher suites. Moments later the client reconnects to the same server offering only SSL 3.0, after an on-path device dropped the first connection attempts. The server accepts SSL 3.0.
stem: Which attack is this, and which server-side change BEST prevents it?

options.text: A downgrade attack, prevented by disabling SSL 3.0 and old TLS versions
options.why: Forcing failures until the client falls back to a weak protocol is a downgrade attack (as in POODLE). If the server refuses obsolete versions, there is nothing weak to fall back to.

options.text: A birthday attack, prevented by switching to a longer hash function
options.why: A birthday attack looks for hash collisions. Nothing here involves finding collisions.

options.text: A replay attack, prevented by adding fresh nonces to every TLS handshake message
options.why: TLS handshakes already use fresh random values. The problem is the server agreeing to an obsolete protocol.

options.text: A collision attack, prevented by replacing the server certificate
options.why: The certificate is not the weakness. Any certificate would still be used over SSL 3.0 if the server allows it.

takeaway: Downgrade attacks need the server to accept weak protocols. Disabling obsolete versions and cipher suites removes the target.

scenario: A red team enters a secure office using a badge that the system logged as belonging to the CFO, who was at home that day. Earlier, a tester had stood behind the CFO in a coffee shop line with a backpack. The building uses 125 kHz proximity cards.
stem: Which attack MOST likely gave the red team access?

options.text: RFID cloning of the CFO's low-frequency proximity card
options.why: 125 kHz proximity cards transmit a fixed ID with no encryption, so a concealed reader nearby can copy it to a blank card, which the system then logs as the real owner.

options.text: Tailgating behind the CFO through the secure door
options.why: The CFO was at home, and the access log recorded a badge read, so nobody was followed through the door.

options.text: Shoulder surfing the CFO's PIN at the badge reader
options.why: A PIN alone would not produce a badge read in the CFO's name. The card's ID was copied.

options.text: Dumpster diving for an old badge the CFO had thrown away
options.why: Possible in theory, but the backpack in the coffee line is the planted clue, pointing to covert reading at close range.

takeaway: Old 125 kHz proximity cards can be skimmed and cloned from a short distance. Encrypted smart cards with mutual authentication and MFA at sensitive doors are the fix.

scenario: Point-of-sale terminals run one payment application and nothing else. Attackers have been planting new memory-scraping malware variants that signature antivirus misses for days at a time.
stem: Which mitigation is MOST effective for these terminals?

options.text: Application allow listing so only the approved payment software can run
options.why: On a single-purpose device, default-deny execution blocks every new malware variant, whether or not a signature exists yet.

options.text: Updating antivirus signatures every hour instead of every day
options.why: Faster updates still depend on someone writing a signature first, and the variants are evading that for days.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on each terminal's storage
options.why: Memory scrapers read card data from RAM while the system runs, which disk encryption does not protect.

options.text: A stronger local administrator password on each terminal
options.why: The malware is not logging in with the admin password, so stronger credentials do not stop it from running.

takeaway: For fixed-function systems (POS, kiosks, ICS consoles), application allow listing beats signature-based detection against new malware.

stem: An analyst is reviewing a domain controller after a suspected compromise. Which TWO observations MOST strongly suggest the attacker tried to hide their activity? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The Security event log was cleared at 03:12 and now starts with event ID 1102
options.why: Event 1102 records that the audit log was cleared. Clearing logs in the middle of the night is a classic attempt to erase evidence.

options.text: There are no logon events at all between 01:00 and 04:00 on a busy server
options.why: A busy domain controller always logs authentications. A total gap points to logging being stopped or records being deleted.

options.text: Several user accounts were locked out after failed password attempts
options.why: Lockouts indicate guessing attempts. They are noisy, not an attempt to hide.

options.text: CPU use rose sharply during the nightly backup window
options.why: High load during a scheduled backup is expected and not a sign of concealment.

options.text: A user signed in from a new laptop after a hardware refresh
options.why: A new device after a refresh has an obvious legitimate explanation.

takeaway: Missing logs and cleared logs (event ID 1102) are indicators that someone is covering tracks. Ship logs off the host to a SIEM so they survive.

scenario: A cloud provider issues an urgent advisory: a flaw in its virtual network driver lets code running inside one customer's virtual machine execute commands on the physical host and read memory from other customers' virtual machines.
stem: Which vulnerability does the advisory describe?

options.text: VM escape
options.why: Breaking out of a guest to the hypervisor or host, and from there into other guests, is VM escape, the worst-case virtualization flaw.

options.text: Resource reuse
options.why: Resource reuse exposes leftover data when memory or disk is reassigned without being cleared. Here the attacker actively executes code on the host.

options.text: VM sprawl
options.why: VM sprawl is unmanaged growth of virtual machines, an operational problem, not an exploit.

options.text: Privilege escalation inside the guest
options.why: Escalation within one VM stays inside that VM. Reaching the host and other tenants crosses the isolation boundary, which is escape.

takeaway: VM escape crosses from guest to host; resource reuse leaks leftovers between tenants; sprawl is unmanaged growth.

scenario: A caller tells the help desk he is the regional VP, is at an airport about to board, and needs his MFA device reset to a new phone right now. He knows his employee ID and manager's name, both of which appear on social media. The help desk agent feels pressured.
stem: Which control would BEST stop this attack without blocking legitimate urgent resets?

options.text: Verify identity through a separate channel, such as a callback to the number on file
options.why: Verification that the attacker cannot complete with public information, such as a call to the registered number or approval from a known manager, defeats pretexting while still allowing real resets.

options.text: Ask the caller extra personal questions such as their date of birth and office location
options.why: Knowledge-based questions often use information that is public or easy to research, which is exactly what this caller already exploited.

options.text: Refuse all MFA resets requested over the phone
options.why: This stops the attack but also blocks legitimate users who have lost their phones, which the question rules out.

options.text: Train the help desk to recognize urgency as a social engineering tactic
options.why: Training helps, but under pressure people still make mistakes. A required verification step is a stronger control than awareness alone.

takeaway: Pretexting plus urgency and authority beats knowledge-based checks. Out-of-band verification against pre-registered contact details is the reliable control.

scenario: A ransomware group publishes samples of stolen data on its leak site and demands payment both to decrypt files and to keep the data private. The victim has tested, immutable offline backups.
stem: Which additional control would have MOST reduced the leverage the attackers still have?

options.text: Egress monitoring and DLP to detect and block the bulk upload before encryption
options.why: Backups solve the encryption half. The remaining leverage is the stolen data, and only detecting and stopping the exfiltration, for example with egress monitoring and DLP, addresses that.

options.text: A second set of immutable backups stored in another region with a separate account
options.why: More backups make recovery even more certain, but they do nothing about the data the attackers already copied.

options.text: Shorter recovery time objectives for the file servers
options.why: Faster recovery helps availability, not the threat to publish stolen data.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on all file servers
options.why: The data was read and copied while the servers were running and decrypted, so disk encryption would not have stopped the theft.

takeaway: Double extortion has two levers: encryption (answered by backups) and data theft (answered by exfiltration detection, DLP and encrypting sensitive data in use).

scenario: A company's MDM report shows several unrooted Android phones with an app installed from an APK file shared in a group chat. The app requests accessibility permissions and has been reading on-screen text, including one-time codes.
stem: Which vulnerability allowed the app onto the phones, and what MDM control BEST prevents it?

options.text: Side loading, prevented by blocking installs from unknown sources
options.why: Installing an APK from outside the official store is side loading, which skips store vetting. MDM can block unknown sources so only approved stores or managed apps can install.

options.text: Jailbreaking, prevented by detecting and blocking rooted devices
options.why: The phones were not rooted. Side loading works on standard devices when unknown sources are allowed.

options.text: A zero-day flaw in Android, prevented by forcing the latest OS update
options.why: The user installed the app and granted it permissions, so no unknown flaw was exploited.

options.text: Bluesnarfing, prevented by disabling Bluetooth when not in use
options.why: The app arrived as a file in a chat, not over Bluetooth.

takeaway: Side loading installs apps from outside the official store; jailbreaking or rooting removes OS restrictions. They are different, and MDM controls each separately.

scenario: A software distributor still signs downloads using MD5 digests. A researcher shows two different installers, one clean and one with a backdoor, that produce exactly the same MD5 value, so the signature on the clean one also validates the backdoored one.
stem: Which attack has the researcher demonstrated?

options.text: A collision attack against the hash function
options.why: Two different inputs producing the same digest is a collision. Because the signature covers the digest, it validates both files, which is why MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer acceptable for signing.

options.text: A downgrade attack that forced the use of an older algorithm
options.why: Nothing was negotiated or forced. The distributor chose MD5 itself.

options.text: A preimage attack that recovered the installer from its hash
options.why: A preimage attack would find an input matching a given hash. Here the researcher crafted two inputs that share a hash, which is easier and is a collision.

options.text: A key compromise of the distributor's signing certificate
options.why: The private key was never needed. The weakness is in the hash, which lets a valid signature cover a second file.

takeaway: Collisions (two inputs, same hash) defeat signatures built on weak hashes. Use SHA-256 or stronger for signing.

scenario: Incident responders at a satellite component maker find an implant that has been present for 14 months. It was delivered through two previously unknown vulnerabilities, uses custom malware seen nowhere else, and copied only engineering drawings for a military contract. No ransom was demanded and nothing was leaked or offered for sale.
stem: Which threat actor and motivation are MOST likely?

options.text: A nation-state actor seeking espionage
options.why: Long dwell time, custom tooling and two zero-days require deep funding, and quietly taking only defense designs with no monetization is intelligence gathering.

options.text: An organized crime group seeking financial gain
options.why: Crime groups turn access into money through ransom, fraud or data sales. Fourteen months of quiet theft with no sale or demand does not fit.

options.text: A hacktivist group acting on political beliefs
options.why: Hacktivists want attention for a cause, so they leak or deface. Nothing here was published or announced.

options.text: An unskilled attacker seeking disruption and chaos
options.why: Unknown vulnerabilities and unique custom malware are the opposite of low sophistication, and nothing was disrupted.

takeaway: High resources, high sophistication, long quiet dwell time and a focus on strategic data with no payout point to a nation-state conducting espionage.

scenario: A school district's web portal is knocked offline by a flood of traffic the evening before final exams. Logs trace the traffic to a cheap online stress-testing service, and a student later boasts on social media that he paid $10 for it. The same service has been used against dozens of unrelated targets this month.
stem: Which set of threat actor attributes BEST fits this attack?

options.text: Unskilled attacker, minimal resources, low sophistication, disruption
options.why: Renting a ready-made service for $10 needs no skill or funding, and taking the portal down before exams is disruption for its own sake.

options.text: Hacktivist, crowd-sourced resources, moderate sophistication, political beliefs
options.why: There is no cause, slogan or message here, which a hacktivist would use to publicize the attack.

options.text: Organized crime, well funded, high sophistication, financial gain
options.why: No extortion demand was made, and renting a booter shows neither high sophistication nor any profit motive.

options.text: Nation-state, extensive funding, advanced sophistication, service disruption
options.why: The motivation of disruption matches, but a $10 rented service used by a student shows none of the resources or skill of a state.

takeaway: An unskilled attacker relies on tools or services built by others. Judge the actor by resources and sophistication, not only by the motivation.

scenario: The day after a mining company announces an open-pit project beside a protected forest, its internal emails about the project appear on a public website under the banner "Stop the Pit". The group behind the leak asks for no money and urges readers to contact regulators.
stem: Which motivation BEST explains this attack?

options.text: Philosophical or political beliefs
options.why: The timing, the slogan and the call to contact regulators show the group is advancing a cause, which is the classic hacktivist motivation.

options.text: Financial gain
options.why: No payment was requested and the data was given away for free, so there is no profit motive.

options.text: Espionage for a competitor's advantage
options.why: Espionage keeps stolen information secret to gain an advantage. Publishing it to the world defeats that purpose.

options.text: Blackmail
options.why: Blackmail threatens to release information unless the victim complies. Here the emails were released at once with no demand attached.

takeaway: Hacktivists publicize. Look for a cause, a slogan and a public release rather than a payment demand or quiet theft.

scenario: Threat intelligence on a ransomware brand shows it runs an affiliate program that splits ransom payments 80/20, staffs a negotiation chat for victims, buys initial access from brokers on criminal forums, and posts data from victims who refuse to pay on a leak site.
stem: Which threat actor type does this profile MOST closely match?

options.text: Organized crime
options.why: Profit sharing, purchased access, negotiators and leak-site pressure are business processes built to maximize revenue, which defines organized crime.

options.text: Nation-state
options.why: Some states use ransomware, but an affiliate revenue split and customer-service style negotiation show a profit business, not state objectives.

options.text: Hacktivist
options.why: Hacktivists pursue a cause and usually publicize their targets. Nothing here is political, and every step is aimed at payment.

options.text: Unskilled attacker
options.why: Individual affiliates may be low skill, but the operation itself is well funded, organized and coordinated across many specialized roles.

takeaway: Ransomware as a service is organized crime: structured, well resourced and driven by financial gain.

scenario: A criminal group buys a valid VPN username and password for a hospital employee on a dark web market, connects at 3 a.m., and exports patient records. The employee was on vacation and had reused that password on a shopping site that was breached last year.
stem: How should the threat actor be classified in the incident report?

options.text: An external actor using compromised internal credentials
options.why: Internal or external describes the attacker's relationship to the organization, not the account used. The group never had legitimate access of its own.

options.text: An insider threat, because the activity came from an employee account
options.why: The employee did nothing during the attack. Calling this an insider threat points the investigation at the wrong person.

options.text: An unintentional insider threat caused by the employee's password reuse
options.why: The reuse was a contributing weakness worth addressing in training, but the actor who stole the records is the outside criminal group.

options.text: Shadow IT, because the shopping site was an unapproved service
options.why: Shadow IT means unapproved systems used for company work. A personal shopping account is not part of the hospital's IT.

takeaway: An outsider holding stolen credentials is still an external actor. Classify by who is acting, not by whose account appears in the logs.

scenario: A CASB discovery report shows a data science team has been using a cloud notebook service, paid for on a manager's corporate card, with copies of customer purchase data. The team says the approved analytics platform takes six weeks to provision. There is no sign the data has been accessed by anyone outside the team.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST response?

options.text: Secure the data, then review the service and approve it or migrate the work
options.why: Shadow IT is usually well meant. Protecting the data, assessing the service and meeting the team's need brings it under governance without driving it further underground.

options.text: Block the service at the web proxy and close the account without any further discussion
options.why: Blocking without meeting the business need tends to push the team to another unapproved tool, and closing the account first loses track of the customer data copies.

options.text: Report the team members to HR as malicious insider threats
options.why: Nothing suggests malicious intent. The team used an unapproved tool to get work done, which is shadow IT, not sabotage.

options.text: Declare a data breach and notify the affected customers
options.why: There is no evidence of unauthorized access by outsiders. Notification decisions follow an assessment, not the discovery of an unapproved tool.

takeaway: Shadow IT is an internal, usually non-malicious threat. Discover it, assess the risk, and bring it into governance while fixing the need that caused it.

scenario: During an armed conflict, hundreds of organizations in one country, including power distributors, are hit at the same moment by malware that encrypts disks and displays a ransom note. Analysts find the payment ID in the note is random and the decryption key is discarded, so no victim can recover even by paying.
stem: Which motivation is MOST likely behind this campaign?

options.text: War
options.why: A coordinated destructive attack on one nation's infrastructure during a conflict, disguised as ransomware, serves military aims. That is the war motivation.

options.text: Financial gain
options.why: The ransom note is a disguise. With a random payment ID and no key, the attackers cannot collect or deliver anything.

options.text: Disruption and chaos
options.why: The campaign is certainly disruptive, but here disruption is a means to a military end. Simultaneous strikes on one nation's infrastructure during a conflict point to war as the motive.

options.text: Blackmail
options.why: Blackmail needs a believable promise to stop if the victim complies. Here nothing the victim does can change the outcome.

takeaway: Fake ransomware that cannot be decrypted is a wiper. Combined with a conflict and infrastructure targets, the motivation is war.

scenario: A procurement director receives an anonymous message containing copies of private emails from her personal account. The sender says the emails will go to her company's board unless she awards an upcoming $4 million contract to a named supplier. No payment is requested.
stem: Which threat actor motivation does this BEST illustrate?

options.text: Blackmail
options.why: The attacker uses threatened exposure of private information to force the victim to act, which is the defining feature of blackmail.

options.text: Revenge
options.why: Revenge aims to harm someone over a past grievance. Here the attacker wants a specific future action and will stay quiet if it happens.

options.text: Espionage
options.why: Espionage quietly collects information for an advantage. This attacker reveals what was taken and uses it as leverage.

options.text: Philosophical or political beliefs
options.why: There is no cause or message, only a demand that benefits a particular supplier.

takeaway: Blackmail is coercion: comply or the information comes out. Look for a threat of exposure tied to a demand.

scenario: A researcher notices that a city's parking payment site shows other drivers' license plates when she changes an ID number in the URL. She confirms the flaw with two records, stops testing, and emails the details to the city's IT department. The city has no bug bounty program, and she asks for nothing in return.
stem: Which statement BEST describes the researcher's motivation?

options.text: Ethical, though unauthorized testing may still break laws or policy
options.why: She tested minimally, stopped and reported privately with no demand, which is ethical motivation. Testing without permission can still carry legal risk.

options.text: Financial gain, because she could later demand payment for staying quiet
options.why: That is speculation. She asked for nothing, there is no bounty, and she reported the flaw privately.

options.text: Philosophical beliefs, because she is protesting the city's parking policy
options.why: Nothing in her report mentions a cause or policy. She simply described the flaw so it could be fixed.

options.text: Data exfiltration, because she viewed records that belong to other drivers
options.why: She viewed only what was needed to confirm the issue and kept nothing. Exfiltration as a motive means the goal is taking data.

takeaway: Ethical motivation means the aim is to fix a weakness. Authorization is a separate question, and testing without it is still risky.

scenario: Analysts at an energy company are attributing two intrusions. Leadership wants to know whether either one points to a nation-state rather than an organized crime group, because that changes who they will notify.
stem: Which observations MOST strongly indicate a nation-state actor? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Three zero-day vulnerabilities used in one campaign with no attempt to monetize access
options.why: Zero-days are expensive. Spending several without seeking any payout signals the large budget and strategic goals of a state.

options.text: Months of quiet access focused on grid control diagrams and operator procedures
options.why: Patient collection of critical infrastructure details supports future sabotage or intelligence, which is a state objective rather than a profit one.

options.text: A ransom note with a payment portal and a 72-hour deadline
options.why: A working payment portal and deadline are the hallmarks of financially motivated organized crime.

options.text: Initial access bought from a broker on a criminal forum
options.why: Buying access from brokers is standard practice in the criminal ransomware ecosystem, so it points toward organized crime.

options.text: A commodity remote access Trojan that is sold openly online
options.why: Commodity tools are cheap and widely available, so on their own they say little about resources and are common in criminal campaigns.

options.text: Stolen data offered for sale to the highest bidder
options.why: Selling data is monetization, which points to financial gain and therefore to criminals rather than a state.

takeaway: Nation-states show high resources and strategic targets with no payout. Payment portals, access brokers and data sales point to organized crime.

scenario: Employees receive emails that appear to come from the HR benefits portal. The body is a single image showing a QR code and the words "Scan to keep your benefits active". The secure email gateway rewrote and scanned every link in these messages but found none, and several staff scanned the code with personal phones.
stem: Which of the following BEST explains why the gateway missed the threat?

options.text: The malicious URL was inside an image, which link scanning does not read
options.why: The gateway inspects text links. A URL encoded in a picture is an image-based vector that only image analysis or QR decoding would catch.

options.text: The message failed SPF, so the gateway skipped its content inspection
options.why: An SPF failure would make the gateway more suspicious, not less, and the scenario says the gateway did scan the messages.

options.text: The phones used cellular data, which bypasses the gateway's link rewriting
options.why: That explains why later network controls never saw the visit, but the gateway had already missed the threat before anyone scanned the code.

options.text: The QR code pointed to a URL shortener that the gateway allowlists
options.why: Nothing suggests an allowlist. The gateway found no link at all, which a shortened text link would not avoid.

takeaway: Image-based vectors hide the payload or link in a picture. Text-based link scanning will not see a QR code unless the gateway decodes images.

scenario: Customers of Northwind Bank report a fake login page after mistyping the bank's address as northwnd-bank.com. Customers who type the correct address reach the real site, and the bank's own web servers show no tampering.
stem: Which attack is this, and which response BEST reduces it?

options.text: Typosquatting; register likely misspellings and seek takedown of the fake
options.why: Only people who mistype the name are affected, which is typosquatting. Owning likely misspellings and removing the fake domain shrink the vector.

options.text: DNS cache poisoning; turn on DNSSEC validation for the bank's resolvers
options.why: Poisoning sends people who type the correct name to the wrong address. Here the correct address works perfectly.

options.text: Watering hole; scan the partner websites that customers often visit
options.why: A watering hole compromises a legitimate site the targets already trust. No legitimate site was compromised here.

options.text: Pharming through altered hosts files; reimage the affected customer computers
options.why: Hosts file changes would misdirect even correctly typed addresses, and only on infected computers, not for anyone who makes a typo.

takeaway: Typosquatting waits for typing mistakes. Defensive registration and takedown help, while DNSSEC addresses forged answers for the correct name.

scenario: Accounts payable forwards the message below, which asks for an urgent wire transfer for a confidential acquisition. The company's real domain is northwind-corp.com, which publishes a DMARC policy of p=reject.
stem: Why did the message pass authentication, and what is the BEST control to add?

options.text: A look-alike domain passed its own checks; tag external mail and call to verify
options.why: SPF, DKIM and DMARC all passed for northwind-corp.co, a domain the attacker owns. External tagging and callback verification stop this impersonation.

options.text: The attacker spoofed the CEO's real address; change the DMARC policy from reject to quarantine
options.why: The real domain was never spoofed, and quarantine is a weaker policy than reject, so this change would make spoofing easier.

options.text: The CEO's mailbox was compromised; reset her password and require MFA
options.why: Mail from a compromised mailbox would come from northwind-corp.com. These headers show a different domain ending in .co.

options.text: The company's SPF record is too permissive; remove third-party senders from it
options.why: The SPF record that passed belongs to the attacker's domain. Editing the company's own record has no effect on it.

takeaway: Email authentication proves a message came from the domain it names, not that the domain is the right one. Cousin domains defeat SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

scenario: A finance clerk gets a call that sounds exactly like the CFO, from a number that displays the CFO's name, asking for an urgent $85,000 payment to a new supplier. Policy requires two approvers for payments over $50,000, but the caller says the second approver is in a meeting and the deal will collapse in an hour.
stem: What should the clerk do FIRST?

options.text: Hang up and call the CFO back on the number in the company directory
options.why: An out-of-band callback on a known number defeats both caller ID spoofing and voice cloning, because the attacker cannot answer the real CFO's phone.

options.text: Proceed, because the caller ID matched the CFO's saved contact entry
options.why: Caller ID is easy to spoof and proves nothing about who is calling, so it cannot justify bypassing the controls.

options.text: Ask the caller a personal question that only the real CFO could answer
options.why: Personal details are often discoverable online, and a live attacker can improvise. It is weaker than verifying through a channel the attacker does not control.

options.text: Send the payment now and have the second approver review it afterward
options.why: This abandons dual approval when it matters most, and a completed wire transfer is very hard to recall after the fact.

takeaway: For voice requests involving money or access, verify through a separate, known channel. A familiar voice and a matching caller ID are not proof of identity.

scenario: During a physical penetration test, testers leave 20 USB drives labeled "Salary review 2027" in the staff parking lot. Six employees plug them into work laptops, and each drive opens a shortcut that launches a built-in system tool to call back to the testers. Antivirus raised no alerts.
stem: Which technical control would MOST effectively stop this vector?

options.text: Endpoint device control that blocks unapproved USB storage devices
options.why: If unapproved storage cannot mount, the shortcut never runs, no matter how the payload is built or which built-in tool it uses.

options.text: Updated antivirus signatures that detect the testers' specific shortcut file
options.why: A signature catches only this exact file. Attackers can trivially change it, and the payload used a legitimate built-in tool.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on every laptop issued to employees
options.why: Encryption protects data if a laptop is lost. It does nothing to stop a user from running files from an inserted drive.

options.text: Quarterly awareness training about the danger of found media
options.why: Training helps and should continue, but it is an administrative control that depends on people, and the question asks for a technical one.

takeaway: Removable media is a threat vector you can close technically with device control. Training reduces clicks but cannot guarantee them away.

scenario: A company is choosing a vulnerability management product. One option installs a client agent on each of its 900 servers. The other is agentless: a central scanner signs in to every server over SSH and WinRM with a privileged service account. The team chooses the agentless option to avoid deploying software.
stem: Which attack surface concern should the team now treat as MOST important?

options.text: Theft of the scanner's privileged account, which works on every server
options.why: Agentless tools concentrate risk in the central credentials. Whoever steals that account can sign in to all 900 servers.

options.text: Exploitable flaws in client software installed on each of the 900 servers
options.why: That is the main attack surface of the agent-based option, which the team did not choose.

options.text: Higher CPU load on the servers during scheduled scan windows
options.why: Performance impact is an operational issue to schedule around, not the most serious security exposure of this design.

options.text: Users disabling the local agent from the notification area
options.why: There is no local agent in an agentless design, and servers rarely have interactive users anyway.

takeaway: Client-based tools add software to every host. Agentless tools add a powerful central credential. Protect whichever surface the design creates.

scenario: Facilities installed 40 IP cameras last month by following the installer's quick-start guide, and nobody changed the admin password because the guide did not mention it. The SOC sees the entries below. The source address does not belong to the company.
stem: Which vulnerability is MOST likely being exploited?
exhibit:
2026-10-12 02:14:07  cam-lobby-03  login  user=admin  src=198.51.100.77  result=success
2026-10-12 02:14:09  cam-lobby-03  config change  stream_url updated
2026-10-12 02:15:31  cam-dock-01   login  user=admin  src=198.51.100.77  result=success
2026-10-12 02:16:02  cam-dock-07   login  user=admin  src=198.51.100.77  result=success

options.text: Default credentials
options.why: Every login succeeds on the first try with the built-in admin account, on cameras whose password was never changed. That is default credentials.

options.text: A zero-day flaw in the camera firmware
options.why: No exploit is needed when ordinary logins succeed. The log shows normal authentication, not a crash or unusual request.

options.text: Password spraying against the camera accounts
options.why: Spraying produces many failed attempts across accounts before a success. These logins succeed immediately with no failures.

options.text: Credential stuffing using leaked passwords
options.why: Stuffing replays passwords leaked from other sites. Staff never set a password here, so there was nothing of theirs to leak.

takeaway: Immediate successful logins to a factory admin account on new devices point to default credentials. Change them during deployment, not later.

scenario: A public web server should serve only an HTTPS website. Administrators manage it over SSH from a jump host, and its database runs on a separate internal server. An external scan of the web server returns the results below.
stem: Which services should be disabled to reduce the attack surface? (Select THREE.)
exhibit:
PORT      STATE  SERVICE
21/tcp    open   ftp
22/tcp    open   ssh
23/tcp    open   telnet
443/tcp   open   https
3306/tcp  open   mysql

options.text: FTP on 21/tcp
options.why: Nothing in the server's role needs file transfer, and FTP sends credentials in cleartext, so it is pure unneeded attack surface.

options.text: Telnet on 23/tcp
options.why: Administrators already use SSH, and Telnet is an unencrypted remote shell that should not run on any internet-facing host.

options.text: MySQL on 3306/tcp
options.why: The database lives on a separate internal server, so a database listener on the public web server serves no purpose.

options.text: SSH on 22/tcp
options.why: SSH is how administrators manage the server. It should be restricted to the jump host's address rather than disabled.

options.text: HTTPS on 443/tcp
options.why: Serving the HTTPS website is the server's only job, so this port must stay open.

takeaway: Every open service port is attack surface. Disable what the role does not need, and restrict what admins need to known sources.

scenario: Attackers stole the remote access credentials of a small refrigeration contractor that monitors a grocery chain's cooling units. Using the contractor's VPN account, they reached the corporate network and then the point-of-sale systems, because the contractor's access was not limited to the cooling controllers.
stem: Which control would have MOST effectively limited the impact of this supply chain vector?

options.text: Confine vendor access to a segment holding only the cooling controllers
options.why: Even with stolen vendor credentials, the attackers could only have reached the cooling controllers, not the corporate network or the tills.

options.text: Require the contractor to complete a detailed security questionnaire every year
options.why: Questionnaires are useful due diligence, but they do not technically stop a breached vendor account from reaching other systems.

options.text: Add a right-to-audit clause to the contractor's service agreement
options.why: A right to audit lets the chain inspect the vendor later. It does nothing to limit where a stolen account can go.

options.text: Install antivirus on all of the point-of-sale terminals
options.why: The terminals were the final target. The root problem was that a vendor account could reach them at all.

takeaway: Supply chain vectors arrive through a trusted partner's access. Give vendors the narrowest network path their job needs.

scenario: An anonymous account posts a fake press release claiming a toy maker is recalling its best-selling product for lead paint, timed for the day before the holiday sales launch. Within hours, thousands of worried parents share the post because they believe it is true.
stem: Which terms BEST describe the original post and the parents' sharing, in that order?

options.text: Disinformation, then misinformation
options.why: The poster knowingly spread a falsehood to cause harm, which is disinformation. Parents sharing it in good faith are spreading misinformation.

options.text: Misinformation, then disinformation
options.why: This reverses the labels. The original author knew it was false, while the parents believed it.

options.text: Disinformation in both cases, because the content is false
options.why: Falseness alone does not decide the label. Intent does, and the parents had no intent to deceive anyone.

options.text: Misinformation in both cases, because nobody was paid to spread it
options.why: Payment is not the test. Deliberate deception by the original poster makes that post disinformation.

takeaway: Disinformation is false information spread on purpose. Misinformation is false information spread by people who believe it.

scenario: Customers who complain about late deliveries on social media get quick replies from an account named after a retailer's support team, using its logo. The replies send them to a "refund form" that asks for card numbers. The retailer's real support account never replied to them.
stem: Which attack is this, and what is the BEST response?

options.text: Brand impersonation; get the account taken down and warn customers
options.why: The attacker poses as the retailer's brand to win customers' trust. Removing the account and telling customers how real support contacts them limits the damage.

options.text: Typosquatting; buy misspelled versions of the retailer's domain name
options.why: Typosquatting relies on people mistyping a web address. Here a fake account contacts victims directly, and new domains would not remove it.

options.text: Watering hole; scan the retailer's own website for injected malicious code
options.why: A watering hole compromises a site the victims already visit. The retailer's site is not involved at all.

options.text: Business email compromise; enable MFA on the support team's mailbox
options.why: BEC uses spoofed or hijacked business email to trick a company into paying. No retailer account was compromised here.

takeaway: Brand impersonation borrows a trusted name and logo to reach customers. Respond with takedowns and clear guidance on how the real brand communicates.

scenario: A visitor waiting in a lobby conference room plugs a laptop into a wall jack and receives an address on the corporate user network, where internal file shares are visible. The jacks are kept active so staff can hold meetings in the room.
stem: Which control would BEST close this unsecure network vector while keeping the jacks usable for staff?

options.text: 802.1X port authentication that admits only authorized devices
options.why: Staff devices that authenticate get corporate access, while unknown devices are refused or placed in a restricted network, so the jacks remain useful.

options.text: Disabling every jack in the conference room
options.why: This closes the vector but breaks the stated requirement that staff can still use the jacks in meetings.

options.text: Port security limiting each jack to the first MAC address it learns
options.why: The first device to connect is simply accepted, MAC addresses are easy to spoof, and no one is actually authenticated.

options.text: SMB encryption on all of the internal file shares
options.why: Encryption protects file traffic in transit, but the visitor still lands on the corporate network with access to everything else.

takeaway: An open wired jack is a network vector. Network access control with 802.1X authenticates the device before it gets on the network.

scenario: Employees receive chat messages in the company's collaboration platform from an external account with the display name "IT Help Desk" and the company logo as its picture. The messages ask them to approve a remote support session. The platform currently accepts chats from any external organization.
stem: Which change would MOST effectively reduce this message-based vector?

options.text: Allow external chat only with approved partners and label outside senders
options.why: This removes the attacker's ability to start the conversation and makes any remaining external message stand out from real IT staff.

options.text: Publish a strict DMARC policy for the company's email domain
options.why: DMARC protects email sent using the company's domain. These messages arrive through the chat platform from another tenant.

options.text: Block every remote support tool at the perimeter firewall and web proxy for all users
options.why: This may break the attack's next step, but the real help desk needs those tools, and the impersonation messages keep arriving.

options.text: Require all employees to change their passwords every 60 days
options.why: Password rotation does not stop an impersonated chat from persuading a user to approve a remote session.

takeaway: Instant messaging is a message-based vector like email. Restrict who can message in from outside, and make external senders obvious.

scenario: A phishing campaign sends fake invoices as .iso disk image attachments. When a user opens one, it mounts as a drive holding a shortcut that runs a script. The email gateway blocks executable attachments, but disk images are not on its blocked list. No one in the company has a business need to receive disk images by email.
stem: Which control would BEST block this file-based vector?

options.text: Block disk image and container attachments at the gateway
options.why: With no business need for these files, blocking container types removes the delivery method entirely before a user can open one.

options.text: Disable Office macros in all documents that arrive from the internet
options.why: Macro restrictions are worthwhile, but this payload is a shortcut and script inside a disk image, not an Office macro.

options.text: Ask users to report suspicious invoices to the security team
options.why: Reporting helps detect campaigns, but it depends on every user spotting the fake, and some will open it first.

options.text: Sign all of the company's outbound mail with DKIM
options.why: DKIM proves that the company's own outgoing mail is genuine. It does nothing to filter incoming attachments.

takeaway: File-based vectors hide payloads in containers and archives to slip past filters. Block file types the business does not need.

scenario: An attacker sees on social media that a warehouse supervisor is on vacation. He phones the payroll office, says he is that supervisor, explains that his bank froze his account after fraud, and asks that his direct deposit be moved to a new account before Friday's run. Payroll makes the change.
stem: Which social engineering techniques did the attacker use? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Vishing
options.why: The attack was carried out over a voice call, which is what makes it vishing rather than email or text phishing.

options.text: Pretexting
options.why: The bank fraud story is an invented scenario that makes an unusual request sound reasonable and urgent, which is pretexting.

options.text: Impersonation
options.why: The attacker claimed to be a specific real employee, chosen because he was away and could not contradict the call.

options.text: Smishing
options.why: Smishing uses SMS text messages. No texts were involved, only a phone call.

options.text: Watering hole
options.why: A watering hole compromises a website the victims visit. Reading a public social media post is reconnaissance, not a watering hole.

options.text: Typosquatting
options.why: Typosquatting relies on mistyped web addresses. No look-alike domain played any part in this attack.

takeaway: One attack often combines several techniques: the channel (vishing), the story (pretexting) and the claimed identity (impersonation).

scenario: During testing, an analyst pastes a 2,048-character string of the letter A into a label printing application's name field, which the form limits to 64 characters on screen. The application crashes and writes the report below. The hexadecimal value 0x41 is the letter A.
stem: Which vulnerability does this MOST likely indicate?
exhibit:
Faulting application: labelprint.exe 4.2.1
Exception code: 0xc0000005 (access violation)
Fault address:  0x41414141
Registers:      EIP=41414141  EBP=41414141  ESP=0019F5A0
Field 'LabelName' received 2048 bytes (buffer 64)

options.text: A buffer overflow that overwrote the saved return address
options.why: The instruction pointer holds 41414141, the tester's own input. Oversized input spilled past the buffer and replaced the return address, a classic overflow.

options.text: A memory leak that gradually exhausted the process's memory
options.why: A leak grows over time and ends in an out-of-memory failure. It would not put the tester's input into the instruction pointer.

options.text: A race condition between two threads writing the same field
options.why: The crash follows a single oversized input to one field. Nothing points to timing between threads.

options.text: An integer overflow in the counter that tracks the field's length
options.why: Integer overflows can lead to memory corruption, but the evidence of input landing in EIP and EBP shows a direct stack buffer overflow.

takeaway: When a crash shows your input in the instruction pointer, the input overflowed a buffer and can redirect execution. Fix it with bounds checking.

scenario: EDR raises the alert below on a user's workstation. Minutes later, the browser process itself, not the downloaded file, starts connecting to an unfamiliar external server.
stem: Which technique BEST describes this activity?
exhibit:
Process:   invoice_view.exe (unsigned)  path: C:\Users\jlee\Downloads\
Action 1:  OpenProcess  target=browser.exe (signed)  access=ALL
Action 2:  VirtualAllocEx in browser.exe  protection=PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE
Action 3:  WriteProcessMemory in browser.exe  size=212 KB
Action 4:  CreateRemoteThread in browser.exe

options.text: Memory injection into a trusted, signed process
options.why: One process writing executable code into another running process and starting a thread there is memory injection, which hides activity inside a trusted program.

options.text: A buffer overflow triggered inside the browser
options.why: An overflow corrupts memory through malformed input to the program itself. Here a separate process wrote into the browser using system calls.

options.text: Privilege escalation through a kernel vulnerability
options.why: Nothing in the alert shows a kernel exploit or a change in privilege level. These are ordinary user-mode calls from one process into another.

options.text: DLL side loading through a library placed beside the browser
options.why: Side loading plants a library where a program loads it at startup. Here code was written into a browser that was already running.

takeaway: Memory injection runs malicious code inside a legitimate process. Alerts on cross-process memory writes and remote threads are the key evidence.

scenario: A code review of a customer portal finds the login lookup below. The developer says it is safe because the login page uses JavaScript to reject email addresses that contain quotation marks.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST fix?

options.text: Use a parameterized query that binds the email as data
options.why: Binding the value means the database never treats user input as part of the SQL command, which removes injection at its root.

options.text: Add server-side code that escapes quotation marks in the input
options.why: Escaping is better than nothing, but it is easy to get wrong across encodings and contexts. Parameterized queries are the reliable fix.

options.text: Keep the JavaScript check and add a web application firewall rule
options.why: Client-side checks are bypassed by sending requests directly. A WAF is a compensating control, not a fix for the code.

options.text: Connect to the database with a read-only account
options.why: Least privilege limits damage, but an attacker could still bypass the login and read every user record.

takeaway: SQL injection happens when input is concatenated into a query. Parameterized queries fix it, and client-side validation never counts as a security control.

scenario: A product review page lets customers post comments. A tester posts a review containing a script tag, and from then on every visitor who opens that product page runs the script, including staff using the moderation console. The review, script included, is saved in the database.
stem: Which vulnerability is this, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: Stored XSS; encode review text for HTML when it is displayed
options.why: The script is saved and served to every viewer, which makes it stored XSS. Output encoding makes the browser show it as text instead of running it.

options.text: Reflected XSS; validate the URL parameters on every incoming request
options.why: Reflected XSS needs each victim to open a crafted link. This script is saved once and runs for everyone afterward.

options.text: SQL injection; switch the review insert to parameterized queries
options.why: The database stored the text correctly as data. The flaw is in how the page renders it, which parameterization does not change.

options.text: Cross-site request forgery; add anti-CSRF tokens to the review form
options.why: CSRF tricks a browser into sending unwanted requests. Here the problem is untrusted script running in visitors' browsers.

takeaway: Stored XSS persists on the server and hits every viewer, while reflected XSS needs a crafted link. Both are fixed with context-aware output encoding.

scenario: Attackers break into a monitoring software vendor's build server and insert a backdoor into the source code before compilation. The vendor's normal pipeline then signs the update with its real code signing certificate, and 18,000 customers install it automatically after their endpoint tools verify the signature.
stem: Why did code signing fail to stop this malicious update?

options.text: A signature proves who published the file, not that its code is safe
options.why: The vendor's own pipeline signed the tampered build, so the signature was genuine. Signing confirms origin and integrity after signing, not the absence of malice.

options.text: The attackers stole the vendor's private key and signed the update themselves
options.why: They did not need the key. The vendor's normal process signed the backdoored build for them.

options.text: The customers' endpoint tools did not check for certificate revocation
options.why: The certificate had not been revoked when the update shipped, so checking revocation would have changed nothing.

options.text: The signature used a hash algorithm too weak to reveal the changes
options.why: The hash matched exactly what was signed. The backdoor was added before signing, so no algorithm would have flagged it.

takeaway: A malicious update signed by the real vendor passes signature checks. Defend with build pipeline security and monitoring of what trusted software does after install.

scenario: A laptop is reimaged from a clean golden image, but the same malware returns within an hour. Forensics finds a modified module in the laptop's UEFI firmware that writes the malware back to the disk at every boot. Secure Boot was disabled on this model.
stem: Which remediation is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Reflash firmware from a vendor-signed image, then enable Secure Boot
options.why: The infection lives in firmware on the motherboard, so only rewriting that firmware with a trusted image removes it. Secure Boot then helps keep untrusted boot code out.

options.text: Reimage the drive again, this time with full-disk encryption turned on
options.why: The firmware is not on the drive, so it survives reimaging and still runs before the operating system starts.

options.text: Replace the hard drive and reinstall the operating system from media
options.why: A new drive does not touch the firmware chip on the motherboard, which will reinfect the new drive at the next boot.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan after booting into safe mode
options.why: Antivirus inside the operating system cannot see or clean code stored in firmware, so the payload simply returns.

takeaway: Firmware malware survives reimaging and drive replacement. Reflash from a trusted source or replace the board, then turn on Secure Boot.

scenario: An asset review flags two systems. A 14-year-old manufacturing control server still receives security patches under an extended vendor support contract. A firewall model bought two years ago has now passed the vendor's end-of-support date, and no further firmware fixes will be released for it.
stem: Which system carries the GREATER patching risk, and why?

options.text: The firewall, because end-of-life means new flaws will never be fixed
options.why: Once a product is end-of-life, every newly found vulnerability stays open permanently. Age alone does not create that problem while support continues.

options.text: The server, because legacy systems by definition can no longer be patched
options.why: Legacy describes an old system, but this one is still receiving vendor patches. Being old is not the same as being unsupported.

options.text: Both carry the same risk, because neither runs current hardware
options.why: Hardware age is not the issue. What matters is whether the vendor still fixes security flaws, and only the server still gets fixes.

options.text: Neither is a risk, because both sit behind other perimeter controls
options.why: Other controls reduce exposure, but they do not make unpatched flaws disappear, especially in the firewall that is itself a perimeter control.

takeaway: Legacy means old; end-of-life means the vendor has stopped fixing it. A young but unsupported device can be riskier than an old supported one.

scenario: A customer of a small cloud host attaches a newly provisioned block storage volume to its virtual machine and runs a file recovery tool on it. The tool recovers fragments of database files and email addresses belonging to another customer, who deleted that volume last week.
stem: Which vulnerability does this BEST demonstrate?

options.text: Resource reuse without sanitization by the provider
options.why: The provider reassigned storage that still held the previous tenant's data. Wiping or crypto-erasing it before reuse is the provider's responsibility.

options.text: VM escape from the guest to the hypervisor
options.why: Nothing broke out of a virtual machine. The customer simply read storage that was legitimately assigned to it.

options.text: VM sprawl across the customer's environment
options.why: Sprawl is the uncontrolled growth of unmanaged virtual machines. It does not explain finding another tenant's data.

options.text: A storage misconfiguration that made the volume public
options.why: The volume was correctly attached to this customer only. The flaw is that its previous contents were never erased.

takeaway: Resource reuse exposes data when memory or storage passes to a new tenant without being sanitized. Ask providers how they wipe released resources.

scenario: A researcher reports that HR export files in a company's cloud object storage can be listed and downloaded by anyone on the internet. The bucket is encrypted at rest with provider-managed keys and has versioning turned on. Its access policy is shown below.
stem: Which of the following BEST explains the exposure and the fix?
exhibit:
{
  "Effect": "Allow",
  "Principal": "*",
  "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"],
  "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::acme-hr-exports",
               "arn:aws:s3:::acme-hr-exports/*"]
}

options.text: The policy allows any principal; limit it to named roles and block public access
options.why: A Principal of "*" grants every requester, signed in or not, the listed actions. Naming specific roles and enabling public access blocks closes it.

options.text: Encryption at rest has failed; rotate the provider-managed encryption key now
options.why: Provider-managed encryption is decrypted automatically for any request the policy allows, so a new key does not change who can read files.

options.text: Versioning exposes older copies; turn versioning off for the bucket
options.why: Versioning keeps older copies of objects, but it grants no access. The policy is what lets anyone read.

options.text: Only listing is the problem; remove ListBucket and keep GetObject for every requester
options.why: Anyone who learns or guesses a file name could still download it. Hiding the list is obscurity, not access control.

takeaway: Cloud data exposure is usually a policy misconfiguration, not a broken cipher. A wildcard principal means everyone, and encryption at rest will not stop them.

scenario: A researcher extracts the firmware from one smart lock and finds the private key the lock uses for TLS with the vendor's cloud service. The identical key is embedded in all 200,000 locks of that model.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes the vulnerability and its fix?

options.text: A cryptographic flaw from one shared key; issue unique per-device keys
options.why: With one key across the fleet, extracting it from any lock exposes all of them. Unique per-device keys contain a compromise to one lock.

options.text: A weak protocol version; upgrade the locks from TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3
options.why: A stronger protocol does not help when the attacker already holds the private key that the protocol relies on.

options.text: A firmware rootkit; reflash every lock with a clean firmware image
options.why: The firmware was not modified, and reflashing the same image puts the same shared key right back.

options.text: A default credential; force every owner to set a new app password
options.why: The owner's app password is separate from the device's TLS key, so changing it leaves the key exposure unchanged.

takeaway: Cryptographic vulnerabilities include poor key management, not only weak algorithms. A key shared across devices turns one extraction into a fleet compromise.

scenario: MDM reports that an executive's iPhone now runs an unofficial package manager, installed after a tool removed the operating system's code signing and sandbox restrictions. The executive says he wanted home screen themes the App Store does not offer. The phone syncs corporate email.
stem: Which term describes what happened, and what is the BEST MDM response?

options.text: Jailbreaking; mark it noncompliant and block corporate access until restored
options.why: Removing iOS restrictions is jailbreaking, which defeats the sandbox the company relies on. Blocking access until the phone is restored protects corporate data.

options.text: Rooting; send an MDM command that removes the root account from the executive's device
options.why: Rooting is the Android term, and MDM cannot simply remove the elevated access a jailbreak or root creates.

options.text: Side loading; add the package manager to the MDM app blocklist
options.why: Side loading installs apps from outside the store without breaking the OS. Here the protections themselves were removed, which blocking one app does not undo.

options.text: Carrier unlocking; ask the mobile carrier to relock the device
options.why: Carrier unlocking only lets a phone use other networks. It has nothing to do with code signing or the sandbox.

takeaway: Jailbreaking (iOS) and rooting (Android) remove OS protections. Side loading only installs outside the official store. Treat jailbroken devices as noncompliant.

scenario: A vendor confirms attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in the file sharing feature of its VPN appliance. No patch exists yet, and the vendor expects one in about ten days. The company's appliance faces the internet, and the file sharing feature is rarely used.
stem: Which actions BEST reduce risk until a patch is released? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Disable the file sharing feature on the appliance
options.why: Turning off the vulnerable feature removes the attack surface entirely, and the business barely uses it.

options.text: Apply the vendor's interim mitigation or IPS rules that block the known exploit traffic
options.why: Virtual patching through vendor workarounds or IPS signatures blocks exploitation attempts while no code fix exists.

options.text: Run an authenticated vulnerability scan to confirm the flaw is present
options.why: Scanners may not yet have a check for a brand new flaw, and confirming it does not reduce the risk.

options.text: Wait for the CVSS score to be published before taking action
options.why: Active exploitation of an internet-facing device is reason enough to act now. A score adds little.

options.text: Update antivirus signatures on all user workstations
options.why: The target is the VPN appliance, not the workstations, so workstation signatures do not protect it.

takeaway: With a zero-day there is no patch to apply. Reduce exposure with compensating controls such as disabling the feature and virtual patching, then patch when available.

scenario: A monthly operating system update fixes a kernel flaw that lets any signed-in standard user gain SYSTEM privileges. The desktop team proposes deferring it for three months because no employee has local administrator rights. Phishing lands malware on a few workstations every month.
stem: Which of the following BEST evaluates the team's reasoning?

options.text: It is flawed, because the bug turns a user-level foothold into full control
options.why: Phishing malware runs as the standard user. This flaw lets that malware jump to SYSTEM, bypassing the very least privilege the team is relying on.

options.text: It is sound, because least privilege already prevents privilege escalation
options.why: Least privilege limits what a user account can do, but a kernel escalation flaw exists precisely to get around those limits.

options.text: It is sound, because the flaw needs local access and is therefore low risk
options.why: Phishing gives attackers local code execution every month, so the local access requirement offers little comfort.

options.text: It is flawed, because standard users can install kernel updates themselves
options.why: Standard users cannot normally install OS updates, and that has nothing to do with whether deferral is safe.

takeaway: Operating system privilege escalation flaws defeat least privilege. When attackers routinely gain user-level footholds, they deserve prompt patching.

scenario: A company's web applications pull in about 400 open-source libraries through a package manager. When a widely used logging library was found to be exploitable, the team needed two days just to work out which applications included it, directly or through other libraries.
stem: Which controls would MOST directly reduce this software supply chain risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Maintain a software bill of materials for every application
options.why: An SBOM lists every component and version, including indirect ones, so the team can find affected applications in minutes.

options.text: Run software composition analysis in the build pipeline
options.why: SCA compares dependencies against known vulnerabilities on every build, flagging risky libraries before and after release.

options.text: Sign the company's own release builds with a code signing certificate
options.why: Signing proves the company's builds were not altered, but it says nothing about flaws inside the third-party libraries.

options.text: Place a web application firewall in front of every application
options.why: A WAF may block some exploit attempts, but it neither finds affected applications nor fixes the vulnerable library.

options.text: Commission a dynamic application security test once a year
options.why: A yearly black-box test is too infrequent and cannot inventory which library versions each application contains.

takeaway: Software supply chain risk starts with knowing what you ship. An SBOM gives the inventory, and SCA keeps checking it against new vulnerabilities.

scenario: A tester requests a nonexistent page on a production web application and receives a full stack trace showing framework version numbers, internal file paths and the database connection string. The developers left the framework's debug mode enabled after the last release.
stem: Which vulnerability category BEST fits this finding, and what is the right fix?

options.text: Misconfiguration; disable debug mode and rotate the exposed credentials
options.why: Debug output in production is a settings problem, not a code flaw. Disabling it stops the leak, and rotation handles credentials already exposed.

options.text: Zero-day; wait for the framework vendor to publish a security patch
options.why: The behavior is a documented setting the developers left on. There is no unknown flaw for a vendor to patch.

options.text: SQL injection; parameterize the queries that build the error page
options.why: No input was injected into a query. The page simply printed internal details because debugging was on.

options.text: Cryptographic failure; encrypt the database connection string stored in the configuration file
options.why: Encrypting the setting at rest is worthwhile, but the debug page would still display details, and the root cause is the setting.

takeaway: Verbose errors and debug modes in production are misconfigurations. Fix the setting, then treat anything the debug output exposed as compromised.

scenario: EDR flags a process on a finance clerk's laptop. The file was dropped by an email attachment she opened yesterday, and the analyst pulls the details shown in the exhibit.
exhibit:
Process : winupdsvc.exe  (PID 6120)  user CORP\mlopez
Path    : C:\Users\mlopez\AppData\Roaming\WinUpd\winupdsvc.exe
API     : SetWindowsHookExW(WH_KEYBOARD_LL)
          GetForegroundWindow + GetWindowTextW every 200 ms
File    : C:\Users\mlopez\AppData\Roaming\WinUpd\k.dat  (grows ~40 KB per day)
Sample  : [Chrome: Online Banking | Sign In] <typed username><TAB><typed password><ENTER>
Network : HTTPS POST 45.77.12.9/upload every 6 hours (contents of k.dat)
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this malware?

options.text: A keylogger that records keystrokes with the active window title
options.why: A low-level keyboard hook, window titles polled every 200 ms and a growing file of typed text sent out every six hours are the signature of a keylogger.

options.text: A remote access Trojan that gives the attacker live control of the desktop
options.why: Nothing shows an inbound command channel or remote control. The only network activity is a one-way upload of the captured file on a fixed schedule.

options.text: Ransomware preparing to encrypt the user's documents
options.why: No files are being encrypted or renamed and there is no ransom note. The program writes to a single log file that keeps growing.

options.text: A rootkit hiding its files by hooking kernel functions
options.why: The hook is a user-mode keyboard hook, not a kernel hook, and the files sit openly in the AppData folder where the analyst found them.

takeaway: A keyboard hook plus a growing file of keystrokes tagged with window titles is a keylogger. MFA limits the damage, because a captured password alone is no longer enough.

scenario: At 10:02 one unpatched workstation in the warehouse VLAN was infected. By 10:20, 140 hosts across three VLANs were infected, although no one opened files or clicked links. The internal firewall logged the traffic in the exhibit.
stem: Which of the following BEST explains how the malware is spreading?

options.text: A worm exploiting a file sharing flaw to copy itself between hosts
options.why: Each newly infected host immediately sweeps other addresses on TCP 445 with no user action, which is how a self-propagating worm spreads.

options.text: A virus infecting files on shared folders that run when users open them
options.why: A virus needs a user or program to run the infected file. Here nobody opened anything and the spread followed automated network sweeps.

options.text: A Trojan that users installed after downloading a fake utility
options.why: Trojans depend on users choosing to install them. Infecting 140 hosts in 18 minutes with no user action rules that out.

options.text: An external attacker scanning to map which hosts expose file sharing
options.why: The sources are internal hosts that were themselves just infected, each starting its own sweep. A reconnaissance scan does not infect what it touches.

takeaway: Spread without user action, where every newly infected host starts scanning the same port, is a worm. Patch the flaw and block SMB between user VLANs to contain it.

scenario: A designer installed a free font manager from a download site, and it works exactly as advertised. A week later the SOC sees the designer's screen being viewed and the mouse moving at night. EDR shows the font manager's helper process holding an outbound TLS connection to an unknown host that sends it commands.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this malware?

options.text: A remote access Trojan hidden inside a working application
options.why: It arrived disguised as useful software that really works, and it gives the attacker interactive control over a command channel. That is a RAT delivered as a Trojan.

options.text: Bloatware that the vendor preinstalled and that wastes resources
options.why: Bloatware is unneeded software shipped with a device. It is not designed to hand an outsider control of the screen, and this was a user download.

options.text: A worm that reached the workstation through a network service flaw
options.why: The designer installed it from a download site. Worms copy themselves across the network by exploiting services, without anyone installing them.

options.text: Spyware that quietly collects the designer's browsing history for advertisers
options.why: Spyware gathers information, but here someone is actively moving the mouse and viewing the screen through a command channel, which is remote control.

takeaway: A Trojan hides malicious function inside software the user chooses to install, and a RAT is the kind that gives the attacker remote control. An application allow list stops unapproved installs.

scenario: The firewall shows a database server sending about 2 GB to an unknown address every night. On the server itself, netstat, Task Manager and the installed antivirus show no unusual process or connection. When the analyst boots the server from trusted forensic media and scans the disk offline, an unknown kernel driver and a hidden folder appear.
stem: Which of the following is MOST likely present on the server?

options.text: A rootkit hiding its processes, files and connections
