options.why: The host's own tools see nothing while the network and an offline scan disagree. Subverting the operating system to hide activity is what a rootkit does.

options.text: Fileless malware running only in memory through built-in tools
options.why: Fileless malware avoids writing to disk, yet the offline scan found a driver and a hidden folder on disk. The OS tools being blind points to deliberate hiding.

options.text: A logic bomb waiting for a trigger date before it activates
options.why: This code is already active every night. A logic bomb is defined by dormant code waiting for a condition, not by concealing itself from the OS.

options.text: Spyware that records user activity for an advertising network
options.why: Spyware collects data about users, but it does not normally load kernel drivers to hide from the system's own tools, and this is an unattended server.

takeaway: When the host's own tools say clean but the network or an offline scan disagrees, suspect a rootkit. Investigate from trusted media and rebuild the system instead of trying to clean it.

scenario: A company bought 300 new laptops. A vulnerability scan finds that each runs a preinstalled vendor support assistant that nobody uses. It listens on a local port and can be told by any web page to download and run an update. There is no sign of attacker activity yet.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this software and how to handle it?

options.text: Bloatware that should be uninstalled and kept out of the image
options.why: It is unneeded preinstalled vendor software, and its exposed update service adds attack surface for no benefit. Uninstalling it from the 300 laptops and the standard image ends the risk.

options.text: A Trojan, so the laptops should be reported as compromised
options.why: A Trojan is deliberately malicious software in disguise. This is legitimate vendor software with a flaw, and there is no sign of compromise yet.

options.text: Spyware, so the vendor's telemetry domains should be blocked at the proxy
options.why: Nothing shows collection of user data. Blocking domains also leaves the local listening service in place for any web page to abuse.

options.text: An unpatched flaw, so the laptops should be isolated until the vendor issues a fix
options.why: Isolating 300 laptops is out of proportion when the software is unused and can simply be uninstalled, which removes the exposure immediately.

takeaway: Bloatware is unneeded preinstalled software. It is not malicious by design, but it adds attack surface, so strip it from the gold image.

scenario: Several programs in a department's shared tools folder have started crashing. A comparison against last month's baseline gives the results in the exhibit. Every changed file was last written from the PC of a technician who runs utilities from a personal USB drive, and no host shows network scanning.
exhibit:
File             Baseline size   Current size   SHA-256 matches
calc_tool.exe       412,160         437,248       no
labelprint.exe    1,088,512       1,113,600       no
report.exe          233,472         258,560       no
readme.txt            2,140           2,140       yes
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this malware?

options.text: A virus that attaches to programs and spreads when they run
options.why: Every executable grew by exactly 25,088 bytes while the text file is unchanged, the classic sign of code appended to host programs. It spreads as infected programs are run.

options.text: A worm that spreads across the network by exploiting a service
options.why: No host is scanning or exploiting services. The spread follows one person running programs from a USB drive, which requires user action.

options.text: A logic bomb a developer planted inside the department's tools
options.why: A logic bomb is dormant code waiting for a trigger in one program. Here many unrelated executables grew by the same amount at once.

options.text: Ransomware encrypting the contents of the shared folder
options.why: The programs still run, if unreliably, and the text file is untouched. Encrypted files would be unreadable, usually renamed, and paired with a ransom note.

takeaway: A virus needs a host file and someone or something to run it, and identical size growth across executables points to file infection. A worm spreads by itself over the network.

scenario: An executive's personal phone, enrolled in MDM for email, has heavy battery drain. MDM finds an app named System Service with no launcher icon. It holds location, microphone, SMS and accessibility permissions and uploads data every 15 minutes. A relative recently offered to set up the phone.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this app?

options.text: Spyware that monitors location, messages and audio
options.why: Hidden from the launcher, granted broad sensing permissions and uploading continuously, the app exists to covertly gather information about the person, which is spyware.

options.text: Bloatware installed by the carrier before the phone was sold
options.why: Carrier bloatware is openly named and visible. It does not hide its icon or quietly request microphone, SMS and accessibility access.

options.text: A keylogger limited to capturing what the user types
options.why: It collects location, audio and messages, far more than keystrokes. Keylogging may be one feature, but it does not describe the whole app.

options.text: Ransomware that will lock the phone until a payment is made
options.why: Nothing is locked or encrypted. Quiet, ongoing collection and upload is the purpose here, not extortion.

takeaway: Spyware covertly gathers information about a person, often with a hidden icon and broad permissions. Battery drain and constant uploads are common indicators on mobile devices.

scenario: Overnight, eight servers in a small server room shut themselves down with thermal alarms, and their CPU use before the shutdown was normal. The HVAC vendor's remote account is shared by several technicians, and the vendor says no one worked that night. The building management system recorded the entries in the exhibit.
exhibit:
01:58  login   user=hvac_vendor  src=185.193.88.14  (VPN portal)
02:03  CRAC-2  setpoint changed 18.0 C -> 35.0 C          user=hvac_vendor
02:04  CRAC-2  high-temperature alarm DISABLED            user=hvac_vendor
03:41  Server room temperature 39.5 C
03:47  SRV-01 .. SRV-08 thermal shutdown
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this attack?

options.text: An environmental attack on the cooling the servers rely on
options.why: The attacker changed the cooling setpoint and disabled its alarm, so the room overheated. Attacking power, cooling or similar conditions is an environmental attack.

options.text: Cryptojacking that overheated the servers with mining workloads
options.why: CPU use was normal before the shutdown. The heat came from the room after cooling was changed, not from the servers' own workload.

options.text: A distributed denial-of-service attack against the servers' services
options.why: A DDoS floods network or application resources. There was no traffic flood here, only manipulated physical conditions.

options.text: A cooling unit failure that the high-temperature alarm should have caught
options.why: The setpoint and the alarm were changed on purpose by a logged-in account, so this is not equipment failure.

takeaway: Attacks on power, cooling or fire suppression are environmental attacks. Treat building systems and shared vendor remote access as part of the attack surface.

scenario: After laptops vanish from a locked storage room, the security manager reviews the access control log for its door. The door has a badge reader, a door-position sensor and a deadbolt. The log entries for that day are shown in the exhibit.
exhibit:
Time      Door      Event                          Badge
18:02:15  STOR-B1   Access granted                 #40218 (K. Osei)
18:02:21  STOR-B1   Door opened
18:02:40  STOR-B1   Door closed
22:47:03  STOR-B1   Door forced open               (none)
22:51:30  STOR-B1   Door closed
23:10:12  STOR-B1   Access denied, invalid card    #00000
stem: Which of the following BEST describes how the thief MOST likely got in?

options.text: Physical brute force, opening the door with no badge read
options.why: A forced-open event means the sensor saw the door open with no valid credential presented, which indicates prying or forcing the door.

options.text: RFID cloning of K. Osei's badge to unlock the door at night
options.why: A cloned badge produces an access granted event under that badge number. The 22:47 opening has no badge read at all.

options.text: Tailgating behind K. Osei during the evening entry
options.why: The 18:02 entry is a normal 19-second open and close. The unexplained opening is the later one, with no badge involved.

options.text: Guessing card numbers at the reader until one was accepted
options.why: The single denied read came after the door had already been forced and closed, and no guess was ever accepted.

takeaway: Read physical access logs like any other log. A forced-open event with no credential is brute force, while a cloned badge appears as a normal grant at an odd time.

scenario: Customers worldwide, on every ISP, reach a fake login page when they visit shop.example. The web servers and the company's internal DNS are untouched, but the registrar account's audit log shows a login from an unfamiliar country yesterday. The analyst runs the query in the exhibit.
exhibit:
$ dig NS shop.example +short
ns1.fastparkdns.example.
ns2.fastparkdns.example.

Company records (expected):
ns1.shop-dns.example.
ns2.shop-dns.example.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this attack?

options.text: Domain hijacking through the compromised registrar account
options.why: The domain's delegation to its authoritative name servers was changed at the registrar, so every resolver on the internet receives the attacker's answers.

options.text: DNS cache poisoning of a recursive resolver
options.why: Poisoning affects users of one resolver's cache. Here customers on every ISP are affected and the public NS delegation itself has changed.

options.text: Hosts file changes made by malware on customer computers
options.why: A hosts file affects one machine at a time. It cannot redirect every customer worldwide or change the domain's public NS records.

options.text: Typosquatting on a look-alike domain registered by the attacker
options.why: Customers typed the correct domain. Typosquatting relies on a misspelled or similar name, not on changing the real domain's name servers.

takeaway: If your own domain's NS records suddenly point somewhere new, the registrar account was hijacked. Protect it with MFA and a registrar lock; cache poisoning only hits one resolver.

scenario: A legacy inventory API on the warehouse network uses HTTP Basic authentication over plain HTTP. The service account inv_sync normally runs only from the scheduler server at 10.20.1.15. After reviewing the log in the exhibit, the analyst concludes the 09:14 requests are a replay of captured credentials.
exhibit:
08:00:02 10.20.1.15  GET  /api/stock   Authorization: Basic <same token>  200
09:00:02 10.20.1.15  GET  /api/stock   Authorization: Basic <same token>  200
09:14:37 10.20.7.88  GET  /api/users   Authorization: Basic <same token>  200
09:14:41 10.20.7.88  POST /api/export  Authorization: Basic <same token>  200
stem: Which TWO changes would BEST prevent this from happening again? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Require TLS for all API traffic so credentials cannot be read in transit
options.why: The attacker could copy the header only because it crossed the network in clear text. Encrypting the channel removes the capture opportunity.

options.text: Replace the static Basic credential with short-lived tokens or client certificates
options.why: A token that expires quickly, or a certificate whose private key never crosses the wire, cannot be reused the way a static Base64 header can.

options.text: Lock the account after five failed attempts
options.why: The log shows no failures at all. Replay uses a credential that already works, so lockout never triggers.

options.text: Lengthen the inv_sync password to 20 characters
options.why: A longer password is captured and replayed just as easily. Replay never needs to guess or crack anything.

options.text: Rotate the inv_sync password every 90 days
options.why: A captured credential still works until the next rotation, which could be almost three months away.

options.text: Block 10.20.7.88 from reaching the API
options.why: That stops this one host, but the credential is still valid and the attacker can capture and reuse it from any other machine on the path.

takeaway: Basic authentication over HTTP is only Base64, so anyone on the path can capture and replay it. Encrypt the channel, use expiring credentials, and alert when service accounts appear from new sources.

scenario: A WIPS at a branch office raises the alerts in the exhibit. Shortly after each burst, the affected clients reconnect to the same corporate access point. The branch uses WPA2-Personal with a passphrase that has not changed in four years.
exhibit:
14:02:10  Deauthentication flood   src=AA:10:4F:22:9C:01 (spoofed BSSID of CORP-AP1)
          dst=ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff     1,240 frames in 3 s
14:02:14  12 clients re-associated to CORP-AP1 (EAPOL 4-way handshake x12)
14:02:15  Unknown device 3C:22:FB:9A:01:77  passive, never associated, RSSI -48 dBm
stem: Which of the following is the attacker MOST likely trying to do?

options.text: Capture the four-way handshake to crack the passphrase offline
options.why: Forcing clients to reconnect makes them repeat the handshake while a nearby passive device records it. A WPA2-Personal handshake can then be attacked offline with a wordlist.

options.text: Lure clients onto an evil twin access point using the same SSID
options.why: The clients rejoined the genuine access point, and no second AP advertising the corporate SSID was detected, which an evil twin requires.

options.text: Jam the 2.4 GHz band so that no client can stay connected
options.why: Jamming is continuous RF noise. This is a short burst of spoofed management frames, after which clients reconnect normally.

options.text: Replay a recorded handshake to join without knowing the passphrase
options.why: The handshake proves knowledge of the key without revealing it, and fresh nonces stop simple replay. The attacker must crack it first.

takeaway: Deauthentication bursts followed by mass reconnects usually mean handshake capture. Long passphrases, WPA3-SAE and 802.11w protected management frames blunt the attack.

scenario: The web server log in the exhibit comes from a product search page. The application never displays database errors, and the returned page looks identical for every request in the log.
exhibit:
Request                                              Status  Size     Time
cat=4                                                 200   1,820 B     41 ms
cat=4' AND SLEEP(5)...                                200   1,820 B  5,043 ms
cat=4' AND (if first letter of db user = a, SLEEP(5))  200   1,820 B     38 ms
cat=4' AND (if first letter of db user = w, SLEEP(5))  200   1,820 B  5,051 ms
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this activity?

options.text: Time-based blind SQL injection extracting data bit by bit
options.why: Each request asks the database a true or false question and the answer shows up only as a five-second delay, which is how blind SQL injection reads data without errors.

options.text: An application-layer denial-of-service attack slowing the search page
options.why: Only certain crafted requests are slow, by exactly five seconds, depending on a condition. That is a signaling channel, not resource exhaustion.

options.text: Reflected cross-site scripting through the category parameter
options.why: There is no script or HTML in the input. The injected text is SQL logic with a delay function, aimed at the database.

options.text: A buffer overflow probe sending oversized input to the parameter
options.why: The inputs are short and well formed. A buffer overflow sends far more data than the field expects, usually causing crashes.

takeaway: When a page never shows errors, attackers ask yes or no questions and time the answers. Parameterized queries stop it, and a fixed delay pattern in the logs gives it away.

scenario: An IDS on a plant network captured the payload in the exhibit, sent to a legacy license server on TCP 27000. Seconds later the license service crashed and restarted, and the server opened a connection back to the sender on TCP 4444.
exhibit:
IDS alert: oversized license request  10.9.4.20 -> 10.9.1.5:27000
  field length 2,310 bytes (protocol maximum for this field: 64)
  content: long run of 0x41 padding, then a run of 0x90, then binary code
10:41:07 license service terminated (access violation), restarted
10:41:09 TCP 10.9.1.5:51122 -> 10.9.4.20:4444 established
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this attack?

options.text: A buffer overflow that overwrites memory to run code
options.why: Input far longer than the field allows, padding, a NOP sled and binary code, followed by a crash and an outbound shell, are the marks of a buffer overflow exploit.

options.text: SQL injection against the license server's database
options.why: There is no SQL syntax anywhere in the payload. It is oversized binary content: padding, a run of NOP instructions and code.

options.text: A replay of a previously captured license request
options.why: A replay resends a legitimate captured message. This is oversized crafted input that crashed the service and gave the sender a shell.

options.text: Directory traversal to read the license file from disk
options.why: Traversal uses ../ sequences in a path to read files. Nothing here references a file, and the result was code execution.

takeaway: Long runs of padding such as 0x41, a NOP sled of 0x90 and machine code, followed by a crash and an outbound shell, signal a buffer overflow. DEP, ASLR and bounds checking defend against it.

scenario: A customer reports that $900 moved from her savings to an unknown payee while she was reading a hobby forum in another tab. She was still signed in to the bank in the same browser, and the request came from her usual home IP address. The bank logged the request in the exhibit.
exhibit:
POST /transfer HTTP/1.1
Host: bank.example
Origin: https://hobbyforum.example
Cookie: session=7f3a9c...e21   (valid, issued 14 minutes earlier)
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

to_account=88120934&amount=900
stem: Which of the following attacks does this request MOST likely show?

options.text: Cross-site request forgery riding the customer's existing session
options.why: A page on another site made her browser send a transfer the bank trusted because the valid session cookie came along automatically, with no anti-CSRF token checked.

options.text: Server-side request forgery that made the bank's server call itself
options.why: SSRF tricks the server into sending requests. Here the customer's own browser sent the request to the bank.

options.text: Session hijacking with a cookie stolen from the customer's device
options.why: A stolen cookie would be replayed from the attacker's machine. This request came from her home address with the forum as its Origin.

options.text: Stored cross-site scripting planted in the bank's transfer page
options.why: Stored XSS would run script inside the bank's own origin. The Origin header shows the request was started by the forum page.

takeaway: CSRF makes a victim's browser send a request it is already authenticated for. Anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies and Origin checks stop it; SSRF is the server being tricked instead.

scenario: A SaaS application lets customers enter a webhook URL and press Test. The application server's outbound request log in the exhibit shows tests submitted by one free-trial account within two minutes. The 10.0.3.0/24 network is not reachable from the internet.
exhibit:
webhook-test acct=trial-5512 GET http://10.0.3.10:22/                 -> "SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6"   3 ms
webhook-test acct=trial-5512 GET http://10.0.3.10:6379/               -> "-ERR wrong number of arguments for 'get' command"  4 ms
webhook-test acct=trial-5512 GET http://10.0.3.11:8500/v1/agent/self  -> 200  4,812 B
webhook-test acct=trial-5512 GET http://10.0.3.12:9200/_cat/indices   -> 200  22,190 B
stem: Which of the following BEST describes this activity?

options.text: Server-side request forgery used to probe internal services
options.why: The trial user supplies internal addresses and ports, and the application server fetches them and returns what it finds. The server is being used to reach places the user cannot.

options.text: An external port scan of the company's internal subnet
options.why: External hosts cannot reach 10.0.3.0/24. Every request came from the application server itself on behalf of the trial account.

options.text: Cross-site request forgery aimed at internal administrators
options.why: CSRF abuses a logged-in user's browser. These requests were generated by the server through its webhook feature.

options.text: Directory traversal through the webhook URL parameter
options.why: There are no ../ sequences or local file paths. The attacker is choosing internal hosts and ports, not escaping a folder.

takeaway: Any feature that fetches a user-supplied URL can become SSRF. Allow-list destinations, block private ranges and metadata addresses, and log what the server fetches.

scenario: A customer portal on a Windows server runs under the low-privilege identity IIS APPPOOL\Portal. Minutes after the portal accepted an unusual file upload, the server's Security log recorded the events in the exhibit.
exhibit:
10:12:40  4688  New process   cmd.exe   parent w3wp.exe   user IIS APPPOOL\Portal
10:13:05  4688  New process   net.exe   parent cmd.exe    user NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
10:13:05  4720  User account created     svc_backup2   by NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
10:13:06  4732  Member added to group    Administrators   member svc_backup2
10:15:30  4624  Logon type 10 (RDP)      svc_backup2   src 198.51.100.23
stem: Which of the following BEST describes what the attacker achieved?

options.text: Vertical privilege escalation from the web app identity to SYSTEM
options.why: Commands started under the low-privilege app pool identity and then ran as SYSTEM, a jump upward that let the attacker create and use an admin account.

options.text: Horizontal privilege escalation into another customer's portal account
options.why: Horizontal escalation moves sideways between accounts at the same level. Here the attacker reached the highest local privilege on the server.

options.text: Credential replay of a captured local administrator password
options.why: No administrator credential was used to reach SYSTEM. The privileged commands came from the web process chain, and the later RDP logon used a brand new account.

options.text: Routine activity by a backup agent that creates its own service account
options.why: A backup agent is not launched by the web worker process after an odd upload, and it would not add itself to Administrators and log in over RDP from the internet.

takeaway: A process chain that starts under a service identity and continues as SYSTEM or root, followed by new members of admin groups (events 4720 and 4732), is vertical privilege escalation with persistence.

scenario: A payment processor tags each transaction with a 64-bit truncated hash and treats two transactions with the same tag as duplicates, silently dropping the second. A tester shows that by generating many slightly different transaction records she can find two that share a tag far sooner than the team expected.
stem: About how many records must she generate for roughly a 50% chance that two share a tag?

options.text: About 2^32, the square root of the number of possible tags
options.why: The birthday paradox means a matching pair appears after roughly the square root of the space, 2^(64/2) (about 1.2 times 2^32 for exactly 50%). The tag offers only about 32 bits of collision resistance.

options.text: About 2^64, since every possible tag value must be tried
options.why: Trying every value is the ceiling for matching one specific tag. Finding any two records that match each other needs only about 2^32.

options.text: About 2^63, since half the tag space is searched on average
options.why: Half the space is the average cost of hitting one chosen target value. Any pair matching comes far sooner because the number of pairs grows with the square of the count.

options.text: About 2^16, since collision effort is a quarter of the tag length
options.why: The birthday bound is half the bit length, not a quarter. 2^16 records form only about 2^31 pairs among 2^64 values, a negligible chance.

takeaway: Birthday attacks find some collision in about 2^(n/2) attempts, so a 64-bit tag gives only about 32 bits of collision resistance. Use full-length hashes such as SHA-256 when collisions matter.

scenario: The identity provider's sign-in log in the exhibit covers one hour. Account lockout is set to 10 failures in 30 minutes. The analyst must decide what the pattern is and which accounts need immediate action.
exhibit:
Time   User        Source IP        Result
09:01  a.chen      45.155.204.11    Failure: bad password
09:01  b.ortiz     45.155.204.12    Failure: bad password
09:02  c.nwosu     45.155.204.13    Failure: bad password
 ...   1,402 accounts, 1 attempt each, all from 45.155.204.0/24
09:31  d.kaplan    45.155.204.40    Success (password), MFA not enrolled
09:33  d.kaplan    45.155.204.40    MFA method registered: new phone
09:40  e.ruiz      45.155.204.71    Success (password), MFA denied by user
09:52  f.grant     10.4.2.18        Failure x3, then Success, MFA approved
stem: Which TWO conclusions are BEST supported by the log? (Select TWO.)

options.text: This is password spraying, which stays below the lockout threshold
options.why: One attempt per account across 1,402 accounts from one address block is spraying. Each account sees a single failure, so lockout never fires.

options.text: d.kaplan is compromised and the attacker has registered an MFA device
options.why: A password success from the spraying range, with no MFA enrolled, followed by a new MFA device gives the attacker access and persistence.

options.text: e.ruiz's account was accessed, because the password step succeeded
options.why: The password is now known and must be reset, but the user denied the MFA prompt, so the attacker never completed the sign-in.

options.text: This is a brute force attack concentrated on a single account
options.why: Brute force hammers one account with many guesses. Here each account receives exactly one attempt.

options.text: f.grant's sign-in shows the attacker succeeding after several guesses
options.why: That sign-in comes from an internal address outside the spraying range, and three typos followed by success is ordinary user behavior.

options.text: Lowering the lockout threshold to 3 failures would have stopped it
options.why: Each account received only one attempt, so any threshold above one would still never trigger.

takeaway: Spraying shows one attempt per account across many accounts, so lockout never fires. A success followed by a new MFA registration is a compromised account with persistence; a denied MFA prompt still means the password must be reset.

scenario: Two weeks after a backup server holding an export of the HR application's user table, with unsalted SHA-1 hashes, was breached, attackers sign in to 37 HR accounts. Each sign-in succeeds on the first attempt, with no failed logins anywhere in the logs. Every compromised account had a password of eight characters or fewer, and no account with a long passphrase was touched.
stem: Which of the following MOST likely explains how the attackers obtained these passwords?

options.text: Offline brute force against the stolen hashes
options.why: Cracking the stolen hashes offline leaves no failed logins, and short passwords fall first while long passphrases resist, which matches the split exactly.

options.text: Online password spraying against the HR login page
options.why: Spraying generates failed logins across many accounts. Here every sign-in succeeded the first time and nothing failed.

options.text: Credential stuffing with passwords leaked from other websites
options.why: Stuffing produces failures for accounts that did not reuse a password, and success would depend on reuse rather than on password length.

options.text: A keylogger installed on HR staff workstations
options.why: A keylogger captures long passphrases as easily as short ones. The length pattern, right after the hash export was stolen, points to cracking.

takeaway: No failed logins plus a pattern where only short passwords fell points to offline cracking of stolen hashes. Salted, slow hashes such as bcrypt or Argon2 and long passwords are the defense.

scenario: A SIEM rule fires on the remote access VPN log in the exhibit. Both source addresses geolocate to the user's own city. The user says she worked from home all afternoon on her one company laptop.
exhibit:
13:05:12  user=pnair  src=73.21.44.190  Connected     device=LT-0442       MFA=push approved
14:22:47  user=pnair  src=98.62.17.5    Connected     device=DESKTOP-8KQ2  MFA=push approved
14:22:47  active sessions for pnair: 2
15:40:03  user=pnair  src=73.21.44.190  Disconnected  device=LT-0442
stem: Which indicator does this log MOST clearly show?

options.text: Concurrent session usage from two devices
options.why: One account holds two live sessions at once from different devices and addresses, and the user owns only one of them. That is concurrent session usage.

options.text: Impossible travel between two distant locations
options.why: Both addresses are in the user's city, so distance is not the problem. The anomaly is two simultaneous sessions.

options.text: Account lockout after repeated failed sign-ins
options.why: There are no failures in the log. Both connections succeeded, including the one from the unknown device.

options.text: Out-of-cycle logging at an unexpected time of day
options.why: Mid-afternoon on a workday is a normal time to connect. The timing is fine; the second device is not.

takeaway: Two live sessions for one user from different devices is concurrent session usage, even when geography looks normal. Here the user also approved a push she did not start, so reset credentials and review MFA.

scenario: The payroll export job is scheduled to run only at 01:00 on the 15th and the last day of each month, from the payroll server itself, and a full export is normally about 48 MB. While reviewing a quiet week, the analyst sees the entries in the exhibit.
exhibit:
2026-09-30 01:00:00  payroll-export started   user=svc_payroll  host=PAY-SRV01
   (no entries Oct 1 to Oct 13)
2026-10-14 13:47:12  payroll-export started   user=svc_payroll  host=WS-ACCT-07
2026-10-14 13:47:58  payroll-export wrote     /exports/full_employee_bank.csv (48 MB)
2026-10-14 13:48:30  sftp upload  dest=203.0.113.88  file=full_employee_bank.csv
stem: Which of the following BEST explains why these entries are suspicious?

options.text: The job ran outside its schedule and was started from a workstation
options.why: A mid-day run on the 14th, launched from an accounting PC and followed by an upload to an outside address, is out-of-cycle activity the schedule cannot explain.

options.text: The 48 MB export file points to excessive resource consumption
options.why: A full export is normally about that size. The size is ordinary; the timing, the source host and the destination are what stand out.

options.text: No entries appear for October 1 through 13, which shows log tampering
options.why: The job is not scheduled on those days, so silence is expected. The gap matches the baseline rather than signaling deleted logs.

options.text: The service account being used at all shows concurrent session usage
options.why: Only one session appears for svc_payroll. The problem is when and where it ran, not two sessions at once.

takeaway: Out-of-cycle logging means events at times or from places the schedule does not explain. Know the baseline, so an expected quiet gap is not mistaken for tampering and a mid-day batch run is not ignored.

scenario: A threat intelligence feed reports that a file of 220,000 records labeled with the company's name is for sale on a criminal forum, and the free sample matches real customers. SIEM, EDR and DLP show no exfiltration from company systems. The sample includes a campaign_segment column that exists only in the monthly export sent to the company's email marketing vendor.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST next step?

options.text: Notify the marketing vendor and start the third-party incident process
options.why: The column unique to the vendor's export ties the leaked data to the vendor's copy, so the investigation and contractual notice should start there.

options.text: Close the report as unfounded because internal monitoring found nothing
options.why: Published data is an indicator in its own right, and the sample matches real customers. Quiet internal logs fit a third-party source; they do not disprove the leak.

options.text: Reimage every server that stores customer data in case of hidden malware
options.why: Nothing links the leak to internal servers, and the unique column points elsewhere. Reimaging would cost a great deal and destroy evidence.

options.text: Buy the full data set from the forum to confirm exactly what was taken
options.why: Paying criminals funds them and may breach law or policy. The sample already identifies the likely source.

takeaway: Published or documented data is an indicator even when internal tools are quiet. Fields unique to one data flow show where the leak happened, often at a third party.

scenario: The help desk reports that the svc_reports account has locked out about every 30 minutes since its password was changed yesterday afternoon. The domain controller events for the lockouts are summarized in the exhibit.
exhibit:
Event 4740  A user account was locked out
  Account Name:          svc_reports
  Caller Computer Name:  RPT-SRV02
  (repeats every 30 to 35 minutes since 2026-10-15 17:10)

Event 4625  An account failed to log on
  svc_reports, workstation RPT-SRV02, logon type 4 (batch)
  5 failures within 2 minutes before each lockout
stem: Which of the following is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: A scheduled task on RPT-SRV02 still configured with the old password
options.why: Logon type 4 is a batch logon, every failure comes from the same server, and the lockouts began right after the password change. A task with a stale credential fits every detail.

options.text: Password spraying against service accounts from the internet
options.why: Spraying tries one guess against many accounts from external sources. Here one account fails repeatedly from one internal server.

options.text: An attacker on RPT-SRV02 brute forcing the svc_reports password
options.why: Nothing suggests an intruder on the server, and the failures began right when the password changed and repeat on a steady cycle. A stale stored credential is the far likelier cause to check first.

options.text: Two administrators sharing the account and creating concurrent sessions
options.why: Concurrent sessions are successful logons. These lockouts come from repeated failed logons.

takeaway: Not every lockout is an attack. Repeated lockouts from one internal host right after a password change usually mean a task, service or mapped drive with stale credentials.

scenario: A user has been on vacation for a week, and her office desktop has been locked the whole time. The web proxy shows the entries in the exhibit from that desktop every night.
exhibit:
02:00:04  10.6.3.41  CONNECT update-cdn-sync.top:443  BLOCKED  category=Newly Registered Domain
02:05:04  10.6.3.41  CONNECT update-cdn-sync.top:443  BLOCKED  category=Newly Registered Domain
02:10:05  10.6.3.41  CONNECT 185.62.190.7:443         BLOCKED  category=Uncategorized IP
02:15:04  10.6.3.41  CONNECT update-cdn-sync.top:443  BLOCKED  category=Newly Registered Domain
stem: Which of the following is the BEST conclusion?

options.text: Malware on the desktop is trying to reach its controller
options.why: Automated attempts every five minutes to a newly registered domain, with an IP fallback, on an unattended machine point to malware trying to call home.

options.text: The proxy is working as intended, so no further action is needed
options.why: The proxy stopped the connection, but something on the desktop is still trying every five minutes. The infection is still there.

options.text: The user is visiting prohibited sites and should be referred to HR
options.why: She is on vacation and the desktop is locked. Retries every five minutes are automated, not a person browsing.

options.text: The domain is a false positive and should be added to the allow list
options.why: A new domain contacted on a fixed interval with an IP fallback looks like command and control. Allowing it would let the malware connect.

takeaway: Blocked content is an indicator, not a resolution. Repeated, automated attempts to reach blocked destinations mean something on the host is still infected.

scenario: Monitoring alerts that free space on a file server's D: drive fell from 400 GB to 12 GB over two nights, while daytime CPU and network use look normal. The analyst finds the folder in the exhibit. It was created by an account that belongs to a contractor whose contract ended last month.
stem: Which of the following is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: Data staging in split archives ahead of exfiltration
options.why: Numbered 4 GB archive parts of engineering drawings, built at night in a hidden folder by an account that should be disabled, show data being gathered and chunked to move out.

options.text: Ransomware encrypting the engineering share in place
options.why: Ransomware encrypts the original files and leaves notes. Here the originals are untouched and copies are being compressed into a hidden folder.

options.text: Log files growing because verbose auditing was left enabled
options.why: Log growth would not produce numbered 7z archives of engineering drawings inside the Recycle Bin.

options.text: A backup job writing its weekly full backup to the wrong drive
options.why: Backups run under a backup service account and write to known targets. They do not hide in the Recycle Bin under a former contractor's account.

takeaway: Sudden disk consumption from split archives in a hidden folder is a staging indicator. Also disable accounts promptly when contracts end, since a leftover account did this.

scenario: At 02:13 on a Saturday, EDR on a file server records the events in the exhibit from a session that began with a domain admin account. No maintenance was scheduled.
exhibit:
02:13:04  Volume shadow copies deleted (all volumes)
02:13:09  Windows backup catalog deleted
02:13:15  Boot configuration: recovery disabled
02:14:30  Service stopped: SQL Server (MSSQLSERVER)
02:15:02  Process started: C:\PerfLogs\svch0st.exe
02:15:40  File renames 6,100 per minute, new extension .k7rz
stem: Which TWO conclusions are BEST supported? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The attacker is removing local recovery options before encrypting
options.why: Deleting shadow copies and the backup catalog and disabling boot recovery are classic ransomware steps to stop the victim restoring locally.

options.text: Files are being encrypted now, so the server should be isolated at once
options.why: Thousands of renames per minute to a new extension mean encryption is under way. Isolating the server limits further damage and spread.

options.text: The activity is routine maintenance because a domain admin account ran it
options.why: No maintenance was scheduled, and admin accounts are a favorite target. Who ran it does not make deleting recovery data routine.

options.text: Stopping SQL Server shows the goal is a denial of service on the database
options.why: Ransomware stops database services so their files are no longer locked and can be encrypted. The goal is extortion, not an outage for its own sake.

options.text: Restoring from the volume shadow copies will recover the files
options.why: The shadow copies were deleted at 02:13, so they are gone. Recovery has to come from offline or immutable backups.

options.text: The misspelled svch0st.exe shows the malware is a self-spreading worm
options.why: The look-alike name shows masquerading, but nothing in the log shows the code spreading to other hosts by itself.

takeaway: Deleted shadow copies and backup catalogs, stopped database services and mass renames to a new extension mean ransomware is running. Isolate first, then recover from offline backups.

scenario: On Monday the two cloud administrators cannot sign in to the company's cloud console root account. Password resets go to an email address neither recognizes, and their MFA prompts never arrive. The provider's audit log for the account is shown in the exhibit.
exhibit:
Sat 23:41  ConsoleLogin          success  src=91.240.118.7  MFA push approved on authenticator (A. Ruiz)
Sat 23:43  UpdateRecoveryEmail   admin@corp.example -> ops.cloudteam@mailbox.example
Sat 23:44  DeactivateMFADevice   authenticator (A. Ruiz)
Sat 23:45  EnableMFADevice       new virtual device
Sun 00:10  CreateAccessKey       key AKIA...7Q2
Sun 00:20  RunInstances          40 x GPU instance type, region ap-south-1
stem: Which TWO conclusions are BEST supported? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The account was taken over and the owners were locked out on purpose
options.why: Changing the recovery email and swapping the MFA device right after an unfamiliar login are deliberate steps to keep the real owners out, which explains the resource inaccessibility.

options.text: An administrator likely approved an MFA push that the attacker started
options.why: The 23:41 login from an unknown address succeeded only because a push was approved on A. Ruiz's authenticator, the original device, before the attacker replaced it. That points to MFA fatigue or a mistaken tap.

options.text: The lockout is a provider outage, since both administrators are affected
options.why: The audit log shows deliberate recovery and MFA changes from an unknown address, not a service failure.

options.text: The 40 GPU instances are a scheduled scaling event
options.why: They were launched with a newly created key minutes after the takeover. Sudden expensive compute is a resource consumption indicator, often of cryptomining.

options.text: The attacker used password spraying, since the log has no failed logins
options.why: Spraying leaves failed logins across many accounts. This log shows one successful login, which says nothing about spraying.

takeaway: Changed recovery details, swapped MFA devices and owners who suddenly cannot get in point to account takeover. Unexpected large compute launches right afterward are a resource consumption indicator.

scenario: At each store, a retailer's payment terminals, store PCs, guest Wi-Fi and security cameras share one flat network. The PCI DSS assessor says every device on that network is in scope. The company wants to shrink the scope and stop a compromised store PC from reaching the terminals.
stem: Which of the following would BEST achieve both goals?

options.text: Move the terminals to a segment that can reach only the processor
options.why: A separate segment with tight firewall rules keeps PCs, guests and cameras away from the terminals and takes those devices out of the cardholder data environment.

options.text: Install endpoint protection on every store PC and security camera
options.why: Endpoint protection helps the PCs, but everything still shares one network, so scope stays the same and many cameras cannot run an agent.

options.text: Enable WPA3 on the guest Wi-Fi so guests cannot eavesdrop on each other
options.why: Stronger Wi-Fi encryption protects wireless traffic, but guests and PCs still sit on the same network as the terminals.

options.text: Require MFA for every sign-in to the store PCs
options.why: MFA reduces stolen-password misuse, but a compromised PC could still reach the terminals and every device would remain in scope.

takeaway: Segmentation limits how far a compromise can spread and shrinks compliance scope. Devices that cannot reach the cardholder data environment can be taken out of scope.

scenario: EDR detects a known credential-stealing tool running on a sales laptop connected over home Wi-Fi. The incident response plan requires preserving memory and disk evidence, the user is in a meeting in another city, and the tool has not reached other hosts yet.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST immediate mitigation?

options.text: Use EDR network containment to isolate the laptop
options.why: Containment cuts the laptop off from everything except the EDR console, stopping spread while keeping memory and disk intact for investigators.

options.text: Tell the user to power off the laptop until IT can collect it
options.why: Powering off stops the tool but erases the memory evidence the plan says must be preserved.

options.text: Remotely wipe and reimage the laptop through device management
options.why: A wipe removes the malware along with every piece of evidence, and it skips learning what the tool already took.

options.text: Block the tool's known command domain at the corporate web proxy
options.why: The laptop is on home Wi-Fi and may not route through the proxy, and the tool can keep running and use other destinations.

takeaway: Isolation stops a host from talking to anything but the security tooling. It contains the threat while preserving evidence, which shutdown and reimaging do not.

scenario: An audit finds that the backup software's service account is a member of Domain Admins because it was easier during installation. The account only needs to read files on 40 servers and write to the backup appliance. Its password is stored in the backup console, which several junior operators can use.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST mitigation?

options.text: Grant only the backup rights it needs, not Domain Admins
options.why: Least privilege limits the account to reading the servers' files and writing to the appliance, so anyone who misuses it no longer controls the domain.

options.text: Rotate the service account's password every 30 days
options.why: Rotation changes the secret but not what the account can do. Whoever holds it at any moment still has full domain control.

options.text: Enable detailed auditing of every logon by the service account
options.why: Auditing helps detect misuse after it happens, but the account keeps rights far beyond its job.

options.text: Move the backup console onto a dedicated management VLAN
options.why: That narrows network access to the console, yet the account inside it still holds domain admin rights that operators can use.

takeaway: Least privilege means each account gets only the rights its job needs. Rotation, auditing and network placement do not shrink an overprivileged account's blast radius.

scenario: A company hardened 200 Linux servers by disabling SSH password login and root login. Six months later a scan finds 37 servers with both settings turned back on, mostly where administrators edited sshd_config by hand while troubleshooting and forgot to revert it.
stem: Which of the following would BEST prevent this from recurring?

options.text: Enforce the SSH baseline with a configuration management tool
options.why: A configuration management tool reapplies the approved settings on a schedule, so a forgotten manual change is corrected automatically.

options.text: Run the vulnerability scan monthly instead of every six months
options.why: More frequent scans find drift sooner, but someone still has to fix each server by hand, and nothing prevents the change.

options.text: Require an approved change request before anyone edits sshd_config
options.why: The drift came from administrators bypassing process while troubleshooting. A policy alone does not enforce or undo anything.

options.text: Re-harden the 37 servers by hand and document the correct settings
options.why: That fixes today's servers, but the same manual troubleshooting will reintroduce the drift later.

takeaway: Configuration enforcement continuously reapplies the approved baseline, so manual changes are corrected automatically. Scans and change control detect or discourage drift but do not undo it.

scenario: A marketing microsite hosted in a cloud storage bucket was retired and the bucket deleted. Its DNS record, promo.example.com as a CNAME to the bucket's provider hostname, was left in place. Weeks later an attacker created a bucket with the same name and served a phishing page at promo.example.com.
stem: Which missed decommissioning step would have prevented this?

options.text: Removing the DNS record that pointed to the bucket
options.why: With the CNAME gone, promo.example.com would point nowhere, and recreating the bucket name would give the attacker nothing under the company's domain.

options.text: Sanitizing the bucket's storage media to NIST SP 800-88
options.why: Media sanitization protects old data, which the provider handles. It does nothing about a live DNS record that anyone can claim.

options.text: Revoking the TLS certificate that was issued for the microsite
options.why: Revocation stops the old certificate, but the attacker who controls the content can obtain a new one because the name still points to them.

options.text: Archiving the microsite's content and access logs for retention
options.why: Retention is good practice but unrelated. The takeover exploited a DNS record that stayed live after the resource was deleted.

takeaway: Decommissioning is not done until every reference is removed: DNS records, firewall rules, accounts and certificates. A dangling CNAME lets anyone who claims the old name take over your subdomain.

scenario: CISA has added a remote code execution flaw in the company's internet-facing VPN appliance to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The vendor released fixed firmware yesterday, and an emergency change can be approved within hours. The IPS vendor has also published a signature for the exploit.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST mitigation?

options.text: Install the fixed firmware through an emergency change
options.why: The flaw is being exploited and a fix exists, so patching removes the vulnerability itself. The emergency change process makes it possible today.

options.text: Enable the IPS signature and patch in the next quarterly window
options.why: Turning on the signature for the few hours before patching is reasonable, but it is a compensating control attackers may evade, and waiting months on an actively exploited flaw leaves it open.

options.text: Increase monitoring of the VPN logs for signs of exploitation
options.why: Monitoring detects compromise after it happens. It does not close a hole that attackers are already using.

options.text: Move the VPN appliance behind the internal firewall
options.why: Remote users must still reach the VPN from the internet, so the vulnerable service stays exposed wherever it sits.

takeaway: When a fix exists for a vulnerability under active exploitation, patching is the mitigation. IPS signatures and monitoring are stopgaps for when a patch truly cannot be applied yet.

scenario: After a breach in which attackers dumped credentials from LSASS memory, the team wants servers to automatically stop any process that tries to read LSASS memory or inject into other processes, even signed admin tools. A HIDS already in place alerted during the breach, but nobody saw the alert until morning.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the requirement?

options.text: A host-based intrusion prevention system with behavioral rules
options.why: A HIPS watches process behavior on the server itself and can block a memory read or injection as it happens, without waiting for a person.

options.text: A network-based IPS at the data center edge
options.why: A network IPS inspects traffic on the wire and cannot see one process reading another process's memory inside a host.

options.text: A host-based firewall that allows only required ports
options.why: A host firewall controls connections in and out of the server, not what processes do to each other's memory.

options.text: Tuning the HIDS to page the on-call SOC analyst by text message
options.why: Faster alerts help, but a HIDS still only detects. The requirement is to stop the behavior automatically.

takeaway: A HIDS detects and alerts; a HIPS can block the behavior on the host as it happens. Network devices cannot see process-level activity such as LSASS reads.

scenario: A penetration tester on a hotel's guest Wi-Fi finds that a traveling employee's laptop answers on TCP 445 and 3389, so she can attempt logins against both. At the office, IT support needs those services, but only from the management subnet. The laptops already use full disk encryption and EDR.
stem: Which of the following BEST mitigates this exposure without breaking support at the office?

options.text: Host firewall rules limiting SMB and RDP to the management subnet
options.why: A host-based firewall travels with the laptop and drops those connections from any other network, including the hotel's, while IT can still connect at the office.

options.text: Disable SMB and RDP entirely on every laptop
options.why: That removes the exposure but also breaks the IT support the office relies on.

options.text: Connect to the VPN only when users need company file shares
options.why: The services keep listening on the hotel network whenever the VPN is down, which is most of the time in this plan.

options.text: Move the RDP listener to a nonstandard high port on every laptop
options.why: Changing the port is obscurity, since a scanner finds it in seconds, and SMB would remain exposed.

takeaway: A host-based firewall protects the device wherever it goes. Scope inbound management ports to the management subnet instead of disabling them or hiding them on odd ports.

scenario: An auditor asks how customer files on laptops would stay protected if a laptop were stolen and never connected to the internet again. The laptops currently use strong login passwords, MDM with remote wipe and EDR.
stem: Which additional control BEST addresses the auditor's concern?

options.text: Full disk encryption with a TPM and a preboot PIN
options.why: Encryption protects the data on the drive even when the laptop stays offline, and the drive cannot be read by removing it and attaching it elsewhere.

options.text: A shorter MDM check-in interval so remote wipe triggers sooner
options.why: A wipe still needs the laptop to connect. A thief who keeps it offline never receives the command.

options.text: A longer minimum length for the Windows login password
options.why: The login password does not protect the disk itself. Removing the drive or booting other media bypasses it.

options.text: GPS location tracking through the MDM agent
options.why: Tracking only works when the device reports in, and finding it does not protect the data meanwhile.

takeaway: Encryption at rest still works when the device is offline and in someone else's hands. Remote wipe and tracking depend on the device checking in.

scenario: Ransomware on one receptionist's PC encrypted 1.2 million files across every department folder on the main file server. The receptionist needs only to read the visitor policy folder and edit the front desk folder. The share and NTFS permissions on the server are Everyone: Full Control.
stem: Which of the following would MOST reduce how many files a similar infection could encrypt?

options.text: Group-based permissions matched to each role's folders
options.why: Malware acts with the rights of the user it runs as. If the receptionist can change only the front desk folder, that is all her infected PC can encrypt.

options.text: Install a second antivirus engine on the file server
options.why: The encryption ran on the PC and reached files over the share with valid rights, so the server's antivirus may never see a malicious file.

options.text: Take hourly snapshots of every file server volume and keep them for 30 days
options.why: Snapshots speed recovery afterward, but the infection could still encrypt every folder before anyone restores.

options.text: Encrypt the file server's volumes at rest
options.why: Encryption at rest protects against stolen disks. Ransomware works through the share with valid access and encrypts the files anyway.

takeaway: Permissions set the blast radius, because malware acts with the rights of the user it runs as. Grant each group only the folders and access level its role needs.

scenario: A new database server is being built from the vendor's default image. In production it will accept connections only from two application servers. The image includes a sample database, a web-based admin console, an FTP service used by the vendor's installer, and the built-in sa account with the documented vendor password.
stem: Which THREE hardening steps should be completed before it goes into production? (Select THREE.)

options.text: Change the sa password or disable the account
options.why: A documented vendor password is the first thing attackers try, so it must be changed or the account disabled.

options.text: Remove the sample database and the unused web console
options.why: Unneeded software adds attack surface and is often less carefully secured than the core product.

options.text: Disable the FTP service and block its port
options.why: The installer is finished with FTP, and leaving an unused clear-text service open only gives attackers another way in.

options.text: Allow the database port from any internal address on the host firewall
options.why: Only two application servers need access, so allowing every internal address is much broader than required.

options.text: Add a second database instance on the same host as a standby
options.why: A standby on the same host adds services to secure and does little for availability, since both fail with the host.

options.text: Rename the sa account but keep the vendor password
options.why: Renaming hides the name, but the documented password would still work for anyone who finds the account.

takeaway: Hardening removes what is not needed and changes what is default: unneeded software and samples, unused services and ports, and vendor passwords.

scenario: A vulnerability scan flags 14 critical issues in an old Java runtime on a file server. The server's owner confirms that nothing on the server uses Java; it was installed years ago for a tool that has since been retired.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST mitigation?

options.text: Uninstall the Java runtime from the server
options.why: Removing software nobody uses ends all 14 issues at once and every future flaw in that package, with no ongoing patching.

options.text: Update Java to the latest version and keep patching it
options.why: Updating fixes today's issues but keeps an unneeded package that will need patching for as long as the server runs.

options.text: Accept the risk because no application uses Java
options.why: Unused software can still be exploited if an attacker reaches it, and acceptance is hard to justify when removal is easy and cheap.

options.text: Deploy IPS signatures for the known Java exploits
options.why: That is a compensating control for software that can simply be removed, and it will not cover new flaws.

takeaway: Software nobody needs should be removed, not patched. Removal ends the vulnerability and every future one in that package.

scenario: A hospital is placing an inline IPS between its emergency department network and the systems that hold patient records and imaging. Clinicians must never lose access during a trauma case. The IPS vendor offers fail-open or fail-closed behavior if the appliance crashes.
stem: Which configuration BEST fits the hospital's priorities, and what is the trade-off?

options.text: Fail-open, accepting that traffic passes uninspected while the IPS is down
options.why: When availability is the overriding need, a crashed IPS should pass traffic rather than cut off clinicians. The trade-off is a window with no inspection, which monitoring and fast repair should cover.

options.text: Fail-closed, accepting that clinicians lose access while the IPS is down
options.why: Fail-closed favors security over availability. Losing access during a trauma case is exactly what the requirement forbids.

options.text: Fail-closed, because a medical environment must always put confidentiality first
options.why: Clinical systems usually put availability and integrity first. Confidentiality matters, but not by blocking care when a security appliance fails.

options.text: Fail-open, because an IPS that fails open still blocks known signatures
options.why: A failed-open IPS is effectively a wire. It blocks nothing until it recovers, so this reasoning is wrong even though the setting is right.

takeaway: Fail-open keeps traffic flowing when a security device fails (availability wins); fail-closed blocks it (security wins). Pick based on what the scenario says matters most.

scenario: Employees may use a sanctioned cloud storage service over HTTPS, but the company wants to block uploads to that service while still allowing downloads and viewing. The current firewall filters on IP address, protocol and port only.
stem: Which capability is required?

options.text: A next-generation firewall with TLS inspection and application-level control
options.why: Telling an upload from a download inside HTTPS requires decrypting the traffic and understanding the application's functions, which is what an NGFW with application awareness and TLS inspection does.

options.text: A stateful firewall rule that blocks TCP 443 to the service's IP range
options.why: Uploads and downloads both use TCP 443 to the same addresses, so a layer 4 rule can only block or allow the whole service.

options.text: A network IDS on a span port with a signature for large outbound files
options.why: An IDS on a span port can only alert. It cannot block the upload, and it cannot see inside the encryption without decryption anyway.

options.text: A site-to-site VPN between the office and the cloud storage provider
options.why: A VPN changes how the traffic travels, not what the user is allowed to do in the application.

takeaway: Controlling functions within an application (upload versus download) needs layer 7 inspection, and for HTTPS that means TLS inspection too.

scenario: A company has closed its offices. All 3,000 employees work from home or travel, and nearly every application is SaaS. Backhauling traffic through the headquarters VPN concentrator makes video calls unusable, but security wants consistent web filtering, CASB and zero trust access for everyone.
stem: Which architecture BEST meets these needs?

options.text: Secure access service edge, delivering security from cloud points of presence near users
options.why: SASE puts secure web gateway, CASB, ZTNA and firewalling in the cloud close to each user, so traffic goes straight to SaaS while still getting consistent policy, with no backhaul.

options.text: A larger VPN concentrator at headquarters with a full tunnel for every user
options.why: A bigger concentrator still forces all traffic through headquarters, which is the source of the latency, and there is no longer an office to protect.

options.text: Split tunneling so that all SaaS traffic goes directly to the internet without inspection
options.why: Split tunneling fixes performance by skipping the security stack, which drops the consistent filtering and CASB the requirement asks for.

options.text: SD-WAN connecting each employee's home router to the data center
options.why: SD-WAN optimizes links between sites. It is not a per-user security service, and these users have no branch site.

takeaway: SASE converges networking and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) as a cloud service near the user, the fit for a remote-first, SaaS-heavy workforce.

scenario: A developer deploys a web application to a platform-as-a-service offering. A scan finds an outdated, vulnerable version of a third-party library bundled with the application, and an outdated version of the language runtime provided by the platform.
stem: Under the shared responsibility model, who fixes each finding?

options.text: The customer updates the bundled library; the provider updates the runtime
options.why: In PaaS the provider manages the operating system and runtime, while the customer owns its code and the dependencies it ships with that code.

options.text: The provider updates both, because the platform hosts the application
options.why: Hosting the application does not make the provider responsible for what the customer packages inside it.

options.text: The customer updates both, because PaaS customers always manage the runtime
options.why: Managing the runtime is the provider's job in PaaS. In IaaS the customer would manage it.

options.text: The provider updates the library; the customer updates the runtime
options.why: This reverses the model. The customer cannot patch the platform's runtime, and the provider does not maintain customer code.

takeaway: Moving from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS, the provider takes on more of the stack. In PaaS the customer still owns application code, its dependencies, data and access.

scenario: A team manages cloud infrastructure with infrastructure as code. A review finds database passwords and an API key written directly in Terraform files that are committed to a Git repository shared by 60 developers.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST remediation?

options.text: Move the secrets to a secrets manager, rotate them and scan commits for secrets
options.why: The secrets are already exposed in history, so they must be rotated. Storing them in a secrets manager keeps them out of code, and commit scanning stops it from happening again.

options.text: Make the repository private and remove the secrets from the files in a new commit
options.why: The secrets remain in the commit history, and 60 developers still had access. Without rotation, the exposure continues.

options.text: Encode the secrets in Base64 inside the Terraform files
options.why: Base64 is encoding, not encryption. Anyone can reverse it instantly.

options.text: Stop using infrastructure as code and configure the cloud by hand
options.why: This throws away IaC's consistency and auditability without solving secret handling, which is the real problem.

takeaway: Secrets do not belong in code or IaC templates. Once committed, assume they are compromised: rotate, move to a vault and add secret scanning.

scenario: A water utility's SCADA network controls chemical dosing. Its PLCs run vendor firmware that can only be updated during an annual shutdown, and an unplanned reboot can disrupt treatment. A consultant recommends weekly automated patching like the corporate network.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST response to the consultant?

options.text: Keep patching to planned windows and rely on segmentation and monitoring in between
options.why: Industrial systems put availability and safety first, so disruptive patching is scheduled, and compensating controls such as strict segmentation and monitoring cover the gap.

options.text: Adopt weekly automated patching because unpatched systems are always the biggest risk
options.why: Unplanned reboots of dosing controllers could create a safety incident. In ICS, the cure would be worse than the disease.

options.text: Connect the PLCs to the corporate network so they receive patches faster
options.why: Bridging SCADA to the corporate network increases exposure dramatically, which is the opposite of what the environment needs.

options.text: Replace the PLCs with general-purpose servers that can be patched weekly
options.why: General-purpose servers do not provide the deterministic, real-time control PLCs exist for, and replacement is not a realistic security fix.

takeaway: ICS, SCADA and RTOS environments trade patch speed for availability and safety. Segmentation, monitoring and planned maintenance windows compensate.

scenario: Two banks want to run a joint fraud model on combined customer data in a public cloud. Each bank's data is encrypted at rest and in transit, but each bank worries that the cloud provider's administrators could read the data while it is being processed.
stem: Which technology BEST addresses this concern?

options.text: Confidential computing with hardware-based secure enclaves
options.why: The gap is data in use. Secure enclaves keep data encrypted in memory and isolated from the host and its administrators while it is processed.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the virtual machines with customer-managed keys
options.why: Disk encryption protects data at rest. Once the VM is running, the data in memory is in plaintext.

options.text: TLS 1.3 with mutual authentication between the banks and the cloud
options.why: TLS protects data in transit, which is already covered. It does nothing once the data is being processed.

options.text: Tokenizing customer identifiers before uploading the data
options.why: Tokenization hides identifiers but the model still processes the remaining data in plaintext in memory, and the fraud model may need the real values.

takeaway: Three states, three answers: at rest (disk, database encryption), in transit (TLS, IPsec), in use (secure enclaves, confidential computing).

scenario: A German health insurer moves to a global cloud provider. Regulators require that personal health data never be stored or processed outside the EU. The provider's default backup policy replicates data to the nearest three regions worldwide.
stem: Which control MOST directly addresses the regulatory requirement?

options.text: Restrict storage, processing and backups to EU regions with location policies
options.why: Data sovereignty is about where data lives and is processed. Region restrictions, applied to backups and replicas too, keep every copy inside the required jurisdiction.

options.text: Encrypt the data with keys held by the insurer before uploading it
options.why: Encryption is valuable, but encrypted data replicated outside the EU is still stored outside the EU, which the regulation forbids.

options.text: Sign a data processing agreement with the provider
options.why: An agreement sets obligations but does not by itself stop the default policy from copying data abroad.

options.text: Tokenize member names before storing the data in the cloud
options.why: Health data tied to tokens is still personal data, and the copies would still leave the EU.

takeaway: Sovereignty and geolocation requirements are met by controlling where every copy, including backups and replicas, is stored and processed.

scenario: After an online store added a load balancer in front of four web servers using round-robin, customers report being logged out and losing their carts at random. Each web server keeps session state in its own memory.
stem: Which change would BEST fix the problem while keeping the load balancing?

options.text: Enable session persistence or move session state to a shared store
options.why: Round-robin sends each request to the next server, which does not have the session. Persistence keeps a user on the same server, and a shared session store lets any server handle any request.

options.text: Switch the load balancer from round-robin to least connections
options.why: Least connections still spreads one user's requests across servers, so the session problem remains.

options.text: Add two more web servers to reduce the load on each one
options.why: More servers make it even more likely that a request lands on a server without the session.

options.text: Switch from active-active to active-passive load balancing for the web pool
options.why: Active-passive avoids the problem only by sending everything to one server, which gives up the load balancing the store wanted.

takeaway: Stateful applications behind load balancers need session persistence (sticky sessions) or shared session storage.

scenario: A company replicates its file servers synchronously to a second data center and considers that its backup strategy. Ransomware encrypts the primary file servers at 14:05. The CIO wants to recover to 14:00 at the latest.
stem: What is the MOST likely outcome, and what should have been in place?

options.text: The replica is encrypted too; frequent immutable snapshots or backups were needed
options.why: Synchronous replication faithfully copies the encrypted files within seconds. Recovering to a point before the attack requires point-in-time copies the attacker cannot modify.

options.text: The replica is clean, because replication only copies data on a schedule
options.why: Synchronous replication writes to both sites at once, so the encryption reached the replica almost immediately.

options.text: The replica is clean, because ransomware cannot cross between data centers
options.why: Replication carries any change, malicious or not, so the ransomware does not need to cross anything itself.

options.text: The replica is encrypted, but an RAID 6 array at the primary site will restore the files
options.why: RAID protects against disk failure, not against encrypted data written by the operating system. It mirrors the damage.

takeaway: Replication and RAID copy mistakes and malware instantly. Backups and snapshots, especially immutable or offline ones, give you a point in time to go back to.

scenario: A payment processor wants to prove that its recovery site can actually process transactions correctly. Regulators will not accept a discussion-only exercise, and the business will not accept any interruption to production.
stem: Which type of test BEST fits?

options.text: A parallel processing test that runs real workloads at both sites side by side
options.why: Running the same transactions at the recovery site while production keeps operating proves real processing capability without interrupting customers.

options.text: A full failover test that moves all production workloads over to the recovery site
options.why: A real failover is the most thorough test but risks interrupting production, which the business has ruled out.

options.text: A tabletop exercise that walks the team through the recovery plan
options.why: A tabletop is discussion only, which regulators said they will not accept.

options.text: A simulation in which the team role-plays a data center outage
options.why: A simulation exercises people and decisions, but it does not prove that the systems at the recovery site can actually process transactions.

takeaway: Tabletop: talk it through. Simulation: rehearse the scenario. Parallel processing: run both sites at once with no outage. Failover: actually switch, the most realistic and most disruptive.

scenario: A data center has a diesel generator that takes about 40 seconds to start and stabilize after a utility power failure. During the last outage, every server rebooted before the generator came online.
stem: Which addition MOST directly prevents this?

options.text: A UPS sized to carry the load for at least the generator's start-up time
options.why: A UPS provides immediate battery power, bridging the seconds between the utility failure and the generator taking over.

options.text: A second generator from a different manufacturer
options.why: A second generator also needs time to start, so the gap that caused the reboots remains.

options.text: Dual power supplies in every server
options.why: Dual supplies protect against a failed power supply or circuit. If both are fed from the same failing source, the servers still lose power.

options.text: A managed PDU with remote outlet control
options.why: A PDU distributes and controls power. It does not store energy to cover an outage.

takeaway: Generators handle long outages but start slowly; a UPS bridges the gap and conditions power. You usually need both.

scenario: Remote employees connect through a VPN that sends only traffic for corporate subnets through the tunnel. An incident shows that a laptop was infected while browsing on hotel Wi-Fi, and corporate web filtering never saw the traffic.
stem: Which change would BEST ensure that all of a remote employee's internet traffic is inspected?

options.text: Switch the VPN to a full tunnel so all traffic passes corporate controls
options.why: The current split tunnel lets internet traffic bypass the corporate stack. A full tunnel routes everything through it, so web filtering and other controls see all traffic.

options.text: Increase the VPN encryption from AES-128 to AES-256
options.why: Stronger encryption protects the tunnel, but the problem is traffic that never enters the tunnel.

options.text: Require all employees to disconnect and reconnect the VPN every eight hours
options.why: Reconnecting more often does not change which traffic goes through the tunnel.

options.text: Move the VPN concentrator into the screened subnet
options.why: Where the concentrator sits does not change the split tunneling that lets browsing bypass inspection.

takeaway: Split tunnel: better performance, less visibility. Full tunnel: everything inspected, more load. The question's priority decides which one is correct.

scenario: The security team needs visibility of all traffic between the data center's web tier and database tier, including malformed packets, at a full 10 Gbps. The network team refuses anything that could drop or delay production traffic if it fails.
stem: Which deployment BEST meets both teams' requirements?

options.text: A passive network TAP feeding an IDS sensor
options.why: A hardware TAP copies every packet, including errored frames, at line rate, and it is passive, so if the sensor fails production traffic is unaffected.

options.text: An inline IPS between the web tier and the database tier
options.why: Inline placement can drop or delay traffic if the device fails or is overloaded, which the network team refuses.

options.text: A SPAN port on the core switch feeding an IDS sensor
options.why: SPAN is passive, but switches commonly drop mirrored packets under heavy load and do not forward malformed frames, so it may not give complete visibility at 10 Gbps.

options.text: NetFlow export from the core switch to the SIEM
options.why: NetFlow summarizes connections without packet contents, so the team would not see malformed packets or payloads.

takeaway: Inline means it can block but can also break things; a TAP is passive and complete; SPAN is passive but can drop packets under load.

scenario: A company is enabling 802.1X on every switch port. Laptops authenticate with certificates, but 200 printers and badge readers cannot run an 802.1X supplicant.
stem: Which approach BEST keeps those devices working without leaving their ports wide open?

options.text: Use MAC authentication bypass with profiling and a restricted VLAN
options.why: Devices without supplicants can authenticate by MAC address, profiling reduces spoofing, and a restricted VLAN limits what a spoofed MAC could reach.
