options.text: Disable 802.1X on every switch port where a printer or badge reader is connected
options.why: This leaves those ports fully open to anyone who unplugs a printer and connects a laptop.

options.text: Give the printers and badge readers a shared username and password
options.why: Devices that cannot run a supplicant cannot use username and password EAP either, and a shared credential would be weak anyway.

options.text: Move the printers and badge readers to the guest wireless network
options.why: Badge readers and printers need internal resources, and the guest network should only reach the internet.

takeaway: 802.1X needs a supplicant. For headless devices, MAC authentication bypass plus profiling and a restricted VLAN is the usual compensating approach.

scenario: An e-commerce platform was split into 35 microservices that call each other over the internal network. A penetration tester who compromised one container could call the payment service's API directly, because internal calls are trusted by network location alone.
stem: Which control BEST addresses this?

options.text: Mutual TLS between services, with each service authorizing which callers it accepts
options.why: mTLS gives every service a verifiable identity, and per-service authorization means a compromised container can only call what its own identity allows.

options.text: A larger perimeter firewall in front of the container platform
options.why: The attacker was already inside the perimeter. The problem is implicit trust between internal services.

options.text: Running every microservice in the same container to reduce network calls
options.why: Collapsing everything into one container removes isolation entirely and undoes the architecture.

options.text: Encrypting the container images stored in the registry
options.why: Encrypted images protect the images at rest. They do not control which running service may call another.

takeaway: Microservices widen the attack surface. Zero trust between services, using authenticated identities such as mTLS plus per-call authorization, replaces trust by network location.

scenario: A licensing server can only run as a single active instance at a time. The business wants it to survive a hardware failure with no more than a few seconds of interruption.
stem: Which design BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: An active-passive cluster with heartbeat monitoring and automatic failover
options.why: Only one node may be active, so the standby waits and takes over automatically when the heartbeat stops, giving a short interruption.

options.text: An active-active cluster with round-robin load balancing
options.why: Active-active runs several instances at once, which this software does not allow.

options.text: Nightly backups restored to new hardware after a failure
options.why: Restoring from backup takes far longer than a few seconds and loses changes since the last backup.

options.text: A cold site with spare hardware and the installation media
options.why: A cold site takes days to bring up, nowhere near a few seconds.

takeaway: Active-active shares load across live nodes; active-passive keeps a standby ready to take over. Software that allows only one live instance needs active-passive.

scenario: A factory sends production data from its plant network to an analytics service in the cloud over the internet.
stem: Which of the following would protect the confidentiality of the data while it is in transit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: An IPsec site-to-site tunnel using ESP between the plant and the cloud network
options.why: ESP encrypts the packets for the whole trip between the two gateways.

options.text: TLS 1.3 between the plant's data collector and the cloud API
options.why: TLS encrypts the application connection end to end between collector and API.

options.text: SHA-256 hashes calculated for each batch of production data
options.why: Hashes detect changes to the data. They do not hide its contents.

options.text: RAID 10 on the analytics service's storage
options.why: RAID provides availability for stored data. It has nothing to do with data moving over the network.

options.text: An IPsec tunnel using AH only
options.why: AH authenticates packets but does not encrypt them, so the data is still readable in transit.

takeaway: Confidentiality in transit comes from encryption: TLS or IPsec ESP. AH and hashing give integrity, not confidentiality.

scenario: Audit logs show 140 workstations have made RDP and SSH connections to domain controllers and network devices over the past month. Only 12 administrators should ever do this.
stem: Which design change BEST reduces this attack surface while still letting administrators work?

options.text: Allow management protocols only from a hardened, monitored jump server
options.why: Forcing all administration through one hardened, logged chokepoint shrinks the attack surface from 140 machines to one and gives a single place to monitor and record sessions.

options.text: Block RDP and SSH completely at every firewall in the network
options.why: Administrators still need these protocols, so a total block stops legitimate work.

options.text: Move the domain controllers to a different subnet with a new address range
options.why: A new address range does nothing unless access is also restricted, and it is easily discovered.

options.text: Change the default RDP and SSH ports on every server
options.why: Non-standard ports are obscurity. Scanners find them quickly and the access remains open to everyone.

takeaway: Jump servers (bastion hosts) concentrate privileged access into one hardened, monitored path into the management zone.

scenario: A startup runs its back end as serverless functions. A review finds that one function, which only reads from a single storage bucket, runs with an identity that has administrator rights to the entire cloud account.
stem: Which risk does this create, and what is the fix?

options.text: A compromise of that function compromises the whole account; scope its role to read that one bucket
options.why: In serverless the customer still owns identities and permissions. A bug or injected input in the function would inherit administrator rights, so least privilege on the function's role is the fix.

options.text: The provider may patch the function's runtime late; move the function to a virtual machine you patch yourself
options.why: Runtime patching is the provider's job in serverless, and moving to a VM adds operational burden without fixing the excessive permissions.

options.text: The function could run out of memory; increase its memory allocation
options.why: Memory limits affect performance and cost, not the security exposure of an over-privileged identity.

options.text: The function's code is stored in plaintext; encrypt the deployment package
options.why: Encrypting the package protects code at rest but leaves the administrator role untouched.

takeaway: Serverless removes server patching from your list but not identity and permissions. Over-privileged function roles are one of the biggest serverless risks.

scenario: A tax preparation firm's systems slow to a crawl every April, the help desk is overwhelmed, and last year the SOC missed alerts because analysts were helping with tickets.
stem: Which activity BEST addresses this recurring problem?

options.text: Capacity planning that covers people, technology and infrastructure for the seasonal peak
options.why: The problem spans staffing, system resources and infrastructure at a predictable peak. Capacity planning addresses all three before the peak arrives.

options.text: A disaster recovery test of the firm's warm site
options.why: Nothing has failed. The systems and people are overloaded by predictable demand, which a DR test does not address.

options.text: A tabletop exercise on responding to a DDoS attack
options.why: The slowdown comes from legitimate seasonal demand, not an attack.

options.text: Doubling the SIEM's log retention period
options.why: Longer retention does not help analysts who are too busy to look at alerts in the first place.

takeaway: Capacity planning considers people, technology and infrastructure. Predictable peaks are a planning problem, not an incident.

scenario: A retailer with 400 stores lets each store manager configure their own store's firewall. Audits find 400 different rule sets, many with any-any rules added to fix connectivity problems quickly.
stem: Which change BEST addresses the root cause?

options.text: Centrally manage store firewalls with a standard template that local staff cannot override
options.why: Decentralized administration produced inconsistent, weak configurations. Central management with an enforced baseline makes every store consistent and auditable.

options.text: Train every store manager on firewall rule writing
options.why: Training helps, but 400 independent administrators will still drift apart. The issue is the decentralized model itself.

options.text: Replace the store firewalls with higher-throughput models
options.why: Throughput is not the problem. The weak rules would simply be copied onto faster hardware.

options.text: Ask each store manager to submit their rule set once a year for review
options.why: Annual reviews catch problems long after they are introduced and do not stop managers adding any-any rules in between.

takeaway: Decentralized administration trades consistency for local flexibility. When consistency fails, centralize management and enforce a baseline.

scenario: A company runs its order database on virtual machines in an IaaS cloud. Attackers exploited a remote code execution flaw in the guest operating system that had a patch available for five months. Management asks who failed to apply it, and the contract includes the responsibility matrix below.
stem: Based on the exhibit, which of the following BEST describes responsibility for the missed patch?
exhibit:
Layer                     On-prem    IaaS       PaaS       SaaS
Physical facilities       Customer   Provider   Provider   Provider
Hypervisor and hosts      Customer   Provider   Provider   Provider
Guest operating system    Customer   Customer   Provider   Provider
Application code          Customer   Customer   Customer   Provider
Data and access settings  Customer   Customer   Customer   Customer

options.text: The customer, because the guest OS is a customer layer in IaaS
options.why: The matrix assigns the guest operating system to the customer under IaaS. The provider stops at the hypervisor and host, so patching inside the VM was the company's job.

options.text: The provider, because it patches the hosts that run every customer VM
options.why: The provider does patch the physical hosts and hypervisor, but that layer is separate from the guest OS running inside the customer's VM.

options.text: Shared equally, because IaaS splits operating system duties between both parties
options.why: The matrix does not split the guest OS row in IaaS. It lists the customer alone, so there is no shared duty to point to.

options.text: The provider, because the flaw was in an image the provider's marketplace supplied
options.why: Even when a VM starts from a provider image, the customer owns the guest OS once it is launched, including every later patch.

takeaway: In IaaS the provider stops at the hypervisor; the guest OS, applications and data belong to the customer. PaaS shifts the OS to the provider and SaaS shifts the application, but data and access settings always stay with the customer.

scenario: A law firm moves its email and document storage to a SaaS suite. The managing partner assumes the provider now handles all of security, and the CISO is writing a one-page summary of what the firm still owns.
stem: Which of the following remain the firm's responsibility? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configuring user accounts, MFA and document sharing settings
options.why: Identity and access settings inside the tenant are always the customer's. A missing MFA policy or an open sharing link is the firm's failure, not the provider's.

options.text: Classifying the firm's documents and deciding who may see them
options.why: Data ownership never moves to the provider. The firm still decides how sensitive each document is and who should have access to it.

options.text: Patching the mail server software that runs the service
options.why: In SaaS the provider runs and patches the application itself. The firm has no access to the servers or the software that runs them.

options.text: Hardening the operating systems of the provider's servers
options.why: The operating systems belong to the provider's layer in SaaS. The firm cannot reach them and is not expected to harden them.

options.text: Maintaining physical security at the provider's data centers
options.why: Physical security is the provider's duty in every cloud model. The firm can review it through audit reports such as SOC 2, but it does not perform it.

takeaway: In SaaS the provider runs everything up to and including the application, but the customer still owns its data, its users and how its tenant is configured.

scenario: A 40-person accounting firm must replace its aging practice management server. It has one part-time IT contractor, nobody available to apply patches, and wants to recover from an outage within one business day without paying for a second site. The shortlist is below.
stem: Which choice BEST fits the firm's stated considerations?
exhibit:
Model                  Who patches OS/app  Recovery approach               Yearly cost
New on-prem server     Firm                Restore from tape               $9,000
IaaS VMs in two zones  Firm                Zone failover, firm managed     $16,000
SaaS practice suite    Provider            Provider multi-region failover  $14,000
Colocated server pair  Firm                Manual failover to rack 2       $21,000

options.text: The SaaS practice suite with provider-managed patching and recovery
options.why: The firm cannot patch or run failover itself. SaaS removes both duties and its multi-region recovery meets the one-day goal at a mid-range cost.

options.text: The new on-premises server, because it has the lowest yearly cost
options.why: Cost was not the stated priority. The firm would still have to patch the server with no staff, and a tape restore of a single server may exceed a day.

options.text: The IaaS VMs, because two availability zones give the strongest resilience
options.why: The zones are resilient, but the firm would still patch the OS and application and manage failover, which it has nobody to do.

options.text: The colocated pair, because a second rack allows fast manual recovery by the contractor
options.why: It is the most expensive option, still leaves patching with the firm, and manual failover depends on a part-time contractor being available.

takeaway: Weigh architecture considerations against the stated constraints. When an organization cannot patch or run recovery itself, patch responsibility and ease of recovery often point to SaaS even when it is not the cheapest option.

scenario: A retailer is moving its loyalty program to a third-party SaaS vendor. The contract includes an indemnification clause, and the retailer carries cyber insurance. The CFO argues that if the vendor is breached all liability moves to the vendor, so a vendor security review is unnecessary.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes the retailer's position?

options.text: It transfers some financial risk but stays accountable for the customer data
options.why: Contracts and insurance shift part of the financial impact, but regulators and customers still hold the data owner accountable, so assessing the vendor remains necessary.

options.text: It has transferred the breach risk entirely through the contract and insurance
options.why: Accountability for customer data cannot be handed off. Breach notification, regulatory penalties and reputational harm still land on the retailer.

options.text: It has avoided the risk, because the data no longer sits on its own systems
options.why: Avoidance means stopping the risky activity. The retailer still collects and uses the loyalty data; it has only changed who hosts it.

options.text: It has accepted the risk, so reviewing the vendor is now optional
options.why: Signing an indemnity and buying insurance is transference, not acceptance, and due diligence on a vendor holding customer data is expected either way.

takeaway: Outsourcing to a third-party vendor and buying insurance are forms of risk transference that move part of the financial impact. Accountability for the data, and the duty to assess the vendor, stay with the organization.

scenario: A company deploys its cloud networks with infrastructure as code. During an outage, engineers opened a security group to 0.0.0.0/0 through the web console and never reverted it. Weeks later, a scheduled pipeline run silently removed a different emergency fix and broke a partner integration.
stem: Which of the following would BEST prevent both problems?

options.text: Make the code the only change path and alert on drift from it
options.why: If every change goes through the code, the open rule would have been reviewed and the emergency fix would live in code, and drift alerts catch any console change that slips through.

options.text: Allow console access only to senior engineers during outages
options.why: Fewer people making untracked console changes is still untracked change. Drift from the code would keep happening, just less often.

options.text: Take daily snapshots of every security group configuration
options.why: Snapshots record state after the fact but do not reconcile it with the code, so neither the open rule nor the overwritten fix would be prevented.

options.text: Stop scheduled pipeline runs so that manual fixes are never overwritten again
options.why: This fixes the second symptom by making drift permanent. The open security group would stay forever and the environment would no longer match its code.

takeaway: Infrastructure as code only delivers consistency when the code is the source of truth. Put emergency changes into the code and use drift detection to catch console changes.

scenario: A platform team will publish one infrastructure-as-code module that 30 business units will use to build their reporting storage. Before it is published, you review the excerpt below.
stem: Which settings should block publication of the module? (Select TWO.)
exhibit:
storage_bucket "reports":
  access_acl      = "public-read"
  versioning      = enabled
  encryption      = kms (customer-managed key)

firewall_rule "admin":
  direction = ingress   port = 22/tcp   source = 0.0.0.0/0

log_group "reports":
  retention_days  = 365

options.text: The public-read access setting on the reports bucket
options.why: A public-read bucket exposes every report to the internet, and because the module is reused, the exposure would be copied into all 30 environments.

options.text: The admin rule allowing port 22 from any source address
options.why: SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0 invites brute force and exploit attempts from the whole internet. Management access should come from a known range or a bastion.

options.text: Versioning enabled on the reports bucket
options.why: Versioning keeps earlier copies of objects, which helps recovery from accidental deletion or ransomware. It is a good default, not a problem.

options.text: Encryption with a customer-managed KMS key
options.why: Encrypting the bucket with a customer-managed key strengthens protection at rest and gives the team control over key access and rotation.

options.text: Log retention of 365 days on the reports log group
options.why: A year of log retention supports investigations and compliance. It adds some storage cost but is not a security flaw.

takeaway: An IaC module multiplies whatever it contains, good or bad. Scan templates in the pipeline for public storage and internet-facing management ports before they are copied to every environment.

scenario: A company runs its order intake as serverless functions. After unusual outbound traffic is traced to the function's account, the incident response team asks for a disk image of the server that ran it. The provider confirms the execution environments were recycled minutes after each run and no host access is offered.
stem: Which of the following should the team have done BEFORE the incident to support this investigation?

options.text: Send function logs and traces to a central, retained log store
options.why: Serverless hosts are short-lived and never exposed to the customer, so evidence has to be captured by design through logging and tracing that outlive each run.

options.text: Take scheduled disk images of the hosts that run the functions
options.why: The customer has no access to the hosts in a serverless model. The provider manages and recycles them, so there is nothing to image.

options.text: Raise the function timeout so instances stay running long enough to review
options.why: A longer timeout only lets a single run last longer. Environments are still recycled, and nobody can log in to inspect them.

options.text: Pin each function to a dedicated server that is kept for evidence
options.why: Serverless platforms do not offer customer-controlled servers. Requiring one means moving away from serverless rather than preparing it for incidents.

takeaway: Serverless functions are ephemeral and the host is never yours to examine. Plan for incidents with centralized logging, tracing and retention configured before anything goes wrong.

scenario: A hosting company will run code uploaded by untrusted customers. Engineers propose packing every customer's workload as containers on a shared fleet of hosts to cut costs. Security worries that one customer could break out of isolation and reach the others.
stem: Which of the following BEST explains the concern and the stronger design?

options.text: Containers share the host kernel; give each customer its own VM
options.why: A kernel exploit inside one container can reach the shared kernel and every other container. Each VM runs its own kernel behind a hypervisor, a much stronger tenant boundary.

options.text: Containers lack network isolation; put each customer on its own VLAN
options.why: Container networking can be isolated with network policies. The core risk is the shared kernel, which a VLAN does nothing to address.

options.text: Container images can be altered; sign every image before it is deployed
options.why: Signing protects the integrity of images the company builds. Here the threat is customer code itself, and signing it does not stop a breakout.

options.text: VMs share the host kernel as well; run each customer on dedicated bare-metal servers
options.why: VMs do not share a kernel; each guest has its own. Bare metal per customer would work but is far costlier than VM isolation requires.

takeaway: Containers isolate processes but share one kernel, so a kernel exploit can cross tenants. Virtual machines each run their own kernel behind a hypervisor, a stronger boundary for untrusted workloads.

scenario: A scan of production finds a critical OpenSSL flaw in 60 running containers that were all built from the same base image. An engineer plans to open a shell in each container and run the package manager to update OpenSSL in place.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST approach?

options.text: Rebuild the image from a patched base, scan it and redeploy
options.why: Fixing the image fixes every future container at once, keeps environments consistent, and the scan confirms the flaw is gone before rollout.

options.text: Patch each running container in place with the package manager
options.why: Changes made inside a running container are lost when it is recreated from the old image, so the flaw returns at the next restart or scale-out.

options.text: Patch the OpenSSL package on the container hosts instead
options.why: Containers carry their own user-space libraries inside the image. Updating the host's copy of OpenSSL does not change the library each container uses.

options.text: Restart the containers so that they pull the latest updates automatically
options.why: A restart launches the same image again. Containers do not update their packages on their own when they start.

takeaway: Treat containers as immutable: fix the image, not the running instance. Rebuild from a patched base image, scan it in the pipeline or registry, and redeploy.

scenario: An audit of a virtualization cluster finds 420 virtual machines, but the inventory lists only 260. Most of the unknown VMs are old test systems built by developers, have no owner and have not been patched in over a year. Two are reachable from the internet.
stem: Which of the following would BEST keep this from happening again? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Require an owner and expiry date on every new VM, with automated reclamation
options.why: Lifecycle rules make someone accountable for each VM and remove the ones nobody renews, which stops forgotten test systems from piling up.

options.text: Run regular discovery scans and reconcile the results against the inventory
options.why: Discovery finds VMs that were created outside the normal process, so gaps between reality and the inventory are caught quickly.

options.text: Patch the hypervisor to prevent VM escape attacks
options.why: VM escape is a different risk. Patching the hypervisor is important but does nothing to find or manage orphaned, unpatched guests.

options.text: Add hosts to the cluster so it can carry the extra VMs
options.why: More capacity treats the symptom and makes it even easier to create VMs that nobody tracks.

options.text: Snapshot every unknown VM before deleting it in a one-time cleanup
options.why: Snapshots can make a cleanup safer, but a one-time cleanup does not stop new untracked VMs from appearing next month.

takeaway: VM sprawl happens when VMs are easy to create and nobody tracks them. Lifecycle rules plus discovery reconciled against the inventory keep unmanaged, unpatched VMs from accumulating.

scenario: A defense contractor keeps its weapons design network physically isolated, with no cabled or wireless connection to any other network. Engineers bring in vendor updates and test data on USB drives. Leadership says that because of the air gap, malware is no longer a realistic threat.
stem: Which of the following is the MOST important control for this environment?

options.text: Controlled, scanned transfer of removable media through a dedicated station
options.why: With network paths removed, removable media becomes the main way in. Scanning and logging every transfer at a dedicated station addresses that remaining path.

options.text: A next-generation firewall at the boundary of the design network
options.why: There is no network boundary to filter, and connecting a firewall would itself break the air gap.

options.text: Logical segmentation of the design network into separate VLANs
options.why: Internal segmentation can limit spread, but it does nothing about infected USB drives, which are the path the scenario describes.

options.text: Disabling the wireless adapters on every workstation in the isolated network
options.why: Removing wireless is part of keeping the gap intact, but the active path for files is USB, which this control leaves untouched.

takeaway: An air gap removes network paths, not every path. Removable media becomes the main way in, as Stuxnet showed, so media transfers must be tightly controlled, scanned and logged.

scenario: A data center is moving to software-defined networking. Forwarding rules for 300 switches will be pushed from a central controller, and automation tools will call the controller's northbound API to change network policy.
stem: Which of the following should the security team prioritize protecting MOST?

options.text: The controller and its API, with strong authentication
options.why: SDN centralizes the control plane. Anyone who controls the controller or its API can reprogram all 300 switches at once.

options.text: The data plane of each switch, with port security on every access port
options.why: Port security is still useful at the edge, but it protects one port at a time while a controller compromise affects the whole network.

options.text: The physical cabling between switches, with tamper-evident seals
options.why: Physical security matters, but it is not the new concentrated risk that a central SDN controller introduces.

options.text: The management interface of each switch, with SNMPv3 on every device
options.why: In SDN the switches take their forwarding rules from the controller, so per-device management is a smaller exposure than the controller itself.

takeaway: SDN separates the control plane from the data plane and centralizes it. That makes the controller and its APIs a single point that can reprogram the network, so protect them first.

scenario: A company is installing 500 smart lighting and occupancy sensors across its offices. The sensors have built-in web interfaces, receive firmware updates only twice a year, and only need to talk to a single vendor cloud service.
stem: Which of the following would BEST reduce the risk these devices add? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Place the sensors on a dedicated segment isolated from user and server networks
options.why: Isolation keeps a compromised sensor from becoming a foothold to reach laptops and servers, which matters because the devices are hard to patch.

options.text: Allow outbound traffic only to the vendor's cloud service endpoints
options.why: The sensors only need one destination, so allowing nothing else blocks command-and-control traffic and abuse of the devices in attacks.

options.text: Install endpoint protection software on each sensor
options.why: Most IoT sensors have no way to run third-party agents, and the vendor would not support it.

options.text: Join the sensors to the main user VLAN for easier management
options.why: Putting weak devices next to user endpoints enlarges the attack surface and gives an attacker a short path to valuable systems.

options.text: Rely on the vendor's twice-yearly firmware updates as the main control
options.why: Updates should still be applied, but six-month gaps in patch availability are the reason network controls are needed.

takeaway: IoT devices are hard to patch and cannot run agents, so control them through the network: isolate them in their own segment and allow only the traffic they need.

scenario: A medical device maker's infusion pump runs a real-time operating system that must respond to sensor input within 2 milliseconds, and the device is certified by regulators as shipped. A hospital security team asks the vendor to install the hospital's standard EDR agent on the pumps.
stem: Which of the following is the MOST likely reason the vendor will refuse, and the BEST alternative?

options.text: An agent could break timing and certification; isolate the pumps
options.why: Extra software can disrupt the RTOS's deterministic timing and void the certified configuration. Segmentation and network monitoring protect the pump without changing it.

options.text: RTOS devices cannot be attacked, so an agent adds nothing
options.why: Real-time and embedded systems have had serious vulnerabilities. They need protection; it just cannot come from a host agent.

options.text: EDR licenses do not cover medical devices; buy a medical license tier
options.why: Licensing is not the technical barrier here. Even a licensed agent would still threaten the pump's timing and certification.

options.text: The agent needs internet access; give the pumps a direct internet route
options.why: Connectivity is not why the vendor refuses, and a direct internet route would greatly increase the pump's exposure.

takeaway: A real-time OS is built for deterministic timing and is often certified as shipped. Protect RTOS and embedded devices with segmentation, network monitoring and vendor-signed firmware rather than host agents.

scenario: A gas pipeline operator's SCADA vendor is overseas and must be able to start remote support within two hours of a call. Today the vendor connects through a remote desktop tool that is always installed and running on an engineering workstation on the control network.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST replacement design?

options.text: Vendor access through an ICS DMZ jump host, enabled per session with MFA
options.why: Brokering access through a DMZ jump host keeps the vendor off the control network directly, and enabling it only for a session with MFA removes the always-open path.

options.text: Keep the remote desktop tool but require a longer vendor password
options.why: A stronger password helps a little, but the always-on direct path into the control network remains.

options.text: A site-to-site VPN from the vendor's network into the control network
options.why: This extends the vendor's whole network into the control network, so any compromise at the vendor becomes a path to the PLCs.

options.text: Remove all remote access and require the vendor to attend on site for every issue
options.why: This is the most restrictive choice, but an overseas vendor cannot meet the two-hour support requirement in person.

takeaway: In ICS environments remote access should never land directly on the control network. Broker it through a DMZ jump host, enable it only when needed, require MFA and record the session.

scenario: A ticketing company's traffic jumps to about 30 times normal for a few hours whenever a major concert goes on sale, roughly 10 times a year. Its on-premises web farm is sized for normal load, and the site crashed during the last two sales.
stem: Which of the following BEST addresses the requirement at a reasonable cost?

options.text: Cloud hosting that scales out automatically during sale events
options.why: Elastic scaling adds capacity for the few hours of each spike and removes it afterward, so the company pays for peak capacity only when it is used.

options.text: Buying enough on-premises servers to carry the peak load
options.why: This would work, but most of that hardware would sit idle for nearly the whole year, which is a poor use of budget.

options.text: Upgrading the existing servers with more CPU and memory
options.why: Vertical scaling has hard limits and cannot realistically deliver 30 times the capacity of the current farm.

options.text: Adding a second on-premises load balancer in an active-passive pair
options.why: A redundant load balancer improves its own availability but adds no web server capacity for the spike.

takeaway: Scalability and elasticity are key reasons to choose cloud: capacity grows for a spike and shrinks after it, so you pay for peak resources only while you need them.

scenario: An agriculture company is deploying soil sensors that must run for eight years on one small battery using a low-power microcontroller. Each reading must be encrypted and authenticated before it is sent over a low-bandwidth radio link.
stem: Which of the following design choices BEST fits these constraints?

options.text: Lightweight authenticated encryption with small ECC keys
options.why: Symmetric authenticated ciphers and elliptic curve keys give strong protection with little computation and small messages, which preserves battery and bandwidth.

options.text: RSA-4096 encryption of every reading for the strongest protection
options.why: Large RSA operations are slow and power hungry on a microcontroller, produce large ciphertexts, and are not meant for encrypting bulk data.

options.text: Unencrypted readings that the gateway encrypts before forwarding
options.why: The radio link would carry readings in the clear, which breaks the requirement to protect each reading before it is sent.

options.text: A full TLS session with certificate revocation checks on each transmission
options.why: Repeated handshakes and revocation lookups cost far more energy and airtime than these sensors can afford over eight years.

takeaway: Embedded and IoT designs are limited by power and compute. Choose lightweight cryptography, such as symmetric authenticated ciphers and ECC instead of large RSA keys, that meets the need without draining the battery.

scenario: A mining company has 25 remote sites that authenticate users against one directory server at headquarters. When a site's satellite link fails, nobody at that site can sign in to local systems, including the safety monitoring consoles.
stem: Which of the following changes BEST improves resilience while keeping consistent control?

options.text: Place read-only directory replicas at each site, managed centrally
options.why: Local replicas let sign-in continue when the link is down, while central management keeps one set of accounts and policies for every site.

options.text: Give each site its own independent directory run by local staff
options.why: Full decentralization survives outages but loses consistent control, so accounts and policies would drift apart across 25 sites.

options.text: Add a second directory server at headquarters for redundancy
options.why: Another server at headquarters does not help a site whose link to headquarters is the thing that failed.

options.text: Let every workstation cache credentials indefinitely so offline logons always succeed
options.why: Cached logons only help users who signed in before, do not cover services and new staff, and indefinite caching delays account revocation.

takeaway: Centralized designs are easier to control but create a single dependency; decentralized ones survive local outages but drift. Central management with distributed replicas is a common middle ground.

scenario: A company's IDS currently watches a copy of internet traffic from a network TAP. Leadership wants it to block attacks automatically, so the team plans to move the single appliance inline between the edge router and the firewall. No second appliance is budgeted.
stem: Which of the following is the MOST important design concern with this change?

options.text: The appliance becomes a single point of failure and adds latency
options.why: Inline, every packet depends on the appliance. Without a bypass, an HA pair or a chosen failure mode, its crash or overload becomes an internet outage.

options.text: The appliance will no longer see the traffic it needs to detect attacks
options.why: An inline device sees every packet in the path, so visibility does not drop. It is the dependency on the device that grows.

options.text: An inline device can only raise alerts, so it still will not block attacks
options.why: This reverses the facts. Inline placement is exactly what lets the appliance drop malicious traffic instead of only alerting.

options.text: The existing TAP will begin dropping packets once the appliance starts blocking traffic
options.why: The TAP is removed or unused in the new design, and a passive TAP never drops traffic because of what a monitoring device decides.

takeaway: Moving from tap or monitor mode to inline makes a device active: it can block, but every packet now depends on it. Plan failure mode, bypass or HA, and throughput before going inline.

scenario: A new IPS is going inline in front of a busy customer portal before a product launch. Its default rule set has thousands of signatures, and the portal team fears that false positives will block real customers during launch week.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST deployment approach?

options.text: Run it in detection-only mode, tune the rules, then enable blocking
options.why: Detect-only mode shows which signatures fire on legitimate traffic. After tuning, blocking can be turned on without cutting off real customers.

options.text: Enable blocking on every signature at once so nothing is missed
options.why: Untuned blocking is exactly what the portal team fears. Every false positive would turn into a customer being cut off.

options.text: Disable all signatures and rely only on anomaly-based detection
options.why: Anomaly detection needs a learned baseline and tends to produce more false positives at first, and it drops coverage of known attacks.

options.text: Deploy it fail-closed so blocked customers are easy to identify in the logs
options.why: The failure mode decides what happens when the IPS crashes. It has nothing to do with false positives and adds outage risk.

takeaway: Tune before you block. Running an IPS in detect-only (IDS) mode first reveals rules that fire on legitimate traffic, so blocking can be enabled without disrupting users.

scenario: A company acquires a smaller firm whose network has an unknown security posture, flat addressing and several unmanaged servers. The business wants the acquired staff to reach three shared applications by next week while full integration is planned.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST way to connect the two networks?

options.text: Place the acquired network in its own zone, allowing only the three apps
options.why: A separate security zone with firewall rules for just the needed flows meets the deadline while keeping the untrusted network away from everything else.

options.text: Join the networks with a routed link and merge the directories now
options.why: A full routed join exposes every corporate system to unmanaged servers whose security nobody has assessed yet.

options.text: Issue corporate VPN accounts that acquired staff use from their own laptops
options.why: This brings unmanaged endpoints straight into the corporate network with broad access, which is wider than the three applications require.

options.text: Wait until every acquired server has been rebuilt before connecting anything
options.why: This is safe, but it ignores the business requirement for access next week when a controlled connection is possible.

takeaway: Group systems of similar trust into security zones and control what crosses between them. An untrusted network gets its own zone with only the specific flows the business needs.

scenario: A retailer connects 300 stores over costly MPLS circuits. It wants to add cheap broadband and LTE links at each store, steer point-of-sale traffic over whichever link performs best, and manage routing policy from one console. Each store keeps its existing firewall for inspection.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Software-defined WAN with application-aware path selection
options.why: SD-WAN manages several transport links from a central controller and picks the best path per application, which is exactly what the retailer describes.

options.text: Secure access service edge with cloud-delivered inspection
options.why: SASE adds security services from the cloud, but the stores keep local inspection. The stated need is WAN path selection and central routing control.

options.text: A full mesh of manually built site-to-site IPsec tunnels
options.why: Manual tunnels between 300 sites are unmanageable and give no application-aware path selection or central policy.

options.text: A second MPLS carrier at each store for added redundancy
options.why: More MPLS increases cost, which contradicts the plan to use cheap broadband and LTE links.

takeaway: SD-WAN centrally manages multiple WAN links and steers traffic by application. SASE combines that networking with cloud-delivered security such as secure web gateway, CASB and ZTNA.

scenario: A school district must filter student web browsing by category, log which sites each student visits, and cache common content to save bandwidth. The district's own web servers already sit behind a separate reverse proxy.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the requirement for student browsing?

options.text: A forward proxy that students' browsers use to reach the internet
options.why: A forward proxy sits between clients and the internet, so it can filter by category, log each user's requests and cache popular content.

options.text: A second reverse proxy placed at the internet connection
options.why: A reverse proxy fronts servers and handles inbound requests. It does not control or log outbound browsing by students.

options.text: A web application firewall in front of the district's web servers
options.why: A WAF protects web applications from inbound attacks. It has no role in filtering what students browse.

options.text: A layer 4 firewall rule allowing only TCP ports 80 and 443 outbound
options.why: Port rules cannot see URLs or categories, cannot log which sites each user visited and do not cache content.

takeaway: A forward proxy sits in front of clients and controls their outbound requests through filtering, logging and caching. A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and handles inbound requests.

scenario: A bank's load balancer terminates TLS so its built-in WAF can inspect requests, then forwards traffic to the web servers over plain HTTP across the data center network. A new policy requires customer data to be encrypted on every network hop.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the new policy while keeping inspection?

options.text: Re-encrypt from the load balancer to the servers (TLS bridging)
options.why: The load balancer still decrypts and inspects, then opens a new TLS session to each server, so no hop carries customer data in the clear.

options.text: Switch to TLS passthrough so the web servers terminate TLS
options.why: Passthrough keeps traffic encrypted end to end, but the load balancer can no longer see requests, so WAF inspection is lost.

options.text: Place the web servers on a separate VLAN from other systems
options.why: Segmentation limits who can reach the traffic, but the policy requires encryption, and the traffic would still be plain HTTP.

options.text: Use IPsec AH between the load balancer and each of the web servers
options.why: AH authenticates packets and protects integrity but provides no encryption, so the data would still be readable.

takeaway: TLS offloading ends encryption at the load balancer. TLS bridging keeps inspection and restores encryption to the back end; passthrough keeps end-to-end encryption but gives up inspection.

scenario: An attacker compromised WEB02, then scanned and logged in to DB01 over several days. The organization's only IDS sensor, placed as shown below, raised no alerts. Both servers are on the same server VLAN behind the core switch.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST change to detect this activity in the future?
exhibit:
Internet ── [Edge router] ── [IDS sensor on TAP] ── [Firewall] ── [Core switch]
                                                                  │
                                                   Server VLAN 10.5.0.0/24
                                                     WEB02   10.5.0.21
                                                     DB01    10.5.0.40

options.text: Add a sensor fed by a TAP or SPAN on the server VLAN
options.why: Traffic between WEB02 and DB01 stays inside the server VLAN and never crosses the edge. A sensor on that segment sees this east-west movement.

options.text: Move the existing sensor to the link just inside the firewall
options.why: That position still sees only north-south traffic through the firewall. Server-to-server traffic in the same VLAN never passes it.

options.text: Replace the sensor with an inline IPS at the internet edge
options.why: An edge IPS has the same blind spot. It can block inbound attacks but never sees traffic that stays inside the data center.

options.text: Raise the frequency of the sensor's signature updates to hourly
options.why: Fresher signatures do not help a sensor that never received the traffic in the first place.

takeaway: A sensor only sees traffic that passes its collection point. Perimeter sensors see north-south traffic; detecting lateral movement needs sensors on internal segments.

scenario: A company will require 802.1X on both wired ports and Wi-Fi. A red team recently captured users' passwords with a rogue access point that imitated the corporate SSID. Every device is company owned and enrolled in MDM, and the company runs an internal PKI.
stem: Which EAP method BEST fits these requirements?

options.text: EAP-TLS with a certificate on each device
options.why: Both sides authenticate with certificates, so there is no password for a rogue access point to capture, and MDM with the internal PKI makes enrollment practical.

options.text: PEAP with MSCHAPv2 using users' domain passwords
options.why: PEAP protects the exchange inside a tunnel, but it is still password based, and clients that skip server validation hand credentials to a rogue AP.

options.text: EAP-TTLS with PAP sent inside the protected tunnel
options.why: The password is protected only by the tunnel. If a client trusts a rogue server, the attacker receives the password itself.

options.text: MAC authentication bypass for every device on the network
options.why: MAB is a fallback for devices that cannot run a supplicant. MAC addresses are easy to spoof, so it is much weaker than any EAP method.

takeaway: EAP-TLS uses certificates on both sides, so there is no password to phish. It needs a PKI and device enrollment, which MDM makes practical.

scenario: A 25-person office has one managed switch and no RADIUS server or budget for one. Visitors have been plugging personal laptops into open wall jacks in the conference room to get on the internal network. Staff desk assignments rarely change.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST control to put in place now?

options.text: Disable unused ports and enable port security with sticky MACs
options.why: The switch can do this today at no cost. Unknown devices on learned ports are blocked, and dead jacks give visitors nothing to plug into.

options.text: 802.1X with EAP-TLS on every switch port
options.why: This is stronger, but it needs a RADIUS server and certificates, which the office does not have and cannot fund.

options.text: A NAC appliance that checks the posture of every device
options.why: NAC would work, but it adds cost and complexity well beyond what a 25-person office with no budget can take on.

options.text: A guest wireless network so that visitors stop using the wall jacks
options.why: Guest Wi-Fi gives visitors an alternative, but it does not prevent anyone from plugging into an open jack.

takeaway: Port security, which limits and learns MAC addresses per port, cheaply stops casual unauthorized devices, though MACs can be spoofed. 802.1X is stronger but needs an authentication server.

scenario: A dental practice with 12 staff and one part-time IT contractor needs a firewall, a VPN for the owner, gateway antivirus, spam filtering and web content filtering. It wants a single device with one management console, and its internet link is 200 Mbps.
stem: Which of the following BEST fits the practice?

options.text: A unified threat management appliance
options.why: UTM bundles firewall, VPN, antivirus, spam and content filtering in one box with one console, which suits a small office with modest bandwidth.

options.text: A web application firewall
options.why: A WAF protects hosted web applications from inbound attacks. The practice does not host applications and needs broad perimeter features.

options.text: A layer 4 stateful firewall plus a separate VPN server
options.why: This lacks antivirus, spam and content filtering and means two devices to manage, against the single-console requirement.

options.text: A pair of high-throughput next-generation firewalls in an HA cluster
options.why: These could do the job, but a pair is two devices against the single-device requirement, and enterprise-sized HA adds cost a 12-person practice does not need.

takeaway: UTM puts many security functions in one appliance with one console, which suits small organizations. The trade-off is a single point of failure and reduced throughput with every feature enabled.

scenario: Backup servers copy data from a storage cluster over a dedicated 40 Gbps segment every night. Security wants a firewall between them that only allows the backup application's ports from the backup servers. No user or internet traffic ever crosses this segment, and throughput is the deciding factor.
stem: Which firewall type is the MOST appropriate choice?

options.text: A high-throughput layer 4 stateful firewall
options.why: Known hosts on known ports only need address, port and state checks. A layer 4 firewall enforces that at line rate without costly deep inspection.

options.text: A next-generation firewall with full application inspection enabled
options.why: Deep inspection on 40 Gbps of backup traffic would be costly and slow, and identifying applications adds little between two fixed sets of hosts.

options.text: A web application firewall in front of the storage cluster
options.why: A WAF inspects HTTP requests to web applications. It does not fit a backup protocol between servers.

options.text: A unified threat management appliance with gateway antivirus enabled
options.why: UTM devices are built for small sites and lose throughput with features on, and virus scanning bulk backup streams adds little value.

takeaway: Select the control that fits the need. Where traffic runs between known hosts on known ports and throughput matters most, a layer 4 stateful firewall is enough; layer 7 inspection adds cost and latency here.

scenario: Two database servers in the same data center replicate directly to each other. Auditors require the replication traffic to be encrypted and authenticated. The servers already route to each other, and the team wants the least overhead without adding a new outer IP header.
stem: Which IPsec configuration BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: ESP in transport mode between the two hosts
options.why: ESP encrypts and authenticates the payload, and transport mode protects host-to-host traffic while keeping the original IP header with minimal overhead.

options.text: AH in transport mode between the two hosts
options.why: AH authenticates packets and protects integrity, but it does not encrypt, so the confidentiality requirement fails.

options.text: ESP in tunnel mode between two security gateways
options.why: This would encrypt the data, but it adds a new outer IP header and gateways that two hosts already routing to each other do not need.

options.text: AH in tunnel mode between two security gateways
options.why: Tunnel mode adds overhead, and AH still provides no encryption, so it misses both goals.

takeaway: ESP provides encryption plus integrity; AH provides integrity only. Transport mode protects the payload between two hosts and keeps the original header; tunnel mode wraps the whole packet for gateway-to-gateway VPNs.

scenario: Two offices are linked with the tunnel configuration below so that they can exchange dynamic routing updates. An auditor's packet capture on the internet link shows file share contents in clear text.
stem: Which of the following BEST fixes the finding while keeping the routing design?
exhibit:
interface Tunnel0
 ip address 172.31.0.1 255.255.255.252
 tunnel source GigabitEthernet0/0
 tunnel destination 203.0.113.50
 tunnel mode gre ip
 ! no crypto map or tunnel protection profile applied
!
router ospf 1
 network 172.31.0.0 0.0.0.3 area 0

options.text: Protect the GRE tunnel with IPsec (GRE over IPsec)
options.why: GRE carries the routing protocol but has no encryption. Wrapping it in IPsec adds confidentiality and integrity while OSPF keeps working over the tunnel.

options.text: Replace GRE with an IPsec AH tunnel between the offices
options.why: AH does not encrypt anything, so file contents would still be readable, and a policy-based IPsec tunnel typically cannot carry the multicast OSPF updates that GRE does.

options.text: Enable OSPF authentication on the tunnel interface
options.why: Routing authentication stops forged route updates, but it does nothing to encrypt the user traffic crossing the tunnel.

options.text: Move the tunnel interfaces to a different private address range
options.why: The tunnel already uses private addressing. Changing the range has no effect on whether the payload is encrypted.

takeaway: GRE is a tunneling protocol with no encryption. GRE over IPsec keeps GRE's ability to carry routing protocols while IPsec adds confidentiality and integrity.

scenario: Forty contractors using their own unmanaged laptops need access to one internal web-based ticketing application for six months. The company will not install software on devices it does not own and does not want contractors to have network-level access to anything else.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: A clientless TLS VPN portal that publishes only the ticketing app
options.why: A browser-based TLS portal needs no software on the laptop and exposes just the one published application, not the internal network.

options.text: A full-tunnel IPsec remote access VPN with a client on each laptop
options.why: This needs a client installed on devices the company does not own and gives network-level access far beyond one application.

options.text: A site-to-site VPN to the contractors' own company network
options.why: This connects the contractor's entire network, not individual users, and opens network-level access in both directions.

options.text: Port forwarding of the ticketing application directly to the internet
options.why: Publishing the app straight to the internet exposes it to everyone, with no gateway authentication in front of it.

takeaway: A clientless, browser-based TLS VPN or similar application gateway gives access to specific web apps without installing software. Full remote access VPNs give network-level access and need a client.

scenario: The SOC's current sensor receives a copy of traffic from a SPAN port and only alerts an analyst after the fact. The SOC wants a replacement that can stop a detected exploit in the middle of the session.
stem: Which device attributes does the new deployment require? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Inline placement in the traffic path
options.why: Only a device that sits in the path can stop the original packets from reaching their destination.

options.text: Active response that drops or resets offending traffic
options.why: Being active means the device acts on what it detects rather than only reporting it, which is what stopping an exploit requires.

options.text: Passive monitoring of a mirrored copy of traffic
options.why: This is the current design. A device that sees only a copy cannot stop the original packets.

options.text: A connection through a network TAP
options.why: A TAP also delivers a passive copy, so it has the same limitation as the SPAN port.

options.text: Fail-open behavior if the device crashes
options.why: The failure mode is a separate availability decision. It is not what gives the device the ability to block.

takeaway: Blocking needs a device that is both inline and active. Passive devices on a TAP or SPAN see a copy and can only alert, and the failure mode is a separate decision.

scenario: A company is redesigning its screened subnet. A recent advisory described a firewall flaw that let attackers bypass all rules on one vendor's devices. The board wants the internal network to stay protected even if one firewall is fully compromised.
stem: Which of the following designs BEST meets the board's requirement?

options.text: Two firewalls from different vendors with the screened subnet between them
options.why: An attacker who defeats the outer firewall still faces a different product with different flaws before reaching the internal network.

options.text: One three-legged firewall with a separate interface for each zone
options.why: A single device protects every zone, so one compromise exposes the internal network directly.

options.text: Two firewalls of the same model in an active-passive HA pair
options.why: An HA pair improves availability, but both units share the same flaw, and only one is in the path at a time.

options.text: Two firewalls from the same vendor placed back to back around the screened subnet
options.why: Layering helps, but a single vendor flaw like the one in the advisory could defeat both firewalls at once.

takeaway: Back-to-back firewalls from different vendors give defense in depth plus platform diversity, so one vendor's flaw does not open the internal network. An HA pair improves availability, not protection.

scenario: An online subscription business stores customers' card numbers so it can charge them every month. Its PCI DSS assessment covers 140 servers because card data flows through order, billing and support systems. The goal is to shrink that scope while still billing monthly.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the goal?

options.text: Tokenization, with the payment processor holding card numbers in a vault
options.why: Internal systems store only tokens that are useless if stolen, and the processor charges the card by token, so most servers can leave PCI scope.

options.text: Encrypting card numbers in every database with AES-256
options.why: Encryption protects the data, but systems that store encrypted card numbers and can reach the keys generally stay in scope, so the 140 servers remain.

options.text: Hashing card numbers with SHA-256 before they are stored in the billing database
options.why: A hash cannot be turned back into a card number, so the business could no longer bill customers each month.

options.text: Masking card numbers so screens show only the last four digits
options.why: Masking changes what users see, but the full numbers are still stored and processed on the same servers.

takeaway: Tokenization swaps sensitive data for a meaningless token and keeps the real value in a separate vault. Systems that only handle tokens can fall out of compliance scope, which encryption alone rarely achieves.

scenario: Call center agents verify callers by asking for the last four digits of their Social Security number. The agents' screen currently shows the full number, and a recent incident involved an agent photographing customer records with a phone.
stem: Which of the following BEST reduces this risk without disrupting verification?

options.text: Mask the field so agents see only the last four digits
options.why: Agents still have exactly what they need to verify the caller, while the full number never appears on screen to be photographed.

options.text: Encrypt the Social Security number column in the database
options.why: The agent application decrypts the value to display it, so agents would still see and could still photograph the full number.

options.text: Replace the number with a random token that agents see instead
options.why: A random token hides the number but also hides the last four digits, so agents could no longer verify callers.

options.text: Hash the number so that the application can never reverse it
options.why: A hash cannot show the last four digits either, which breaks the verification process the call center depends on.

takeaway: Masking hides part of a value at display time so people see only what their task needs. The full value still exists behind the mask and must be protected separately.

scenario: A company's mobile app contains a proprietary pricing algorithm that competitors have reverse engineered from the installed app package. The code must run on customers' phones, because the app must work offline and the logic cannot move to a server.
stem: Which of the following BEST slows down further reverse engineering?

options.text: Obfuscate the compiled code so it is hard to read and analyze
options.why: Obfuscation scrambles names, structure and control flow without changing behavior, which raises the effort needed to recover the algorithm.

options.text: Encrypt the app package so it cannot be read on the phone
options.why: The phone must decrypt the code to run it, and the key has to live on the device, so a determined analyst can still extract it.

options.text: Hash the algorithm's source code and publish the digest
options.why: A published hash lets someone check integrity. It does nothing to hide how the algorithm works.

options.text: Tokenize the algorithm's variables before the app is compiled
options.why: Tokenization replaces data values with references to a vault. It is not a way to protect program logic running offline.

takeaway: Obfuscation makes code or data hard to understand without changing what it does. It slows reverse engineering but does not stop a determined analyst, so keep truly critical logic server side when possible.

scenario: A beverage company has decided not to patent its flavor formula, because a patent would require publishing the recipe and protection would expire after 20 years. Only six employees know the full formula, and the company wants to keep it protected indefinitely.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes how this data must be treated?

options.text: As a trade secret, protected only while it stays secret
options.why: A trade secret keeps its legal protection only as long as reasonable steps keep it confidential, so access control, NDAs and need to know are essential.

options.text: As patented intellectual property, protected even if it leaks
options.why: The company chose not to patent, so there is no registration to fall back on if the recipe is disclosed.

options.text: As public data, since a recipe is not covered by any regulation
options.why: Lack of regulation does not make data public. The formula is among the most valuable data the company owns.

options.text: As regulated data, since food recipes fall under consumer privacy laws
options.why: Privacy laws cover personal data about individuals. A product recipe is business data, not regulated personal data.

takeaway: A trade secret is protected only while it is kept secret, so strict access control, NDAs and need to know matter even more than for patented intellectual property, whose protection comes from public registration.

scenario: A regional clinic that also sells wellness products online to customers in the EU is labeling the data on its file server ahead of a compliance audit. The auditor asks which records are regulated data.
stem: Which of the following are regulated data? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Patient treatment records that include diagnoses
options.why: Health information tied to identified patients is protected health information under HIPAA, a regulation with specific handling rules.

options.text: Order histories of identified customers in the EU
options.why: Personal data about EU residents falls under GDPR, which regulates how it is collected, stored and transferred.

options.text: The source code of the clinic's appointment app
options.why: Source code is intellectual property. It is valuable and confidential, but no regulation governs it as such.

options.text: A draft marketing brochure for a new service
options.why: A draft brochure is internal until it is published, but it contains nothing a law or regulation governs.

options.text: The internal schedule of staff meetings
options.why: Meeting schedules are ordinary internal data with low sensitivity and no regulatory handling requirements.

takeaway: Regulated data is data that a law or regulation governs, such as health records under HIPAA or personal data of EU residents under GDPR. Valuable data such as source code is intellectual property, not regulated data.

scenario: A logistics firm prints 2D barcodes on parcel labels that encode each recipient's name, phone number and home address. Staff argue the labels need no protection because people cannot read the codes, and returned labels are thrown into open recycling bins.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes the risk?

options.text: The codes are non-human-readable but any phone can decode them
options.why: Barcodes are an encoding, not protection. Anyone collecting discarded labels can read the personal data with a free app, so the labels need secure disposal.

options.text: The barcodes are encrypted by design, so the data is protected
options.why: Standard 2D barcodes encode data in an open format. They provide no confidentiality at all.

options.text: The data is public because it is printed on the outside of parcels
options.why: Showing an address to a courier for delivery does not make thousands of records public, and bulk collection creates a privacy breach.

options.text: Only human-readable records are covered by privacy regulations
options.why: Privacy rules apply to personal data in any format, including barcodes, binary files and encoded fields.

takeaway: Non-human-readable data such as barcodes, QR codes and encoded fields is not protected just because people cannot read it. Classify and handle it by its content.

scenario: A retailer encrypts card data at rest in its databases and in transit with TLS to its processor. Malware was still found on store registers, and its output file held full card numbers. An excerpt is below.
stem: Which of the following BEST addresses this attack?
exhibit:
[mem-scan] process=POSClient.exe pid=4120
  match track2 4111111111111111=2812101000000000
  match track2 5555555555554444=2711201000000000
  ...
  wrote 8,412 records to C:\ProgramData\svc\log.dat

options.text: Point-to-point encryption that starts inside the card reader
options.why: With P2PE the reader encrypts card data before the register ever handles it, so memory-scraping malware on the register finds only ciphertext.

options.text: Stronger TLS settings between the registers and the processor
options.why: The malware reads card data from memory before it is sent, so better transport encryption does not change what it captures.

options.text: Full disk encryption on every store register
options.why: Disk encryption protects data at rest on a powered-off device. Running malware reads decrypted data straight from memory.

options.text: Hashing card numbers before they are written to the database
options.why: The theft happened in register memory, not in the database, so hashing stored values would not stop it.

takeaway: Data in use sits decrypted in memory, where RAM-scraping malware reads it. Encrypting at the point of capture means the register only ever handles ciphertext.

scenario: A web application's database server uses full disk encryption with keys sealed in a TPM. An attacker used SQL injection through the application and downloaded 200,000 customer records in clear text. A manager asks how that was possible when the data was encrypted.
stem: Which of the following BEST explains what happened?

options.text: FDE protects a powered-off or stolen disk, not data a running system serves
options.why: Once the server boots, the disk is unlocked and the database reads plain data for any query, including the attacker's injected ones.

options.text: The TPM released the encryption key to the attacker's session
options.why: The attacker never needed the key. The running system was already decrypting data for the application.

options.text: SQL injection is able to break the AES encryption on the disk
options.why: Injection does not attack cryptography at all. It abuses the application's legitimate access to the database.

options.text: The records were in transit, and stronger TLS would have stopped the theft
options.why: The attacker's own session would be protected by TLS too. Transport encryption does not stop an application from answering a malicious query.

takeaway: Full disk encryption protects data at rest against physical theft. On a running system, data is decrypted for any process with access, so application flaws need application controls, least privilege and field-level encryption.

scenario: A payroll provider allows access to its admin portal only from IP addresses that geolocate to the United States, where all its staff work. Logs show a successful login with a stolen password from a US cloud hosting address, made by an attacker later traced overseas.
stem: Which of the following BEST explains the gap and the improvement?

options.text: IP location is easily faked with VPNs; add MFA and device checks
options.why: The attacker simply routed through a US address. Geographic restrictions are a useful layer, but stronger authentication and device trust must back them up.

options.text: The geolocation database was outdated; update it every week
options.why: The lookup was accurate: the address really was in the US. A fresher database would have allowed the same login.

options.text: Block all cloud provider address ranges instead of using geolocation
options.why: This may stop this attempt, but attackers also rent residential proxies, and it breaks legitimate traffic from cloud-hosted services.

options.text: Allow logins only from the state where the headquarters is located
options.why: A narrower region has the same weakness, because an attacker can rent an address in that state just as easily.

takeaway: Geographic restrictions add a layer, but IP location is easy to fake with VPNs and proxies. Combine them with strong authentication and device trust rather than relying on them alone.

scenario: A hotel chain processes card payments with an application on 12 servers. Those servers share a flat network with 900 other systems, so the assessor treats all 912 systems as in scope for PCI DSS.
stem: Which of the following would MOST reduce the number of systems in scope?

options.text: Segment the 12 payment servers into an isolated zone
options.why: PCI scope follows connectivity. Once the other 900 systems cannot reach the cardholder data environment, they can be removed from scope.

options.text: Encrypt the hard drives of all 912 systems
options.why: Disk encryption protects data at rest but does not change which systems can connect to the payment servers, so scope stays the same.

options.text: Mask card numbers on the front desk screens across the chain
options.why: Masking limits what staff see, but the flat network still connects every system to the payment environment.

options.text: Run quarterly vulnerability scans on all 912 in-scope systems
options.why: Scanning is required for in-scope systems anyway. It keeps them compliant but does nothing to reduce how many there are.

takeaway: Segmentation isolates sensitive data in its own zone. In PCI DSS, systems that cannot connect to the cardholder data environment can fall out of scope, shrinking both risk and audit effort.

scenario: An HR share holds salary and disciplinary files. The share is encrypted at rest and reachable only from the corporate network, but a review finds the folder grants Modify to the Domain Users group, so any employee can open or change the files.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST fix?

options.text: Restrict folder permissions to the HR group by least privilege
options.why: The exposure comes from who is allowed in. Limiting access to the HR group closes it directly.

options.text: Re-encrypt the share using a stronger encryption algorithm
options.why: Encryption at rest is transparent to authorized users, and every employee is currently authorized, so stronger encryption changes nothing.

options.text: Move the share to a network segment for HR staff only
options.why: Segmentation would help but does not fix the overbroad permission, which still applies to anyone who reaches the share another way.

options.text: Enable file access auditing on the share to record every access
options.why: Auditing records who opened the files but still allows every employee to read and change them.

takeaway: Encryption protects data from people without access; permission restrictions decide who has access. If the permissions let everyone in, encryption at rest simply decrypts the files for them.

scenario: An analyst needs to send a spreadsheet with 3,000 customers' names, account numbers and balances to the external audit firm. The company's data classification policy is summarized below.
stem: According to the policy, which of the following is the BEST way to send the file?
exhibit:
Label         Examples                           External sharing rule
Public        Press releases, published prices   Allowed
Internal      Org charts, internal procedures    Partners under NDA, any method
Confidential  Customer PII and account data      Approved recipients, encrypted transfer only
Restricted    Encryption keys, M&A plans         Not shared externally without CISO approval

options.text: Label it Confidential and send it to the approved auditor by encrypted transfer
options.why: Customer account data matches the Confidential examples, and that label's rule requires an approved recipient and encrypted transfer.

options.text: Label it Internal and email it to the auditor under the existing NDA
options.why: Customer account data is listed under Confidential, not Internal, so the looser Internal handling rule does not apply.

options.text: Label it Restricted and wait for the CISO to approve sending it
options.why: Restricted covers keys and M&A plans. Over-classifying adds delay without matching the policy's definitions.

options.text: Label it Confidential and email it to the approved auditor as a normal unencrypted attachment
options.why: The label is right, but an ordinary attachment is not the encrypted transfer the Confidential rule requires.

takeaway: Classification drives handling. Label data by the policy's definitions, then follow that label's handling rule; the right label with the wrong handling still breaks the policy.

scenario: An application server talks to its database over the internal data center network using an unencrypted database protocol. A developer argues encryption is unnecessary because both servers are behind the firewall, but during a test an insider on the same network captured database passwords and query results.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST response?

options.text: Enable TLS on the database connections inside the data center
options.why: The capture proves the traffic is readable on the internal path. Encrypting the connection protects credentials and results from anyone who can sniff it.

options.text: Move the database onto the same VLAN as the application server
options.why: Sharing a VLAN does not encrypt anything, and an attacker on that VLAN can still capture traffic, for example through ARP poisoning.

options.text: Enable full disk encryption on the database server
options.why: Disk encryption protects data at rest. The data was captured in transit, which disk encryption does not cover.

options.text: Add a firewall rule limiting the database port to the application server only
options.why: Restricting who can connect is good practice, but the traffic between the two servers would still cross the network in clear text.

takeaway: Data in transit needs protection on internal networks too, because insiders and attackers with a foothold can capture traffic. Being inside the firewall is not the same as being trusted.

scenario: A file server's disks failed on Friday at 08:00. Every job in the backup catalog below completed successfully, and the administrator must rebuild the server to its state at the last backup.
stem: Which backup sets are needed to restore the server to its state at Thursday 22:00?
exhibit:
Day        Time   Type          Captures changes since
Sunday     22:00  Full          (everything)
Monday     22:00  Incremental   Sunday full
Tuesday    22:00  Incremental   Monday backup
Wednesday  22:00  Incremental   Tuesday backup
