Thursday   22:00  Incremental   Wednesday backup

options.text: The Sunday full plus the Monday through Thursday incrementals
options.why: Each incremental holds only the changes since the previous backup, so the full and every incremental after it must be restored in order.

options.text: The Sunday full and the Thursday incremental only
options.why: Thursday's incremental contains only changes since Wednesday's job, so Monday to Wednesday changes would be missing.

options.text: The Thursday incremental only, because it is the most recent backup
options.why: An incremental is not a complete copy. On its own it holds one day of changes and cannot rebuild the server.

options.text: The Sunday full and the Wednesday and Thursday incrementals
options.why: Skipping Monday's and Tuesday's incrementals loses the changes captured on those days, leaving an inconsistent restore.

takeaway: Incrementals capture changes since the last backup of any type, so a restore needs the last full plus every incremental after it, in order. They are fast to take and slow to restore.

scenario: A company takes a full backup every Saturday night and a differential every other night, as shown below. Its database server was corrupted on Thursday at 14:00, and the last successful job was Wednesday night's.
stem: Which backup sets are needed to restore to the most recent possible point? (Select TWO.)
exhibit:
Sat 23:00  Full
Sun 23:00  Differential
Mon 23:00  Differential
Tue 23:00  Differential
Wed 23:00  Differential   (last successful job)
Thu 14:00  Database corrupted

options.text: Saturday's full backup
options.why: Every differential is measured against the last full backup, so the full is the base of any restore.

options.text: Wednesday's differential
options.why: A differential holds all changes since the full, so the latest one already includes everything from Sunday through Wednesday.

options.text: Sunday's differential
options.why: Its changes are already included in Wednesday's differential, so restoring it adds nothing.

options.text: Monday's differential
options.why: Wednesday's differential supersedes it, because each differential contains everything changed since Saturday's full.

options.text: Tuesday's differential
options.why: It is older than Wednesday's differential and is fully contained in it, so it is not needed.

takeaway: A differential holds all changes since the last full backup, so a restore needs only the full plus the latest differential. Differentials grow daily but make restores simpler than incrementals.

scenario: A payment gateway's contract guarantees 99.99% availability measured over a calendar year. Last year the service had three outages, lasting 18, 22 and 25 minutes. The customer is claiming a service credit, and the provider's account manager asks you to check the math.
stem: Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Missed: 99.99% allows about 53 minutes a year, and downtime was 65
options.why: A year has 525,600 minutes, and 0.01% of that is about 52.6 minutes. The three outages total 65 minutes, which exceeds the allowance.

options.text: Met: 99.99% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime per year
options.why: About 8.76 hours a year is the allowance for 99.9%, not 99.99%. Each extra nine cuts the allowance by a factor of ten.

options.text: Met: each outage stayed under the 26 minutes allowed per incident
options.why: Availability is measured on total downtime over the period. The contract sets no per-incident allowance, and the outages add up.

options.text: Missed: 99.99% allows only about 5 minutes of downtime per year
options.why: The SLA was missed, but about 5.3 minutes a year is the allowance for 99.999%, so the reasoning is wrong.

takeaway: Each extra nine cuts allowed downtime by ten: 99.9% is about 8.76 hours a year, 99.99% about 52.6 minutes, and 99.999% about 5.3 minutes. Add up every outage in the measurement period.

scenario: A store's only internet link has 99% availability, and its card terminals need internet access to work. The owner adds a second link from a different provider over a different physical path, also rated at 99%, with automatic failover. Assume the two links fail independently.
stem: What is the expected availability of internet access now?

options.why: Access fails only when both links are down at once: 0.01 times 0.01 is 0.0001, so availability is 1 minus 0.0001, or 99.99%.
This understates the benefit. The chance of both independent links failing together is one in ten thousand, not one in a thousand.
Multiplying 0.99 by 0.99 is the formula for components in series, where both must work. Here either link is enough.
Redundancy reduces the chance of an outage but cannot remove it. Both links can still fail together, and failover itself can fail.

takeaway: For redundant components in parallel, availability is 1 minus the product of their failure rates; two 99% links give 99.99%. For components in series, multiply the availabilities, which lowers the total.

scenario: A distribution company's disaster recovery plan sets an RTO of 48 hours for its warehouse systems. A hot site would cost $400,000 a year, which the board rejected. A cold site is cheap, but ordering and installing servers there would take about three weeks.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the RTO at the lowest reasonable cost?

options.text: A warm site with hardware and links in place, restoring data at failover
options.why: Equipment and connectivity are ready, so only data restore and configuration remain, which fits within 48 hours at far less than a hot site.

options.text: A cold site, with servers ordered when a disaster is declared
options.why: Three weeks to obtain and install hardware is far longer than the 48-hour RTO.

options.text: A hot site, because it is the only option that can meet a 48-hour RTO
options.why: A hot site can recover in minutes, but a 48-hour RTO does not need that speed, and the board already rejected its cost.

options.text: Offsite backup tapes only, with no recovery site arranged
options.why: Backups protect the data, but without anywhere to restore it the company would face the same hardware delay as a cold site.

takeaway: Hot sites recover in minutes to hours at the highest cost, warm sites in hours to a few days, and cold sites in days to weeks. Choose the cheapest site that still meets the RTO.

scenario: A Gulf Coast bank placed its disaster recovery site 12 miles from its primary data center to make staff travel easy. Both buildings are on the same power grid and inside the same hurricane evacuation zone. Last season a single storm forced both sites offline for four days.
stem: Which of the following BEST addresses the weakness?

options.text: Relocate the recovery site outside the region
options.why: The problem is shared regional risk. Geographic dispersion puts the sites under different weather, power grid and evacuation conditions.

options.text: Upgrade the recovery site from a warm site to a hot site
options.why: Faster failover does not help when the same storm takes the recovery site offline along with the primary.

options.text: Add generators with four days of fuel at the primary site
options.why: Generators address power loss only. Flooding, evacuation and blocked roads would still close both buildings.

options.text: Replicate data synchronously between the two existing sites
options.why: Synchronous replication improves the RPO, but both copies still sit in the same disaster zone and fail together.

takeaway: Geographic dispersion means recovery sites far enough apart that one disaster, such as a storm, earthquake or grid failure, cannot take out both. Distance trades off against latency and staff travel.

scenario: A faulty update from a company's single endpoint security vendor crashed every Windows server and workstation at once. Recovery took two days, because the domain controllers, DNS servers and jump hosts all ran the same software and failed together.
stem: Which resilience principle would have MOST reduced the impact?

options.text: Platform diversity for critical services
options.why: If critical services ran on different platforms or security products, one bad update would have left some of them running to support recovery.

options.text: Geographic dispersion of the company's data centers
options.why: The update reached every system regardless of location, so distance between sites would not have helped.

options.text: Load balancing across a larger number of domain controllers
options.why: Extra domain controllers running the same software would have crashed in exactly the same way.

options.text: More frequent backups of the affected servers
options.why: Backups support recovery, but they do not stop every system from failing at once, which drove the two-day outage.

takeaway: Platform diversity, meaning different vendors, operating systems or technologies for critical functions, keeps one bug, bad update or exploit from taking down everything at once. It adds management cost, so apply it where it matters most.

scenario: An airline runs its booking system in two regions of one cloud provider. Last year an identity service outage at that provider made every region unusable for six hours. The board now requires the booking system to survive a provider-wide failure.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the requirement?

options.text: Run the booking system across two different cloud providers
options.why: Only a second provider is independent of the first provider's shared services, so a provider-wide outage leaves one side running.

options.text: Add a third region with the same cloud provider
options.why: All regions still depend on the provider's shared global services, which is exactly what failed last year.

options.text: Spread instances across more availability zones in each region
options.why: Zones protect against data center failures within a region, not against a provider-wide control plane outage.

options.text: Buy a premium support contract with faster response times
options.why: Faster support may shorten troubleshooting, but it cannot keep the service running during the provider's outage.

takeaway: Multi-zone and multi-region designs survive failures inside one provider. Only multi-cloud survives a provider-wide failure, at the cost of more complexity and broader skills.

scenario: A company has just written its first disaster recovery plan. Executives and department heads have never worked through it together, and the budget does not allow any production downtime or a separate test environment this quarter.
stem: Which type of exercise should the company run FIRST?

options.text: A tabletop exercise walking the plan's owners through a scenario
options.why: A tabletop costs little, needs no systems and shows whether people understand their roles, which is the right first step for a new plan.

options.text: A failover test that switches production to the recovery site
options.why: A failover test risks production downtime, which is not allowed, and is premature before the plan has been reviewed.

options.text: A parallel processing test at the recovery site
options.why: Parallel processing needs a working recovery environment running real workloads, which the budget does not cover yet.

options.text: A simulation that runs injected events against lab copies of systems
options.why: A simulation needs a test environment the company does not have, and it fits better after a tabletop has fixed the plan's obvious gaps.

takeaway: Start with a tabletop, a low-cost discussion that shows whether people know their roles and where the plan has gaps. Move to simulations, parallel processing and failover tests as the plan matures.

scenario: Every server in a rack has dual power supplies, but both supplies are plugged into the same power strip, which is fed by a single UPS. When that UPS failed during a self-test, the whole rack lost power even though utility power was normal.
stem: Which of the following BEST removes this single point of failure?

options.text: Feed each supply from a separate PDU, UPS and circuit
options.why: With independent power paths, losing one UPS, strip or circuit still leaves every server running on its other supply.

options.text: Replace the failed UPS with a larger model that has a longer runtime
options.why: A bigger UPS is still one device. The next time it fails, every server in the rack goes down again.

options.text: Install a standby generator to back up the utility feed
options.why: Utility power was fine during this outage. A generator protects against grid failure, not a failed UPS in the path.

options.text: Disable the UPS self-test so that it cannot trigger another outage
options.why: The self-test exposed a weak UPS. Disabling it hides the problem and leaves the single path in place.

takeaway: Dual power supplies only add resilience when each is fed by an independent path. Use separate PDUs, UPS units and circuits so one failure cannot drop the whole rack.

scenario: An insurance portal has a stateless web tier and a database that allows only one writable instance at a time using shared storage. The architect must keep both tiers running if any single server fails.
stem: Which of the following design pairings is BEST?

options.text: Load balance the web tier and use a failover cluster for the database
options.why: Stateless web servers are interchangeable, so a load balancer spreads requests and skips failed nodes, while a cluster fails the single-writer database over to a standby node.

options.text: Cluster the web tier and load balance the database across nodes
options.why: This is backward. The database cannot accept writes on several nodes at once, so spreading requests across them would fail.

options.text: Load balance both tiers across active-active nodes
options.why: The web tier suits this, but a database allowing one writable instance cannot run active-active.

options.text: Cluster both tiers with active-passive failover between paired nodes in each tier
options.why: This would survive failures, but it leaves standby web servers idle instead of using them to share load.

takeaway: Load balancing spreads requests across interchangeable, usually stateless nodes. Clustering keeps a stateful service, such as a single-writer database, available by failing over between nodes that share state.

scenario: An order database gets a full backup every night at 01:00. The business sets an RPO of 15 minutes for orders, and live replication alone was rejected because it would copy any corruption to the standby instantly.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets the RPO?

options.text: Transaction log (journal) backups every 15 minutes
options.why: The journal records every change, so after restoring the nightly full, the logs replay to a point no more than 15 minutes before the failure, or just before corruption began.

options.text: Hourly snapshots of the database storage volume
options.why: Snapshots every hour allow up to 60 minutes of lost orders, four times the RPO.

options.text: A second full backup each day at 13:00
options.why: Two fulls a day still leave up to 12 hours between recovery points.

options.text: Synchronous replication to a standby database server
options.why: This gives near-zero data loss but copies corruption instantly, which is the reason the business rejected it.

takeaway: Journaling records every change so a restore can replay to a precise point in time. It is how databases meet short RPOs without copying corruption the way live replication does.

scenario: A company encrypts its offsite backup tapes with AES-256. A fire destroyed the primary data center, including the backup server, which was the only place the encryption keys were kept. The tapes in the offsite vault are intact but cannot be read.
stem: Which of the following would have prevented this outcome? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Escrowing the backup keys in a separate, secure offsite location
options.why: Keys stored away from both the primary site and the tapes survive a site disaster, so the encrypted backups stay recoverable.

options.text: Regular restore tests from offsite media at the recovery site
options.why: A restore test away from the primary site would have revealed that the keys existed only on the backup server.

options.text: No longer encrypting backups that are sent offsite
options.why: This trades a key management problem for exposed data during transport and storage. The flaw was key storage, not encryption.

options.text: Storing the keys on the same tapes as the backup data
options.why: Anyone holding the tapes could then decrypt them, which defeats the purpose of encrypting backups.

options.text: Switching the tapes to a stronger encryption algorithm
options.why: AES-256 was not the problem. Any algorithm leaves the data unreadable once the key is lost.

takeaway: Encrypted backups are only as recoverable as their keys. Escrow keys separately from both the primary site and the media, and prove recovery with restore tests from offsite copies.

scenario: A clinic's scheduling database has an RPO of 4 hours. Backups currently run once a day, as shown below, and the server failed at 19:30 today with its disks unrecoverable.
stem: How much data was lost, and which schedule would meet the RPO?
exhibit:
Job          Schedule      Last success      Next run
DB-daily     00:00 daily   today 00:00       tomorrow 00:00

Server failure: today 19:30

options.text: About 19.5 hours; back up at least every 4 hours
options.why: Everything since the 00:00 backup, 19.5 hours of changes, is gone. Backup intervals no longer than 4 hours keep any loss within the RPO.

options.text: About 19.5 hours; add a second daily backup at 12:00
options.why: Two backups a day still leave 12-hour gaps. A failure at 19:30 would lose 7.5 hours, beyond the 4-hour RPO.

options.text: About 4 hours; the current schedule already meets the RPO
options.why: The RPO is a target, not the actual loss. The last good backup was at 00:00, so 19.5 hours were lost.

options.text: About 7.5 hours; back up at least every 8 hours
options.why: Loss is measured from the last good backup at 00:00, and an 8-hour interval would still exceed the 4-hour RPO.

takeaway: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time, so backup or journal intervals must be no longer than the RPO. Actual loss is the time between the last good backup and the failure.

scenario: A scan returns two findings. Finding 1: CVSS 9.8 remote code execution on a lab server on an isolated network with no route to production. Finding 2: CVSS 7.5 authentication bypass on the internet-facing VPN appliance; the CVE appears on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. The team can only patch one system this week.
stem: Which should be remediated FIRST, and why?

options.text: The VPN appliance, because it is exposed and actively exploited
options.why: Prioritization weighs exploitability and exposure, not just the base score. An internet-facing system with a flaw already being exploited in the wild carries far more real risk than an isolated lab box.

options.text: The lab server, because CVSS 9.8 is critical and must always be fixed before a 7.5
options.why: The base score ignores environment. An isolated lab server with no route to production is hard to reach, so its real-world risk is lower.

options.text: Neither, until a credentialed scan confirms that both findings are real
options.why: Confirmation matters, but a known exploited flaw on an exposed VPN should not wait for a second scan. You can validate and patch in the same window.

options.text: The lab server, because remote code execution is always worse than an authentication bypass on any network
options.why: Bypassing authentication on a VPN can give an attacker the whole network. The type of flaw matters less than how reachable and how exploited it is.

takeaway: CVSS base scores rank severity in a vacuum. Real prioritization adds exposure, active exploitation (such as KEV) and the asset's importance.

scenario: A non-credentialed scan flags 30 Red Hat servers as vulnerable to an OpenSSH CVE because the banner shows an old version number. The operations team says Red Hat backports security fixes without changing the upstream version string.
stem: What should the analyst do NEXT?

options.text: Validate with a credentialed scan or the vendor's package advisory
options.why: Version banners often hide backported fixes. A credentialed scan or the vendor's errata shows whether the fixed package is actually installed, which confirms or dismisses the finding.

options.text: Mark all 30 findings as false positives because the operations team vouched for them
options.why: Accepting an explanation without evidence risks dismissing a real vulnerability. Findings should be verified, not waived on someone's word.

options.text: Upgrade OpenSSH from source on all 30 servers to remove the old version string from the banner
options.why: Replacing vendor packages with source builds breaks supportability and future patching, and may not even be necessary.

options.text: Change the SSH banner so the scanner stops reporting the version
options.why: Hiding the banner only suppresses the symptom. It does not tell you whether the servers are actually vulnerable.

takeaway: Confirm before you remediate or dismiss. Banner-based findings on distributions that backport fixes are a common source of false positives.

scenario: A quarterly scan of 800 Windows servers reports almost nothing beyond open ports, yet the patch team knows dozens of servers are missing months of updates.
stem: Which change would MOST improve the accuracy of the results?

options.text: Run credentialed scans with a least-privilege scanning account
options.why: A credentialed scan logs in and checks installed patches, versions and configuration, producing far fewer false negatives than looking at the server from outside.

options.text: Increase the scan frequency from quarterly to weekly using the same settings
options.why: Scanning more often with the same blind spot just repeats the same false negatives more often.

options.text: Switch to an intrusive scan that attempts to exploit each open port
options.why: Exploit attempts can crash servers and still would not reveal missing patches for services that are not exposed.

options.text: Scan from the internet so that the results reflect what an attacker sees
options.why: An external view sees even less of the patch state than the current internal, non-credentialed scan.

takeaway: Non-credentialed scans show the attacker's outside view and miss a lot; credentialed scans see installed software and missing patches.

scenario: A critical patch for a payroll application server will break the vendor's software, and the vendor's fix is 90 days away. The business cannot run payroll without the application.
stem: Which response is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A documented, time-limited exception with compensating controls, approved by the risk owner
options.why: When remediation is not possible, a formal exception records the risk, sets an expiry date, names who accepted it and adds compensating controls such as isolation and monitoring until the fix arrives.

options.text: Install the patch anyway because critical vulnerabilities must always be patched within 14 days
options.why: Breaking payroll causes certain business harm. Policy deadlines usually allow approved exceptions for exactly this situation.

options.text: Remove the server from the vulnerability scanner's scope until the vendor releases the fix
options.why: Hiding the finding removes visibility without reducing risk, and the system could be forgotten after 90 days.

options.text: Transfer the risk by asking the vendor to sign an indemnity letter
options.why: An indemnity letter may shift some financial impact, but it leaves the server exposed and does nothing to stop an attack.

takeaway: Can't patch yet? Document an exception or exemption with an owner, an expiry and compensating controls. Never just hide the finding.

scenario: The server team reports that the 42 critical findings from last month's scan have been remediated, and the ticket is ready to close.
stem: What is the BEST way to validate the remediation?

options.text: Rescan the affected systems and confirm the findings no longer appear
options.why: Validation means independent evidence. Rescanning shows whether each fix actually took effect, catching missed servers or failed installs.

options.text: Ask the server team to sign off that every patch was installed
options.why: Self-attestation is not verification. Patches fail silently, and servers get missed.

options.text: Close the ticket and check again during next quarter's scheduled scan
options.why: Waiting a quarter leaves any failed remediation exposed for months without anyone knowing.

options.text: Review the change tickets to confirm that changes were approved
options.why: Approved changes show intent, not outcome. They do not prove the vulnerabilities are gone.

takeaway: Vulnerability management ends with validation: rescan, audit or otherwise verify, then report.

scenario: A company is retiring 300 laptops with self-encrypting SSDs that held customer data. The laptops will be sold to a refurbisher, so the drives must remain usable, and auditors require proof of sanitization.
stem: Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Cryptographic erase of each SSD, with a certificate of sanitization per drive
options.why: Crypto erase destroys the drive's encryption key, instantly making the data unrecoverable while leaving the drive reusable, and the certificates satisfy the auditors.

options.text: Degauss each SSD and record the serial numbers before the laptops are shipped out
options.why: Degaussing works on magnetic media only. It does not erase flash memory and it provides false assurance.

options.text: Shred each SSD and obtain a certificate of destruction from a vendor
options.why: Shredding is thorough and well documented, but it destroys the drives, which conflicts with selling the laptops.

options.text: Format each SSD with a quick format and reinstall the operating system
options.why: A quick format leaves most data recoverable, especially on SSDs where wear leveling keeps old blocks around.

takeaway: Reuse means sanitize (crypto erase or secure erase for SSDs); no reuse means destroy. Degaussing only works on magnetic media. Keep certificates either way.

scenario: A law firm wants to buy phones for its attorneys, keep full management control including remote wipe, and still let attorneys use the phones for personal email and photos.
stem: Which mobile deployment model fits BEST?

options.text: COPE
options.why: Corporate-owned, personally enabled: the firm buys and fully manages the phone, while allowing reasonable personal use.

options.text: BYOD, with an MDM agent installed on the personal devices that the attorneys already own
options.why: BYOD means the attorneys own the phones, but the firm wants to buy them, and full control of a personal device is hard to justify.

options.text: CYOD, where attorneys pick a model from an approved list for business use only
options.why: Choose your own device lets users pick from a list, but the scenario's key point is allowing personal use on a company-owned, fully managed phone.

options.text: VDI, with attorneys reaching a hosted mobile desktop from any device they happen to have
options.why: VDI is a way to deliver desktops, not a device ownership model, and it does not provide a managed phone.

takeaway: BYOD: user owns it. COPE: company owns it, personal use allowed. CYOD: user chooses from an approved list. Ownership and personal use are the deciding facts.

scenario: A company is evaluating a commercial file-parsing library delivered only as a compiled binary. The vendor will not provide source code. Security wants to find crashes and memory corruption bugs before deployment.
stem: Which testing approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Dynamic analysis by fuzzing the library with malformed files
options.why: Without source code, the practical way to find parsing bugs is to run the library and feed it huge numbers of malformed inputs, watching for crashes and memory errors.

options.text: Static code analysis of the library's source code before it is integrated into the product
options.why: Static analysis needs source code, which the vendor will not provide.

options.text: A manual peer code review of the integration code written by the in-house developers
options.why: Reviewing in-house code is useful, but the bugs in question would be inside the vendor's library, which the review cannot see.

options.text: Verifying the library's code signing certificate
options.why: A valid signature proves who published the library and that it was not altered. It says nothing about bugs inside it.

takeaway: Static analysis reads code without running it; dynamic analysis and fuzzing run it with crafted inputs, which is the only option for a black-box binary.

scenario: A university's mailing list forwards messages from external senders to 5,000 subscribers. After the receiving mail servers start enforcing DMARC, forwarded messages from domains with strict policies are rejected. Investigation shows SPF fails on the forwarded copies.
stem: Why does SPF fail, and which mechanism can still pass DMARC for these messages?

options.text: The forwarder's IP is not in the sender's SPF record; an intact DKIM signature still passes
options.why: SPF checks the connecting server's IP, which is now the university's, not the original sender's. DKIM signs the message itself, so if the list does not alter the signed parts, the signature still verifies and satisfies DMARC.

options.text: Forwarding strips the sender's DMARC record; republishing it with a longer TTL fixes it
options.why: DMARC records are looked up in DNS by receivers. Forwarding does not strip them, and TTL has nothing to do with this failure.

options.text: SPF only works over TLS; enabling STARTTLS on the list server makes SPF pass again
options.why: SPF is unrelated to transport encryption. It fails because the sending IP changed.

options.text: The subscribers' own SPF records block forwarding; asking them to add the list server fixes it
options.why: SPF is evaluated against the sender's domain, not the recipients'. Recipients' records play no part.

takeaway: SPF validates the sending IP and breaks on forwarding; DKIM validates a signature on the message and survives forwarding if the content is not modified. DMARC passes if either aligns.

scenario: Attackers keep spoofing a company's domain in phishing emails. The company uses a CRM platform, a marketing service and a ticketing system that all send mail as its domain, and nobody is sure which other services do. Its DMARC record does not exist yet.
stem: Which approach BEST stops the spoofing without breaking legitimate mail?

options.text: Publish DMARC at p=none, align every legitimate sender from the reports, then enforce
options.why: Monitoring mode reveals every service sending as the domain. Once all of them are aligned with SPF or DKIM, enforcing quarantine and then reject blocks spoofing without collateral damage.

options.text: Publish DMARC at p=reject immediately so that all spoofed mail is blocked starting today
options.why: Rejecting before inventorying senders would bounce legitimate CRM, marketing and ticketing mail, and possibly others nobody knew about.

options.text: Add every known sender to the SPF record and skip DMARC entirely
options.why: SPF alone tells receivers nothing about what to do with failures and does not check the visible From address, so spoofing continues.

options.text: Block the company's own domain at the inbound email gateway
options.why: This might stop some spoofed internal mail, but it does nothing for customers and partners receiving spoofed messages, and it breaks real internal mail.

takeaway: Roll DMARC out in stages: p=none to discover senders, align them with SPF or DKIM, then quarantine, then reject.

scenario: Sales staff spend most of their time on hotel and customer Wi-Fi without a VPN. The company wants to block access to known malicious and newly registered domains on those laptops wherever they are, with as little performance impact as possible.
stem: Which solution BEST fits?

options.text: An agent-based DNS filtering service that applies policy on any network
options.why: A lightweight agent sends lookups to a filtering resolver from any network, blocking bad domains before a connection is made, with almost no performance cost.

options.text: A proxy server in the headquarters data center with a PAC file on each laptop
options.why: A central proxy only filters traffic routed back to headquarters, adding latency for staff who rarely use the VPN.

options.text: A next-generation firewall at the headquarters internet edge
options.why: Laptops on hotel Wi-Fi never pass through the headquarters firewall.

options.text: Host file entries for known malicious domains pushed by group policy
options.why: Static hosts entries cannot keep up with constantly changing malicious and newly registered domains.

takeaway: Roaming users need protection that travels with the device: agent-based DNS filtering or a cloud SWG, not a central appliance they never pass through.

scenario: A web server was compromised through a vulnerable plugin, and the attacker read files outside the web root. The audit log shows SELinux recorded "avc: denied" messages for every one of those reads, yet the reads succeeded.
stem: What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: SELinux was in permissive mode, which logs violations without blocking them
options.why: Denial messages for actions that still succeeded are the signature of permissive mode. Enforcing mode would have blocked the reads and logged the same messages.

options.text: SELinux was disabled, so the kernel ignored its policy entirely
options.why: A disabled SELinux would not log any avc messages at all.

options.text: The attacker had root, and SELinux cannot restrict the root user
options.why: SELinux mandatory access control does restrict root processes, which is one of its main purposes.

options.text: The policy allowed the reads, and the logged denials were only false positives
options.why: If the policy allowed them, SELinux would not log denials. The log shows the policy forbade the reads.

takeaway: SELinux permissive mode logs what it would block but enforces nothing. Production systems need enforcing mode.

scenario: Engineers occasionally copy design files labeled Confidential to USB drives to work at home. Network DLP on the email gateway and web proxy is already in place, but it never sees these copies.
stem: Which control BEST closes this gap?

options.text: Endpoint DLP that blocks copying labeled files to removable media
options.why: Copying to USB never touches the network, so only an agent on the endpoint can see the file's label and block or log the copy.

options.text: A firewall rule that blocks outbound connections from the engineering VLAN to the internet
options.why: Copying to a USB drive does not use the network at all, so firewall rules cannot see it.

options.text: Full-disk encryption on the engineers' laptops
options.why: FDE protects the laptop if it is stolen. It does nothing to stop a logged-in user copying files to a USB drive.

options.text: A CASB that monitors sanctioned and unsanctioned cloud application use by the engineering team
options.why: A CASB governs cloud application use. It does not see local copies to removable media.

takeaway: Network DLP sees what crosses the network; endpoint DLP sees local actions such as USB copies, printing and clipboard use.

scenario: An audit finds employees who changed departments years ago still hold access from their old roles. The company already removes access when people leave.
stem: Which process would BEST catch this privilege creep going forward?

options.text: Periodic access reviews in which managers attest to each user's current access
options.why: Regular recertification asks managers to confirm or revoke each person's access, catching rights left over from earlier roles.

options.text: Stronger password requirements for accounts that have access to sensitive systems
options.why: Password strength does nothing about whether the person should hold the access at all.

options.text: Disabling accounts after 90 days of inactivity
options.why: These users are active, so inactivity rules never trigger. The problem is excess access, not unused accounts.

options.text: Identity proofing when each employee is first hired
options.why: Proofing confirms who someone is at onboarding. It does not track how their access accumulates later.

takeaway: Deprovisioning handles leavers; access reviews and attestation handle movers whose old permissions linger (privilege creep).

scenario: A hospital wants clinicians to open a patient chart only if they are assigned to that patient's care team, are on shift, are on a hospital-managed device and are on the hospital network. Assignments change hourly.
stem: Which access control model BEST supports these rules?

options.text: Attribute-based access control
options.why: ABAC evaluates many attributes together (user, resource, device and environment), which is what care-team membership, shift, device and location require, and it adapts as attributes change.

options.text: Role-based access control with a separate role for each care team that clinicians join and leave
options.why: Roles would explode in number with hourly team changes, and RBAC alone does not consider device or location.

options.text: Mandatory access control with classification labels on charts
options.why: MAC matches clearances to labels. It does not handle shifts, care-team assignments or device posture.

options.text: Discretionary access control in which each patient's physician grants access to colleagues
options.why: Leaving access to individual owners is inconsistent and does not enforce the device, shift and network conditions.

takeaway: When access depends on several changing conditions at once (who, what, when, where, which device), the answer is ABAC.

scenario: Twelve engineers hold permanent Domain Admin membership but use it only a few times a month. An attacker who phished one engineer immediately had full domain control.
stem: Which change MOST reduces this exposure while still letting engineers do admin work?

options.text: Just-in-time elevation that grants Domain Admin for an approved, time-limited task
options.why: With no standing privileged membership, a phished account normally holds no admin rights. Elevation happens only on request, for a limited time, and is logged.

options.text: Requiring the engineers to use 20-character passwords and change them every 60 days
options.why: Phishing captures whatever the password is, so length and rotation would not have prevented the attack.

options.text: Moving the twelve engineers into a single shared administrator account that is vaulted
options.why: Sharing one account removes accountability and still leaves a standing admin credential to steal.

options.text: Monitoring Domain Admin logons with a SIEM alert
options.why: Alerts help detect misuse but do not reduce the standing privilege the attacker used.

takeaway: Standing privilege is the risk. Just-in-time access, password vaulting and ephemeral credentials shrink it.

scenario: The same web server has been reinfected with a web shell three times in two months. Each time, the team removed the shell, restored the site and closed the incident.
stem: Which step did the team MOST likely skip?

options.text: Root cause analysis to find and fix how the attacker keeps getting in
options.why: Removing the web shell treats the symptom. Without finding the entry point, such as a vulnerable plugin or stolen credentials, the attacker simply returns.

options.text: Notifying law enforcement about the repeated compromise
options.why: Notification may be appropriate, but it would not stop the reinfections.

options.text: Restoring the server from a backup taken before the first infection
options.why: A clean restore does not close the hole the attacker used, so reinfection would follow.

options.text: Increasing the retention of the web server access logs
options.why: Better logs help investigation, but only if someone actually performs the investigation.

takeaway: Recurring incidents mean the root cause was never found. Eradication is incomplete until the entry point is fixed.

scenario: Legal counsel tells the CISO that a former employee is likely to sue the company. The email system automatically deletes messages older than 180 days.
stem: What should the CISO do FIRST?

options.text: Place a legal hold that suspends deletion for the relevant mailboxes and records
options.why: Once litigation is reasonably anticipated, relevant data must be preserved. A legal hold overrides the normal retention schedule so evidence is not destroyed.

options.text: Export every mailbox in the company to offline storage
options.why: Overcollecting is costly and unnecessary. A hold should cover the relevant custodians and data.

options.text: Let the 180-day deletion policy continue because it was in place before the dispute
options.why: Allowing deletion after litigation is anticipated can be treated as spoliation of evidence, even if the policy is routine.

options.text: Start e-discovery and send the relevant messages to opposing counsel
options.why: Production through e-discovery comes later, through counsel. The first step is preservation.

takeaway: Anticipated litigation triggers a legal hold first: preserve, then collect and produce through e-discovery.

scenario: An investigator removes the hard drive from a suspect's powered-off workstation. The case may go to court, so the defense will challenge whether the evidence was altered.
stem: Which procedure BEST preserves the drive's integrity as evidence?

options.text: Image it through a write blocker, hash both drive and image, and log the custody
options.why: A write blocker prevents any change to the original, matching hashes prove the image is identical, and the custody record shows who handled it and when.

options.text: Boot the workstation once more to confirm that the drive still works before imaging it
options.why: Booting writes to the drive (logs, timestamps, swap), altering the evidence before it is preserved.

options.text: Copy the user's files to an external drive with the operating system's copy function
options.why: A file copy misses deleted data and slack space and changes access metadata. It is not a forensic image.

options.text: Encrypt the original drive so that nobody else can tamper with it
options.why: Encrypting the original modifies it, which destroys its value as unaltered evidence.

takeaway: Forensic acquisition: write blocker, bit-for-bit image, hashes of original and copy, and an unbroken chain of custody.

scenario: A phishing email delivered a ZIP file to 40 users. The analyst must determine which users actually opened the archive and ran the program inside, and what it launched.
stem: Which data source would BEST answer this?

options.text: Endpoint logs from EDR, showing process creation and the parent processes
options.why: Only the endpoint sees a program execute and what it spawns. EDR process telemetry shows who ran the file and the process tree that followed.

options.text: Email gateway logs, showing which recipients received the message and the attachment
options.why: Gateway logs show delivery, not whether anyone opened the archive or ran the program.

options.text: Firewall logs, showing outbound connections from each workstation during the day
options.why: Firewall logs might show suspicious traffic later, but they cannot show which program ran on which host.

options.text: NetFlow from the core switch
options.why: NetFlow records conversations between addresses. It has no visibility into processes on endpoints.

takeaway: Pick the data source that observes the event directly: execution is seen on the endpoint, delivery at the gateway, and connections at the firewall.

scenario: An analyst knows a workstation transferred about 2 GB to an external address last night over an unencrypted protocol. Legal now needs to know exactly which files were sent.
stem: Which data source can answer this question?

options.text: A full packet capture of the traffic
options.why: Packet captures contain the payloads, so the transferred files can be reconstructed from an unencrypted session. Metadata sources cannot do this.

options.text: NetFlow records for the workstation
options.why: NetFlow shows who talked to whom, when and how many bytes. It contains no file names or content.

options.text: The firewall's connection log
options.why: Connection logs record addresses, ports, actions and byte counts, not the content.

options.text: DNS query logs
options.why: DNS logs show which names were looked up. They cannot show what data was sent afterward.

takeaway: Metadata (NetFlow, firewall and DNS logs) shows that something happened; only packet captures show what was in it.

scenario: An audit of network management finds FTP used to move configuration backups, SNMPv2c with the community string "public" for monitoring, and Telnet used to administer switches.
stem: Which replacements BEST address the findings? (Select THREE.)

options.text: SFTP for the configuration backups
options.why: SFTP runs over SSH, encrypting both credentials and file contents, unlike FTP which sends both in clear text.

options.text: SNMPv3 with authentication and privacy enabled
options.why: SNMPv3 adds per-user authentication and encryption, replacing clear-text community strings.

options.text: SSH for switch administration
options.why: SSH encrypts the management session, replacing Telnet's clear-text logins.

options.text: TFTP for the configuration backups
options.why: TFTP has no authentication or encryption at all, so it is worse than FTP.

options.text: SNMPv2c with a longer, random community string
options.why: A longer community string is still sent in clear text and offers no real authentication.

options.text: HTTP-based web management on the switches
options.why: Plain HTTP sends credentials in clear text, the same weakness as Telnet.

takeaway: Know the secure replacements: FTP to SFTP or FTPS, Telnet to SSH, SNMPv1/v2c to SNMPv3, HTTP to HTTPS, LDAP to LDAPS.

scenario: A security analyst must collect evidence from a running Windows server suspected of hosting a memory-resident backdoor. The server will be rebuilt afterward.
stem: Which actions are appropriate? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Capture a memory image before shutting the server down
options.why: A memory-resident backdoor lives in RAM, which is lost at power-off, so memory comes first in the order of volatility.

options.text: Record a hash of each image and keep a chain of custody log
options.why: Hashes prove the evidence has not changed, and the custody log documents everyone who handled it.

options.text: Run a full antivirus scan on the server before collecting anything
options.why: Scanning changes files and timestamps and may remove artifacts before they are preserved.

options.text: Reboot into safe mode so that the backdoor cannot run during collection
options.why: Rebooting destroys the volatile memory that holds the backdoor.

options.text: Copy suspicious files to the analyst's laptop using drag and drop
options.why: Ad hoc copies alter metadata and are not forensically sound images.

takeaway: Volatile first, hash everything, document custody, and do not let tools or reboots change the evidence before it is preserved.

scenario: Users on the warehouse floor keep dropping off Wi-Fi near the loading docks. A tool shows a strong unknown signal on the same channel, and coverage maps are years out of date.
stem: What should the wireless team do FIRST?

options.text: Perform a site survey and produce a heat map of coverage and interference
options.why: A site survey measures actual signal strength, dead zones and interference sources, giving the evidence needed to move access points, change channels or find the unknown transmitter.

options.text: Double the transmit power on every access point across the whole warehouse floor
options.why: Raising power without data often increases co-channel interference and can extend the network into the parking lot.

options.text: Switch the SSID from WPA2 to WPA3 to stop the disconnections
options.why: The symptoms are coverage and interference, which the security mode does not affect.

options.text: Hide the SSID so that the unknown device cannot see the network
options.why: Hiding the SSID does not stop interference and offers almost no security benefit.

takeaway: Wireless problems start with measurement: a site survey and heat map show coverage, dead zones, overlap and rogue or interfering signals.

scenario: Tier 1 analysts spend most of their shift on the same steps for every reported phishing email: extract URLs and attachments, check reputation services, search for other recipients and delete copies. Response times are falling behind.
stem: Which solution BEST reduces the workload while keeping responses consistent?

options.text: A SOAR playbook that automates the enrichment, search and removal steps
options.why: Repetitive, well-defined steps are what orchestration and automation are for. A playbook runs them the same way every time and frees analysts for judgment calls.

options.text: A larger SIEM storage allocation so that more email logs can be searched
options.why: More storage does not perform any of the manual steps the analysts are drowning in.

options.text: An additional email gateway from a second vendor in front of the current one
options.why: A second gateway might catch more phishing, but it does nothing about handling the reports that still arrive.

options.text: A policy requiring users to delete suspicious emails without reporting them
options.why: Ignoring reports loses the early warning they provide and leaves the same message in other inboxes.

takeaway: SIEM collects and correlates; SOAR orchestrates and automates the response. Repetitive playbook steps are the SOAR use case.

scenario: A SIEM rule alerts whenever any account fails to log in five times in ten minutes. It fires 1,800 times a day, almost all from a service account with an expired password and from users mistyping passwords on Monday mornings. Analysts now ignore it.
stem: Which action BEST improves this rule's value?

options.text: Fix the service account and tune the rule's thresholds and context
options.why: Alert tuning removes known benign sources and adds context (many accounts from one source, failures followed by success) so the rule fires on attacks rather than noise.

options.text: Disable the rule because failed logins are already blocked by account lockout
options.why: Disabling it removes visibility into password spraying and brute force, which lockout does not always stop.

options.text: Raise the alert's severity so that analysts cannot ignore it
options.why: Making a noisy alert louder makes alert fatigue worse, not better.

options.text: Forward every alert from the rule to the CISO's inbox for review
options.why: Moving the noise to someone else does not make it useful.

takeaway: Alert fatigue is fixed by tuning (thresholds, exclusions, context), not by turning rules off or turning them up.

scenario: Twice this year, an attacker changed the web server's configuration to inject a credit card skimmer script, and nobody noticed for weeks. The server's files rarely change outside approved releases.
stem: Which control would detect this kind of change MOST quickly?

options.text: File integrity monitoring on the web root and configuration files
options.why: FIM baselines file hashes and alerts on unexpected changes, which is exactly what injecting a script into rarely changing files produces.

options.text: A weekly vulnerability scan of the web server from an internal scanner
options.why: A vulnerability scan looks for known weaknesses, not for unexpected changes to files.

options.text: A web application firewall blocking SQL injection attempts on the site
options.why: A WAF may block some attacks, but it would not notice a configuration file already being modified.

options.text: NetFlow monitoring of the web server's outbound traffic
options.why: Skimmers often send card data from the customer's browser, not from the server, so NetFlow may show nothing unusual.

takeaway: FIM detects unauthorized changes to files that should be stable, such as web content, configs and system binaries.

scenario: A threat intelligence report describes a group that persists by creating scheduled tasks named like legitimate updaters and moves laterally with remote WMI. No alerts have fired in the company's environment.
stem: Which activity BEST uses this intelligence?

options.text: A hypothesis-driven threat hunt for such scheduled tasks and WMI use
options.why: Threat hunting assumes a breach may already have happened and proactively searches for the described behavior, which catches activity that slipped past existing detections.

options.text: Waiting for the SIEM to raise an alert before investigating
options.why: That is reactive by definition, and the report suggests the group may evade existing alerts.

options.text: Running a penetration test against the external perimeter
options.why: A pen test checks whether someone could get in. It does not look for an adversary who may already be inside.

options.text: Blocking all scheduled tasks on every endpoint
options.why: Scheduled tasks are used by legitimate software, so a blanket block would break systems and is not an investigation.

takeaway: Threat hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven, often seeded by threat intelligence, and looks for what alerts missed.

scenario: A company wants to make sure that 6,000 Windows laptops all enforce the same screen lock timeout, disable legacy SMBv1, and block running executables from user download folders, and that local users cannot change these settings.
stem: Which tool is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Group Policy applied from Active Directory
options.why: Group Policy centrally enforces operating system settings on domain-joined Windows machines and reapplies them if users try to change them.

options.text: A SIEM correlation rule that alerts when settings differ
options.why: A SIEM can detect differences, but it does not apply or enforce the settings.

options.text: A vulnerability scanner with a Windows hardening policy
options.why: A scanner reports configuration gaps. It does not push settings to 6,000 laptops.

options.text: A one-time configuration script run by the help desk during deployment
options.why: A one-off script cannot stop users or software from changing settings afterward.

takeaway: Configuration enforcement at scale uses central policy tools (Group Policy, MDM or UEM), not detection tools or one-time scripts.

scenario: A company automated user provisioning with dozens of scripts written by one engineer, who has now left. A change in the HR system's API silently broke account deprovisioning, and nobody understands the scripts well enough to fix them quickly.
stem: Which automation drawback does this BEST illustrate?

options.text: Technical debt and complexity that create a single point of failure
options.why: Undocumented, person-dependent scripts are technical debt, and when they break, a critical process (deprovisioning) fails with nobody able to support it.

options.text: Reduced reaction time, because automation is slower than manual work
options.why: Automation usually improves reaction time. The problem here is supportability, not speed.

options.text: Inability to enforce baselines, because scripts cannot apply standards
options.why: Enforcing baselines is a benefit of automation. The failure here is maintainability.

options.text: Lower employee retention, because automation makes jobs less interesting
options.why: Automation is usually cited as improving retention by removing tedious work, and the scenario is about a broken integration.

takeaway: Automation drawbacks to know: complexity, cost, single point of failure, technical debt and ongoing supportability.

scenario: A federal contractor must prove that 900 Linux servers comply with a published hardening benchmark and produce machine-readable results for auditors every month.
stem: Which approach BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Automated SCAP scans against the benchmark's checklist
options.why: SCAP-compatible tools evaluate systems against standardized benchmark content (such as CIS or DISA STIG) and produce machine-readable compliance reports at scale.

options.text: Manual review of a random sample of 20 servers each month
options.why: Sampling does not prove that all 900 comply, and manual results are not machine-readable.

options.text: A penetration test of the Linux servers once a year
options.why: A pen test looks for exploitable weaknesses, not line-by-line compliance with a benchmark, and once a year misses the monthly requirement.

options.text: NetFlow analysis of traffic to and from the Linux servers
options.why: Traffic patterns say nothing about whether the servers' configurations match the benchmark.

takeaway: SCAP plus benchmarks (CIS, STIG) gives automated, standardized, machine-readable configuration compliance checks.

scenario: Contractors plug their own laptops into conference room ports. The company wants unmanaged or unpatched devices to reach only a remediation portal and the internet, while compliant corporate laptops get full access.
stem: Which control BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Network access control with posture checks and VLAN assignment
options.why: NAC checks each device's identity and health when it connects and places it in the right VLAN: full access for compliant corporate devices, a restricted network for everything else.

options.text: Port security that allows only one MAC address per conference room port
options.why: Port security limits how many devices use a port, but it does not check health or decide what network a device should be on.

options.text: A web filter that blocks contractors from risky website categories
options.why: Web filtering does not stop an unmanaged laptop from reaching internal systems.

options.text: Disabling all conference room ports and providing guest Wi-Fi
options.why: This removes wired access for corporate laptops too and does not assess device health.

takeaway: NAC decides what a device may reach based on who it is and whether it is healthy, often by assigning VLANs.

scenario: A company built a hardened baseline for its 250 Linux web servers from the CIS benchmark and deployed it through a golden image last year. This month's compliance report is shown in the exhibit. Administrators admit they loosened settings by hand while troubleshooting and never put them back.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST way to maintain the baseline from now on?
exhibit:
Baseline compliance: web tier (250 servers)
Check                              Pass   Fail
SSH PermitRootLogin no             148    102
SSH PasswordAuthentication no      161     89
Telnet service disabled            240     10
Host firewall default policy drop  152     98

options.text: Use configuration management to detect drift and automatically restore baseline settings
options.why: Maintaining a baseline means continuously comparing systems against it and correcting drift. A configuration management tool enforces the approved state on every run, so manual changes cannot linger.

options.text: Rebuild every web server from the golden image once a year before the compliance audit
options.why: A yearly rebuild restores compliance for a moment, but drift builds up again for months in between. It treats the symptom on a schedule instead of enforcing the baseline continuously.

options.text: Write a new baseline that adopts the settings administrators changed during troubleshooting
options.why: Rewriting the standard around the drift would bless insecure settings such as root login over SSH. The baseline content is fine; the gap is that nothing enforces it.

options.text: Run a weekly credentialed vulnerability scan and email the results to the server team
options.why: A scan reports problems but fixes nothing, and the team already ignored drift once. Detection without enforcement leaves the servers out of compliance between reports.

takeaway: Secure baselines have three phases: establish, deploy and maintain. Maintaining means detecting and correcting drift continuously, and updating the baseline itself only through change control.

scenario: During a physical assessment, a tester plugged a laptop into a wall jack in a vacant lobby office and received an address on the employee VLAN. The office has been empty for a year and no devices are planned for it. The company wants a fix it can apply today without new infrastructure.
stem: Which switch hardening step BEST addresses this finding?

options.text: Shut down the unused ports and assign them to an unused VLAN
options.why: An unused port should not be live at all. Disabling it removes the access immediately at no cost, and parking it in an unused VLAN limits the damage if someone re-enables it by mistake.

options.text: Deploy 802.1X authentication with a RADIUS server on every access port
options.why: 802.1X is a strong control for ports that must stay active, but it needs a RADIUS server, supplicants and a rollout plan. That is new infrastructure, and a vacant port simply does not need to be on.

options.text: Replace Telnet with SSH for management of the access switches
options.why: Encrypting management traffic is good hardening, but the tester never touched the management plane. The live data port in the lobby would still hand out an employee VLAN address.

options.text: Enable DHCP snooping on the employee VLAN to block rogue servers
options.why: DHCP snooping stops rogue DHCP servers from answering clients. The tester's laptop was a client, and it would still receive a lease from the legitimate server.

takeaway: Disable unused switch ports and park them in an unused VLAN. Controls such as 802.1X and port security are for ports that must stay in service.

scenario: Facilities installed 60 smart thermostats and conference room displays that join the corporate network. A scan shows they still accept the manufacturer's default admin password and sit on the same VLAN as employee laptops. The devices cannot run third-party software.
stem: Which of the following should the security team do to harden these devices? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Change the default credentials on every device to unique strong passwords
options.why: Default passwords are published in manuals and attacker tools, so changing them closes the most common way IoT devices are taken over.

options.text: Move the devices to an isolated VLAN that allows only the traffic they need
options.why: Segmentation limits what a compromised thermostat or display can reach. It is the standard control for devices that cannot run security agents.

options.text: Install an EDR agent on each device to watch for signs of compromise
options.why: The scenario says the devices cannot run third-party software. Embedded IoT systems rarely support agents, which is why other controls are needed.

options.text: Enable UPnP so the devices can open the firewall ports they require
options.why: UPnP lets devices open ports on their own without review. That expands the attack surface instead of hardening it.

options.text: Turn off automatic firmware updates so device behavior stays predictable
options.why: Firmware updates are the main way vendors fix flaws in embedded systems. Disabling them leaves known vulnerabilities in place.

options.text: Give each device a static IP address so it is easier to track
options.why: Static addressing may help inventory and firewall rules, but by itself it neither removes the default password nor separates the devices from laptops.

takeaway: IoT and embedded devices that cannot run agents are hardened by changing defaults, keeping firmware current and isolating them on their own segment.

scenario: A startup's three administrators share one password for the cloud provider's root account and use it for their daily work. MFA is not enabled. The company is preparing for its first security assessment of its cloud infrastructure.
stem: Which of the following actions BEST harden this account structure? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable MFA on the root account and reserve it for the few tasks that require it
options.why: The root account has unlimited power over the whole environment. Protecting it with MFA and locking it away for rare break-glass tasks is a core cloud hardening step.

options.text: Create individual administrator identities with least-privilege roles for daily work
options.why: Named accounts give accountability for every action, and least-privilege roles limit the damage if one administrator is phished.

options.text: Generate root access keys so the administrators can stop typing the shared password
options.why: Root access keys are long-lived credentials with unlimited rights. Providers advise against creating them because a leaked key gives full control.

options.text: Store the shared root password in a team vault so all three can keep using it
options.why: A vault protects how the password is stored, but daily shared use of root remains. There is still no MFA and no way to tell which person did what.

options.text: Turn on default encryption for every storage bucket in the account
options.why: Encryption at rest is worthwhile, but it does nothing about the weak, shared, all-powerful identity that the assessment will flag.

options.text: Rotate the root password every 30 days and email it to the administrators
options.why: Rotation does not fix sharing or the missing MFA, and sending the password by email creates a new place for it to leak.

takeaway: Harden cloud identity first: MFA on the root account, root kept for break-glass use only, and individual least-privilege identities for daily administration.

scenario: A consulting firm lets employees read company email and documents on their personal phones. Most employees refused to enroll because the current MDM policy would let IT wipe the entire phone, including personal photos. The firm will not buy phones but must be able to remove company data when someone leaves.
stem: Which approach BEST meets both needs?

options.text: Containerize company apps and data so IT can selectively wipe only the work profile
options.why: A managed container or work profile keeps corporate data separate on a BYOD phone. IT can wipe that container without touching personal data, which addresses the employees' objection.

options.text: Switch to a COPE model so the firm owns each phone and can wipe it whenever needed
options.why: COPE gives full control because the company owns the device, but the firm has said it will not buy phones. The question is how to protect data on personal devices.

options.text: Keep full-device enrollment and promise employees that IT will wipe only in emergencies
options.why: A promise does not change what the policy can technically do, so the privacy concern and low enrollment remain.

options.text: Allow browser-based webmail only and drop mobile device management entirely
options.why: Without any management, the firm cannot enforce a screen lock or remove cached documents. It gives up the control it needs when someone leaves.

takeaway: On BYOD devices, containerization (a managed work profile) lets the company wipe its own data selectively while leaving personal content alone.

scenario: Warehouse staff use company-managed Android phones paired with Bluetooth barcode scanners. An assessor in the parking lot found the phones in discoverable mode all shift and paired a laptop to one after a worker accepted an unexpected pairing prompt. The scanners must keep working, and the rugged phones' MDM can control discoverability and keep an allow list of paired devices.
stem: Which control BEST reduces this risk?

options.text: Use MDM to turn off discoverable mode and allow pairing only with approved scanners
options.why: Managing the Bluetooth connection method through MDM removes the advertising that let the assessor find the phones and blocks pairing with unknown devices, while the approved scanners keep working.

options.text: Disable Bluetooth on every warehouse phone through the MDM policy
options.why: This removes the Bluetooth risk completely, but the scanners rely on Bluetooth. The scenario requires the scanners to keep working.

options.text: Train warehouse workers to reject pairing prompts they did not expect
options.why: Training helps, but it depends on busy workers making the right choice every time. A technical restriction is more reliable.

options.text: Replace the Bluetooth scanners with models that connect over the warehouse Wi-Fi network instead
options.why: Changing hardware is expensive and slow, and it introduces a new connection method to secure. A policy change solves the problem with the current devices.

takeaway: Secure mobile connection methods with MDM: keep Bluetooth non-discoverable and restrict pairing to approved devices instead of relying on users to reject prompts.

scenario: A company enabled WPA3-Personal in WPA2/WPA3 transition mode so older laptops could connect. An inventory last month confirmed every device now supports WPA3. A wireless survey produced the exhibit, and some laptops began WPA2 handshakes with the third access point listed.
stem: Which action BEST closes this weakness?
exhibit:
SSID      BSSID              CH   SECURITY
CorpNet   3c:84:6a:12:40:01  36   WPA3-SAE / WPA2-PSK
CorpNet   3c:84:6a:12:40:11  44   WPA3-SAE / WPA2-PSK
CorpNet   da:a1:19:7e:02:5c  44   WPA2-PSK

options.text: Disable transition mode and run the SSID as WPA3 only
options.why: Transition mode keeps WPA2 alive, so a rogue access point can advertise WPA2 only and capture handshakes for offline cracking. With every device WPA3-capable, WPA3-only removes the downgrade path.

options.text: Change the passphrase but keep transition mode for compatibility
options.why: A new passphrase helps if the old one leaked, but the downgrade path stays open. Compatibility is no longer needed because all devices support WPA3.

options.text: Lower the access points' transmit power so the signal stays inside the building
options.why: Reducing power trims coverage outside, but the rogue device is the attacker's own transmitter. It does nothing about clients falling back to WPA2.

options.text: Enable WPS so users can reconnect quickly with a PIN after a disconnect
options.why: WPS PIN mode has a well-known brute-force weakness. It adds an attack path instead of removing one.

takeaway: WPA2/WPA3 transition mode is a temporary compatibility setting. Once every client supports WPA3, switch to WPA3 only to remove downgrade attacks.

scenario: A university's staff Wi-Fi uses WPA2-Enterprise with PEAP-MSCHAPv2 and a RADIUS server. Attackers ran an evil twin with the same SSID and collected staff credential hashes, because laptops were set to accept any server certificate. The university cannot issue client certificates to 4,000 devices this year.
stem: Which change BEST stops this credential harvesting within these constraints?

options.text: Configure clients to validate the RADIUS server certificate, its CA and its name
options.why: PEAP protects the inner password exchange only if the client checks it is talking to the real RADIUS server. Enforcing certificate validation makes the evil twin's certificate fail before credentials are sent.

options.text: Migrate to EAP-TLS so that every device authenticates with its own client certificate
options.why: EAP-TLS is the strongest option, but it needs a client certificate on every device. The university has said it cannot issue those this year.

options.text: Replace the RADIUS server with TACACS+ for wireless authentication
options.why: TACACS+ is used for administrator access to network devices, not 802.1X wireless authentication. It would not stop the evil twin.

options.text: Switch the staff SSID to WPA3-Personal with a long shared passphrase
options.why: A passphrase shared by 4,000 people will leak, and it removes individual authentication and accountability. It trades one weakness for another.

takeaway: In PEAP and EAP-TTLS, the tunnel protects credentials only when the client validates the server certificate. Without that check, an evil twin can harvest logins.

scenario: A data leak was traced to a device with IP address 10.40.8.77 on the corporate Wi-Fi at 14:12 yesterday. The Wi-Fi uses WPA2-Enterprise, with each user authenticating to a RADIUS server. The access points log only MAC addresses, and DHCP logs map IP addresses to MAC addresses.
stem: Which record would MOST directly tie the session to a named user?

options.text: RADIUS accounting records showing user, MAC address, start and stop times
options.why: The accounting part of AAA records who connected, from which device and for how long. Matched against the MAC from the DHCP lease and the time of the leak, it names the authenticated user.

options.text: DHCP lease logs that map 10.40.8.77 to a MAC address
options.why: DHCP logs are a useful step, but they identify a MAC address, not a person. MAC addresses can be spoofed or shared.

options.text: Access point association logs for the floor where the device was connected at the time
options.why: Association logs show which MAC was on which access point. They place the device but still do not identify the user.

options.text: TACACS+ command logs from the wireless LAN controller
options.why: TACACS+ records what administrators did on the controller. It does not log end users' network sessions.

takeaway: AAA means authentication, authorization and accounting. RADIUS accounting is the record that ties a network session to a specific authenticated user and time.

scenario: A penetration tester reports two findings on a shopping site. An injected script read the session cookie through document.cookie, and the same cookie was sent in cleartext when a user followed an old http:// link to the site. The response header is shown in the exhibit.
stem: Which cookie attributes should be added to address both findings? (Select TWO.)
exhibit:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Set-Cookie: sessionid=8f2c91ab77e0d4; Path=/; Domain=shop.example.com

options.text: HttpOnly
options.why: HttpOnly stops client-side scripts from reading the cookie through document.cookie, which blocks the theft by injected script.

options.text: Secure
options.why: The Secure attribute tells the browser to send the cookie only over HTTPS, so it is never sent in cleartext on an http:// request.

options.text: Domain=.example.com
options.why: Widening the domain sends the cookie to every subdomain of example.com, which increases exposure instead of reducing it.

options.text: Expires set one year in the future
options.why: A long expiry turns the session cookie into a persistent one, which lengthens the window in which a stolen cookie is useful.

options.text: SameSite=None
options.why: SameSite=None allows the cookie on cross-site requests, which weakens CSRF protection. It does not stop scripts reading the cookie or cleartext sending.

takeaway: Secure cookies need Secure (HTTPS only), HttpOnly (no script access) and usually SameSite (limits cross-site sending). Each attribute stops a different attack.

scenario: Developers added JavaScript to an order form so the quantity field accepts only whole numbers from 1 to 50. A tester used an intercepting proxy to change the quantity to -20 after the browser had checked it, and the checkout issued a credit to the tester's card.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST fix?

options.text: Validate the quantity on the server against the allowed range
options.why: Anything the browser checks can be changed afterward in transit. Server-side input validation against an allow list or range is the control the attacker cannot skip.

options.text: Obfuscate the form's JavaScript so testers cannot read the validation
options.why: The tester did not need to read the script; the proxy edits the request after the browser runs it. Hiding the code does not stop that.

options.text: Use parameterized queries for every database call in the checkout service
options.why: Parameterized queries stop SQL injection, but -20 is a valid integer and would pass straight through. This is a business logic flaw, not an injection.

options.text: Encode the quantity value whenever the application writes it into a page
options.why: Output encoding prevents cross-site scripting when data is displayed. It does nothing to stop a negative quantity from being processed.

takeaway: Client-side validation is for user convenience. Input validation that protects the application must happen on the server, where the attacker cannot bypass it.

scenario: Administrators run dozens of PowerShell maintenance scripts from a file share through scheduled tasks under a privileged service account. An attacker with write access to the share added a line to one script that created a new domain admin. The team wants altered scripts to be refused at run time.
stem: Which control BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Sign approved scripts and configure hosts to run only signed scripts
options.why: Code signing binds each approved script to a trusted publisher. The attacker can edit the file but does not hold the signing key, so any edit breaks the signature and a host that requires signed scripts refuses to run the altered one.

options.text: Run static code analysis on each script before it is copied to the share
options.why: Static analysis checks code before deployment, but it cannot notice an edit made afterward. The tampered script would still run.

options.text: Encrypt the file share so that only authorized accounts can read the scripts
options.why: Encryption protects confidentiality from outsiders. The attacker already had write access, and the scheduled task would still run whatever the share contains.

options.text: Record each script's hash in the change ticket when it is approved
options.why: A recorded hash helps someone prove tampering later, but nothing checks it before the script runs. It is documentation, not enforcement.

takeaway: Code signing proves who published code and that it has not changed since. It only protects you when systems are set to refuse unsigned or altered code.

scenario: An email gateway's signature antivirus keeps missing malicious Office attachments that are unique to each campaign, so no signature exists when they arrive. The company will accept a few minutes of delivery delay for attachments from external senders.
stem: Which control would BEST catch these attachments before users open them?

options.text: Detonate attachments in a sandbox and block any that behave maliciously
options.why: A sandbox opens the file in an isolated environment and watches what it does, such as launching scripts or calling out. It detects new malware by behavior, which signatures cannot do.

options.text: Update the gateway's antivirus signatures every hour instead of once a day
