options.why: Faster updates still need someone to have seen the sample first. Files unique to each campaign have no signature when they arrive.

options.text: Deploy a honeypot mailbox that attracts phishing campaigns for study
options.why: A honeypot collects intelligence about attackers, but it does not inspect messages being delivered to real employees.

options.text: Block attachments whose file hash appears on a reputation blocklist
options.why: Hash reputation is another form of signature. A file that is unique to one campaign has no reputation yet, so it passes.

takeaway: Sandboxing runs untrusted code in isolation to observe its behavior, which catches new or unique malware that signature and hash checks miss.

scenario: An audit found that departments had bought 37 SaaS tools with corporate credit cards. Several store customer data, and security reviewed none of them before purchase. Finance wants departments to keep the ability to buy software quickly.
stem: Which of the following BEST prevents this from happening again?

options.text: Route all software purchases through a procurement process with a security review
options.why: Building security into acquisition means tools are assessed before data goes into them. A streamlined procurement step keeps buying quick while closing the gap at its source.

options.text: Block every SaaS domain at the web proxy unless IT has approved that service in advance
options.why: Blanket blocking is blunt and slows the business, and it does nothing for tools used off the corporate network. It treats the symptom rather than how the tools are acquired.

options.text: Run a CASB discovery report each quarter to find new cloud applications in use
options.why: Discovery is useful, but it is detective. By the time a quarterly report finds a tool, customer data may already be in it.

options.text: Ask each SaaS vendor for a SOC 2 report after the contract has been signed
options.why: Vendor assurance belongs before the purchase, when the company can still walk away. Asking after signing is the right idea at the wrong phase.

takeaway: Asset management starts at acquisition: route purchases through procurement so security reviews a product before the company commits to it or puts data in it.

scenario: To save 40% on a branch refresh, a manager wants to buy core switches from an online reseller that is not on the manufacturer's authorized partner list. The listing says the units are new, sealed and include full support.
stem: What is the MOST significant security concern with this purchase?

options.text: The hardware or firmware could be counterfeit or tampered with
options.why: Unauthorized channels are a known source of counterfeit and modified network gear, and the manufacturer may not honor support or firmware updates. That is a supply chain risk at the core of the network.

options.text: The switches will arrive with the manufacturer's default administrator credentials
options.why: Every new switch ships with defaults, whichever channel it comes from. Changing them is a normal hardening step, not a risk specific to this reseller.

options.text: The switches will need a hardened configuration baseline applied before deployment
options.why: Any switch needs a baseline before going into production. That is routine work and does not distinguish this purchase from an authorized one.

options.text: The reseller's price might rise before the order is approved and shipped
options.why: A price change is a budget issue, not a security concern. It does not affect the integrity of the equipment.

takeaway: Buy hardware through authorized channels. Gray-market equipment risks counterfeit or tampered firmware and may have no valid support or update entitlement.

scenario: A critical finding on a database server has stayed open for five months. The infrastructure team says the application team owns it, the application team says it belongs to a project that ended, and the CMDB entry lists no owner.
stem: Which of the following would MOST effectively prevent this kind of stall in the future?

options.text: Require an accountable owner on record for every asset in the inventory
options.why: Assignment and accounting give each asset a named owner who must remediate, accept the risk or retire it. Without an owner, findings fall between teams.

options.text: Escalate findings older than 90 days to the CIO automatically
options.why: Escalation adds pressure, but without a recorded owner the CIO inherits the same argument about whose server it is.

options.text: Have the security team apply the database patch directly to close the finding
options.why: This fixes one finding, but patching an application nobody owns can break it, and the next orphaned server will stall the same way.

options.text: Scan the database server weekly instead of monthly to track the finding
options.why: The finding is already known. More frequent scanning measures the problem more often but does not assign anyone to fix it.

takeaway: Every asset needs a recorded owner. Ownership is what turns a vulnerability finding into someone's task to remediate, accept or decommission.

scenario: An employee reports a laptop stolen from a car. The asset inventory lists its serial number and model but not who it was assigned to or what kind of data it handled, so the privacy office cannot tell whether breach notification laws apply.
stem: Which change to asset management would BEST prevent this uncertainty next time?

options.text: Record each asset's assigned user and the classification of data it handles
options.why: Assignment and classification in the inventory let the privacy office see immediately whose device it was and whether regulated data was involved, which drives the notification decision.

options.text: Require full-disk encryption on every laptop before it is issued to an employee
options.why: Encryption is an excellent control and can reduce notification duties, but it is a protection measure. It still would not tell the privacy office who had the laptop or what it held.

options.text: Attach barcode asset tags to every laptop for faster physical audits
options.why: Barcode tags speed up counting hardware, but they record the device, not its user or the sensitivity of its data.

options.text: Run a monthly discovery scan to confirm which laptops are still online
options.why: Discovery shows whether a device is present on the network. It says nothing about ownership or data classification.

takeaway: Asset accounting records more than make and serial number. Recording the assigned owner and data classification tells you how much a lost asset matters.

scenario: The company's inventory system relies on an installed agent and lists 1,180 devices. The CISO suspects that personal laptops, printers and unmanaged appliances are also on the network and wants them found and added to the inventory.
stem: Which method would BEST enumerate the devices the current inventory is missing?

options.text: Active network discovery combined with DHCP lease and switch MAC table data
options.why: Network-side enumeration sees anything that talks on the network, whether or not it runs an agent. Comparing the results with the agent inventory reveals the unmanaged devices.

options.text: Push the inventory agent to all devices through the software distribution system
options.why: Software distribution reaches only devices that are already managed. Personal laptops and appliances would never receive the agent.

options.text: Ask every department manager to submit a list of the equipment their team uses
options.why: Manual lists are incomplete and slow, and managers are unlikely to know about devices that were plugged in without approval.

options.text: Reconcile purchase orders from the past three years against the current inventory
options.why: Purchase records show what the company bought. Personal devices and gifted or borrowed equipment never appear on them.

takeaway: Agent-based inventory sees only managed assets. Enumerating the network itself (discovery scans, DHCP and switch tables) finds what the inventory does not know about.

scenario: Eight SSDs from a records server have failed and no longer power on. They held unencrypted patient data and are not self-encrypting. The manufacturer offers free replacements if the failed drives are shipped back.
stem: What should the hospital do with the failed drives?

options.text: Keep them, have them shredded and obtain a certificate of destruction
options.why: A failed SSD can still have readable flash chips. Physical destruction with documented certification is the only reliable option when the drive cannot be sanitized logically.

options.text: Ship them back for the free replacements, since the drives no longer function
options.why: A dead controller does not erase the flash memory, and a lab can read the chips directly. Patient data would leave the hospital's custody.

options.text: Degauss the drives and then ship them back to claim the warranty replacements
options.why: Degaussing works on magnetic media, not on the flash memory in SSDs. The data would remain readable.

options.text: Run a multi-pass overwrite on each drive and then return them under warranty
options.why: The drives will not power on, so an overwrite cannot run. Overwriting is also unreliable on SSDs because of wear leveling.

takeaway: When media cannot be sanitized logically, destroy it physically and keep a certificate of destruction. Degaussing does not work on SSDs or flash media.

scenario: A finance application server is being decommissioned after a migration. The migration moved only the last two years of transactions to the new platform. Regulations require keeping seven years of financial records, and the server is scheduled to be wiped tomorrow.
stem: What should happen BEFORE the server is sanitized?

options.text: Archive the older records to retained storage as the retention policy requires
options.why: Decommissioning must respect data retention. The five years of records that were not migrated must be preserved in protected storage before the disks are wiped.

options.text: Sanitize the server as scheduled, since the new platform is now the system of record
options.why: The new platform holds only two years of data. Wiping now would destroy records the company is legally required to keep.

options.text: Keep the old server running indefinitely in case the older records are ever requested
options.why: This keeps the data, but leaves an unmaintained server running for years. Archiving meets the retention duty without that exposure.

options.text: Obtain a certificate of sanitization from the vendor that will wipe the disks
options.why: A certificate documents the wipe after it happens. It is the right step at the wrong time and does nothing to preserve the records.

takeaway: Check retention requirements before sanitization. Data that must be kept is archived first, and only then are the disks wiped and the wipe certified.

scenario: A web server that hosted an internal application is being retired. Its disks will be sanitized next week and the hardware will go to a certified recycler.
stem: Which of the following should also be part of decommissioning this server? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Revoke its certificates and disable its service accounts
options.why: Credentials tied to a retired server are easy to forget and can be reused by an attacker. Revoking and disabling them removes access that no longer has a purpose.

options.text: Update the asset inventory to show the server as retired
options.why: The inventory must reflect disposal so the asset is no longer scanned, licensed or counted, and so auditors can trace it to its certificate.

options.text: Leave its DNS record in place so that old links still resolve
options.why: A record pointing at an address that may later be reused can be hijacked. Stale DNS entries should be removed during decommissioning.

options.text: Keep its firewall rules in case the server is rebuilt later
options.why: Stale rules leave openings for whatever system later receives that address. Rules should be removed with the server they served.

options.text: Copy its local administrator password to the replacement server
options.why: Reusing a password across systems means one compromise unlocks both. The replacement should have its own unique credential.

takeaway: Decommissioning is more than wiping disks: remove the asset's accounts, certificates, DNS records and firewall rules, and update the inventory.

scenario: The security team is most worried about an unauthenticated attacker on the internet who can trigger a flaw without any action by a user. The scan report lists the four findings and CVSS vectors shown in the exhibit.
stem: Which finding matches that threat?
exhibit:
Finding  Vector                                         Base
A        CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H   8.8
B        CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N   7.5
C        CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H   7.8
D        CVSS:3.1/AV:P/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H   6.8

options.text: Finding B
options.why: AV:N, PR:N and UI:N mean it is exploitable over the network with no privileges and no user interaction. Its impact is confidentiality only, but it is the one that fits the threat described.

options.text: Finding A
options.why: It has the highest score, but UI:R means a user must take an action, such as opening a file or link, before the attack works.

options.text: Finding C
options.why: AV:L and PR:L mean the attacker needs local access and an account on the system. An unauthenticated remote attacker could not use it directly.

options.text: Finding D
options.why: AV:P means the attacker must physically touch the device. It cannot be exploited from the internet.

takeaway: Read the vector, not just the score: AV shows where the attacker must be, PR the privileges needed and UI whether a user has to help.

scenario: A vendor publishes the CVSS vector in the exhibit for a flaw in a reporting tool. In this company, the tool runs on an isolated segment reachable from only two admin workstations and holds no confidential data. The analyst wants the internal score to reflect this while keeping the vendor's rating on record.
stem: Which CVSS metric group should the analyst adjust?
exhibit:
Vendor advisory
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N   Base score 9.1 (Critical)

options.text: Environmental metrics
options.why: The environmental group lets an organization modify base metrics and set its own security requirements, producing a score for its environment without changing the published base score.

options.text: Base metrics
options.why: Base metrics describe the flaw's intrinsic characteristics and should stay as the vendor published them. The analyst explicitly wants to keep that rating.

options.text: Temporal metrics
options.why: Temporal metrics (called threat metrics in CVSS 4.0) track exploit maturity and fix availability over time. They do not describe this company's network or data.

options.text: Impact subscore
options.why: The impact subscore is part of the base calculation, not a separate group the consumer adjusts. Changing it would alter the vendor's base rating.

takeaway: CVSS base scores describe the flaw everywhere; environmental metrics tailor the score to your exposure and data. Prioritize on the environmental result.

scenario: A web application passed its monthly vulnerability scan with no findings. Two weeks later a penetration tester found SQL injection on the account settings page, which is reachable only after logging in. No code changed between the scan and the test, and the scanner had been given only the site's home page URL.
stem: Which of the following BEST describes the scan result?

options.text: A false negative caused by the scan never reaching pages behind the login
options.why: The flaw existed during the scan but was not reported, which is a false negative. An unauthenticated scan cannot test pages it cannot reach, so it needs credentials for the application.

options.text: A false positive, because the scanner reported the application as clean
options.why: A false positive is a reported flaw that is not really there. Here a real flaw was missed, which is the opposite error.

options.text: A true negative, because the flaw must have been added after the scan ran
options.why: The scenario states that no code changed between the scan and the test, so the flaw was present and missed.

options.text: A zero-day, because no scanner signature existed for this SQL injection flaw
options.why: SQL injection is a long-known class that scanners test for generically. The problem was coverage of the site, not an unknown flaw.

takeaway: A false negative is a real vulnerability the tool did not report. Unauthenticated web scans commonly miss everything behind a login page.

scenario: A development team builds a customer portal from about 300 open-source packages. Last year it took the team nine days just to learn it was affected by a critical flaw in a widely used logging library. The team wants to know within hours whenever a new CVE affects any package it ships.
stem: Which identification method BEST meets this goal?

options.text: Package monitoring that checks the dependency list against vulnerability databases
options.why: Package monitoring (software composition analysis against an SBOM) watches every dependency and alerts as soon as a new CVE is published for a version in use.

options.text: Static analysis of the team's own source code on every commit to the shared repository
options.why: Static analysis looks for insecure patterns in first-party code. It is not built to tell you that a third-party library just received a new CVE.

options.text: Dynamic analysis of the running portal as part of each release cycle
options.why: Dynamic testing probes the running application at release time. A CVE published between releases would go unnoticed until the next test.

options.text: An annual penetration test of the portal by a third-party firm
options.why: A yearly test is a point-in-time check. It could not deliver an alert within hours of a new CVE.

takeaway: Static and dynamic analysis test your own code; package monitoring tracks known vulnerabilities in the third-party components you depend on.

scenario: A regional hospital's small security team wants threat intelligence about attacks on healthcare providers, including indicators peer hospitals saw in the last few days. It also wants a trusted forum where it can share details of its own incidents confidentially.
stem: Which source BEST fits these needs?

options.text: Membership in the healthcare sector's information sharing and analysis center
options.why: An ISAC is an information-sharing organization for one sector. Members exchange timely, sector-specific indicators and discuss incidents under agreed confidentiality rules.

options.text: A commercial threat feed that covers every industry in every region of the world
options.why: A proprietary feed may include healthcare indicators, but it is a one-way product. It offers no peer forum for confidential sharing.

options.text: OSINT collected from security blogs, vendor reports and public advisories
options.why: Open-source intelligence is free and useful, but it is public, often slower, and gives no confidential channel for sharing with peers.

options.text: Monitoring dark web marketplaces for the hospital's name and domains
options.why: Dark web monitoring can reveal stolen data for sale. It does not provide sector-wide indicators or a sharing community.

takeaway: Information-sharing organizations such as ISACs give sector-specific, peer-shared intelligence; OSINT is public, proprietary feeds are purchased, and dark web monitoring watches for stolen data.

scenario: A retailer learned of its last breach only when a bank reported fraud, three months after customer records had been offered for sale online. Leadership wants earlier warning if company credentials or customer data are being traded by criminals.
stem: Which of the following would MOST directly provide that warning?

options.text: Dark web monitoring for company domains, credentials and data samples
options.why: Criminal marketplaces and forums are where stolen data is advertised. Monitoring them for the company's domains and records gives warning that data is already out.

options.text: A bug bounty program that pays researchers for reporting new vulnerabilities
options.why: A bug bounty finds weaknesses before they are exploited. It would not reveal that data has already been stolen and listed for sale.

options.text: Membership in an information-sharing organization for the retail sector
options.why: Sector sharing gives indicators and attack trends, but it would not specifically flag this retailer's records being traded.

options.text: Weekly authenticated vulnerability scans of the e-commerce environment
options.why: Scanning shows exposure, not evidence of theft. A breach that already happened would not appear in a scan report.

takeaway: Dark web monitoring is a threat feed for one question: is our data or are our credentials already being sold?

scenario: Security researchers sometimes email a software company's sales address about flaws they find, and one went public after two months without a reply. The company wants a published way for researchers to report issues and a promise not to take legal action over good-faith testing. It has no budget for rewards.
stem: Which of the following BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: A responsible disclosure program with a published policy and safe harbor terms
options.why: A disclosure program gives researchers a clear channel, scope and response timeline, and safe harbor language removes the legal fear. It does not require paying rewards.

options.text: A bug bounty program that pays researchers according to the severity of each finding
options.why: A bug bounty would meet the reporting need, but it pays cash rewards, and the company has no budget for them.

options.text: An annual third-party penetration test of the company's software products
options.why: A penetration test finds flaws from the company's chosen testers. It gives outside researchers no channel and no legal assurance.

options.text: A dedicated mailbox for reports with no published scope or testing rules
options.why: A mailbox fixes the routing problem, but without published rules and safe harbor, researchers still face legal uncertainty about testing.

takeaway: A responsible disclosure program sets the channel, scope and safe harbor for researchers; a bug bounty adds payment for valid findings.

scenario: After patching, segmentation and improved backups, a manufacturer's assessment still estimates that a successful ransomware attack could cost several million dollars in downtime and recovery. The board agrees that the remaining likelihood cannot be reduced further at a reasonable cost but wants the financial impact limited.
stem: Which response BEST addresses the board's goal?

options.text: Purchase cyber insurance to transfer part of the financial impact
options.why: Insurance is the response that limits financial loss when likelihood cannot reasonably be reduced further. It transfers part of the cost of an incident to the insurer.

options.text: Grant a formal exception for the remaining unpatched vulnerabilities
options.why: An exception documents why a specific flaw is not being fixed. It leaves the full financial impact with the company.

options.text: Add another layer of segmentation between the manufacturing plants
options.why: The board has already concluded further reduction is not cost-effective. Segmentation also lowers likelihood rather than limiting the cost of an attack.

options.text: Accept the risk and record it in the risk register with no further action
options.why: Acceptance keeps the entire financial exposure in house, which is the opposite of what the board asked for.

takeaway: Vulnerability response options include patching, segmentation, compensating controls, exceptions and insurance. Insurance limits financial impact; it does not reduce likelihood.

scenario: The monthly vulnerability report for the CISO must flag every finding that has passed the remediation deadline set by the company's policy. The policy and the open findings are shown in the exhibit.
stem: Which finding is out of compliance with the policy?
exhibit:
Policy: Critical 9.0-10.0 = 15 days | High 7.0-8.9 = 30 days | Medium 4.0-6.9 = 90 days

Host     Finding                           CVSS   Days open
web-01   OpenSSL buffer overflow           9.8    12
db-02    PostgreSQL privilege escalation   8.8    34
app-03   Weak TLS cipher suites            5.9    71
fs-04    SMB signing not required          5.3    88

options.text: db-02 PostgreSQL privilege escalation
options.why: A CVSS 8.8 score is High, which has a 30-day deadline. The finding has been open 34 days, so it is the one past its deadline.

options.text: web-01 OpenSSL buffer overflow
options.why: This is the most severe finding, but Critical items have 15 days and it has been open 12. It is urgent but still within policy.

options.text: fs-04 SMB signing not required
options.why: At 88 days it is the oldest finding, but a 5.3 score is Medium with a 90-day deadline, so it is close but not yet overdue.

options.text: app-03 Weak TLS cipher suites
options.why: A 5.9 score is Medium with a 90-day deadline, and the finding has been open 71 days. It is within policy.

takeaway: Check overdue findings against the deadline for their severity band, not against their age alone or their score alone.

scenario: A penetration test found that customers could view other customers' invoices by changing the invoice number in the URL. The company's automated scanner had never flagged this issue. Developers now say the authorization check is fixed and want the finding closed.
stem: Which is the BEST way to validate the remediation?

options.text: Have a tester repeat the original steps against the fixed application
options.why: Validation must use a method that can actually detect the flaw. Repeating the tester's steps verifies that changing the invoice number no longer exposes other customers' data.

options.text: Rerun the automated vulnerability scan and close the finding if it is clean
options.why: The scanner never detected this authorization flaw, so a clean scan proves nothing. It would report clean whether or not the fix works.

options.text: Review the developers' commit message and code change describing the fix
options.why: Reading the change is a useful check, but it is not testing. The fix could be incomplete, or other endpoints could still accept the altered number.

options.text: Add the finding to the scope of next year's internal audit for review
options.why: Deferring validation for a year leaves the company unsure whether customer data is still exposed. Verification should happen now.

takeaway: Validate remediation with a method that can see the flaw: rescanning works for scanner findings, while logic flaws found by testers need a retest.

scenario: The same CVE, with a CVSS base score of 7.8, appears on two Linux servers. The team can patch only one tonight and will patch the other next week.
stem: Which facts would justify patching Server A first? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Server A is reachable from the internet, while Server B is internal only
options.why: Exposure is an environmental variable that raises real risk. An internet-facing server can be reached by far more attackers.

options.text: Server A stores cardholder data covered by PCI DSS
options.why: Data sensitivity and regulatory impact raise the organizational impact of a compromise, which justifies higher priority.

options.text: Server A was added to the scanner's target list before Server B
options.why: The order in which hosts were added to a scan has nothing to do with how risky the vulnerability is.

options.text: Server A runs an older kernel version than Server B
options.why: Both servers have the same CVE. An older kernel might have other issues, but it does not make this vulnerability more dangerous on Server A.

options.text: Server A has more CPU and memory than Server B
options.why: Hardware capacity does not change exposure, data value or exploitability. It is irrelevant to patch priority.

takeaway: When the CVSS score is identical, prioritize on environmental variables (exposure) and industry or organizational impact (data, regulation, criticality).

scenario: An unpatched flaw affects a manufacturing control server valued at $400,000. Analysts estimate that an exploit would cause $100,000 of damage to the asset and expect an exploit about once every four years.
stem: What are the exposure factor and the annualized loss expectancy?

options.text: Exposure factor 25%, ALE $25,000
Exposure factor 25%, ALE $100,000
options.why: The exposure factor is right, but $100,000 is the single loss expectancy. It has not been multiplied by the annual rate of 0.25.

options.text: Exposure factor 75%, ALE $75,000
options.why: This uses the share of the asset that survives instead of the share that is lost. EF is the percentage of value lost in one event.

options.text: Exposure factor 25%, ALE $400,000
options.why: This multiplies by four years instead of by the annual rate. An event every four years means an ARO of 0.25, not 4.

takeaway: Exposure factor is the share of asset value lost in one event. SLE = asset value x EF, and ALE = SLE x ARO.

scenario: The network operations center polls 400 switches with SNMP every five minutes. When a switch's redundant power supply failed last week, nobody knew until the next poll. The team wants each switch to report hardware faults the moment they happen, and the monitoring system already supports SNMPv3.
stem: Which change BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Configure the switches to send SNMPv3 traps to the monitoring system
options.why: A trap is an unsolicited message the device sends as soon as an event occurs, so the NOC hears about a fault immediately. SNMPv3 adds authentication and encryption.

options.text: Shorten the SNMP polling interval for all 400 switches to every ten seconds
options.why: Faster polling narrows the gap but never closes it, and polling 400 switches every ten seconds adds heavy load to the devices and the monitoring system.

options.text: Export NetFlow records from every switch to a central flow collector
options.why: NetFlow describes traffic flows: who talked to whom and how much. It does not report hardware health such as a failed power supply.

options.text: Enable SNMPv2c traps that use the default community string
options.why: Version 2c traps would push the event, but they send a cleartext community string, and the default one is widely known. SNMPv3 is available and should be used.

takeaway: SNMP polling asks devices for status on a schedule; SNMP traps let the device push an alert the moment something happens. Use SNMPv3 for security.

scenario: A retailer wants to see which hosts at its 60 stores talk to which external addresses, how much data they send and when, so it can spot unusual transfers. The links to the stores are slow, and storing full packet captures from every store is not affordable.
stem: Which data source BEST fits these needs?

options.text: NetFlow or IPFIX records exported from each store's router
options.why: Flow records summarize every conversation by source, destination, ports, bytes and time without the payload. They answer who, where, when and how much at a fraction of the size of captures.

options.text: Full packet captures at each store, uploaded to headquarters every night
options.why: Captures contain everything, including payloads, but the scenario rules them out because of link speed and storage cost.

options.text: SNMP interface counters polled from each store's router every five minutes
options.why: Interface counters show total traffic on a link, but they cannot show which internal host talked to which external address.

options.text: Antivirus logs collected from the point-of-sale terminals at each store
options.why: Antivirus logs record malware detections on endpoints. They do not describe network conversations or data volumes.

takeaway: NetFlow gives metadata (who, where, when, how much) about traffic; packet capture gives content. Choose flows when you need breadth at low cost.

scenario: A company must check the configuration of 120 vendor-managed network appliances against its hardening standard every week. The support contract is void if any third-party software is installed on them, but each appliance accepts SSH logins from a read-only account.
stem: Which monitoring approach BEST fits these constraints?

options.text: Agentless scanning that logs in over SSH with the read-only account
options.why: Agentless checks connect with existing protocols and credentials, read the configuration and compare it with the standard. Nothing is installed, so the contract is not affected.

options.text: A lightweight compliance agent installed on each of the 120 appliances
options.why: An agent would give detailed results, but installing third-party software voids the vendor's support contract.

options.text: Unauthenticated network scans that check which ports each appliance has open
options.why: An unauthenticated scan sees only what is exposed on the network. It cannot read the configuration settings the standard covers.

options.text: A review of the vendor's published security guide for each appliance model
options.why: A vendor guide describes recommended settings, not what is actually configured on the company's appliances each week.

takeaway: Agentless monitoring uses existing access such as SSH, WMI or APIs and suits systems where agents cannot be installed; agents suit devices you fully manage.

scenario: Most of a consulting firm's 900 laptops connect to the corporate network only a few days a month. The weekly vulnerability scan runs from the data center on Tuesday nights, and the latest report covered only 210 laptops.
stem: Which change would MOST improve scan coverage of the laptops?

options.text: Deploy scanning agents that assess each laptop and report over the internet
options.why: An agent runs on the laptop itself and reports results whenever the device has an internet connection, so coverage no longer depends on being on the corporate network.

options.text: Run the network vulnerability scan every night instead of once a week
options.why: More frequent network scans still miss laptops that are off the corporate network or asleep, which is most of them on most nights.

options.text: Require consultants to connect to the VPN every Tuesday evening
options.why: This depends on hundreds of people remembering and leaving their laptops awake. Coverage would remain unreliable.

options.text: Switch the network scan to credentialed mode with a scanning account
options.why: Credentialed scans find more on each host they reach, but they do not reach more hosts. Coverage is the problem here.

takeaway: Network scans only see devices that are present when the scan runs. Agents cover roaming and remote endpoints wherever they connect.

scenario: After a breach, investigators found the attacker had cleared the Security event log on three compromised servers, erasing evidence of how they moved between them. Each server kept its logs only on its own disk.
stem: Which control would BEST have preserved this evidence?

options.text: Forwarding logs in near real time to a central log platform
options.why: Log aggregation copies each event off the server as it happens. Clearing the local log afterward would not remove the copies the attacker cannot reach.

options.text: Increasing the maximum size of each server's local Security log
options.why: A bigger log keeps more history, but an attacker with administrator rights can still clear it in one command.

options.text: Backing up each server's event logs to tape every Sunday night
options.why: Weekly backups leave days of events unprotected. Anything cleared between backups is lost.

options.text: Alerting the server team when a local Security log becomes 90% full
options.why: This alert is about capacity, not tampering. It would neither preserve the events nor reveal that the log was cleared.

takeaway: Aggregate logs centrally and quickly. Local logs can be cleared by anyone who controls the host, so the evidence must already be elsewhere.

scenario: A payment processor's SIEM keeps 90 days of searchable logs and then deletes them. PCI DSS requires at least one year of audit log history, with the most recent three months immediately available for analysis. Expanding the SIEM's searchable storage to a full year would triple its licensing cost.
stem: Which approach BEST meets the requirement at a reasonable cost?

options.text: Archive logs older than 90 days to low-cost, tamper-resistant storage for a year
options.why: Archiving keeps the three months the standard requires immediately available in the SIEM and retains the rest more cheaply, protected from alteration until it can be deleted.

options.text: Expand the SIEM's searchable storage so that it holds a full year of logs
options.why: This meets the requirement, but at triple the cost, and the standard only needs the most recent three months to be immediately available.

options.text: Keep 90 days in the SIEM and rely on each device's local logs for the rest
options.why: Local logs roll over and can be altered on the device, so there is no assurance a year of history will survive.

options.text: Produce monthly summary reports from the SIEM and then delete the raw logs
options.why: Summaries are not audit log history. Investigators and auditors need the original events.

takeaway: Archiving moves older logs to cheaper, protected storage to meet retention rules, while the SIEM keeps the recent data needed for fast searching.

scenario: The antivirus policy on engineering workstations deletes any detected file immediately. Last week it deleted a licensed simulation tool flagged by a new heuristic rule; the detection was a false positive, and engineers lost two days reinstalling. Security still wants detected files made harmless right away.
stem: Which policy change BEST balances these needs?

options.text: Quarantine detected files so they can be analyzed and restored if benign
options.why: Quarantine moves the file to an isolated location where it cannot run, which neutralizes real malware at once while keeping the file available for analysis and restoration.

options.text: Set the antivirus to alert only and take no action when it detects a file
options.why: Alert-only mode avoids false positive damage, but real malware would remain able to run until someone responds.

options.text: Exclude the engineering software folders from antivirus scanning
options.why: An exclusion stops this false positive but creates a blind spot where real malware could hide.

options.text: Disable heuristic detection and rely only on signature-based detection
options.why: Turning off heuristics removes detection of new and modified malware just to avoid one false positive.

takeaway: Quarantine is the safe default response for detected files: it stops execution immediately but keeps the file for analysis and easy restoration.

scenario: An analyst tuned a noisy SIEM rule that detects credential dumping from LSASS memory by excluding a backup product's process. Alerts dropped from 300 a day to 2. The team wants to be sure the tuned rule still catches real attacks.
stem: What is the BEST way to validate the change?

options.text: Simulate the credential dumping technique on a test host and confirm the alert fires
options.why: Validation means proving the rule still detects the behavior it exists for. Running the technique in a controlled test shows whether tuning created false negatives.

options.text: Check that the daily alert count stays low for the next 30 days
options.why: A low count could mean the tuning worked or that the rule no longer detects anything. It cannot distinguish the two.

options.text: Ask the backup vendor to confirm its process no longer triggers the rule
options.why: This confirms the false positives are gone, which is only half the goal. It says nothing about whether real attacks still alert.

options.text: Raise the severity of the tuned rule so the remaining alerts get attention
options.why: Severity changes how alerts are handled, not whether the rule detects attacks. It does not validate anything.

takeaway: After alert tuning, validate in both directions: false positives should drop, and a simulated true positive must still trigger the alert.

scenario: Network DLP on the web proxy has reported no violations in months. An investigation then shows a departing employee uploaded customer spreadsheets to a personal cloud storage site through that proxy. The site uses HTTPS, and the proxy passes HTTPS traffic through without inspecting it.
stem: Which change would BEST allow the DLP to detect such uploads?

options.text: Enable TLS inspection on the proxy for cloud storage site categories
options.why: Network DLP can only match content it can read. Decrypting uploads to cloud storage sites at the proxy lets the DLP policies see the spreadsheets.

options.text: Add more customer data patterns and keywords to the DLP policy
options.why: Better patterns cannot match content that is still encrypted. The DLP never sees the data inside the HTTPS session.

options.text: Use NetFlow from the proxy to flag unusually large outbound transfers
options.why: Flow data could show a large upload, but not what was in it. It is not DLP and cannot tell customer data from a large video.

options.text: Move the DLP sensor to the internet edge outside the web proxy
options.why: Traffic is still encrypted at the edge, so the sensor would be just as blind there.

takeaway: Network DLP needs to see content. For HTTPS traffic that means TLS inspection, usually with exceptions for categories such as banking and health sites.

scenario: Each event in the exhibit is below the alert threshold of the system that logged it: the VPN alerts only after 20 failed logins, and the file server never alerts on reads. Together, they suggest a guessed password followed by bulk access to finance files.
stem: Which capability would BEST detect this pattern automatically?
exhibit:
02:14:07 VPN      user=jlee  result=FAIL     src=185.220.101.4
02:14:11 VPN      user=jlee  result=FAIL     src=185.220.101.4
02:14:16 VPN      user=jlee  result=FAIL     src=185.220.101.4
02:16:40 VPN      user=jlee  result=SUCCESS  src=185.220.101.4
02:19:02 FILESRV  user=jlee  action=read   count=2314  share=\\fs01\finance

options.text: A SIEM correlation rule linking login failures, a success and mass file reads
options.why: Correlation joins events from different sources by user and time. A rule for failures, then a success, then unusual file access catches the pattern no single system flags.

options.text: Lowering the VPN's failed-login alert threshold to three attempts for all users
options.why: A lower threshold would flag the failures, but it would also generate heavy noise from mistyped passwords and still ignore the file access that matters most.

options.text: SNMPv3 traps sent from the VPN concentrator to the network monitoring system
options.why: SNMP traps report device health and status events. They do not tie user logins to file access.

options.text: A scheduled antivirus scan of the finance file share on the file server
options.why: Antivirus looks for malicious files. Reading spreadsheets with valid credentials is not malware.

takeaway: A SIEM's value is correlation: linking individually harmless events across sources into one alert that reflects attacker behavior.

scenario: A network team wants to monitor CPU load, interface errors and link utilization on 30 routers, and also see which hosts generate the most traffic through them. Policy forbids installing any software on the routers.
stem: Which tools should the team use? (Select TWO.)

options.text: SNMPv3 polling of the routers from a monitoring system
options.why: SNMP is built into routers and reports CPU, interface errors and utilization without installing anything. Version 3 adds authentication and encryption.

options.text: NetFlow exported from the routers to a flow collector
options.why: Routers export flow records natively, showing which hosts send the most traffic and to where, which SNMP counters cannot show.

options.text: EDR agents installed on each router's operating system
options.why: Policy forbids installing software on the routers, and EDR is designed for endpoints rather than network devices.

options.text: Endpoint DLP deployed to the network team's laptops
options.why: DLP watches for sensitive data leaving endpoints. It gives no visibility into router health or traffic volumes.

options.text: Static code analysis of the routers' firmware images
options.why: Static analysis is an assessment of code for flaws. It does not monitor live device health or traffic.

takeaway: For infrastructure monitoring without agents, SNMP covers device health and counters, and NetFlow covers who is talking to whom and how much.

scenario: A factory's isolated OT network runs antivirus on 40 engineering workstations. Because the network has no internet access, the signatures were last updated eight months ago. Connecting the network to the internet is not permitted.
stem: Which of the following is the BEST way to keep the antivirus effective?

options.text: Bring in hash-verified signature updates through a controlled transfer process
options.why: Updates can reach an isolated network through a managed path, such as scanned and verified media or a one-way transfer to an internal update server. Isolation is kept and protection is current.

options.text: Allow the workstations to reach the vendor's update servers through the firewall
options.why: This would update the signatures, but it opens the isolated network to the internet, which policy forbids.

options.text: Uninstall the antivirus because signatures that old provide no protection at all
options.why: Old signatures still detect older malware, and removal leaves the workstations with no detection at all.

options.text: Let engineers copy signature files from home onto USB drives when they remember
options.why: Uncontrolled personal media is a classic way malware enters isolated networks, and updates would be irregular and unverified.

takeaway: Isolated networks still need updates. Use a controlled, verified transfer path instead of either connecting the network or letting protections go stale.

scenario: Security policy says SSH to the public web server 203.0.113.20 is allowed only from the admin network 198.51.100.0/24. The firewall log shows SSH sessions from dozens of unknown internet addresses being permitted to that server. The rule base is shown in the exhibit.
exhibit:
FW-EDGE inbound rules (top to bottom, first match wins)
#  Source            Destination      Proto  Port  Action
1  Any               203.0.113.20     TCP    443   Allow
2  Any               203.0.113.0/24   TCP    Any   Allow
3  198.51.100.0/24   203.0.113.20     TCP    22    Allow
4  Any               203.0.113.20     TCP    22    Deny
5  Any               Any              Any    Any   Deny
stem: Which change BEST fixes the problem while keeping the intended access?

options.text: Remove rule 2, or narrow it to only the ports the subnet actually needs to publish
options.why: Rule 2 permits every TCP port to the whole subnet, so internet SSH matches it and is allowed before rules 3 and 4 are ever evaluated. Removing or narrowing it lets the admin allow and the SSH deny work as written.

options.text: Move rule 4 above rule 3 so that the SSH deny is evaluated before the admin allow
options.why: This changes the wrong pair of rules. Internet SSH would still match rule 2 first, and the admins would now be blocked by the deny.

options.text: Delete rule 5 and rely on the firewall's implicit deny at the end of the list instead
options.why: An explicit and an implicit final deny behave the same, and traffic never reaches rule 5 because rule 2 already allowed it.

options.text: Restrict rule 1 so that TCP 443 is accepted only from the admin network 198.51.100.0/24
options.why: Rule 1 handles HTTPS, not SSH. Narrowing it would break the public website and leave the SSH exposure through rule 2 untouched.

takeaway: With first match wins, an overly broad allow placed above specific rules silently overrides them. Read the list top down and find the first rule each packet hits.

scenario: At 3 a.m. an internal file server suddenly opened SMB sessions to 700 workstations, something it has never done before. The attackers used a custom tool, and the signature-based IPS, which is fully up to date, raised no alert.
stem: Which change to the IPS would MOST likely detect this kind of activity in the future?

options.text: Subscribe to a second commercial signature feed so that the IPS receives new rules every hour
options.why: More signatures help only for known tools. A custom tool has no signature in any feed, so the gap remains.

options.text: Enable anomaly-based detection that baselines normal traffic and alerts on deviations
options.why: Behavior or trend-based detection compares activity with a learned baseline, so a server that has never talked SMB to workstations stands out even without a signature.

options.text: Switch the sensor from inline prevention mode to passive monitoring through a network tap
options.why: Moving to passive mode changes whether the device can block, not what it can recognize. It would still miss the unknown tool.

options.text: Write a custom signature for the attacker's tool based on the hashes found in this incident
options.why: A custom rule catches this exact tool next time but nothing new. The question asks for detection of activity that has no signature.

takeaway: Signature detection finds what is already known with few false positives; anomaly or trend-based detection finds the unknown by spotting changes from a baseline, at the cost of more tuning.

scenario: During a test, a red team delivered a well-known exploit kit to a user's browser. The inline IPS at the internet edge blocked the payload when it was served over HTTP but raised nothing when the same payload came over HTTPS. The IPS signatures are current.
stem: Which change would BEST let the IPS stop the HTTPS delivery?

options.text: Replace the signature set with a vendor feed that publishes updates several times per hour
options.why: The signature already exists and matched over HTTP. Faster updates do not help when the IPS cannot read the encrypted payload.

options.text: Add an anomaly-based engine that baselines each user's HTTPS traffic volume and destinations
options.why: A single small download looks normal in volume, and an anomaly engine still cannot see inside the encrypted session.

options.text: Enable TLS inspection on the forward proxy and pass the decrypted traffic to the IPS
options.why: The IPS failed only because the payload was encrypted. Decrypting at the proxy lets the existing signatures see and block it.

options.text: Move the IPS from the internet edge to a tap behind the core switch in passive mode
options.why: The traffic is still encrypted at the core, and passive mode would remove the ability to block.

takeaway: An IPS can only inspect what it can read. When a known attack passes over TLS but is caught in plaintext, the fix is decryption, not more signatures.

scenario: A company already blocks malicious domains with DNS filtering on every laptop. HR now wants staff to keep using a large social site's messaging and company pages but be blocked from its marketplace and gaming sections. Staff work remotely and do not use a VPN.
stem: Which solution BEST meets this new requirement?

options.text: Add the social site's domain to the DNS filtering block list for all users
options.why: DNS filtering sees only the domain name, so blocking it removes the whole site, including the messaging and pages HR wants to keep.

options.text: Send all web traffic through a centralized proxy in the head office data center
options.why: A head office proxy could filter by URL path, but remote staff without a VPN would bypass it unless their traffic is backhauled, which is not the case here.

options.text: Deploy an agent-based web filter that applies URL path and content category rules
options.why: An endpoint agent filters wherever the laptop is and can match full URLs and categories, so it can block specific sections of a site while allowing the rest.

options.text: Create reputation-based block rules that deny any site with a low reputation score
options.why: A large, popular social site has a good reputation. Reputation scoring cannot separate its acceptable sections from the ones HR wants blocked.

takeaway: DNS filtering works at the domain level only; blocking part of a site needs URL filtering, and for off-network users that means an agent-based filter or a cloud proxy.

scenario: A phishing email sent users to a credential harvesting page on a domain registered six hours earlier. The web filter blocks the phishing, malware and spyware categories, but logs show it allowed the page because the domain was classified as "uncategorized."
stem: Which web filter change would BEST prevent this type of miss?

options.text: Add the specific phishing domain to the web filter's custom block list
options.why: Blocking this one domain is reactive. The next campaign will use another freshly registered domain.

options.text: Expand the category block list to include social media, file sharing and personal storage sites
options.why: Those categories do not cover a brand-new uncategorized domain, and they would block business use without fixing the gap.

options.text: Block or isolate uncategorized and newly registered domains using reputation data
options.why: New phishing domains have no category and no reputation yet. A rule that blocks, warns or opens them in isolation covers that window.

options.text: Require security awareness training on spotting phishing links for all staff each quarter
options.why: Training is worthwhile but is not a web filter change, and the question asks how the filter should stop pages like this one.

takeaway: Category filtering misses brand-new domains because they are not yet classified. Reputation rules for uncategorized and newly registered domains close that gap.

scenario: Harborline's own domain, harborline.com, publishes SPF, DKIM and a DMARC policy of p=reject. An accounts payable clerk received the message in the exhibit and nearly sent a wire transfer before calling the CFO.
stem: Which control would BEST help stop messages like this one?

options.text: Change the DMARC record for harborline.com to strict SPF and DKIM alignment
options.why: Alignment settings apply to mail claiming to be from harborline.com. This message is from a different domain the attacker controls, so it passes its own checks.

options.text: Email gateway rules that flag lookalike sender domains and tag external messages
options.why: The attacker registered harb0rline.com and authenticated it properly, so only lookalike detection and external sender warnings on the gateway catch it.

options.text: Rotate the DKIM signing keys for harborline.com and lengthen them to 2048 bits
options.why: Stronger keys protect mail signed for harborline.com. They have no effect on a domain the company does not own.

options.text: Change the SPF record for harborline.com so that it ends in -all instead of ~all
options.why: With p=reject already in place, the SPF qualifier is not the gap. The message never claimed harborline.com.

takeaway: SPF, DKIM and DMARC prove a message came from the domain it names. They cannot stop a lookalike domain the attacker owns; the email gateway has to catch that.

scenario: Email DLP blocks outbound messages containing more than five customer account numbers. A departing employee emailed the full customer list to a personal address inside a password-protected ZIP file. The DLP log entry reads "attachment could not be inspected: encrypted," and the message was delivered.
stem: Which change would BEST close this gap?

options.text: Lower the DLP threshold so that a single customer account number triggers a block
options.why: The threshold is not the problem. DLP could not read any of the content, so no threshold would have matched.

options.text: Fingerprint the customer list so that DLP recognizes even partial copies of it in messages
options.why: Fingerprinting still requires DLP to read the attachment, which it cannot do while the ZIP is encrypted.

options.text: Quarantine outbound attachments that DLP cannot inspect, such as encrypted archives
options.why: Content that cannot be inspected is the blind spot. Holding it for review or blocking it unless sent through approved encryption stops this bypass.

options.text: Deploy endpoint DLP that prevents copying files labeled Confidential to removable USB drives
options.why: Endpoint USB control is useful but covers a different channel. The data left through email, which is where the gap is.

takeaway: DLP can only match content it can read. Decide what happens to encrypted or otherwise uninspectable files, or they become the easy way around every rule.

scenario: External auditors connect their own laptops to wired guest ports for a two-week engagement. Policy requires checking that antivirus is running and the OS is patched before granting access, but the audit firm will not allow permanent software to be installed on its laptops.
stem: Which NAC approach BEST meets both requirements?

options.text: A dissolvable agent that runs the posture check and removes itself
options.why: A temporary agent performs a full posture assessment for the session and leaves nothing installed, which fits both the policy and the auditors' restriction.

options.text: A persistent agent installed on each auditor laptop for the length of the engagement
options.why: A persistent agent gives detailed posture data, but the audit firm has already refused permanent software on its devices.

options.text: MAC address filtering on the guest ports using a list of the auditors' laptops
options.why: MAC filtering identifies devices loosely and is easy to spoof. It checks nothing about antivirus or patch level.

options.text: 802.1X on the guest ports using certificates issued by the company to each auditor
options.why: Certificates authenticate the device or user but do not assess posture, and enrolling them means installing company configuration on the laptops.

takeaway: NAC posture checks come in persistent, dissolvable and agentless forms. Dissolvable agents suit visitors who need a real posture check but cannot keep software installed.

scenario: In the last incident, a phishing email led to a stolen session token and then a malicious inbox rule in the cloud mailbox. Analysts took nine hours to connect the events because email security, identity, endpoint EDR and cloud tools each have separate consoles. The team wants detections correlated automatically and response actions from one place, without writing and maintaining its own correlation rules.
stem: Which solution BEST fits?

options.text: Upgrade the EDR agents to the vendor's newest release with longer local telemetry retention
options.why: Better endpoint data does not help with an attack that ran mostly through email, identity and the cloud mailbox.

options.text: Extended detection and response (XDR)
options.why: XDR natively combines endpoint, email, identity and cloud telemetry into correlated incidents with built-in response actions, which is exactly the requirement.

options.text: A SIEM that collects logs from every tool so analysts can write correlation searches
options.why: A SIEM can centralize the logs, but the team would still have to build and maintain the correlation rules, which it wants to avoid.

options.text: User behavior analytics focused on detecting unusual activity by individual accounts
options.why: UBA would flag unusual account behavior but does not correlate across email, endpoint and cloud or provide response actions for them.

takeaway: EDR covers endpoints; XDR extends detection and response across endpoints, email, identity, network and cloud with built-in correlation.

scenario: An engineer's account signed in from the corporate VPN with a valid password and MFA at 2 a.m. and cloned 600 source code repositories in one night. The engineer normally touches about five a week. No signature or SIEM rule fired, and the repositories carry no DLP classification labels.
stem: Which capability would MOST likely have detected this activity?

options.text: DLP policies that block transfers of documents labeled Confidential or Restricted
options.why: DLP relies on labels or content patterns, and these repositories have no labels, so the policy would not match.

options.text: An IPS with updated signatures for known data exfiltration tools and techniques
options.why: The activity used normal Git operations over an approved connection. There is nothing malicious for a signature to match.

options.text: Network access control with posture checks on every device that connects to the VPN
options.why: NAC checks the device when it connects. A healthy corporate laptop with valid credentials would pass.

options.text: User behavior analytics that compares each account with its own normal baseline
options.why: UBA learns what is normal for each user, so a jump of more than 100 times the usual number of in repositories accessed at an unusual hour stands out even when every login is valid.

takeaway: When credentials, MFA and the device all look legitimate, the remaining signal is behavior. UBA detects compromised or malicious insiders by deviation from each user's baseline.

scenario: An administrator used mv to move a website's files from a home directory into /var/www/html. The site now returns 403 Forbidden. File permissions are 644 and owned by apache, and SELinux is in enforcing mode. The audit log shows the entry in the exhibit.
exhibit:
type=AVC msg=audit(1760612400.123:812): avc:  denied  { read } for
  pid=2214 comm="httpd" name="index.html"
  scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0
  tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:user_home_t:s0
  tclass=file permissive=0
stem: Which action BEST fixes the problem without weakening security?

options.text: Run setenforce 0 so that SELinux logs the denial but no longer blocks Apache's reads
options.why: Permissive mode makes the site work by removing mandatory access control for the whole system. That weakens security instead of fixing the label.

options.text: Restore the default SELinux context on /var/www/html with restorecon -R
options.why: mv kept the user_home_t label from the home directory. restorecon relabels the files as httpd_sys_content_t, which the httpd_t policy allows Apache to read.

options.text: Change the file permissions to 777 so that every account, including apache, can read them
options.why: The denial comes from SELinux, not from standard Linux permissions. 777 would not stop the AVC denial and would let anyone modify the site.

options.text: Configure Apache to run as root so that it can read files regardless of their ownership
options.why: Running the web server as root does not bypass SELinux type enforcement and would make any compromise of Apache a full system compromise.

takeaway: An SELinux denial with correct file permissions usually means a wrong security context. Fix the label with restorecon or semanage rather than disabling enforcement.

scenario: The company's recursive DNS resolvers were poisoned with forged answers that sent users to a fake payroll site, even though the payroll domain is signed by its owner. The security team needs the resolvers to reject forged answers for signed zones. Hiding which names users look up is not a requirement.
stem: Which change BEST meets this requirement?

options.text: Configure clients to send their queries to the resolvers using DNS over HTTPS
options.why: DoH encrypts traffic between clients and the resolver, protecting privacy, but it does nothing to verify answers the resolver receives from upstream servers.

options.text: Add the fake payroll domain to the company's DNS filtering block list
options.why: The attack forged answers for the real payroll name. Blocking the fake site's domain does not stop the next forged record for a legitimate name.

options.text: Enable DNSSEC validation on the recursive resolvers
options.why: DNSSEC validation checks the digital signatures on records from signed zones, so forged answers fail validation and are discarded instead of cached.

options.text: Require all DNS traffic between the resolvers and upstream servers to use TCP port 53
options.why: Using TCP makes some spoofing harder but does not authenticate the data. DNSSEC is the control designed to prove records are genuine.

takeaway: DNSSEC gives DNS integrity and origin authentication but no confidentiality; DoH and DoT give confidentiality but do not prove an answer is genuine.

scenario: Remote staff reach the company mail server from the internet with desktop mail clients. They send mail through the server and download it with POP3; delivery between mail servers is handled by a separate relay. A new standard says no client session may start in plaintext, because a STARTTLS downgrade could expose credentials.
stem: Which ports should the edge firewall allow from the internet to this server? (Select TWO.)

options.text: TCP 465
options.why: Port 465 is message submission over implicit TLS. The TLS handshake happens before any SMTP command, so nothing is ever sent in plaintext.

options.text: TCP 995
options.why: POP3S on 995 uses implicit TLS from the first byte, which meets the standard for downloading mail with POP3.

options.text: TCP 587
options.why: Submission on 587 starts in plaintext and upgrades with STARTTLS. It ends up encrypted, but the session begins in the clear, which the standard forbids.

options.text: TCP 110
options.why: Plain POP3 starts unencrypted. Even with the STLS upgrade command, the session begins in plaintext before encryption starts.

options.text: TCP 993
options.why: IMAPS on 993 is implicit TLS and would meet the standard, but staff download mail with POP3, so nothing would use it.

options.text: TCP 25
options.why: Port 25 is SMTP relay between mail servers, which the separate relay handles. It also starts in plaintext, with STARTTLS optional.

takeaway: Implicit TLS encrypts from the first byte: submission 465, IMAPS 993, POP3S 995. STARTTLS (SMTP on 25 and 587, and the upgrade on 110 and 143) starts in plaintext and then switches to TLS.

scenario: Threat intelligence lists 40 command-and-control domains used by a malware family. The domains rotate through hundreds of IP addresses every day. The security team wants to stop infected machines from reaching the C2 servers and also learn which internal hosts are infected, without installing new software on endpoints.
stem: Which approach BEST meets these goals?

options.text: Block the current IP addresses of the C2 servers at the edge firewall and review its deny log
options.why: The deny log would show some infected hosts, but the domains move to new addresses daily, so the block list is always out of date.

options.text: DNS filtering that answers queries for the listed domains with a sinkhole address and logs the source
options.why: Blocking at the name level works no matter which IP the domain points to, and every query to the sinkhole identifies an infected host.

options.text: Add the C2 domains to the web proxy's block list under the malware category
options.why: Malware often talks to C2 directly rather than through the proxy, and non-HTTP channels never touch it, so coverage and visibility would be partial.

options.text: Ask the EDR vendor for a new detection signature and deploy it to all endpoints
options.why: This needs endpoint coverage and a signature that may not exist yet. It also does not block the domains at the network level as asked.

takeaway: For C2 that rotates IP addresses, block at the DNS layer. A sinkhole both cuts the callback and turns every lookup into a list of infected hosts.

scenario: A mobile app offers "Sign in with Partner Portal." After the OAuth 2.0 flow, the app treats any valid access token it receives as proof of who the user is. A tester showed that an access token issued to a different app for the same user could be replayed to sign in to this app as that user.
stem: Which change BEST fixes this design flaw?

options.text: Shorten the lifetime of every access token the portal issues to five minutes
options.why: A shorter lifetime narrows the replay window but leaves the core mistake in place: an access token still does not prove the user signed in to this app.

options.text: Use OpenID Connect and validate the ID token's issuer, audience and signature
options.why: OAuth access tokens authorize API calls; they are not meant for the app to learn who signed in. An OIDC ID token is issued for this specific app (audience) and is the standard proof of authentication.

options.text: Add PKCE to the authorization code flow that the mobile app already uses
options.why: PKCE stops an intercepted authorization code from being redeemed. It does not stop the app from accepting a token that was issued to another client.

options.text: Replace the flow with SAML 2.0 assertions because OAuth cannot be used by mobile apps
options.why: OAuth works well on mobile, and SAML is built mainly for browser-based web SSO. Switching protocols is a larger change than needed and rests on a false premise.

takeaway: OAuth 2.0 is for authorization (what an app may access). OpenID Connect adds authentication on top with an ID token; SAML does authentication through signed assertions.

scenario: A scheduling startup's web app needs to read and create events in employees' corporate calendars through the calendar provider's API. The company will not let the app store employee passwords, and each employee must be able to revoke the app's access without changing a password.
stem: Which technology BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: OAuth 2.0 with scoped access tokens
options.why: OAuth lets the user consent to specific scopes such as calendar read and write. The app gets a revocable token for the API and never sees the password.

options.text: SAML 2.0 assertions issued by the corporate identity provider to the startup's app
options.why: SAML signs a user in to a service provider. It does not give the app delegated, scoped access to call another provider's API.

options.text: An LDAP bind from the app to the directory using a dedicated service account and password
options.why: This stores a credential in the app, grants directory access rather than calendar API access, and cannot be revoked per employee.

options.text: OpenID Connect ID tokens presented to the calendar API as proof of each employee's identity
options.why: ID tokens tell the client app who signed in. APIs authorize requests with access tokens and scopes, not ID tokens.

takeaway: Delegated access to an API without sharing a password, with consent and revocation, is OAuth. If the question is about proving who the user is, think OIDC or SAML.

scenario: After weekend maintenance on the company's identity provider server, users can no longer sign in to any SaaS application through SSO. They enter their credentials at the IdP successfully, then each SaaS app shows an error. One provider sent the log in the exhibit.
exhibit:
SP log, crm.example-saas.com (provider time 2026-10-14T13:02:11Z)
SAML Response rejected: Assertion is not yet valid
  Issuer        https://idp.corp.example
  Signature     valid
  Audience      match
  NotBefore     2026-10-14T13:09:40Z
  NotOnOrAfter  2026-10-14T13:14:40Z
stem: Which is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: The IdP's token signing certificate expired during the maintenance window
options.why: The log shows the signature validated. An expired or replaced signing certificate would fail signature checks instead.

options.text: The entity ID configured for the SaaS application no longer matches the audience
options.why: The log reports that the audience matched, so the assertion was addressed to the right service provider.

options.text: The IdP server's clock is several minutes fast, so assertions arrive before they are valid
options.why: The assertion's NotBefore time is about seven minutes after the provider's receive time. An IdP clock running fast after maintenance fits, and fixing NTP restores sign-in to every app.

options.text: The users' directory passwords expired over the weekend and must be reset at the IdP
options.why: Users already authenticated at the IdP, and the IdP issued an assertion. Expired passwords would stop them before that point.

takeaway: SAML assertions carry validity windows, so clock skew between the IdP and service providers breaks SSO even when signature and audience are correct. Keep both sides on NTP.

scenario: A company has acquired a competitor. Each has its own directory and identity provider. Within two weeks, the competitor's 900 employees need access to 15 of the parent company's web applications, and the directories will not be merged for at least 18 months.
stem: Which approach BEST provides this access?

options.text: Create a second account in the parent directory for each competitor employee
options.why: Duplicate accounts double the passwords users must manage, and when someone leaves the competitor, the parent account is easily missed during deprovisioning.

options.text: Establish a federation trust so the parent apps accept the competitor IdP's assertions
options.why: Federation lets employees authenticate at their home IdP while the parent company's apps trust the assertions. Leaving the home company still removes their access in one place.

options.text: Migrate every competitor account into the parent company's directory before the deadline
options.why: This is the long-term plan, but it cannot be done safely in two weeks and is not needed to grant access now.

options.text: Provide a small set of shared accounts in the parent directory for each competitor department
options.why: Shared accounts destroy individual accountability and make revoking one person's access impossible without affecting the whole department.

takeaway: Federation extends trust between separate identity domains so users sign in once with their home credentials. It is the standard answer for mergers and partner access.

scenario: A systems administrator will be terminated at a 10 a.m. meeting. The administrator has VPN access, cloud console admin rights, knowledge of several shared service passwords and an active email session on a phone. Legal wants the mailbox and files preserved for a possible investigation.
stem: Which actions should happen at the time of notification? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Disable the user's accounts instead of deleting them
options.why: Disabling cuts off access immediately while keeping the mailbox, files and account history that legal wants preserved.

options.text: Revoke active sessions and tokens, and rotate the shared passwords the admin knew
options.why: Disabling an account does not always end existing sessions on phones or in the cloud console, and shared passwords stay valid until they are changed.

options.text: Delete all of the user's accounts so that none can be reused
options.why: Deletion stops access but can destroy the mailbox and files that legal needs to preserve.

options.text: Change only the domain password and leave the accounts enabled for handover
options.why: A password change does not end sessions or tokens already issued, and the shared service passwords would still work.

options.text: Remotely wipe the administrator's laptop before collecting it from the meeting
options.why: Wiping destroys potential evidence. The device should be collected and preserved instead.

takeaway: For a hostile departure, disable rather than delete, kill existing sessions and tokens, and rotate any shared secrets the person knew, all at the moment of notification.

scenario: New remote hires receive their first password from the help desk by phone, at a number they give during onboarding. An attacker posing as a new hire got the credentials, enrolled his own authenticator app at first sign-in and accessed HR data for a week.
stem: Which control would BEST have prevented this?

options.text: Require new hires to enroll in MFA during their very first sign-in
options.why: That already happened here, and it helped the attacker: whoever holds the first password enrolls their own MFA device.

options.text: Require managers to attest each quarter that their team members still need their access
options.why: Attestation reviews whether existing access is still appropriate. It does not verify a person's identity before an account is handed over.

options.text: Verify identity against a government ID and live video check before issuing credentials
options.why: Identity proofing confirms that the person receiving the account is the person HR hired, closing the gap the attacker used.

options.text: Make the initial password longer and more complex, and require a change at first sign-in
options.why: A stronger initial password does not matter when it is delivered to the wrong person.

takeaway: Identity proofing happens before provisioning: confirm the real person first, then issue credentials. MFA and attestation cannot fix an account given to an impostor.

scenario: A defense contractor labels documents Confidential, Secret or Top Secret, and each employee holds a clearance. A project lead who creates a Secret document must not be able to share it with an uncleared colleague, even though he owns the file. The operating system must enforce this centrally.
stem: Which access control model BEST fits?

options.text: Discretionary access control
options.why: DAC lets owners decide who gets access, which is exactly what must be prevented here.

options.text: Role-based access control
options.why: RBAC grants permissions by job role. It does not compare classification labels with clearances or stop owners from sharing.

options.text: Mandatory access control
options.why: MAC enforces system-wide labels and clearances that users, including owners, cannot change, so a Secret document is readable only by someone cleared for Secret or higher.

options.text: Rule-based access control
options.why: Rule-based control applies global conditions such as time or source address to everyone. It is not built around classification labels and clearances.

takeaway: Labels and clearances that even owners cannot override mean MAC. If owners decide, it is DAC; job roles mean RBAC; global conditions mean rule-based; many attributes mean ABAC.

scenario: An audit of a small design firm's file server finds no security groups and no central policy. Each folder's creator sets its permissions, and one designer granted Everyone Full Control on a folder of client contracts to make sharing easier.
stem: Which access control model is this environment MOST likely using?

options.text: Discretionary access control
