options.text: The router is pushing a scheduled backup over FTP; switch the backup job to FTPS
options.why: The laptop sent the read request and the router is answering it. The protocol is TFTP on UDP 69, not FTP on TCP 20 and 21.

takeaway: TFTP (UDP 69) has no login and no encryption. Move device configurations with SCP or SFTP over SSH (TCP 22), and limit management protocols to the management network.

scenario: A public web server at 203.0.113.31 runs its application and its database on the same host. The edge firewall log is shown, and the database's authentication log shows thousands of failed logins for the root account.
stem: Which service is being attacked, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: MySQL on TCP 3306; lock the database root account after five failed login attempts
options.why: Lockout slows guessing but leaves the database exposed to the internet, and locking root can itself cause an outage. Removing the exposure is better.

options.text: RDP on TCP 3306; require Network Level Authentication for remote logins
options.why: RDP is TCP 3389. Port 3306 is MySQL, and NLA has nothing to do with database logins.

options.text: Microsoft SQL Server on TCP 1433; close 1433 at the firewall
options.why: The 1433 attempts were already denied and aimed at a different address. The attempts that got through went to 3306, which is MySQL.

options.text: MySQL on TCP 3306; close 3306 at the firewall and bind the database to localhost
options.why: 3306 is MySQL. Because the application runs on the same host, the database needs no network listener at all; binding to 127.0.0.1 and removing the firewall rule removes the attack surface.

takeaway: Database ports: 1433 Microsoft SQL Server, 3306 MySQL and MariaDB, 1521 Oracle, 5432 PostgreSQL. Databases belong behind the application tier, never directly on the internet.

scenario: A company is moving its phones to a hosted SIP provider. A security review requires that call setup and authentication be encrypted across the internet and that the voice itself be encrypted as well. The firewall team asks what to configure toward the provider.
stem: Which configuration meets the requirement?

options.text: SIP over TLS on TCP 5061, with SRTP for the voice media
options.why: 5061 is SIP over TLS, which encrypts call setup and the authentication exchange. SIP carries only signaling, so the voice stream needs SRTP to be encrypted too.

options.text: SIP on UDP 5060, with SRTP for the voice media
options.why: SRTP protects the audio, but 5060 is clear-text SIP, so call setup details can be read and the authentication exchange captured.

options.text: SIP on TCP 5060, because TCP adds reliable delivery for the call signaling
options.why: TCP adds reliability, not encryption. SIP on 5060 is clear text whether it runs over UDP or TCP.

options.text: SIP over TLS on TCP 5061, with plain RTP for the voice media
options.why: TLS protects the signaling, but plain RTP carries the voice unencrypted, so anyone on the path could record the calls.

takeaway: SIP 5060 is clear text over UDP or TCP; SIP over TLS uses 5061. SIP only sets up the call, so the audio needs SRTP to be protected.

scenario: After users moved into a new VLAN, 10.60.3.0/24, domain logons still mostly work, but some applications report authentication errors and domain controller 10.1.1.10 logs a sharp rise in NTLM authentications from that VLAN. The firewall log for one workstation is shown.
stem: What is the MOST likely cause and its security impact?

options.text: LDAP on port 389 is blocked, so clients cannot look up accounts in the directory
options.why: The log shows 389 allowed. The denied traffic is on port 88.

options.text: SMB on port 445 is blocked, so Group Policy cannot be downloaded to the clients
options.why: The log shows 445 allowed, and blocking it would not by itself drive up NTLM authentications.

options.text: LDAPS on port 636 is not allowed, so directory queries are now sent in clear text instead
options.why: Nothing in the log shows 636 attempts, and a missing LDAPS rule would not explain the jump in NTLM authentications.

options.text: Kerberos on port 88 is blocked, so clients fall back to weaker NTLM authentication
options.why: Port 88, TCP and UDP, is Kerberos. When it is unreachable, Windows falls back to NTLM where allowed, which is weaker and open to relay and pass-the-hash. Allow 88 to the domain controllers.

takeaway: Port 88 is Kerberos (TCP and UDP), 389 LDAP, 636 LDAPS, 445 SMB, 3268 and 3269 the global catalog. Blocking 88 may not cause outright failures; the silent fallback to NTLM is the security problem.

scenario: In a lab, four test PCs connect to an old hub, and the hub's uplink plugs into port 12 of a managed switch that also serves 30 office PCs. A contractor connects a laptop running a packet sniffer to a spare port on the hub. No port mirroring is configured.
stem: Whose unicast traffic can the contractor's laptop capture without any further attack?

options.text: Only the office PCs' traffic, because the switch copies everything it forwards to the uplink port
options.why: A switch copies traffic to another port only when a SPAN session is configured. By default it forwards unicast frames only to the port where the destination MAC lives.

options.text: The traffic of every one of the 34 PCs, because they all share one broadcast domain
options.why: Sharing a broadcast domain means the laptop sees broadcasts such as ARP from all of them. Unicast frames between office PCs are switched only to their destination ports.

options.text: Only the four lab PCs' traffic, including anything they exchange with office PCs
options.why: A hub repeats every frame out of every port, so all devices on it share one collision domain and see each other's traffic. The switch sends office PCs' unicast frames only to their destination ports, so office-to-office traffic reaches the hub only in brief floods for unknown destinations.

options.text: No other device's traffic, because every port on a hub is its own collision domain
options.why: That describes a switch. A hub is a layer 1 repeater with one shared collision domain across all its ports.

takeaway: Hub: layer 1, repeats everything, one collision domain. Switch: layer 2, forwards unicast by its MAC table, one collision domain per port. Router: layer 3, separates broadcast domains.

scenario: Printer VLAN 20 admits devices by a MAC address allow list. The inventory says printer 0017.c8a4.31be is on port Gi0/22 in the copy room, and Gi0/7 is a normally unused wall jack in the lobby. The switch logs the message shown, and NAC reports web browsing from the printer's address.
exhibit: %SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF: Host 0017.c8a4.31be in vlan 20 is flapping between port Gi0/22 and port Gi0/7
stem: What is MOST likely happening, and which control BEST prevents it?

options.text: The printer was moved to the lobby jack by facilities; update the asset inventory
options.why: A moved printer would not alternate between two ports, and printers do not browse the web. Two devices are using one MAC.

options.text: A spanning tree loop is making the printer's MAC bounce between ports; enable BPDU guard on access ports
options.why: Loops do cause MAC flapping, but usually for many MACs on uplinks during a broadcast storm, not one printer MAC on two access ports while it browses the web.

options.text: The switch's MAC table has overflowed and is flooding frames; enable port security limits
options.why: An overflowing table shows thousands of random MACs, not one known MAC moving between two ports.

options.text: A lobby device is spoofing the printer's MAC; replace MAC filtering with 802.1X
options.why: The same MAC alternating between two access ports means two devices claim it. MACs are trivial to change, so an allow list is weak; 802.1X makes the device prove its identity, with MAB plus profiling for printers that cannot do 802.1X.

takeaway: A switch learns source MACs per port, so one MAC on two access ports means a duplicate or a spoof. MAC filtering is easy to bypass; 802.1X authenticates the device itself.

scenario: Headquarters reaches a partner's network, 10.50.0.0/16, through a site-to-site VPN. Since early this morning, traffic to the partner's payment server 10.50.3.7 has been seen unencrypted on the internal network. The edge router's routing table is shown, and the network team does not recognize 10.255.0.66.
exhibit:
Destination      Next hop        Interface  Source
0.0.0.0/0        203.0.113.1     outside    static
10.0.0.0/8       10.255.0.1      inside     static
10.50.0.0/16     172.31.0.2      vpn-tun0   static
10.50.3.0/24     10.255.0.66     inside     OSPF, learned 02:13 today
stem: Where does the router send packets for 10.50.3.7, and why?

options.text: To 10.255.0.66, because the /24 is the longest prefix match for that address
options.why: Routers choose the most specific matching route. 10.50.3.7 matches the /0, /8, /16 and /24, and the /24 wins, so a rogue device that injected it through OSPF is now on the path. Require OSPF authentication.

options.text: To 203.0.113.1, because traffic to another company's network always uses the default route
options.why: The default route is used only when nothing more specific matches, and three more specific routes match 10.50.3.7.

options.text: To 172.31.0.2 over the VPN, because static routes always beat routes learned through OSPF
options.why: Administrative distance only breaks ties between routes to the same prefix. A more specific prefix wins first, so the /24 is used.

options.text: To 10.255.0.1, because 10.0.0.0/8 is the first internal route listed in the table
options.why: Table order does not matter. The longest matching prefix does, and the /8 is the least specific internal route.

takeaway: Routing uses the longest prefix match first; administrative distance only decides between equal prefixes. An injected, more specific route is a classic way to insert an on-path device, so authenticate routing protocols.

scenario: An attacker plugs a laptop into SW2 and starts a rogue DHCP server and an ARP poisoning tool. Neither switch has any VLANs beyond the default, and R1 has no DHCP relay configured. The topology is shown.
exhibit:
[R1 router]
                /           \
          Gi0/0               Gi0/1
     10.1.10.0/24          10.1.20.0/24
          |                     |
        [SW1]                 [SW2]
      22 hosts          15 hosts + attacker laptop
stem: Which hosts are exposed to these broadcast-based attacks?

options.text: All 37 hosts for ARP, but only SW2's hosts for DHCP, since ARP crosses routers
options.why: ARP is also a broadcast and never crosses a router. It only resolves addresses on the local segment.

options.text: Only the 15 hosts on SW2, since R1 stops broadcasts at its interfaces
options.why: DHCP discovers and ARP requests are broadcasts, and broadcasts stop at a router interface. Each router interface is its own broadcast domain, so SW1's hosts never hear the rogue offers or the forged ARP.

options.text: None of the hosts, because each switch port is a separate broadcast domain
options.why: Each switch port is a separate collision domain, not a broadcast domain. A switch floods broadcasts to every port in the VLAN, so SW2's hosts receive them.

options.text: All 37 hosts, because both switches connect to the same router and share its gateway
options.why: A router separates broadcast domains. With no DHCP relay forwarding requests, SW1 hosts' broadcasts never reach SW2.

takeaway: Switches flood broadcasts within a VLAN; routers stop them. DHCP and ARP attacks therefore reach one broadcast domain (one VLAN or subnet) unless a relay forwards DHCP.

scenario: A penetration tester on an access port in VLAN 1 crafts frames carrying two 802.1Q tags: an outer tag for VLAN 1 and an inner tag for VLAN 50, the server VLAN. The trunk between the switches uses VLAN 1 as its native VLAN. The tester's packets reach a server in VLAN 50, but no replies come back.
stem: Which attack is this, and which change BEST prevents it?

options.text: Switch spoofing; disable DTP trunk negotiation on every user-facing access port of the switch
options.why: Switch spoofing negotiates a trunk to get two-way access to many VLANs. Here no trunk was formed, and the traffic only flows one way.

options.text: ARP poisoning; enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on VLAN 50
options.why: ARP poisoning redirects traffic within a single VLAN. It cannot move frames from VLAN 1 into VLAN 50.

options.text: MAC flooding; enable port security on the tester's access port
options.why: MAC flooding makes a switch flood frames inside one VLAN. It does not deliver frames into a different VLAN.

options.text: Double tagging; move the native VLAN to an unused ID and keep users out of it
options.why: The first switch strips the outer tag because it matches the native VLAN, and the next switch reads the inner tag and delivers the frame into VLAN 50. The attack is one-way, which matches the missing replies.

takeaway: VLAN hopping has two forms: switch spoofing (negotiate a trunk, two-way) and double tagging (abuse the native VLAN, one-way). Fixes: static access ports with DTP off, and an unused, tagged native VLAN.

scenario: A hosting company puts 40 customer web servers in one screened subnet VLAN. A penetration test shows that one compromised customer server can scan and attack the other customers' servers directly, even though the firewall between the VLAN and the internet is correct. Re-addressing every server would take months.
stem: Which control BEST stops server-to-server traffic inside the VLAN with the least redesign?

options.text: Stricter inbound and outbound rules on the perimeter firewall between the VLAN and the internet
options.why: The perimeter firewall sees only traffic that leaves the VLAN. Server-to-server frames are switched locally and never reach it.

options.text: 802.1Q trunking on every server port so that each frame carries a VLAN tag
options.why: Tagging only marks which VLAN a frame belongs to. It does nothing to stop two hosts in the same VLAN talking to each other.

options.text: A separate VLAN and subnet for every customer, with all traffic routed through the firewall
options.why: This is strong segmentation, but it requires re-addressing all 40 servers, which the scenario rules out as too slow.

options.text: Private VLANs with isolated ports, so each server reaches only the promiscuous gateway port
options.why: Traffic between hosts in one VLAN is switched directly and never passes the firewall. Isolated private VLAN ports block host-to-host frames while keeping the shared subnet and gateway.

takeaway: VLANs separate broadcast domains, but hosts inside one VLAN talk directly. Private VLANs (isolated or community ports) or host firewalls stop that lateral traffic without re-addressing.

scenario: A small switch in the public lobby serves only guest kiosks in VLAN 40 and is managed in VLAN 99. Its uplink trunk to the core is shown. VLAN 10 is staff and VLAN 20 is finance.
exhibit:
SW-LOBBY# show interfaces trunk
Port     Mode   Encapsulation  Status    Native vlan
Gi0/48   on     802.1q         trunking  1

Port     Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/48   1-4094

Port     Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/48   1,10,20,40,99
stem: Which change BEST limits the damage if someone tampers with the lobby switch?

options.text: Change the native VLAN from 1 to 40 so that untagged traffic lands in the guest VLAN
options.why: Making a user VLAN native helps double tagging from the kiosk ports. The native VLAN should be an unused ID, and the change does not stop tagged staff frames.

options.text: Enable port security on the kiosk ports so that only the kiosks' MAC addresses are learned
options.why: Port security helps against rogue devices on kiosk ports, but if the switch itself is reconfigured, the trunk still delivers staff and finance traffic to it.

options.text: Enable MACsec on the trunk so frames between the switches are encrypted
options.why: MACsec stops eavesdropping on the cable, but a tampered switch decrypts the frames itself and still has every VLAN delivered to it.

options.text: On the core switch, prune the trunk to only the VLANs the lobby switch needs
options.why: The trunk carries every VLAN, so whoever controls the lobby switch can put a port into staff or finance. Allowing only 40 and 99 on the core's end means a tampered lobby switch cannot simply re-add the other VLANs and reaches only those segments.

takeaway: Trunks carry every VLAN unless pruned. Allow only the VLANs each switch needs (on the upstream end, which the edge switch cannot change) and use an unused native VLAN, so a compromised edge switch reaches only its own segments.

scenario: Right after a change that enabled DHCP snooping on access switch SW-ACC3, every PC on that switch lost network access. Gi0/48 is the uplink toward the core, where the core switch relays DHCP to the real DHCP server. The output from one PC and the switch log are shown.
exhibit:
C:\> ipconfig
   Autoconfiguration IPv4 Address. . : 169.254.71.33
   Subnet Mask . . . . . . . . . . . : 255.255.0.0
   Default Gateway . . . . . . . . . :

SW-ACC3 log:
%DHCP_SNOOPING-5-DHCP_SNOOPING_UNTRUSTED_PORT: DHCP_SNOOPING drop message on
untrusted port, message type: DHCPOFFER, MAC sa: 7c21.0e4a.9b41, interface Gi0/48
stem: What is the cause, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: A rogue DHCP server sits behind Gi0/48; shut down the uplink port
options.why: The uplink leads to the real DHCP server. Shutting it would cut the switch off from everything, and the drops began exactly when snooping was enabled.

options.text: The uplink is untrusted, so the real DHCP offers are dropped; mark Gi0/48 as trusted
options.why: With snooping on, every port is untrusted by default, and server messages such as OFFER and ACK are dropped on untrusted ports. The legitimate offers arrive on the uplink, so it must be trusted. Without them the PCs fall back to APIPA.

options.text: Snooping is blocking the PCs' DHCP discovers; mark every user access port on the switch as trusted
options.why: Access ports should stay untrusted, so clients can send DISCOVER and REQUEST but cannot answer as servers. Trusting them would let a rogue server back in.

options.text: The DHCP scope is exhausted; increase the pool size on the server
options.why: An exhausted pool means no offers are sent. Here offers are being sent, and the switch is dropping them.

takeaway: DORA: Discover and Request come from clients; Offer and Ack come from servers. DHCP snooping drops server messages on untrusted ports, so trust only the ports toward real servers or relays.

scenario: During an external penetration test, the tester runs the command shown from the internet against the company's public authoritative DNS server and receives the full record list, including internal hostnames and private addresses.
exhibit:
$ dig axfr example.com @ns1.example.com
example.com.         3600 IN SOA  ns1.example.com. hostmaster.example.com. 2026101601 ...
vpn.example.com.     3600 IN A    203.0.113.40
hr-db.example.com.   3600 IN A    10.20.5.12
dc01.example.com.    3600 IN A    10.1.1.10
...
;; XFR size: 412 records (messages 1, bytes 13871)
stem: Which change BEST fixes this finding?

options.text: Enable DNSSEC signing on the public zone so that every record is authenticated
options.why: DNSSEC proves records are authentic but does not hide them. A signed zone can still be transferred in full.

options.text: Move the internal hostnames into TXT records instead of A records
options.why: A zone transfer returns every record type, so this hides nothing. Internal names belong in a separate internal zone (split DNS).

options.text: Restrict zone transfers to the IP addresses of the authorized secondary DNS servers
options.why: AXFR copies the whole zone, normally over TCP 53, and should be allowed only to the secondaries that need it. Limiting it by address, ideally with TSIG keys, stops anyone else from dumping the zone.

options.text: Block UDP 53 from the internet to the public authoritative DNS server so it cannot be queried
options.why: A public authoritative server must answer queries on UDP 53 or customers cannot find the website. Zone transfers also use TCP 53, so this blocks the wrong thing.

takeaway: Zone transfers (AXFR, TCP 53) should go only to authorized secondaries, ideally with TSIG. Keep internal records in a separate internal zone so the public server never holds them.

scenario: A company shut down its cloud-hosted shop six months ago but left its DNS records unchanged. Today shop.example.com shows a page selling counterfeit goods under the company's name. The cloud provider lets any customer claim an unused application name. A lookup is shown.
exhibit:
$ dig shop.example.com +noall +answer
shop.example.com.                   300  IN  CNAME  example-shop.cloudapp.example.net.
example-shop.cloudapp.example.net.   60  IN  A      20.84.113.9
stem: What is the root cause, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: The MX record still points at the old cloud service; update it to the new mail provider
options.why: MX records route email, not web traffic. The website is controlled by the CNAME for shop.example.com.

options.text: The company's DNS server was cache poisoned; enable DNSSEC validation on its resolvers
options.why: Poisoning plants false answers, but these are the company's own published records working exactly as written. Validation would confirm them as authentic.

options.text: The domain's registrar account was hijacked; reset the registrar password and enable MFA
options.why: A registrar takeover would change the name servers or many records. Here the company's own unchanged CNAME points to a name an outsider now owns.

options.text: A dangling CNAME let an outsider claim the old cloud name; remove or repoint the record
options.why: A CNAME aliases one name to another. The company's alias still points at a cloud name it gave up, so whoever claims that name controls what shop.example.com serves. Delete records when services are retired.

takeaway: A = name to IPv4, AAAA = IPv6, CNAME = alias to another name, MX = mail, TXT = SPF, DKIM, DMARC and verification, PTR = reverse lookup. A CNAME to a released cloud name invites subdomain takeover.

scenario: The default gateway for VLAN 2 is 10.2.2.1, a router configured never to send ICMP redirects. An analyst captures the traffic shown, and afterwards the workstations send their traffic for data center servers 10.9.0.20 and 10.9.4.11 to 10.2.2.99, an unmanaged Linux host. Dynamic ARP Inspection is enabled and has logged no violations.
stem: Which technique is the attacker using, and what BEST stops it?

options.text: A rogue DHCP server handing out 10.2.2.99 as the gateway; enable DHCP snooping
options.why: Rogue DHCP would change the default gateway for all traffic at the next lease. Here only traffic to two data center servers moved, right after the redirects.

options.text: Forged ICMP redirects (type 5); configure hosts to ignore redirects and filter them
options.why: ICMP type 5 tells a host to use a better next hop. These redirects claim to come from the gateway, which never sends them, and reroute traffic through 10.2.2.99 without touching ARP, which is why DAI saw nothing. Disabling redirect acceptance on hosts stops it.

options.text: ICMP echo requests used for a ping sweep of the VLAN; block ICMP type 8 at the edge firewall
options.why: Echo requests (type 8) only discover live hosts. They do not change where a host sends its traffic.

options.text: ARP poisoning of the gateway; enable Dynamic ARP Inspection on VLAN 2
options.why: DAI is already enabled with no violations, and the exhibit shows ICMP redirect messages, not forged ARP replies.

takeaway: ICMP types: 0 echo reply, 3 destination unreachable (code 3 port, code 4 fragmentation needed), 5 redirect, 8 echo request, 11 time exceeded. Forged redirects are an on-path technique that bypasses ARP defenses.

scenario: A hosting provider reports SSH brute-force attempts against its server 192.0.2.80 from the company's only public address, 203.0.113.10, source port 40112, at 14:02:17 UTC. 300 employees share that address. The firewall's translation log, in UTC, is shown.
stem: Which internal host should the analyst investigate?

options.text: 10.30.8.14, because it is the first translation recorded in that minute
options.why: Log order does not identify an attacker. 10.30.8.14 went to a different server on port 443 through a different public port.

options.text: 10.30.8.51, matched by the public source port 40112 and the timestamp
options.why: With port address translation many hosts share one public IP, and the public source port plus the time picks out one translation. Port 40112 at 14:02:17 maps to 10.30.8.51, which also made a second SSH attempt.

options.text: All 300 hosts, because every host shares the public address 203.0.113.10
options.why: They share the address, but the translation log records which internal socket used each public port, so the source narrows to one host.

options.text: 10.30.8.77, because it connected to 192.0.2.80 in the same second
options.why: 10.30.8.77 did connect at 14:02:17, but to port 443 on public port 40113. The reported port 40112 belongs to a different translation.

takeaway: Behind PAT a public IP alone identifies nobody. Keep NAT translation logs (inside address and port, public port, time) with synchronized clocks so external reports can be traced to one host.

scenario: The firewall lets workstations send DNS only to the internal resolvers, which forward queries to the internet. A SIEM rule flags workstation 10.40.2.19. Part of the resolver's query log is shown, and no other host has ever queried this domain.
exhibit:
10:14:02 client 10.40.2.19  query TXT  mzxw6ytboi4dqnrqgezdgnbvgy3tqojq.x7k.datasync-cdn.example
10:14:02 client 10.40.2.19  query TXT  nfxgq2lbmvzsa3dpm5ugk4tthjwge3dt.x7k.datasync-cdn.example
10:14:03 client 10.40.2.19  query TXT  ojsxg5dfmrxw4idbonzwk5dtfzrwg33n.x7k.datasync-cdn.example
...      41,000 similar queries from 10.40.2.19 in two hours
stem: What is MOST likely happening?

options.text: A CDN client is resolving content servers, which normally use long generated names
options.why: CDNs do use generated hostnames, but not 41,000 unique TXT queries from one host in two hours to a domain no one else uses.

options.text: The workstation's resolver is being cache poisoned by the external domain
options.why: Poisoning corrupts answers held in a resolver's cache. The exhibit shows one client sending unique queries, which is outbound data, not forged answers.

options.text: Data is being exfiltrated by DNS tunneling, encoded in the subdomain labels
options.why: Long random labels under one new domain, TXT queries and tens of thousands of unique names from one host is the tunneling pattern. The data rides in the query names to the attacker's authoritative server, through the company's own resolvers.

options.text: The workstation is taking part in a DNS amplification attack against the resolver
options.why: Amplification sends small spoofed queries to open resolvers so that large answers hit a victim. These are unique queries from one internal host to its own resolver.

takeaway: DNS tunneling signs: long or random subdomain labels, many unique names under one domain, unusual TXT or NULL queries, and high volume from one host. Forcing DNS through internal resolvers enables detection but does not block it.

scenario: After a threat feed reported that 198.51.100.0/24 is attacking the company, an administrator added rule 3 to the edge firewall shown. The next day, logs show 198.51.100.23 still logging in to 10.1.1.20 over SSH.
exhibit:
#  Action  Proto  Source            Destination   Port
 1  permit  tcp    any               10.1.1.10     443
 2  permit  tcp    any               10.1.1.0/24   22
 3  deny    ip     198.51.100.0/24   any           any
 4  permit  udp    any               10.1.1.53     53
    (implicit deny ip any any)
stem: Why did rule 3 fail, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: Rule 2 matches first, so move the block for 198.51.100.0/24 above it
options.why: Firewalls read rules top-down and stop at the first match. 198.51.100.23 to 10.1.1.20 on TCP 22 matches rule 2's any source before rule 3 is reached. Block lists belong above broad permits.

options.text: Rule 3 needs the destination set to 10.1.1.20 instead of any before it can take effect
options.why: A destination of any already includes 10.1.1.20. Narrowing it would not help, because rule 2 still matches first.

options.text: The implicit deny overrides rule 3, so the explicit deny is ignored
options.why: The implicit deny only applies when nothing above it matches. Here rule 2 matches and permits the traffic before either deny is reached.

options.text: Rule 3 uses ip instead of tcp, so it does not match the SSH traffic
options.why: ip matches every IP protocol, including TCP. The problem is the rule's position, not its protocol.

takeaway: ACLs are read top-down and the first match wins. Put specific denies such as block lists above broad permits; the implicit deny only catches what nothing else matched.

scenario: Group policy configures browsers to use the company's explicit web proxy, which filters categories and logs every request. Logs show several developers reaching blocked sites after removing the proxy setting. The firewall allows any internal host out on TCP 80 and 443.
stem: Which change BEST closes this gap?

options.text: Block the restricted categories on the DNS resolver instead of the proxy
options.why: DNS filtering is a useful layer, but users who change DNS servers or use DNS over HTTPS skip it, and the direct firewall path remains open.

options.text: Permit outbound web ports only from the proxy, or redirect web traffic to it transparently
options.why: While the firewall lets every host out directly, the proxy is optional. Allowing web traffic out only from the proxy, or intercepting it transparently, forces every request through filtering.

options.text: Push the proxy setting again through group policy with a much shorter refresh interval
options.why: Developers can still change the setting between refreshes or use tools that ignore it, and the direct path through the firewall stays open.

options.text: Deploy a reverse proxy in the screened subnet to inspect the developers' outbound web requests
options.why: A reverse proxy fronts inbound access to the company's own servers. It does not sit in the path of employees browsing outbound.

takeaway: Forward proxies serve outbound users (explicit needs client settings, transparent intercepts in the network); reverse proxies front inbound access to servers. A proxy enforces policy only if the firewall blocks the route around it.

scenario: A branch gateway sitting behind its ISP's NAT router must build an IKEv2 IPsec site-to-site tunnel to the headquarters firewall. The headquarters firewall allows only listed traffic in from the internet, and the tunnel will not come up.
stem: Which inbound rules must headquarters allow from the branch's public address? (Select TWO.)

options.text: UDP 1701
options.why: UDP 1701 is L2TP, which runs inside IPsec in L2TP/IPsec remote access. A plain IKEv2 site-to-site tunnel does not use it.

options.text: IP protocol 50 (ESP)
options.why: Raw ESP carries the traffic when there is no NAT. With NAT traversal active, ESP travels inside UDP 4500, so this tunnel does not need a protocol 50 rule.

options.text: UDP 4500
options.why: When IKE detects NAT in the path, it switches to NAT traversal on UDP 4500 and wraps ESP inside UDP on that port.

options.text: UDP 500
options.why: IKE starts its negotiation on UDP 500, so the very first exchange fails without it.

options.text: TCP 1723
options.why: TCP 1723 is PPTP, an obsolete VPN protocol, not part of IPsec.

options.text: IP protocol 51 (AH)
options.why: AH authenticates the IP header, which NAT rewrites, so AH fails through NAT and is not used for this tunnel.

takeaway: IPsec: IKE on UDP 500, NAT traversal on UDP 4500, ESP is IP protocol 50 and AH is protocol 51 (AH breaks with NAT). Legacy: PPTP TCP 1723, L2TP UDP 1701. TLS VPNs use TCP 443.

scenario: A 12-person design studio uses WPA2-Personal. A visitor captured the four-way handshake from the parking lot and later recovered the passphrase with an offline dictionary attack. The studio has no server room, no RADIUS server and no budget for a managed identity service, and every device supports WPA3.
stem: Which change BEST prevents a repeat of this attack?

options.text: Keep WPA2-Personal and switch its encryption from AES-CCMP to TKIP
options.why: TKIP is the older, weaker WPA cipher. The weakness exploited was the PSK handshake, and TKIP would make things worse.

options.text: Keep WPA2-Personal and hide the SSID so outsiders cannot see the network
options.why: Hidden SSIDs still appear in probe and association frames, and the handshake can still be captured and cracked offline.

options.text: Move to WPA3-Enterprise with 802.1X and a RADIUS server for each user's login
options.why: Enterprise mode is stronger and gives per-user credentials, but it needs a RADIUS or identity service that the studio does not have and cannot pay for.

options.text: Move to WPA3-Personal, whose SAE handshake resists offline dictionary attacks
options.why: SAE replaces the PSK handshake, so a captured exchange cannot be tested offline against a word list and every guess needs a live attempt. It still uses a shared password, which suits a studio without RADIUS.

takeaway: WPA2-Personal handshakes can be cracked offline; WPA3-Personal (SAE) stops that. WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X with RADIUS) adds per-user credentials when the infrastructure exists. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filters are not security.

scenario: A branch router protects the internal network 10.5.0.0/16 with the inbound access list shown. A penetration tester sends TCP packets with only the ACK flag set to many internal addresses and gets RST replies from live hosts, mapping the network even though only one web server should be reachable.
exhibit:
ip access-list extended INBOUND
 10 permit tcp any 10.5.0.0 0.0.255.255 established
 20 permit tcp any host 10.5.1.10 eq 443
 30 deny   ip any any log
stem: Why does this work, and what is the BEST fix?

options.text: Live hosts answer the ACK probes only because inbound ICMP is permitted; block ICMP from the internet
options.why: The RST replies are TCP, not ICMP. Blocking ICMP does not stop TCP ACK packets from reaching the hosts.

options.text: The ACL has no explicit deny at the end; add a deny ip any any line after the existing rules
options.why: Rule 30 already denies everything else. The problem is that rule 10 permits the forged ACKs before rule 30 is reached.

options.text: The established keyword passes any packet with ACK set; replace the ACL with a stateful firewall
options.why: A stateless ACL cannot know whether a real session exists; established simply matches packets with ACK or RST set. A stateful firewall checks each packet against its connection table and drops ACKs for sessions never opened.

options.text: Rule 20 lets the scan through to every host; remove it
options.why: Rule 20 matches only 10.5.1.10 on port 443. The ACKs to other hosts are matched by rule 10.

takeaway: Stateless filters judge each packet alone, so flag tricks like forged ACKs pass rules meant for replies only. Stateful firewalls track sessions and drop packets that belong to no known connection.

scenario: An analyst is reconstructing a capture from a freshly booted laptop, with empty ARP and DNS caches, that browsed to https://portal.example.com. The DNS server and the portal are both in other subnets. To spot where an attack could have been inserted, the analyst first writes down the expected order of events.
stem: Which order of events is correct?

options.text: ARP for the gateway, DNS query, TLS handshake, TCP handshake to port 443, HTTP GET
options.why: TLS runs on top of TCP, so the three-way handshake must finish before the TLS handshake can begin.

options.text: DNS query, ARP for the portal's IP address, TCP handshake to port 443, TLS handshake, HTTP GET
options.why: ARP resolves only local addresses. The portal is remote, so the laptop ARPs for the gateway, and it must do that before even the DNS query can leave.

options.text: ARP for the gateway, DNS query, TCP handshake to port 443, HTTP GET, TLS handshake
options.why: With HTTPS the HTTP request is sent only after TLS is established, so the path and headers are encrypted. Sending the GET first would be plain HTTP.

options.text: ARP for the gateway, DNS query, TCP handshake to port 443, TLS handshake, HTTP GET
options.why: Before any packet can leave the subnet the laptop needs the gateway's MAC, so ARP comes first. Then DNS returns the portal's IP, TCP connects, TLS secures the channel, and only then is the HTTP request sent inside it.

takeaway: One HTTPS request: ARP for the gateway, DNS for the name, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, then HTTP inside TLS. ARP spoofing hits step 1, DNS poisoning step 2, TLS downgrade or stripping step 4.

scenario: A company's next-generation firewall does not decrypt TLS. Employees browse a cloud file-sharing site over HTTPS with TLS 1.3, and Encrypted Client Hello is not in use. Management asks what the firewall can still see when writing policies for this traffic.
stem: Which information can the firewall see without decrypting the sessions? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The full URL path, such as /share/upload
options.why: The path is part of the HTTP request, which travels inside the encrypted TLS tunnel.

options.text: The session cookies the browser sends
options.why: Cookies are HTTP headers, so they are encrypted inside TLS along with the rest of the request.

options.text: The destination IP address and TCP port 443
options.why: IP and TCP headers sit outside the TLS layer, so addresses and ports are always visible to devices on the path.

options.text: The HTTP status codes the site returns
options.why: Status codes are part of the encrypted HTTP response, so they are not visible on the wire under TLS.

options.text: The names of the files being uploaded
options.why: File names travel in the HTTP request headers or body, which TLS encrypts, so seeing them requires TLS inspection.

options.text: The server hostname in the TLS Server Name Indication field
options.why: Without Encrypted Client Hello, the client sends the SNI hostname in clear text in its ClientHello, which is how firewalls categorize HTTPS without decrypting it.

takeaway: Without TLS inspection a firewall sees IPs, ports, the SNI hostname (unless ECH is used) and DNS queries (unless DNS is encrypted), but not URLs, headers, cookies or content.

scenario: After the HR application moved to a new server VLAN with the address 10.20.8.40, users get a connection error when browsing to https://hr.example.com. The help desk ran the commands shown from a user's PC. The application team says the service is running and listening on 443.
exhibit:
PS> Resolve-DnsName hr.example.com
Name             Type  TTL   IPAddress
hr.example.com   A     300   10.20.8.40

PS> Test-NetConnection hr.example.com -Port 443
ComputerName     : hr.example.com
RemoteAddress    : 10.20.8.40
RemotePort       : 443
PingSucceeded    : True
TcpTestSucceeded : False
stem: At which step does the request fail, and what is the MOST likely cause?

options.text: At the TCP handshake; a firewall or ACL is blocking TCP 443 to the new VLAN
options.why: DNS returned the new address and ping works, so name resolution and routing are fine. The TCP connection to 443 fails before TLS can start, which points to a filter dropping port 443 between the users and the new VLAN.

options.text: At DNS resolution; the A record still points to the server's old address in the old VLAN
options.why: Resolve-DnsName returned 10.20.8.40, the new address, and the test reached it, so DNS is correct.

options.text: At routing; the users' default gateway has no route to the new VLAN
options.why: Ping to 10.20.8.40 succeeded, so packets are routed to the subnet and back. The failure is specific to TCP 443.

options.text: At the TLS handshake; the server's certificate does not match the hostname
options.why: A certificate problem appears after TCP connects, as a browser certificate warning. Here TCP never connects.

takeaway: Troubleshoot a web request in order: DNS answer, IP reachability, TCP handshake to the port, TLS, then HTTP. Ping working while the TCP test fails points to a port filter.
